people.name: More Adey
people.bio: Translator and editor who published the first English translation of Ibsen's Brand (1891) under the pseudonym William Wilson, later ran the Carfax picture gallery with Robert Ross, and was joint editor of the Burlington Magazine, 1911-19. The editors of the Complete Letters describe him as a 'Close friend of Robert Ross'; the two shared lodgings at 24 Hornton Street, Kensington, and both were Roman Catholics - Wilde in 1897 teased 'you and More, especially More' as a unit for treating him 'as a Dissenter'. It was to Adey that Ross addressed, in installments, his narrative of Wilde's final illness, death and funeral (14 December 1900), and a rosary Adey had given Ross was placed around Wilde's neck at the laying-out.
people.bio_note: Born/died, Brand translation, 'Close friend of Robert Ross' and Carfax partnership from the biographical footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 577 n. 2 (repo PDF 629; Burlington Magazine editorship also in the elided portion of that note, which cites Siegfried Sassoon, Siegfried's Journey, 1945, for his later years). Shared lodgings from the editorial note at p. 781 n. 2 (PDF 832): 'More Adey and Robert Ross shared lodgings at 24 Hornton Street, Kensington'. 'You and More' and the editors' 'Ross and Adey were both Roman Catholics' from p. 866 and n. 1 (PDF 916). Death-narrative addressee and rosary from the Epilogue, pp. 1219 and 1221 (PDF 1264, 1266).

sources.quote: My dear More, I hear with great regret from Robbie of the loss you have sustained. You were so kind to my mother, so sympathetic and gentle in your delicate attentions to her up to the last, that I know you will let me express my sorrow at the death of your mother: it seems to me that I have almost a right to do so: for friends have all things in common. I wish you could come out here: one is healed at Rome of every trouble: and I should like to go with you to the Vatican, where I hope you will some day walk gravely in mediaeval dress, with the gold chain of office, and guide pilgrims to the feet of the Pope.
sources.context: Wilde to More Adey, [postmark 26 April 1900], c/o Cook and Son, Rome (MS Clark). Adey's mother had died on 9 April; Wilde's own had died in February 1896 while he was in prison, and Adey had attended her. AFTER TWO YEARS OF BLAMING HIM in the letters of 1897 - 'incapable of managing affairs of tomtit in a hedge' - this is Wilde writing to him with unqualified tenderness.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That the quarrel ended, and what Adey had done for Wilde's mother.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1230; printed folio 1184 confirmed on the rendered page image.

context_engagements.note: This letter is the parent of a fragment that had sat unattributed in the reading log - the three questions at the top of printed 1024 had no owner until the preceding folio was read.

sources.quote: My dear More, I see your beautiful handwriting on the cover of the Echo, which reached me this morning. Many sincere thanks. It is a capital review, but, of course, I want the literary papers to criticise it. It is not altogether a pamphlet on prison-reform. I wonder what that good kind fellow Major Nelson thinks of it. I sent him a copy. I wish you could come over here and see me, but I suppose that is difficult. The intellectual atmosphere of Paris has done me good, and I now have ideas, not merely passions. Naples was fatal. … Are you writing? Are you in love? Are you happy?
sources.context: Wilde to More Adey, Monday [21 February 1898], Hôtel de Nice (text from a copy in Stuart Mason's hand, Clark). The Echo review of The Ballad had appeared on 19 February; Major Nelson was the governor of Reading. THE ORPHAN IS CLOSED: 'Are you writing? Are you in love? Are you happy?' had been logged as an unattributed fragment at the top of printed 1024 with no addressee established. Reading printed 1023 identifies the letter as this one. NAPLES WAS FATAL is Wilde's own verdict on the Posillipo months with Douglas, given to the friend he had spent 1897 blaming for everything.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's verdict on Naples, and three questions to a friend that are the warmest thing in the letter.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 1069-1070; printed folios 1023 and 1024 both confirmed on the rendered page images.

sources.quote: I have lately been reading your brother's lovely lyrical poems, so you see you have both of you given me that rare thing happiness.
sources.context: Wilde to Laurence Housman, 9 August 1897, Chalet Bourgeat, Berneval-sur-Mer (MS Bryn Mawr) - the close of the letter thanking him for All-Fellows. THE EDITORS' NOTE ON THE SAME PAGE carries the rest: Robert Ross 'told me that when he visited his friend in jail he learnt some of the poems by heart and recited them to him', and A. E. Housman wrote to Seymour Adelman in 1928 that A Shropshire Lad 'was published while Mr Wilde was in prison, and when he came out I sent him a copy myself'.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Both directions of the contact: the poems carried into Reading by Ross, and the book sent on release.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 973; printed folio 923 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: A. E. Housman
people.bio: Poet and classical scholar (1859-1936), author of A Shropshire Lad (1896) and elder brother of Laurence Housman. He never met Wilde. Robert Ross learned poems from A Shropshire Lad by heart and recited them to Wilde in Reading Gaol, and Housman sent Wilde a copy of the book himself when he came out. Wilde, writing to his brother, said the two of them had given him 'that rare thing happiness'.

people.name: George Alexander
people.bio: Actor-manager of the St James's Theatre, born George Alexander Gibb Samson (1858-1918) and knighted in 1911. He acted with Irving from 1881, went into management on his own in 1889, and held the St James's from 1891 until his death. He commissioned Lady Windermere's Fan, paying Wilde £50 in advance in January 1890, and produced both it (1892) and The Importance of Being Earnest (1895). Thirteen of Wilde's letters to him survive, from 1890 to four months before Wilde's death; Wilde addressed him throughout as Aleck. At the bankruptcy Alexander bought the acting rights to both plays, made voluntary payments to Wilde afterwards, and left the rights to Wilde's son Vyvyan when he died.
people.bio_note: THE THIRTEEN LETTERS are at repo PDF 443, 483, 506, 532, 534, 535, 634, 647, 651, 662, 672, 685 and 1239. TWELVE OF THE THIRTEEN have been read at the page — printed 421, 463, 486, 512, 515, 582, 595, 599, 610, 620, 633 and 1193 — every folio confirmed on its own page image. ONE remains unread (repo PDF 534): it is the first half of a mid-February 1892 rehearsal letter whose second half was read at printed 515, and both halves are staging notes on Lady Windermere's Fan. DATES AND NAME are from the editors' note at printed 421. THE 1892 REHEARSAL LETTERS are not quoted beyond the one at printed 512: they are line-by-line direction ('Lord A's coat is too horsy'), and the only human sentence in them is 'I write from bed which accounts for pencil', and the openings visible in the OCR mirror run 'Dear Aleck' and 'My dear Aleck'. DATES: the death year comes from the editors' note at printed 1193; no birth year is given there and none is inferred. (printed 1111, located in the mirror, not yet read at the page).

context_engagements.period: Professional friendship 1890-1900; the correspondence runs the whole of it
context_engagements.note: Two of the thirteen are long play scenarios — the first sketch of The Importance of Being Earnest at printed 595, and the plot later sold to Frank Harris as Mr and Mrs Daventry at printed 599 — and several more are staging, rights and money.

sources.quote: Dear Aleck, I beg to acknowledge with thanks your cheque for £50 on account of fees for my play. I find that we are not leaving town till Thursday, so if you have any stalls left my wife and I would like very much to come to your première of Carré's play. But perhaps you have given away all your seats. Believe me yours
sources.context: Wilde to George Alexander, [? late January 1890], 16 Tite Street (MS Morgan) — the earliest of the thirteen, quoted whole. The receipt Wilde signed for the £50 is printed beneath it. Kept for the second paragraph: the Wildes asking Alexander for seats, which is the friendship before it had anything to be tested by.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The beginning of the correspondence, and its social side — Wilde and Constance wanting to come to his opening night.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 443; printed folio 421 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Aleck, I am not satisfied with myself or my work. I can't get a grip of the play yet: I can't get my people real. The fact is I worked at it when I was not in the mood for work, and must first forget it, and then go back quite fresh to it. I am very sorry, but artistic work can't be done unless one is in the mood; certainly my work can't. Sometimes I spend months over a thing, and don't do any good; at other times I write a thing in a fortnight.
sources.context: Wilde to George Alexander, [2 February 1891], 16 Tite Street (MS Arents). The play is Lady Windermere's Fan, which Alexander had commissioned and paid for in advance a year earlier. The elision drops news of The Duchess of Padua's New York production. This is the first of the four letters in which Wilde tells him something he did not have to.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde admitting to his manager that the commissioned play is not working, and why — candour rather than excuse.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 483; printed folio 463 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Alick, Of course I am in your debt £50 and I am very much disappointed I have not been able to write the play, but I want you not to ask me to pay you at present, as I am in a great mess about money, and really will not have any till September, when The Duchess of Padua goes on tour in America. Do let me wait till then, and believe me to be, with great regret for not having done the play, sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to George Alexander, [? Summer 1891], 16 Tite Street (MS Morgan) — quoted whole. The content is a debt and a missed commission; what it records about the two of them is the register, nine years before the last letter: 'My dear Alick', and a man telling his manager plainly that he is in a mess about money.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The early register of the friendship, and the candour in it.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 506; printed folio 486 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Aleck, I heard by chance in the theatre today – after you had left the stage – that you intended using the first scene a second time – in the last act. I think you should have told me this, as after a long consultation on the subject more than four weeks ago you agreed to have what is directed in the book of the play … My object, however, in writing is not to reproach you in any way – reproaches being useless things – but to point this out.
sources.context: Wilde to George Alexander, [mid-February 1892], 16 Tite Street (MS Hyde) — during rehearsals for Lady Windermere's Fan, which opened at the St James's on 20 February. The elision drops several paragraphs of stage-management argument. Kept for how Wilde handles a grievance with him: he states it, then disarms it in the same breath.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The working relationship under strain, and Wilde's care to keep a disagreement from becoming a quarrel.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 532; printed folio 512 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Aleck, I dare say you have seen in the papers that I have given Hare the refusal of my next play, and I am anxious to send you a few lines to explain to you my reasons in doing so. I shall always remember with pride and with pleasure the artistic manner in which you produced my first play, and the artistic care you showed, down to the smallest detail of production, that my work should be presented in the best manner possible, and it would be a great delight to me to have some other play of mine produced by you at your charming theatre, but I have always been anxious to have some work of mine produced by Hare, whose wonderful stagecraft no one appreciates more than you do, and as he
sources.context: Wilde to George Alexander, [? January 1894], 16 Tite Street (MS Texas). The editors mark the rest of the letter missing, and it breaks off mid-sentence here. Wilde had read in the papers that Alexander would have learned of the snub from the press, and wrote at once so that he would not.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The care taken not to wound: a letter written for no reason except that a friend might otherwise feel passed over.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 634; printed folio 582 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Aleck, I can't make out what could have become of your letter. I thought from your silence that you thought the play too farcical in incident for a comedy theatre like your own, or that you didn't like my asking you to give me some money. … No: I want to come back to you. I would like to have my play done by you (I must tell you candidly that the two young men's parts are equally good) … I may mention that the play is an admirable play. I can't come up to town, I have no money. … Write me your views – about this whole business. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to George Alexander, [? September 1894], 5 Esplanade, Worthing (MS Arents) — the letter placing The Importance of Being Earnest, which Alexander would produce the following February. The elisions drop a long argument about American touring rights and what sort of actor Alexander is, which is trade rather than friendship.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The loyalty underneath the business — 'I want to come back to you' — and Wilde poor enough at Worthing to say so plainly.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 662; printed folio 610 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Aleck, I have been ill in bed for a long time, with a sort of malarial fever, and have not been able to answer your kind letter of invitation. I am quite well now, and, as you wished to see my somewhat farcical comedy, I send you the first copy of it. It is called Lady Lancing on the cover: but the real title is The Importance of Being Earnest. When you read the play, you will see the punning title's meaning. … I read charming accounts of your banquet at Birmingham, and your praise of the English dramatist. I know and admire Pinero's work, but who is Jones? Perhaps the name as reported in the London papers was a misprint for something else. I have never heard of Jones. Have you? Give my kind regards to Mrs Aleck, and believe me, sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to George Alexander, [circa 25 October 1894], 16 Tite Street (MS Arents) — sending the typescript of The Importance of Being Earnest, still stamped Lady Lancing. The elision drops a paragraph arguing the play is unsuited to Alexander's line, which is trade. 'Who is Jones?' is a joke at the expense of Henry Arthur Jones, whose play Alexander had produced six months earlier and whom Wilde knew perfectly well.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The friendship at its most companionable — illness, a joke shared at a rival's expense, and regards to the wife who greets him again in the last letter of 1900.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 672; printed folio 620 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Aleck, I am much obliged to you for your cheque for £300. If it is possible could you let me have the balance as soon as possible. I am already served with writs for £400, rumours of prosperity having reached the commercial classes, and my hotel is loathsome to me. I want to leave it. On Sunday I hope to send you, or read you, the vital parts of my Florentine play. I think you will like it. In any case, some day soon I would like to talk to you about it. I am sorry my life is so marred and maimed by extravagance. But I cannot live otherwise. I, at any rate, pay the penalty of suffering. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to George Alexander, [February 1895], St James's Theatre (MS Hyde) — quoted whole. The Importance of Being Earnest had opened there on 14 February; Queensberry left his card at the Albemarle on the 18th. Nothing in the letter is off the subject of the two of them, so nothing is cut.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Wilde told Alexander about himself weeks before the collapse — the trust in the friendship, measured by the confession rather than by any endearment.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 685; printed folio 633 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Aleck, It was really a great pleasure to see you again, and to receive your friendly grasp of the hand after so many years. Nor shall I forget your dear wife's charming and affectionate greeting of me. I know now how to value things like that. With regard to your proposal to spread the payment for the plays over a certain time, I know it was dictated by sheer kindness and the thoughtfulness of an old friend. … I would then have before me a year free from worry, and perhaps may do something you would like. Could you do this for me? I was delighted to see you so well, and so unchanged. Kindest wishes to your wife. Sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to George Alexander, [? 21 July 1900], Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris (MS Arents) - four months before Wilde's death, and eighteen months after Alexander had cut him in the street at Napoule. The elision drops the standing-order instructions and Robert Ross's street address. The editors' note 2 records that Alexander had bought the acting rights to Lady Windermere's Fan and The Importance of Being Earnest at the bankruptcy, 'made some voluntary payments to Wilde and bequeathed the rights to Wilde's son Vyvyan on his death in 1918'.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The warmth of the friendship at the very end of Wilde's life, and what he had learned to value - a handshake, and a wife's greeting.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1239; printed folio 1193 confirmed on the rendered page image. The OCR mirror attributes this letter to printed 1192; the page image gives 1193.

sources.quote: My dear Aleck, I am not satisfied with myself or my work. I can't get a grip of the play yet: I can't get my people real. The fact is I worked at it when I was not in the mood for work, and must first forget it, and then go back quite fresh to it. I am very sorry, but artistic work can't be done unless one is in the mood; certainly my work can't. Sometimes I spend months over a thing, and don't do any good; at other times I write a thing in a fortnight.
sources.context: Wilde to George Alexander, [2 February 1891], 16 Tite Street (MS Arents). The play is Lady Windermere's Fan, which Alexander had commissioned and would produce the following year. The letter continues about The Duchess of Padua's anonymous New York production. THE SAME FOLIO carries the Horne and Clifton letters already on this map; this one had been logged as read-but-unentered and is now closed.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde admitting to his manager that he cannot work to order.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 483; printed folio 463 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Alphonse
people.bio: A young man of Wilde's Paris circle in December 1898, described to Reginald Turner as 'your little friend Alphonse'. He was arrested one night for blackmail after demanding fifteen francs, being given ten and a cab-fare, and making a scene on being put out of the house. Wilde's verdict: 'quite an imp, though attractive in love-scenes'.
people.bio_note: the General Index entry 'Alphonse (boy), 1107'.

people.name: André
people.bio: One of two people Wilde reported meeting on a three-day trip to Nice with Harold Mellor in January 1899, while Wilde was staying at La Napoule on the Riviera. Wilde described him to Robert Ross as 'one beautiful person, called André, with wonderful eyes'. No surname, age, occupation, dates or further trace appear in the letter, and nothing else about him was found in the pages read.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, Thursday [? 12 January 1899], Napoule, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1118 (repo PDF 1164, printed folio confirmed on the rendered page image, 2026-08-03; transcription and provenance reused unchanged). He is on the roster under the 2026-08-03 decision to give the exile-years liaison tier nodes rather than a collective footnote; the collective mentions on the same tier (the Riviera fishing population, the Napoule fisher-lads) name no individual and stay in the collective context_engagement on wilde.json. DATES: NONE RECORDED. Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel treats the Nice trip at printed p. 245 (repo PDF 259) and names 'two young men named André and Pietro, the former "with wonderful eyes"' without adding anything the letter does not already say. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and none is likely to be: the record preserves a first name (or a trade) in another man's correspondence and no surname to search by.

people.name: Kit Anstruther-Thomson
people.bio: Scottish artist and writer on aesthetics, born 1857, known as "Kit". She replaced Mary Robinson as Vernon Lee's close companion from 1887 to 1900 and became her collaborator: the two ran experiments on bodily response to art informed by Robert Vischer's theory of Einfuhlung, the term Edward Titchener Englished in 1909 as "empathy". Their article "Beauty and Ugliness" (Contemporary Review, October 1897) drew a plagiarism charge from Bernard Berenson, later retracted, and the work was collected as Beauty and Ugliness (1912), co-written with Lee. Anstruther-Thomson died in 1921; Lee wrote a substantial introduction to her posthumous Art and Man (1924) as a tribute.
people.bio_note: Dates (1857-1921), the companion years (1887-1900) and the collaboration from Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography of Vernon Lee (2018/2019).

people.name: Armando
people.bio: A young Roman whom Wilde knew in April 1900, described to Robert Ross as 'a very smart elegant young Roman Sporus' and, at greater length, as being 'so absurdly like the Apollo Belvedere that I feel always as if I was Winckelmann when I am with him'. Wilde gave him up over the cost of his clothes, took up his best friend instead, and had forgiven him within a fortnight. He survives under a first name only.
people.bio_note: HE IS THE BEST-DOCUMENTED OF THE ROME COHORT: two folios, both read at the page, one of them carrying a sustained physical description of a kind Wilde wrote about almost nobody else this late. 'Sporus' was Nero's boy-favourite and is not an ambiguous word in Wilde's vocabulary; 'Winckelmann' is Johann Joachim Winckelmann, to whom Pater devoted a chapter of The Renaissance and whose name in this circle carries the whole freight of adult male desire for young men modelled on Greek sculpture. The gap existed because only Armando has his own General Index entry ('Armando (boy), 1182, 1184'); the other two appear inside the same paragraphs and are indexed nowhere.

sources.quote: I now like Arnaldo: he was Armando's greatest friend, but the friendship is over.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Rome, April 1900, in the sentence immediately after giving up Armando. The whole of the record for Arnaldo.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That Wilde replaced one young Roman with his best friend, and said so plainly.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1228; printed folio 1182 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Arnaldo
people.bio: A young Roman, Armando's closest friend, whom Wilde took up in April 1900 when he gave Armando up. He survives in one sentence: 'I now like Arnaldo: he was Armando's greatest friend, but the friendship is over.'
people.bio_note: The gap existed because only Armando has his own General Index entry ('Armando (boy), 1182, 1184'); the other two appear inside the same paragraphs and are indexed nowhere.

people.name: I. D. W. Ashton
people.bio: English companion of Wilde's exile years, otherwise untraced: the editors of the Complete Letters have only a visiting-card enclosed in one of Wilde's letters, inscribed 'Mr I. D. W. Ashton. Piccadilly Club, W', and record that 'Further than that he has not been traced.' He was in Naples for about a month by 11 November 1897, during Wilde's Naples months with Lord Alfred Douglas, and Wilde - who saw 'a great deal' of him there - introduced him by letter to Reginald Turner as 'a most charming and delightful fellow' who 'has been a very good friend to me'. He appears again in Paris in December 1898, travelling from St Malo, and was expected to go to the States by January 1899. Wilde's letters record two attachments of his - to Joseph in Paris and to a youth named Walter - and Wilde's verdict on him as 'capital company, and a very astounding person in his capacity for pleasure, grand in his cups, and with a heart of gold'. Nicknamed 'Sir John', the name under which he appears throughout the correspondence.
bio_sources: Identity and the untraced verdict: 'Enclosed in this letter is a visiting-card inscribed "Mr I. D. W. Ashton. Piccadilly Club, W". Further than that he has not been traced. Meyerfeld says that he was nicknamed Sir John, and this is corroborated by the complementary references to him and St Malo on pp. 1118-9. See also p. 1067.' - Holland & Hart-Davis, editors' footnote, Complete Letters (2000), p. 979n (repo PDF 1027, printed folio confirmed on rendered page image, 2026-08-03).

Naples, 1897: 'This is to introduce to you our friend Ashton, who has been in Naples for a month, and of whom we have seen, I am glad to say, a great deal. He is a most charming and delightful fellow, and has been a very good friend to me, so I am anxious for you to know him.' - Wilde to Reginald Turner, 11 November [1897], Villa Giudice, Posilippo; p. 979 (repo PDF 1027, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).

Wilde's summing-up, and the States: 'Poor Sir John! However, I think he may do well in the States. … but Sir John was capital company, and a very astounding person in his capacity for pleasure, grand in his cups, and with a heart of gold.' - Wilde to Robert Ross, [? 12 January 1899], Napoule; p. 1118 (repo PDF 1164, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).
people.bio_note: The 'Sir John' = Ashton identity key is verified in the source twice over: the editors' note at 979n, and the editors' cross-reference footnote at 1107n2, which reads in full 'See note 1, p.979'. Not read so far: printed 1023, 1049, 1067, 1109-10, 1121, and the St Malo corroboration the editors cite at 1118-9 - printed 1118 was read and carries no St Malo reference, so the corroborating passage is presumably at 1119. DATES: NONE RECORDED, AND THE EDITORS SAY SO IN TERMS. Their footnote, re-read as a page image so far with the printed folio 979 confirmed, is the whole of the identification: 'Enclosed in this letter is a visiting-card inscribed "Mr I. Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel discusses him at printed pp. 142 and 240 (repo PDF 156, 254) purely as the 'homosexual friend named Ashton' of Wilde's letters, adding no particulars. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted; the man is a set of initials and a club address.

people.name: Fred Atkins
people.bio: Billiard-marker, bookmaker's clerk and music-hall comedian — 'I am twenty years old' on oath in April 1895 — introduced to Taylor by Schwabe in November 1892 and taken to Paris by Wilde that month as nominal private secretary. He lived and worked blackmail with the bookmaker James Burton; on the stand he denied any impropriety with Wilde, and on recall was proved to have lied on oath about a Rochester Row arrest (a gentleman found naked in bed with him, money demanded) and was ordered from the box. The judge's summing-up called him 'a most reckless, unreliable, unscrupulous, and untruthful witness' (as quoted by the Letters editors), and the jury found Wilde not guilty on every Atkins count.
bio_sources: Atkins's testimony and recall, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 206-210, 216-218 (p. 207 read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03; rest djvu OCR)
Hyde, Trials (1948), Introduction pp. 72, 74 (perjury; not-guilty verdict; djvu OCR)
Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 714 n 1 (the judge's phrase; Wilde acquitted of the Atkins charges; read at rendered PDF p. 765, 2026-08-03)
people.bio_note: Mary Applegate's stained-sheets testimony (Hyde p. 211) is the only circumstantial support for the Paris allegation and is preserved in the dossier. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED FROM THE SOURCES CONSULTED. The age is now verified in the source rather than from OCR: Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, printed p. 206 - 'FREDERICK ATKINS, examined by Mr. Read as a page image in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, IA PDF p. 247), printed folio 206 confirmed; Mr Justice Charles repeats it in his summing-up ('Atkins is now twenty years of age', located in the same OCR text at printed p. 266 region, not read in the source). SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web. The Complete Letters editors' note at printed p. 714 gives his occupations and the judge's 'most reckless, unreliable, unscrupulous, and untruthful witness', but no dates. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted.

people.name: Florence Balcombe
people.bio: Florence Anne Lemon Balcombe, daughter of a retired lieutenant-colonel who had fought in the Crimea, living at 1 Marino Crescent, Clontarf, Dublin. Wilde courted her from August 1876 - he drew her that month and called the courtship 'a memory of two sweet years' - until her engagement in 1878; the editors caption her plate 'Wilde's first love'. She married Bram Stoker on 4 December 1878 at St Anne's Church, Dublin, appeared as a Priestess in Tennyson's The Cup at the Lyceum in January 1881, and remained on cordial terms with Wilde, who sent her Salome in 1893.
people.bio_note: Born/died (1858-1937), parentage and Clontarf address from the main-particulars footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 47 n. 3 (repo PDF 72, folio confirmed), which also records Wilde's August 1876 drawing of her. 'Wilde's first love' from the List of Illustrations, p. vi (repo PDF 6). 'Two sweet years' from Wilde's letter of [? 30 September 1878], p. 71 (repo PDF 98). Stoker marriage from p. 72 n. 1 (repo PDF 99). The Cup casting from p. 107 n. 1 (repo PDF 132). Salome presentation letter at p. 552 (repo PDF 604). DATES 1858-1937 confirmed 2026-08-06 from the editors' note at printed 47, which gives her as Florence Anne Lemon Balcombe, daughter of a retired lieutenant-colonel of 1 Marino Crescent, Clontarf, Dublin, and records that Wilde's own drawing of her, dated August 1876, is at the University of Texas.

people.name: John Evelyn Barlas
people.bio: Scottish poet and revolutionary Socialist, friend of William Morris, author of eight volumes of verse. On Bloody Sunday, 13 November 1887, he was arrested in the Trafalgar Square riot and took a policeman's truncheon to the head, a blow the editors of Wilde's letters say affected his reason. On 31 December 1891 he fired a revolver outside the Speaker's House at Westminster, saying 'I am an anarchist. What I have done is to show my contempt for the House of Commons.' Wilde guaranteed half his £200 bail. He died in a lunatic asylum.
people.bio_note: BOTH LETTERS READ AT THE PAGE: printed 511 and 512 (repo PDF 531 and 532), folios confirmed. Dates 1860-1914, the biography and the bail are from the editors' note at printed 511.

context_engagements.period: January-February 1892, around Barlas's arrest and bail

sources.quote: My dear friend and poet, Thanks, a thousand thanks, for your charming letter. Whatever I did was merely what you would have done for me or for any friend of yours whom you admired and appreciated. We poets and dreamers are all brothers. I am so glad you are feeling better. I now know nerves myself, what they are, and what rest can do for them. We will have many days of song and joy together when the spring comes, and life shall be made lovely for us, and we will pipe on reeds. I must come and see you soon. Your affectionate friend
sources.context: Wilde to John Barlas, [postmark 19 January 1892], 16 Tite Street (MS Hyde) — quoted whole. Barlas had been bound over three days earlier in the sum of £200, half guaranteed by Wilde; the editors say this letter is clearly the answer to Barlas's letter of gratitude. 'Whatever I did' is the bail.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde making light of standing surety for him, and the terms he puts the friendship in: brothers, spring, days of song and joy, 'Your affectionate friend'.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 531; printed folio 511 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear poet, With great pleasure. Have I a form to fill up? Or is a letter what is necessary? In all things command me. The question of the 'particular purpose'. Only your wish to read in a public museum is a general question addressed to all, as many illiterate persons seek admission, whose sole object is either to read the Family Herald, or to write it, which is worse. Send me a line, poet and scholar, and know me for ever your friend
sources.context: Wilde to John Barlas, [postmark 4 February 1892], 16 Tite Street (MS Hyde) — quoted whole. Barlas wanted a reader's ticket for the British Museum and needed a recommender; the editors record that he was admitted on a six-month ticket the following day.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde vouching for him a second time within a month — and the sign-off, which is the warmest formula in either letter.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 532; printed folio 512 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Natalie Clifford Barney
people.bio: American heiress, poet, and Paris salon hostess who, per McDermott, 'saw herself as a latter day Sappho', and whose Quelques Portraits-Sonnets de Femmes (1900) made her notorious for openly lesbian verse. She opened a correspondence with Olive Custance after Opals (1897), wooed her with love poems, hosted her in Paris, and travelled with her in Italy around 1901; her memoir Souvenirs Indiscrets (1960) recounts the episode, including a plan to gather Custance and Renée Vivien into a Sapphic community at Mytilene. Her later, celebrated Left-Bank circle (Vivien, Romaine Brooks, and others) lies outside this web's scope.
people.bio_note: Dates (1876-1972) and the wooing account from Sarah Parker's Y90s Custance biography (read in full 2026-08-03); pursuit/Italy details from McDermott's Fortnightly Review profile (2020); 'rumoured entanglements' framing from Parker 2011 (AM p. 1), citing Wickes 1977 and Souhami 2004.

people.name: Mabel Batten
people.bio: Singer, known as "Ladye", 1856-1916. The Harry Ransom Center's biographical sketch of Radclyffe Hall calls her Hall's first lover and a "singer and society beauty" who "introduced her into a circle of artistic and intellectual women, many of them lesbians" - which places her, in the surviving record, as the person who brought Hall into queer society. She was the cousin of Una Troubridge, who met Hall in 1915 and became Hall's partner after Batten's death in 1916. Batten does not appear in Wilde's Complete Letters; her link to this map is through Hall.

people.name: Aubrey Beardsley
people.bio: Artist (1872-98). He was working in an insurance office until 1892; his drawings were first published in February 1893, he illustrated the English Salomé, and he was art editor of the Yellow Book and then the Savoy before dying of tuberculosis at twenty-five. One letter from Wilde to him survives - an invitation to dinner at Kettner's with Robert Ross - but the warmer document is an inscription Wilde wrote in a copy of Salomé in March 1893: 'For Aubrey: for the only artist who, besides myself, knows what the dance of the seven veils is, and can see that invisible dance.'
people.bio_note: the volume's General Index. THE EDITORS NOTE THE LETTER IS 'APPARENTLY THE ONLY SURVIVING LETTER FROM WILDE TO BEARDSLEY' and that it cannot be dated within six months - they include it anyway for that reason, which is worth recording as an editorial decision. HIS OWN INDEX ENTRY RECORDS A COOLING: 'his dislike of W' (printed 919n) at Dieppe in 1897, alongside his being supported by [[raffalovich]] and his connection to [[smithers]], who published the Savoy. Those folios are unread and the falling-out is not documented here.

sources.quote: My dear Aubrey, I am charmed to find you are in town. Will you join Bobbie and me at dinner tonight at Kettner's (Church St, Soho) at 7.30. We are not going to dress. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Aubrey Beardsley, [? December 1893], 10 & 11 St James's Place (MS Yale) - quoted whole, and the only surviving letter between them. 'Bobbie' is Robert Ross, who is on this map: the dinner is the three of them. The editors record that the word 'Aubrey' has been erased from the manuscript but remains legible.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The only surviving letter, and that Wilde, Ross and Beardsley dined together.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 630; printed folio 578 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: March '93. For Aubrey: for the only artist who, besides myself, knows what the dance of the seven veils is, and can see that invisible dance.
sources.context: Wilde's inscription in a copy of the original French Salomé (1893), recorded by the editors, which survives in the Sterling Library at the University of London. Written months before Beardsley illustrated the English edition. It is the warmest thing Wilde is recorded as writing to him, and it is not a letter - which is why the correspondence alone understates the relation.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Wilde thought Beardsley alone could see.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 630; printed folio 578 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: George Bedborough
people.bio: Editor of The Adult, a magazine promoting freedom in sexual relations outside marriage, and secretary of the Legitimation League, which campaigned for the legal recognition of children born out of wedlock. In 1898 he published Havelock Ellis's Sexual Inversion - the first English study of homosexuality - at his Watford University Press, and on 31 May that year he was arrested for selling a copy of it to a plain-clothes policeman. Ten weeks earlier he had sent Wilde a bound edition of his essays and a Salomé illustrated by Max Beerbohm, and Wilde had written back to thank him.
people.bio_note: found in the volume's General Index at printed 1239 and read at the page the same hour. NOT YET READ: the Legitimation League and Sexual Inversion material lies outside this volume.

sources.quote: My dear Sir, I must thank you very much for the books: the edition of my essays is a masterpiece of lovely binding and I was charmed to receive my dear father's book, and also Salomé with the dainty drawings of Max Beerbohm in his Oxford days. You really have been most kind to me and I do hope to see you. I am worried over the sordid things of life, so cannot write - at least intelligently - but I beg you to accept again my sincere thanks and I hope you will review The Ballad of Reading Gaol somewhere. You have been so charming to the author, that you may be charming also to the work. Truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to George Bedborough, [postmark 15 March 1898], Hôtel de Nice, Paris (MS Texas) - quoted whole. Bedborough had had Wilde's essays bound up out of the periodicals they first appeared in and inscribed the volume 'To the author from Geo. Bedborough, 5 March 1898'. READ THE DATES TOGETHER: this is 15 March; Bedborough reviewed The Ballad in the April Adult, hoping Wilde's next song would be 'signed with the old familiar name'; and on 31 May he was arrested for selling Havelock Ellis's Sexual Inversion to a plain-clothes policeman. 'My dear father's book' is one of Sir William Wilde's.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The whole of the correspondence, ten weeks before Bedborough's arrest.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1083; printed folio 1037 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear good Friend, I am installed here in a little inn by the sea. It is very nice, and there is no one in the whole hotel, so I am quite alone. I am still filled with wonder at the beauty of the world, and with gratitude to God for still considering me worthy to enjoy it, or perhaps I should say making me worthy of such a privilege. Do write to me, and tell me all about yourself, and your artistic plans. Have you any plays going? I know you are reciting, and envy those who hear that wonderful rich voice of yours that Browning, and indeed all poets, used to admire so much, and can watch your lithe panther-like grace of movement, and become dominated by the exquisite tyranny of your personality. However, I think of you every day, and the sea-birds, whom the wind here blows about like white flowers, seem aware of the fact, and are, apparently, quite indignant about it, if screaming counts as a sign! Send me a photograph of yourself, if you can. I want to look at your shadow: and please like and store as a secret my new name. Your affectionate friend
sources.context: Wilde to Mrs Bernard Beere, [circa 2 June 1897], Hôtel de la Plage, Berneval-sur-Mer (MS Yale) - quoted whole, and signed SEBASTIAN MELMOTH. A fortnight out of prison. The Browning who admired her voice is Robert Browning. 'Please like and store as a secret my new name' is the alias being entrusted to her, which is the same discretion machinery visible in the Dieppe letter to Ada Leverson where Ross and Turner travelled under each other's names.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: One of the first friends written to after prison, and the alias entrusted to her.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 925; printed folio 875 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Mrs Bernard Beere
people.bio: Actress, and one of Wilde's oldest theatrical friends - she created Mrs Arbuthnot in A Woman of No Importance. Nine of Wilde's letters to her survive, running from 1880 to 1897. The last of them was written from Berneval a fortnight after he came out of prison, and he signed it with his new name and asked her to keep it a secret.
people.bio_note: NINE LETTERS at printed 152, 161, 330, 416, 590, 592, 631, 846 and 875; ONE read at the page.

people.name: Bernhard Berenson
people.bio: American art historian and connoisseur, a friend and Richmond-circle neighbour of Katharine Bradley and Edith Cooper - the two women who wrote together as Michael Field. For a period in the 1890s Cooper had a crush on him.

people.name: Carlos Blacker
people.bio: A gentleman of independent means, linguist and friend of Wilde's from the 1880s, who stood by him for years and to whom Wilde wrote some of the warmest letters of his exile. Fifteen survive, from 1897 to 1898. Blacker was living in Freiburg with knowledge of the Dreyfus affair; the friendship later broke over it.
people.bio_note: FIFTEEN LETTERS at repo PDF 961, 970, 971, 985, 986, 995, 1081, 1085, 1090 and others; ONE read at the page (printed 911, folios confirmed). DATES NOT RECORDED - the editors give none on the page read, and none is inferred. That was true of the pages then read and false as a description of the volume: the General Index lists folios 1085-8, and printed 1085 carries Wilde's own account - Blacker 'has behaved like a hypocritical ass to me', an accusation of an anonymous attack, 'I wrote him a very strong letter' - together with the Dreyfus entanglement the old note had relegated to hearsay.

sources.quote: My dear old Friend, I need not tell you with what feelings of affection and gratitude I read your letter. You were always my staunch friend and stood by my side for many years. Often in prison I used to think of you: of your chivalry of nature, of your limitless generosity, of your quick intellectual sympathies, of your culture so receptive, so refined. What marvellous evenings, dear Carlos, we used to have! What brilliant dinners! What days of laughter and delight! To you, as to me, conversation - that τερπνὸν κακόν as Euripides calls it - that sweet sin of phrases - was always among the supreme aims of life, and we tired many a moon with talk, and drank many a sun to rest with wine and words. You were always the truest of friends and the most sympathetic of companions. … Many friends, such as Will Rothenstein, the artist, Conder, who is a sort of Corot of the sunlight, Ernest Dowson, the poet, and others have come to see me for a few days: and next month I hope to see Ricketts and Shannon, who decorated all my books for me, dear Robbie Ross, and perhaps some others.
sources.context: Wilde to Carlos Blacker, 12 July 1897, Chalet Bourgeat, Berneval-sur-Mer (MS Koch, Yale). Seven weeks out of prison. The elision drops a description of the chalet and the beach. τερπνὸν κακόν is Euripides' 'delightful evil'; Wilde renders it himself as 'that sweet sin of phrases'. THE ROLL-CALL AT THE END is a list of who actually came: Rothenstein, Dowson, Ricketts, Shannon and Ross are all on this map.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Wilde thought a long friendship had been made of, and who came to Berneval.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 961; printed folio 911 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: C. Blacker has behaved like a hypocritical ass to me, and finally wrote me a letter accusing me of having written some attack on him that appeared in some Paris paper. I need hardly say I never read the paper, or saw the attack, and that I never write anonymous attacks on people anywhere. I was so angry, I wrote him a very strong letter. He has got into a mess here through being Reinach's 'homme de paille' in his Dreyfus-Syndicat campaign and I should not wonder if he were expelled. … The comic thing about him is the moral attitude he takes up. To be either a Puritan, a prig, or a preacher is a bad thing. To be all three at once reminds one of the worst excesses of the French Revolution.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Monday, 27 June [1898], Nogent-sur-Marne (MS Clark). The elision drops the detail of Blacker's connection with Conybeare and a dismissed army officer. 'homme de paille' is a straw man or front. THIS CORRECTS THIS NODE. Its bio_note asserted until 2026-08-06 that the break with Blacker 'is NOT documented on any page read here' - a true statement about the pages then read, which the volume's own General Index contradicted by listing folios 1085-8. Reading them shows the quarrel documented in Wilde's own hand AND shows it is the Dreyfus affair, which the same note had described as merely 'in the general literature'. The editors also point to a scholarly account: J. Robert Maguire, 'Oscar Wilde and the Dreyfus Affair', Victorian Studies, Autumn 1997.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The break with Blacker, in Wilde's own words, and its entanglement with the Dreyfus affair.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1131; printed folio 1085 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Mary Bliss
people.bio: E. P. Warren's first cousin, to whom he had dedicated his privately printed fairy tale The Prince Who Did Not Exist (1900), and who married his partner John Marshall on 5 November 1907. Fothergill's memoir has her arriving at Lewes House and courting 'Ned and Marshall, either of which she was well prepared to marry', and thinking naively that the marriage would bind Marshall closer to Warren. She died at the Villa Buonvisi, Bagni di Lucca, in 1925; all three of them share the tomb there.
people.bio_note: Her birth year is not recorded by Sox, who calls her 'Ned's spinster cousin' and 'a middle-aged cousin' at the time she came to Lewes House, before 1901. json, 2026-08-05; the source moved with her unchanged, verified at the printed page. Sox's own verdict on the union: 'Neither love nor sex had anything to do with the union of Mary and John Marshall, but she was an extremely beneficial help-mate in his collecting at the Metropolitan Museum.'

people.name: Harold Bloodworth
people.bio: 'Pug' of George Ives's household - a working-class former footballer who joined in 1909, outlived Ives, and inherited the Adelaide Road house jointly with 'Elephant'. Cook records Ives's diary grief when Pug was away, and his paternal framing of the household as his 'children'.
bio_sources: Cook, London and the Culture of Homosexuality (2003), p. 148
people.bio_note: Footballer identity, survival of Ives and the joint inheritance from Cook 2014 printed p. 96 (repo PDF 107, folio confirmed); the diary passage on sleeping beside Pug and Cubby at printed p. 101 (repo PDF 112, folio confirmed); both. The 1909 move-in is from Cook 2003 p. 148. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED. Cook names him at printed pp. 96, 109 and 110 (repo PDF 107, 120, 121) - footballer, joined the household, outlived Ives, inherited jointly, executor of the will, 'had lived with Ives at this point for around 30 years' - and attaches no dates to him anywhere. Searched so far, WITHOUT RESULT: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), repo PDF - every occurrence of the surname in the whole book, plus the endnotes and bibliography for the household chapter; the Ives repo transcripts (ives_diaries_burnet.txt, ives_letters_burnet_collated.txt, ives_letters_burnet_transcription.txt, ives_lewis_correspondence_2026-06.md), which contain no occurrence of any of the household surnames; and the open web, which returned only the Palgrave chapter version of Cook's same text ('George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family') and no dates. Cook is the only scholar to have written this household up and he dates their arrivals, their departures and Ives's will, but never a person: he gives no birth or death date for any member of the household. Unresolved without census, GRO index and probate research on common English surnames. Ives's own proved will (Cook, printed pp. 109-110), which leaves the Adelaide Road house to Bloodworth and Saunders, names Bloodworth an executor and portions the Goddards, is the natural documentary starting point, since a grant of probate fixes addresses and often identifies legatees.

sources.quote: Dear Sphinx, Your aphorisms must appear in the second number of the Chameleon: they are exquisite. 'The Priest and the Acolyte' is not by Dorian: though you were right in discerning by internal evidence that the author has a profile. He is an undergraduate of strange beauty. The story is, to my ears, too direct: there is no nuance: it profanes a little by revelation: God and other artists are always a little obscure. Still, it has interesting qualities, and is at moments poisonous: which is something. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Ada Leverson, [early December 1894], Albemarle Club (MS Clark) - quoted whole. The editors identify the anonymous author as John Francis Bloxam, editor of The Chameleon and an undergraduate of Exeter College, and record that the story was attributed to Wilde and that 'much play was made' with it at his trial - along with Wilde's own aphorisms in the same issue and Douglas's poem 'Two Loves'. 'Dorian' here is John Gray, who is on this map.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's only recorded description of him - and his verdict on the story that would be used against him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 677; printed folio 625 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: John Francis Bloxam
people.bio: An undergraduate of Exeter College, Oxford, who founded and edited The Chameleon and wrote for its first and only issue, anonymously, 'The Priest and the Acolyte' - a story of a priest's love for a boy. The story was widely attributed to Wilde, and much was made of it at his trial. Wilde, who had aphorisms in the same issue, described its author privately as 'an undergraduate of strange beauty'.
people.bio_note: NO LETTERS BETWEEN THEM SURVIVE: he has no entry in the Index of Recipients, and the evidence here is a sentence in a letter to [[leverson]] (printed 625, read at the page 2026-08-06). DATES NOT RECORDED and none inferred.

people.name: Harold Boulton
people.bio: Harold Edwin Boulton (1859-1935), a Balliol undergraduate from 1878 who edited Waifs and Strays, in which Wilde published two poems, and who wrote the words of 'The Skye Boat Song'. He succeeded his father as second baronet in 1918. Four of Wilde's letters to him survive from his Oxford years, and the first of them is a complaint that he has not written and that he seems to prefer somebody else's company.
people.bio_note: FOUR LETTERS at repo PDF 93, 110, 111 and 144; ONE read at the page (printed 66, folios confirmed). DATES 1859-1935 from the editors' note at printed 66.

people.name: An actor, Bradfield
people.bio: A performer in the Greek play at Bradfield College in 1898, whom John Fothergill watched from the audience and then wrote to. The record preserves no name and no age. Fothergill's memoir calls him only 'a boy on the stage' and, sixty years later, 'that boy' - and 'boy' in this period was used of grown men as readily as of children, so nothing about his age follows from it. Fothergill bought a photograph of the cast with him in the middle, wrote to him the same night on hotel notepaper, and had two letters back before a firm of solicitors intervened and raised the police. The memoir closes the episode by noting that he much later saw the man mentioned 'in some official capacity; he too had retired.'
bio_sources: Sox, Bachelors of Art (1991), pp. 142-143, quoting Fothergill's unpublished memoir
people.bio_note: From Fothergill's memoir as printed in Sox, printed pp. 142-143 (repo PDF 158-159), folios confirmed and. Sox's passage describes a Greek play at a school but never identifies him as a pupil. No name, and no birth or death date in any source consulted. The year 1898 is fixed by Sox's next paragraph, 'It was also the same year - 1898 -'.

people.name: Katharine Bradley
people.bio: Poet, born 1846, the elder half of "Michael Field" and the aunt of her collaborator and life partner Edith Cooper (1862-1913), whom she raised. "Michael Field" is not a person but the single joint pen name under which Bradley and Cooper published everything: eight volumes of poetry, some twenty-seven verse dramas, and a joint diary, Works and Days. Wilde addressed his letters to "Michael Field", writing to the pair as one correspondent. Bradley and Cooper came from a well-off Birmingham family, read classics at University College, Bristol, and lived together first in Reigate and finally in Richmond; on the Y90s account Bradley was the older and the more glamorous and expansive of the two, and was "Michael" (also the Simiorg, or All-Wise-Fowl) in the private mythology of the diary. Wilde corresponded with "Michael Field" between 1890 and 1893 about their verse dramas and about placing A Question of Memory with J. T. Grein's Independent Theatre. Bradley survived Cooper by less than a year and died in 1914.
people.bio_note: Dates (1846-1914) from the editors' identifying footnote to Wilde's letter to "Michael Field", Complete Letters (2000), p. 449, read at the rendered page image 2026-08-03 (the editors print the forename "Katherine"; the roster form "Katharine" follows the Y90s biography and her own usage).

sources.quote: Dear Michael Field, Write to Miss Elisabeth Marbury, c/o Low's Exchange, New York City, USA. She manages all my plays. I have written to her. I am a wretch not to have answered sooner, but I have no excuse; so you will forgive me. Your third act was quite admirable - a really fine piece of work - with that touch of terror our stage lacks so much. I think the theatre should belong to the Furies. Caliban and Silenus, one educated and the other sober, seem now to dominate, in their fallen condition, our wretched English drama. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to 'Michael Field', [? late October 1893], Albemarle Club (MS Clark) - quoted whole. He is helping them place a play in America and praising their third act. The Caliban and Silenus line is Wilde on the contemporary English stage.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde acting for them professionally, and what he thought of their play.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 626; printed folio 574 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Pietro Branca-d'Oro
people.bio: A young Italian whom Wilde added to his circle in the spring of 1900, between Palermo and Rome. He survives in one sentence to Robert Ross: 'I have added one Pietro Branca-d'Oro to the group. He is dark, and gloomy, and I love him very much.' Wilde had seven months to live.
people.bio_note: the volume's General Index entry 'Branca-d'Oro, Pietro (boy), 1181' - the same '(boy)' form the editors use for Georges, André, Alphonse and Armando. This is a different man: Palermo and Rome, April 1900, printed 1181, and Wilde introduces him as a new arrival - 'I have ADDED one Pietro Branca-d'Oro to the group'.

people.name: Romaine Brooks
people.bio: American portrait painter, and Natalie Barney's companion from 1915 for the rest of Barney's life. Souhami's Wild Girls is a joint life of the two of them. She painted Barney as 'L'Amazone' in 1920 and Élisabeth de Gramont around 1912, so the three women at the centre of this cluster are also her sitters. Barney called her Angel, or Angel Birdie; Brooks called Barney Nat Nat. Brooks resisted the terms Barney lived by - Souhami records that she did not want a sustained one-to-one relationship, and found Barney's other affairs hard to endure.
people.bio_note: Sole source read: Souhami, Wild Girls, printed 137 (repo PDF 171, folio confirmed on the rendered page image), chapter 22 'Natalie and Romaine'. No birth or death date is recorded from the pages read.

people.name: A 'brown faun', Naples
aka: the wanton sylvan boy of Italy
people.bio: One of the Neapolitans Wilde called 'my dear Neapolitans', and the one he singled out. He is known from a single sentence written to Leonard Smithers from Paris on 2 September 1900, three months before Wilde's death, after the group had gone home to Naples: Wilde misses 'that brown faun with his deep woodland eyes and his sensuous grace of limb', and says that the Egyptian waiter at the Cafe d'Egypte 'does not console me for the loss of the wanton sylvan boy of Italy'. Both phrases describe this same man. No name, age, occupation or date of meeting is recorded, and nothing else about him survives.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [Postmark 2 September 1900], Paris; Complete Letters printed 1196 (repo PDF 1242), read on the rendered page 2026-08-04. PROVENANCE CAVEAT, from the editors' own footnote 1 to this letter: 'The text of this incomplete letter is taken from Forty Years in my Bookshop by W. Spencer (1923), corrected and supplemented by the American Art Association catalogue of 1 February 1928.' The heading carries no manuscript line, unlike the Ives letter lower on the same page ('MS Texas'), so this text descends from a printed memoir and a saleroom catalogue rather than a surviving manuscript, and the letter is incomplete.

people.name: Diana Bryn
people.bio: Louis Wilkinson's third wife, married after Ann Reid's death in 1932 and divorced at an unrecorded date. Nothing else about her appears in anything read - she is the least documented of the four wives, resting on a single Who Was Who mention.
people.bio_note: Eliot letter of 9 February 1929; Ann Reid to Wilkinson's own Seven Friends (1953) dedication and to Friedman (2002), with her 1932 death to Elwin (1946), p. 207; Diana Bryn to Who Was Who; Joan Lamburn to his Times obituary.

people.name: James Burton
people.bio: A bookmaker, known in the ring as 'Watson', with whom Fred Atkins lived at Osnaburgh Street, Tachbrook Street and elsewhere between about 1891 and 1894, and with whom he worked blackmail. The Rochester Row incident of June 1891 - a gentleman found in bed with Atkins, the charge afterwards dropped - belonged to that partnership, and the charge-sheet from it was the perjury trap that destroyed Atkins's credibility as a Crown witness in April 1895.

context_engagements.period: Osnaburgh Street, Tachbrook Street and elsewhere, 1891-1894

sources.quote: Have you ever lived with a man named Burton?—Yes, at Osnaburgh Street, Tachbrook Street, and other places.
sources.context: Fred Atkins cross-examined by Sir Edward Clarke, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895
sources.supports: cohabitation with Burton across multiple addresses
