people.name: Edward P. Cattell
people.bio: Farm hand at Kirkwood, New Jersey, and a friend of the Stafford family, whom Whitman met in May 1876 and met again by Timber Creek and by the pond on moonlight nights through the following year. Whitman noted his age as 'about 25 or 6' in 1876, which is as close to a birth year as the record comes; his people lived at Gloucester, and his grandfather or great-grandfather Jonas Cattell was a Revolutionary soldier and celebrated runner, whom Whitman thought interesting enough to write up in the Philadelphia Times in 1879. In January 1877 Whitman wrote asking him to stop calling at the Stafford farm and to tell nobody, while assuring him of 'unalterable love'. Cattell wrote back that October, in his own spelling, that he loved him and always would. **No dates of birth or death are recorded for him anywhere consulted** - the paper thins exactly where the money does, and he is on this map for the same reason the unnamed men of Wilde's exile are.

people.name: Philibert de Clermont-Tonnerre
people.bio: French marquis, and Élisabeth de Gramont's husband: she married him at twenty-one, and it is from him that she takes the title Duchesse de Clermont-Tonnerre under which she is usually named. Souhami describes him as reactionary and dictatorial, a man who tried to bend her to his views, and records that she spoke of him as a cruel gaoler.
people.bio_note: Source read at the rendered page: Souhami, Wild Girls, printed 72 (repo PDF 98, folio confirmed). DATES: NONE RECORDED — neither his years nor the year of the marriage is given on the page read; it says only that she was twenty-one, and her own birth year is not stated there either, so nothing is inferred.

people.name: Arthur Clifton
people.bio: A solicitor and friend of Wilde's from the 1880s, later a director of the Carfax Gallery. Seven of Wilde's letters to him survive. He was among the small number of people Wilde asked to dinner to meet other friends, and one of the letters is Wilde going over a poem of his line by line.
people.bio_note: SEVEN LETTERS at repo PDF 396, 404, 407, 432, 482, 483 and 537; TWO read at the page (printed 410 and 463, folios confirmed). DATES NOT RECORDED and none inferred.

sources.quote: My dear Arthur, The new last line 'Paradise' is charming. 'Vice' does not do as it is a word tainted in its signification with moral censure - vitium: what is faulty. The evening was charming. I enjoyed it all. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Arthur Clifton, [postmark 28 January 1891], [16 Tite Street] (MS Clark) - quoted whole. Wilde is editing a poem of Clifton's and reaches for the Latin: vitium means a flaw or defect, and his argument is that the English word has been contaminated by moralising and no longer means what its root means.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde refusing the vocabulary of moral censure, in private, four years before it was used on him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 483; printed folio 463 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Arthur, Do you really wish to buy the necklace? £6 is a heap of money. Ever yours … I shall call at the Club (N. L.) tonight about 10.30 if I can. But write at once.
sources.context: Wilde to Arthur Clifton, [postmark 8 August 1889], 16 Tite Street (MS Private) - quoted whole including the postscript; the ellipsis marks only the signature falling mid-letter. The club is the National Liberal. Trivial in content and kept for the register: Wilde calling in at half past ten at night and wanting an answer the same day. ADDED 2026-08-05 during the page sweep - it was on a folio read for Kersley and not logged.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The everyday footing of the friendship.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 432; printed folio 410 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Many friends, such as Will Rothenstein, the artist, Conder, who is a sort of Corot of the sunlight, Ernest Dowson, the poet, and others have come to see me for a few days: and next month I hope to see Ricketts and Shannon, who decorated all my books for me, dear Robbie Ross, and perhaps some others.
sources.context: Wilde to Carlos Blacker, 12 July 1897, Berneval-sur-Mer (MS Koch, Yale). The roll-call of who came after prison. Corot is the French landscape painter, and the compliment is to Conder's light.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That he came to Berneval, and what Wilde thought of his painting.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 961; printed folio 911 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Conder is now a vineyard: the Youngs are very serious about him, and there is a moral atmosphere about Dieppe that you should come over and dissipate.
sources.context: Wilde at Berneval, August 1897, on the same printed page as the second Laurence Housman letter. 'A vineyard' appears to be a joke at the expense of some improving influence being exerted on Conder at Dieppe; the sense is not explained on the page and nothing is inferred.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Conder in the Dieppe circle, and Wilde's tone about him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 978; printed folio 928 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Charles Conder
people.bio: Painter, celebrated for watercolours on silk and for painted fans. He was one of the friends who came out to Berneval to see Wilde in the summer of 1897, alongside Rothenstein and Dowson, and Wilde described him to Carlos Blacker as 'a sort of Corot of the sunlight'. He drew the landscape and figures on a picture postcard Wilde sent Leonard Smithers from Napoule at the end of 1898.

people.name: Constance Lloyd
people.bio: Constance Mary Lloyd (1858-1898), daughter of Horace Lloyd QC (1828-74), first met Wilde in London in June 1881 and accepted his proposal in Dublin, announcing the engagement to her brother Otho on 26 November 1883. They married at St James's Church, Sussex Gardens, on 29 May 1884, honeymooned in Paris, and had two sons, Cyril and Vyvyan. After the 1895 catastrophe she, like her brother, took the name Holland; she visited Wilde in Reading Gaol on 19 February 1896 to break the news of his mother's death - their last meeting. She died at Genoa on 7 April 1898, aged forty, and was buried in the Protestant cemetery there; 'Wife of Oscar Wilde' was added to her gravestone only in 1963.
people.bio_note: All facts from Complete Letters (2000) pages read as images 2026-08-03: p. 221 n. 1 (dates, parentage, 1881 meeting, Holland name change 'like his sister'); p. 222 (engagement letter); p. 227 n. 2 (wedding card: church, date, hour); pp. 227-9 (honeymoon letters); p. 555 ('my two boys') and plate captions 80-81 (sons' names); p. 652 n. 4 (Reading visit 19 Feb 1896, last meeting); p. 1054 n. 1 (death at Genoa, aged forty); plate caption 82 (grave, 1963 inscription). LETTER COUNT ESTABLISHED 2026-08-06 from the volume's Index of Recipients (printed 1236): 'Wilde, Constance - 241, 633, 637'.
bio_sources: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 221 n. 1
Complete Letters (2000), plate captions 80-82 (plate section between printed pp. 550-551)

people.name: Alphonse Conway
people.bio: A Worthing boy — son of a widow who let lodgings, keen to go to sea — whom Wilde and Douglas met launching a boat on the beach in August 1894; for six weeks he was, in Wilde's contemporaneous letter, 'my only companion,' sailing to Littlehampton and bathing with Wilde, and receiving an inscribed cigarette case, a photograph, a novel, a walking-stick and a blue serge suit before the twenty-four-hour Brighton trip of about 27 September. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at Worthing and the Albion Hotel, Brighton; the allegation, outside the Central Criminal Court's jurisdiction, was never charged, and Conway — seen outside the Court in May 1895 — never testified.
bio_sources: Wilde's libel-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 137-139 (djvu OCR)
Wilde's final-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 318-319 (djvu OCR)
Queensberry's plea, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 344 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)

Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas [August 1894], Complete Letters (2000), p. 602, with the editors' note 'Alphonse Conway, a newspaper boy whom Wilde had met on the beach at Worthing' (p. 602 n 5; read at rendered PDF p. 654, 2026-08-03)

Antony Edmonds, Oscar Wilde's Scandalous Summer (2014), extract at oscarwilde.org.uk - 1891 baptism record giving 10 July 1878; Richard Wood, 'The Later Fate of Alphonse Conway', oscarwilde.org.uk - argued identification with Harold Payne, d. 15 Jan. 1915
people.bio_note: No birth/death dates found in sources read so far, and NO AGE appears in the plea as printed by Hyde (verified in the source image): Wilde on oath estimated 'a youth of about eighteen,' the Letters editors call him 'a newspaper boy' (undated), and Wilde denied he sold papers. Edmonds corroborates the year from the April 1891 census, where Sarah Conway's son 'Alphus', born at Bognor, is twelve. Wood builds this from census, birth, service, death and probate records and calls it 'surely beyond sheer coincidence'; it is nonetheless an argued identification rather than a record naming the trial witness, so no death date is entered here and the call is left open. Two things in the repo record corroborate the name-change premise independently: Queensberry's plea as printed by Hyde names him 'Alfonso Harold Conway' - the middle name Wood's argument turns on - and the Letters editors call him 'Alphonse Conway, a newspaper boy whom Wilde had met on the beach at Worthing' (p. 602 n. 5). SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web.

people.name: Edith Cooper
people.bio: Poet, born 1862, the younger half of "Michael Field" and the niece of her collaborator and life partner Katharine Bradley (1846-1914). "Michael Field" is not a person but the single joint pen name under which Bradley and Cooper published everything: eight volumes of poetry, some twenty-seven verse dramas, and a joint diary, Works and Days. Wilde addressed his letters to "Michael Field", writing to the pair as one correspondent. On the Y90s account Cooper was the more retiring and fragile of the two and tended to follow her aunt's lead; in the diary's private mythology she was "Field", Henry, or the Persian Puss. Evangelista notes that despite the two women's constant devotion to each other Cooper was prone to heterosexual infatuations, including a period of attachment to their friend Bernhard Berenson. She died of cancer in 1913; Bradley followed within the year.
people.bio_note: Dates (1862-1913) from the editors' identifying footnote to Wilde's letter to "Michael Field", Complete Letters (2000), p. 449, read at the rendered page image 2026-08-03, and corroborated in Evangelista's Y90s biography of Michael Field (2015).

sources.quote: Dear Michael Field, Write to Miss Elisabeth Marbury, c/o Low's Exchange, New York City, USA. She manages all my plays. I have written to her. I am a wretch not to have answered sooner, but I have no excuse; so you will forgive me. Your third act was quite admirable - a really fine piece of work - with that touch of terror our stage lacks so much. I think the theatre should belong to the Furies. Caliban and Silenus, one educated and the other sober, seem now to dominate, in their fallen condition, our wretched English drama. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to 'Michael Field', [? late October 1893], Albemarle Club (MS Clark) - quoted whole. He is helping them place a play in America and praising their third act. The Caliban and Silenus line is Wilde on the contemporary English stage.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde acting for them professionally, and what he thought of their play.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 626; printed folio 574 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Arthur Cruttenden
people.bio: A saddler by trade and a fellow prisoner of Wilde's in Reading, released before him. In June 1897, within weeks of his own release, Wilde had him to stay at Berneval-sur-Mer, tried to find him a friend who could put him back into business, and wrote twice in one day to Reggie Turner to introduce him - once formally, once to say he sang and wrote songs and should be seen "as a friend of mine". Wilde's phrase for him is "gentle and unassuming and grateful", and "very sensitive to kindness". No dates and no later trace survive.
people.bio_note: From two letters to Reggie Turner of 16 June 1897, both printed on p. 900 and read at the rendered page 2026-08-04; surfaced by the mechanical sweep.

people.name: Olive Custance
people.bio: Poet, born 7 February 1874, eldest daughter of Colonel Frederic Hambledon Custance of Weston Old Hall, Norfolk; she published in The Yellow Book from 1894 and issued four collections — Opals (1897), Rainbows (1902), The Blue Bird (1905), and The Inn of Dreams (1911). Courted around 1901 by both Natalie Barney and Lord Alfred Douglas, she jilted her fiancé George Montagu and eloped with Douglas on 4 March 1902; their son Raymond was born that November. The marriage was worn down by Douglas's litigations and the custody fight for Raymond, and the couple separated in 1913 without divorcing; from 1932 she lived near Douglas in Hove, seeing him nearly every day. She died on 12 February 1944.
people.bio_note: Dates and facts from Sarah Parker's Y90s biography (https://1890s.ca/custance_bio/, read in full 2026-08-03), corroborated by Parker's Volupté article (2019, at p. 61) and, for the courtship/marriage, by Douglas's Autobiography (1929) read at IA page images (pp. 188-200; partisan). Parker (Volupté 2.1 (2019), p. 61) describes her 'sexual identity as an aristocrat and a queer woman'; Parker 2011 reads her poetry as expressing 'bisexual desire'.

context_engagements.note: Custance's official fiancé at the moment of the elopement — Douglas's memoir (p. 197, image-verified) has the King's letter congratulating Mrs Custance on 'her daughter's engagement to George' days before the 4 March 1902 wedding; McDermott calls him 'a rich school friend of Douglas's, George Montague', heir to an earldom.

sources.quote: My dear Young, The saltimbanques cannot come to Berneval so I don't know if there are enough attractions to drag you and Mrs Young out so long a way.
sources.context: Wilde to Dalhousie Young, [? 2 June 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe (MS Hyde). The saltimbanques are travelling acrobats. Wilde had been out of prison a fortnight and Young, who had defended him in print two years earlier while a stranger, was proposing to visit with his wife.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That Young came to see him within a fortnight of his release.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 925; printed folio 875 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: To sum up shortly: I do not see any evidence that Mr Wilde's love for beauty was a pose; and if there were such evidence it would not affect me in the least. His books do not seem to me to contain any element that is morbid or immoral. I can find no trace of bad influence in his friendships; and for the question of his life, as he was convicted (rightly or wrongly, it makes no difference) of breaking a law, he is being punished for breaking a law. As regards sin, even if we know, or think we know what a man has done, we know nothing about the motive or the manner; and under these circumstances, any outside judgment is a mere impertinence.
sources.context: The close of Young's pamphlet Apologia pro Oscar Wilde, dated 31 May 1895 - six days after the conviction - quoted in full by the editors. YOUNG WAS A STRANGER TO WILDE WHEN HE WROTE IT. The editors add that he also contributed £50 to the fund More Adey collected for Wilde's release. This is Young's own voice, not Wilde's, and is the reason the node exists.
sources.speaker: Dalhousie Young
sources.supports: A public defence of Wilde published by a stranger six days after the conviction.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 925; printed folio 875 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Dalhousie Young
people.bio: English composer and pianist (1866-1921), a pupil of Leschetizky and Paderewski, who made his début in Rome in 1893 and in London in 1895. Within days of Wilde's conviction that spring - and while a complete stranger to him - he published a pamphlet, Apologia pro Oscar Wilde, dated 31 May 1895. He also gave £50 to the fund More Adey collected to support Wilde on his release. Seven of Wilde's letters to him survive, all from the Berneval summer of 1897.
people.bio_note: the volume's Index of Recipients. SEVEN LETTERS at printed 875, 881, 936, 943, 945, 948 and 949; ONE read at the page.

people.name: James Darmesteter
people.bio: French orientalist and professor at the College de France, who married the poet Mary Robinson in August 1888, having been accepted by her the year before. The engagement is what ended her eight-year attachment to Vernon Lee, who suffered a long depression after it. He died in October 1894 after a short illness, leaving her widowed at thirty-seven.
people.bio_note: THE YEAR CONFLICT IS RESOLVED HERE, not left open: Pulham's Y90s biography of Vernon Lee says the attachment lasted 'until Mary married in 1887' and Wikipedia says 1888, but the standard scholarly edition of Lee's correspondence distinguishes the two events - it dates Robinson's acceptance of Darmesteter to 1887 and states that 'the marriage took place in August 1888'.

people.name: Hugo Gerald de Bathe
people.bio: Lillie Langtry's second husband, twenty-eight to her forty-five when they married at St Saviour's Church, Jersey, on 27 July 1899, with her daughter Jeanne Marie the only person present besides the officials. He succeeded as fifth Baronet in 1907, making her Lady de Bathe - the name she died under. By the end they lived apart, she at Monaco and he at Vence.
people.bio_note: Dates 1871-1940 from the Wikipedia article; the baronetcy succession in 1907 is from the Complete Letters editors at p. 91 n. 2, already on langtry.json.

people.name: Élisabeth de Gramont
people.bio: French aristocrat and memoirist, daughter of the Duc de Gramont and Princesse Isabelle de Beauvau-Craon, known as 'Lily' and, by marriage, as the Duchesse de Clermont-Tonnerre. Natalie Barney's lover from 1910 and her companion for the rest of de Gramont's life. At twenty-one she had married the Marquis Philibert de Clermont-Tonnerre, whom Souhami describes her speaking of as a cruel gaoler. Proust consulted her while writing À la Recherche du Temps Perdu, and she wrote four volumes of memoirs; she dedicated her Almanack des Bonnes Choses de France to Barney.
people.bio_note: Both statements were read at the rendered page: Souhami, Wild Girls, printed 72 (repo PDF 98, folio confirmed on the page image) opens its chapter 'Lily de Gramont'; Wickes, The Amazon of Letters, printed 122 (repo PDF 124, folio confirmed) states the relationship independently. DATES: NONE RECORDED. The title in the Souhami footnote at printed 72 is given as Duchesse de Clermont-Tonnerre; Wickes anglicises it to Duchess de Clermont-Tonnerre, and both spellings are carried as aka.

people.name: Isidore de Lara
people.bio: Composer (1858-1935), born Isidore Cohen, whose operas were produced at Monte Carlo under the patronage of the Princess of Monaco. Wilde inscribed a copy of his Poems to him in June 1887: 'To my friend Isidore de Lara, the poet of the musicians, in sincere admiration and affection.'
people.bio_note: BOTH INDEXES CHECKED BEFORE DECIDING: he has NO entry in the Index of Recipients - no letter to him survives - and a single General Index entry, 'De Lara, Isidore, 1136n'. So one footnote really is all there is, which is now a conclusion rather than an assumption. NOT CONSULTED: Osbert Sitwell's pen portrait of him in Noble Essences (1950), which the editors name.

sources.quote: To my friend Isidore de Lara, the poet of the musicians, in sincere admiration and affection, Oscar Wilde, June '87.
sources.context: Wilde's inscription in a copy of his Poems (fifth edition, 1882), recorded by the editors in a note on de Lara's opera, produced at Monte Carlo under the patronage of Princess Alice of Monaco. NOT A LETTER: no correspondence between them survives and he has no entry in the Index of Recipients. The editors point to Osbert Sitwell's Noble Essences (1950) for a portrait.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The whole of the record: one inscription, in Wilde's hand, calling him a friend.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1182; printed folio 1136 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Didaco
people.bio: Florentine actor whom Wilde met at Genoa on his journey from the Riviera to Gland in the early months of 1899, and with whom he spent three days. Wilde described him to Reginald Turner as 'a beautiful young actor, a Florentine, whom I wildly loved', bearing 'the strange name of Didaco' and 'the look of Romeo, without Romeo's sadness'. No surname, age, dates or further trace appear in the letter, and nothing else about him was found in the pages read.
people.bio_note: Everything known here comes from one paragraph of Wilde to Reginald Turner, postmark 20 March 1899, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1132 (repo PDF 1178, printed folio confirmed on the rendered page image). The letter runs over onto printed 1133 and ends there with no further mention of Didaco (repo PDF 1179, folio confirmed), so that paragraph is the whole record on this page-pair. DATES: NONE RECORDED. Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel retells the Genoa meeting at printed p. 248 (repo PDF 262), independently confirming Genoa rather than Naples, and gives no surname, age or dates. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and none is likely to be: the record preserves a first name (or a trade) in another man's correspondence and no surname to search by.

people.name: Lord Alfred Douglas
people.bio: Lord Alfred Bruce Douglas, born 1870, third son of John Sholto Douglas, eighth Marquess of Queensberry, and Sybil Montgomery (who divorced the Marquess in 1887); educated at Winchester and Magdalen College, Oxford, which he left without a degree. Lionel Johnson brought him to see Wilde at Tite Street in 1891, and Wilde dated the friendship proper from May 1892, when Douglas appealed to him over a blackmail scrape. A poet, he was the dedicatee and translator of Wilde's Salome and published Poems in 1896; he later said he destroyed 150 of Wilde's letters to him, including those from Holloway. He arrived in Paris the day after Wilde's death and followed the coffin at the funeral on 3 December 1900. He married Olive Custance by special licence at St George's, Hanover Square, on 4 March 1902; their only child, Raymond Wilfrid Sholto Douglas, was born on 17 November 1902 and from 26 August 1927 lived, with brief intervals, at St Andrew's Hospital, Northampton. Douglas was received into the Catholic Church in May 1911, and was made bankrupt on a money-lender's petition on 14 January 1913. He edited the Academy from 1907, and the rest of his middle life ran through the courts: the Ransome libel trial of 1913, which he lost; Robert Ross's criminal prosecution of him in 1914; a series of actions of his own; and finally his conviction for criminal libel of Winston Churchill, for which Mr Justice Avory sentenced him to six months in the second division. He was taken to Wormwood Scrubs on 13 December 1923 and released for good behaviour on 12 May 1924. In prison he wrote In Excelsis, seventeen sonnets - begun 20 February 1924 and finished on Good Friday, 18 April - which the prison authorities confiscated at his release and which he never recovered; it was published from memory, in the London Mercury in October 1924 and in book form that December. His marriage broke down in 1913 and again after a short reconciliation, but he and Olive were reconciled in later life; she died on 12 February 1944. His late books were the Autobiography (1929) and Without Apology (1938), and his last lyric poem was written in 1927. He died at about four in the morning on Tuesday 20 March 1945, in the Colmans' farmhouse at Lancing where he had spent his last months, and was buried, as he had asked, with his mother in the cemetery of the Franciscan Friary at Crawley.
people.bio_note: Facts to 1900 from Complete Letters (2000) pages read as images 2026-08-03: editorial headnote p. 461 (birth year, parentage, schooling, 1891 introduction, May-1892 dating); p. 575 n. 1 (mother, divorce 1887); p. 574 n. 2 (Salome translation and dedication); p. 648 n. 1 (Poems, 1896); p. 646 n. 1 (destruction of 150 letters); p. 1222 (funeral). Marriage: 'Thus, on 4 March 1902, Lord Alfred Douglas and Olive Custance became man and wife at St George's, Hanover Square.' - Murray, Bosie (2020 edn), PDF p. 141 (repo PDF page read as image 2026-08-03; edition carries no printed folios).
Son: 'the birth of his grandson, on 17 November 1902 … Christened Raymond Wilfrid Sholto Douglas' - Murray, Bosie (2020 edn), PDF p. 143 (read as page image 2026-08-03).

Conversion: 'Douglas's opinions had been entrenched for some time before, in May 1911, he faced up to what he had in the past described as ‘tomfoolery’ and became a Catholic.' - Murray, Bosie (2020 edn), PDF p. 164 (read as page image 2026-08-03).

Sentence and prison: 'Douglas was taken to Wormwood Scrubs in a Black Maria on 13 December. … At fifty-three, he was in no state to survive six months in the Wormwood Scrubs of the 1920s.' and 'In every other respect, Douglas had been sentenced to six months’ hard labour.' - Murray, Bosie (2020 edn), PDF p. 241 (read as page image 2026-08-03). Avory's words of sentence, including the surety to keep the peace 'particularly to Mr Winston Churchill', are at PDF p. 240 (text layer only ⧖).

Death: 'In the early hours of the morning of Tuesday 20 March, Douglas’s night nurse called the Colmans to his room. … at about four in the morning, Lord Alfred Douglas breathed for the last time.' and 'Douglas had mentioned several years earlier that he wished to be buried with his mother, in the cemetery of the Franciscan Friary in Crawley.' - Murray, Bosie (2020 edn), PDF p. 318 (read as page image 2026-08-03).

people.name: Ernest Dowson
people.bio: English poet of the Decadence and one of the Rhymers' Club - the loose association of young poets, meeting at the Cheshire Cheese in Fleet Street, whose two Books of the Rhymers' Club (1892, 1894) carried his work alongside Yeats, Lionel Johnson and Arthur Symons. He met Wilde in 1890 and, with Robert Sherard, visited him at Oakley Street 'in the dark days between his trials'. Living at Arques-la-Bataille near Dieppe in the summer of 1897, he was among the first friends to reach Wilde after his release, dining at Berneval on 3 June and seeing him constantly until his own return to London in mid-July; the twelve surviving letters from Wilde to him are the largest cluster of the Berneval/Dieppe months, and travel from 'Cher Monsieur le Poete' to 'Tout a toi'. Frankel calls him at this period 'one of his closest confidantes' and credits the friendship - together with Wilde's reading of A. E. Housman - as a spur to the composition of The Ballad of Reading Gaol. The correspondence resumed from Naples that October, by then largely about a debt of some 18-20 pounds Dowson owed Wilde; he died at Robert Sherard's house at Catford on 23 February 1900, nine months before Wilde, who asked Smithers to put flowers on his grave.
people.bio_note: The year-pair is from the editors' main-particulars footnote at Dowson's first appearance in the text - Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), printed p. 877 n. 1 (repo PDF 927): 'English poet (1867-1900). The exact death date is from the editors' footnote to Wilde's letter of condolence to Smithers, printed p. 1173 n. 2 (repo PDF 1219): 'Ernest Dowson died in Robert Sherard's house at Catford on 23 February 1900. BIO SOURCING: the Rhymers' Club membership from the editors' footnote at Complete Letters printed p. 422 n. 2 (repo PDF 444, OCR mirror only, unverified in the source), which names the Cheshire Cheese meetings and the two Books of the Rhymers' Club (1892, 1894) with 'W. The 1890 meeting and the Oakley Street visit between the trials from printed p. 877 n. 1 as above (independently asserted, without Sherard, at Sox, Bachelors of Art (1991), printed p. 141). The Berneval/Dieppe period from Wilde's letters at printed pp. 877-926 and from Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), printed p. 113 (repo PDF 127, folio confirmed on the rendered page): Dowson 'now one of his closest confidantes, whom Wilde had known back in London and who resided near Dieppe, at Arques-la-Bataille, until his departure for London in mid-July'; the Ballad claim at Frankel printed p. 121 (repo PDF 135, OCR/text layer). The Naples debt from Wilde to Dowson, printed pp. 957, 965, 969, 971. Frankel's 'just nine months before his own' at printed p. 114 (repo PDF 128, folio confirmed on the rendered page). NOT RECORDED AS A CONTEXT ENGAGEMENT, but on the record: Fothergill, in his unpublished memoir as printed by Sox at p. 141, 'commented that Dowson was in love with the owner of the Cafe Royal, but was "faithful only after his fashion"'; and the Complete Letters editors, glossing Wilde's otherwise 'inexplicable' 1898 reference to a 'Mrs Dowson' (printed p. 1018 n. 3), note that 'Ernest Dowson never married and his mother had died in 1895' and read the phrase as 'probably a reference to a newly acquired mistress or one of the prostitutes whose company he enjoyed'.

people.name: Peter Doyle
people.bio: Irish-born American transit worker, and the companion to whom Walt Whitman wrote the letters published in 1897 as Calamus. Born in Limerick on 3 June 1843 and raised in the American South, he enlisted in the Confederate army in 1861 and was discharged after being wounded; he was in the audience at Ford's Theatre on the night Lincoln was shot. After the war he worked in Washington as a conductor on the Pennsylvania Avenue horsecars, which is how he and Whitman met one winter's evening in 1865 - Doyle twenty-one, Whitman forty-five and the car's only passenger. He later worked for the Pennsylvania Railroad, first as a brakeman and then as a baggage master, and in the mid-1880s settled in Philadelphia and visited Whitman weekly across the river in Camden. He kept Whitman's letters, entrusted them to Richard Maurice Bucke in 1880, and allowed him to publish them in 1897 - a decision without which almost nothing of this relationship would survive. He attended Whitman's funeral. He died in Philadelphia on 19 April 1907, aged sixty-three, and is buried in Congressional Cemetery, Washington.
people.bio_note: Murray's entry on Doyle in Walt Whitman: An Encyclopedia, read in full on the Whitman Archive 2026-08-04 (the site 403s to automated fetching; it was read in a browser). Murray is the author of the fullest published biography of Doyle.

people.name: Émile Duclaux
people.bio: French microbiologist and chemist, a student of Pasteur and his successor at the Institut Pasteur, and Mary Robinson's second husband. She married him in 1902, eight years after Darmesteter's death, and was widowed again in 1904. She lived on among his children, took his name, and died at Aurillac in 1944.
people.bio_note: THE MARRIAGE YEAR IS IN CONFLICT AND IS NOT RESOLVED: Wikipedia says 1902, Wikidata's P580 qualifier says 1901, and NEITHER CARRIES A REFERENCE. 1902 is entered because it is the fuller of the two statements and sits in continuous prose, but a later pass should settle it from the ODNB entry for Mary Duclaux or from Patricia Rigg's Blackwell encyclopedia article.

people.name: Jean Dupoirier
people.bio: Proprietor of the Hôtel d'Alsace in the rue des Beaux-Arts, Paris, where Wilde lived for the last eighteen months of his life and where he died on 30 November 1900. Wilde addressed him as 'Mon cher Patron' and signed to him as Sebastian Melmoth. He kept Wilde's things for him between journeys, and let him run up a bill he could not pay. Many years later he gave an interview about Wilde's last days in which, the editors record, he remembered him with affectionate sympathy.
people.bio_note: Mikhail's Interviews and Recollections (1979) - is named by the editors and has NOT been consulted; it is the obvious next source and would be his own voice.

sources.quote: Mon cher Patron, Je ne retournerai pas avant le premier juin, et par conséquence vous pouvez louer mon appartement: c'est inutile de le garder, et sans doute vous aurez beaucoup de touristes au mois de mai pour l'Exposition. Je vous prie d'avoir la bonté de conserver toutes mes choses pour moi, comme vous l'avez fait l'année passée. J'espère que Madame et la petite se portent bien. Je vous remercie pour mes lettres. Recevez mes compliments.
sources.translation: My dear Patron, I shall not return before the first of June, and consequently you may let my apartment: it is useless to keep it, and no doubt you will have a great many tourists in May for the Exhibition. I beg you to have the goodness to keep all my things for me, as you did last year. I hope Madame and the little one are well. I thank you for my letters. Receive my compliments.
sources.context: Wilde to Jean Dupoirier, [postmark 18 April 1900], chez Cook et Fils, Rome - quoted whole, and signed SEBASTIAN MELMOTH rather than with his own name. The Exhibition is the Paris Exposition Universelle of 1900. He asks after Dupoirier's wife and small child. Wilde would be dead in the Hôtel d'Alsace seven months later. THE SAME FOLIO carries the letter naming Pietro Branca-d'Oro and the 'Homer' passage.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The ordinary arrangement that kept Wilde housed, and that his things were kept for him a second year running.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1227; printed folio 1181 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Edward Langtry
people.bio: An Ulster landowner and widower who married Emilie Charlotte Le Breton in Jersey in 1874 and brought her to London, where she became the most photographed woman in England. She became an American citizen in the course of her US touring and divorced him at Lakeport, California, on 13 May 1897; he died later the same year.
people.bio_note: Holland and Hart-Davis (Complete Letters (2000), p. 91 n. 2 - the repo source, already used on langtry.json) describe him as 'an Irish widower of thirty' whom she married 'in her teens'. Wikipedia dates the wedding to 9 March 1874 and makes her twenty and him twenty-six. Both cannot stand: on either candidate birth year for her (1852 on the person file, following the editors; 1853 per Wikipedia and Wikidata) she was past nineteen in March 1874.

people.name: John Ellingham Brooks
people.bio: English translator, resident on Capri, whose life's work was an English version of Heredia's sonnets. He married Romaine Brooks on 13 June 1903 and gave her the surname she kept and painted under. The marriage was a bargain rather than an attachment on either side: she wanted a name of her own, out of reach of her mother and brother, and he wanted an income and his debts paid. He was himself homosexual — Souhami records Somerset Maugham's first affair with a man as having been with him — and Romaine left within weeks.
people.bio_note: Read at the rendered page: Souhami, Wild Girls, printed 113 (repo PDF 147, folio confirmed); the Maugham detail is at repo PDF 139, located in the text layer and NOT yet read at the page. DATES: NONE RECORDED for him.

people.name: Harry Elvin
people.bio: A soldier, and a fellow prisoner of Wilde's in Reading Gaol. Wilde gives his age as twenty in 1897, which would put his birth around 1877, and calls him the friend he liked best of everyone left inside; the two walked together and talked at length in the prison yard. Elvin was due for release on 6 November 1897. Wilde, by then in Naples and short of money himself, borrowed £2.10 from Reggie Turner so that a letter with a postal order in it would be waiting for him at the Post Office when he came out. **No dates, no trade beyond the army, and no later trace** - the record holds him for the length of one paragraph.
people.bio_note: Everything known here is in a single letter, Wilde to Reggie Turner, postmark 30 October 1897, printed p. 976, read at the rendered page 2026-08-04.

people.name: Eolo
people.bio: An Italian boy in Harold Mellor's household, whose father sold him to Mellor for 200 lire and who had christened all seventeen of his children out of a mythological dictionary. He travelled with Mellor on the Riviera in 1898-99, bicycling over to Wilde at Napoule, and was still with him in Paris in September 1900, by which time Wilde was calling him Mellor's 'slave'. He is presumably the unnamed 'pretty Italian boy' of Wilde's first Mellor letter of 27 December 1898.
people.bio_note: A third mention is indexed at printed 1128; that page has not been read, so it stays a pointer.

people.name: Eric Ward
people.bio: A chorister of Magdalen College, Oxford, from 1874 to 1878. He survives in the record of Wilde's circle as four words in a letter - 'young Ward the quire boy' - and in an editor's footnote giving his full name and his years in the choir. Nothing else about him is known here: not his birth, not his death, not what he made of the evening Wilde saw him in a private box at a Dublin theatre with an older Magdalen man.
people.bio_note: The whole of note 7 at printed 28 is 'Eric Richard Ward, Magdalen chorister 1874-8' - no parentage, no relation, nothing further.

people.name: Ernest Leverson
people.bio: Ada Leverson's husband, a businessman. He appears in Wilde's letters only as 'Ernest' and 'dear Ernest', but he appears steadily: he is named in the same breath as his wife in the letter thanking her for taking Wilde in, he sent Wilde a Shakespeare in Holloway, and he was at Dieppe to meet him when he came out of prison. Whatever the Leversons did for Wilde in May 1895, they did it as a household.
people.bio_note: DATES NOT RECORDED - the editors give none on the pages read, and none is inferred.

people.name: Ernest Troubridge
people.bio: Royal Navy officer, later Admiral Sir Ernest Troubridge, who in October 1908 married Una Taylor as his second wife; their daughter Andrea was born in 1910. She met Radclyffe Hall in 1915 and by 1919 the Troubridges were legally separated because of it - the same year his knighthood made her Lady Troubridge. The marriage ended in law only with his death in 1926, and she kept the title until her own in 1963.
people.bio_note: THE WEDDING DAY IS DELIBERATELY NOT NARROWED: Wikipedia and the Ransom Center both give only 'October 1908', and although Wikidata sharpens it to 10 October, its two references are an online genealogy network and a library blog post - neither a register entry - so the day is left open per this module's rule about dates no source documents. json, 2026-08-05.

sources.quote: My dear Arthur, I was charmed to get your letter, and it was delightful of you to remember my birthday. Though we see each other so rarely, I always think of you as one of my real friends, as I hope you will always think of me. Ricketts has just done for me a lovely cover for Dorian Gray - grey pastel-paper with a white back and tiny gold marigolds. When it appears I will send you a copy. How happy you must be in your little house; there are only two things in the world of any importance, Love and Art; you have both; they must never leave you. Let me send my kindest regards to your wife; I like to think that the wives of my friends are my friends also; and believe me, sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to Arthur Fish, [circa 16 October 1890] - quoted whole; the editors take the text from Cassell's Weekly of 2 May 1923. Wilde's birthday was 16 October, so this is written on or about it, thanking someone for remembering. The Ricketts is Charles Ricketts, who is on this map, and the cover is the 1891 Dorian Gray.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde on his own birthday naming someone one of his real friends, and what he thought the only two important things were.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 477; printed folio 455 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Arthur Fish
people.bio: Wilde's assistant on The Woman's World, and afterwards a friend he saw rarely and thought of often. Eight of Wilde's letters to him survive, from 1887 to 1892. In one, written on his own birthday, Wilde calls him 'one of my real friends' and tells him there are only two things in the world of any importance, Love and Art, and that he has both.
people.bio_note: He is here because printed 455 was opened for Galton and Symons and read whole - the third letter on it is his, and it is much the warmest of the three. EIGHT LETTERS at printed 386, 404, 440, 444, 455, 491, 497 and 531; ONE read at the page. DATES NOT RECORDED and none inferred.

people.name: Richard Fisher
people.bio: A member of E. P. Warren's Lewes House household, John Marshall's friend from Liverpool College, and 'Fishlet' to the others there. Sox lists 'Matt Prichard's alliance with Richard Fisher' among the jealousies and rivalries that marked Warren's relationships; Fothergill's memoir has Prichard growing jealous of Fothergill and Marshall, taking 'little Fisher' with him to the North Room and never appearing in the upper rooms again. The two left together for the Boston Museum of Fine Arts in 1901, which Warren read as going over to the enemy.
people.bio_note: Transcription and provenance reused unchanged from the context_engagement on prichard.json, where he was held off-roster until 2026-08-05. 'Alliance' is Sox's own word and nothing read characterises the bond further; the Fothergill passage (p. 150, rendered) describes the pairing-off and the retreat to the North Room, and the 1901 Boston departure is at p. 40. Warren's 'going over to the enemy' is at p. 70 and was read in the text layer only, so it stays a pointer rather than a quotation.

people.name: Fortuné
people.bio: One of the two young men at La Napoule whom Wilde called his 'two special friends' in a letter to Laurence Housman of about 28 December 1898, singling them out from the local fisher-folk. Wilde wrote that both were 'quite perfect, except that they can read and write'. No surname, age, dates or further trace appear in the letter, and nothing else about him was found in the pages read.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Laurence Housman, [Circa 28 December 1898], Hôtel des Bains, Napoule, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1113 (repo PDF 1159, printed folio 1113 confirmed at the foot of the rendered page image). DATES: NONE RECORDED. Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel repeats the Housman letter at printed p. 243 (repo PDF 257) and adds nothing further about either of the two men. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and none is likely to be: the record preserves a first name (or a trade) in another man's correspondence and no surname to search by.

people.name: John Fothergill
people.bio: Architect-trained aesthete, art dealer and later celebrated innkeeper; per Sox the one member of E. P. Warren's Lewes House brotherhood to become well known in Britain. Born 27 February 1876, son of George Fothergill of a fairly well-off Westmorland family; met Wilde at 19 through Robbie Ross and Reggie Turner, put in brief stints at the London School of Architecture (a pupil of architecture at 30 Manchester Street, 'to be near Sir Arthur Blomfield') and the Slade School of Art, dabbled in classical archaeology, and managed the Carfax Gallery. Wilde inscribed Fothergill's copy of The Ballad of Reading Gaol 'To Rowland Fothergill, the Architect of the Moon'. Ran the Spreadeagle at Thame near Oxford as innkeeper-author - the innkeeping diaries published in the 1930s and 1940s made his name - and died in a modest terraced house in Rugby on 26 April 1957, aged 81.
people.bio_note: All facts read in the source 2026-08-03 in Sox (1991). Introduction printed pp. vii-viii (repo PDF 11-12, roman-folio offset +4): died 26 April 1957 in Rugby aged 81; 'dabbled in classical archaeology, put in brief stints studying at the London School of Architecture and the Slade School of Art, and managed the Carfax Gallery'; 'the one member of the Lewes House brotherhood to become well known in Britain'. P. 133 (PDF 149): born 27 February 1876, son of George Fothergill, 'fairly well-off Westmorland family'; full name John Rowland Fothergill, called Rowland by some friends and Roland or Ronald by others; innkeeping diaries of the 1930s-1940s. P. 137 (PDF 153): met Wilde at 19 through Ross and Reggie Turner. P. 138 (PDF 154): architecture pupil at 30 Manchester Street near Blomfield; the Ballad inscription. Sox's caveat on his main source (p. 133): Fothergill's unpublished 81-page memoir (written 1954, three years before his death) is unfinished, 'highly disorganized', with 'few dates given'. Warren bond NOT entered under context_engagements: in pages read so far Sox says only that Fothergill had 'taken up with Warren in Rome' (p. 142) - no explicit romantic/sexual characterization read in the source; see dossier.

people.name: Francesco
people.bio: One of three coachmen - cocchieri - who drove Wilde out to Monreale during the eight days he spent at Palermo in April 1900. Wilde named the three to Robert Ross as the most favoured, and said he had loved them all. Francesco is named as one of the three most favoured.

people.name: Frank Harris
people.bio: Editor of the Fortnightly Review and later the Saturday Review, and afterwards the author of a famously unreliable biography of Wilde. Thirty-seven of Wilde's letters to him survive. In the exile years he paid Wilde a monthly allowance, bought him clothes, and took him to Napoule for a month so that he might write something. Wilde called him 'a dear good friend of mine'.
people.bio_note: THIRTY-SEVEN LETTERS at repo PDF 489, 555, 895, 944, 1065, 1070, 1075, 1079, 1082 and others; FOUR read at the page (printed 845, 894, 1024-5 and 1097, folios confirmed). DATES NOT RECORDED and none inferred. The first pass had kept only the two letters about money and missed both letters about the friendship itself - printed 894 and 1024-5 - which are the best things in the correspondence.

sources.quote: My dear Frank, Just a line to thank you for your great kindness to me, for the lovely clothes, and for the generous cheque. You have been a real good friend to me, and I shall never forget your kindness: to remember such a debt as mine to you - a debt of kind fellowship - is a pleasure. About our tour, later on let us think about it. My friends have been so kind to me here that I am feeling happy already. Ever yours … If you write to me please do so under cover to R. B. Ross, who is here with me.
sources.context: Wilde to Frank Harris, [circa 20 May 1897], Hôtel Sandwich, Dieppe (MS Yale) - quoted whole, written within a day or two of coming out of prison and printed on the same page as the letter to Ada Leverson. The postscript is the same discretion machinery: letters to Wilde had to be addressed to somebody else.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The first thanks, and the clothes he came out of prison in.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 895; printed folio 845 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Frank, I know you do not like writing letters, but still I think you might have written me a line in answer, or acknowledgement of my letter to you from Dieppe. I have been thinking of a story to be called 'The Silence of Frank Harris'. I have, however, heard during the last few days that you do not speak of me in the friendly manner I would like. This distresses me very much. I am told that you are hurt with me because my letter of thanks to you was not sufficiently elaborated in expression. This I can hardly credit. It seems so unworthy of a big strong nature like yours, that knows the realities of life. I told you I was grateful to you for your kindness to me. Words, now, to me signify things, actualities, real emotions, realised thoughts. I learnt in prison to be grateful. I used to think gratitude a burden. Now I know that it is something that makes life lighter as well as lovelier for one. I am grateful for a thousand things, from my good friends down to the sun and the sea. But I cannot say more than that I am grateful. I cannot make phrases about it. For me to use such a word shows an enormous development in my nature. Two years ago I did not know the feeling the word denotes. … But I must say again that I no longer make roulades of phrases about the deep things I feel. When I write directly to you I speak directly. Violin-variations don't interest me. I am grateful to you. If that does not content you, then you do not understand, what you of all men should understand, how sincerity of feeling expresses itself.
sources.context: Wilde to Frank Harris, 13 June 1897, Hôtel de la Plage, Berneval-sur-Mer (MS Texas), three weeks out of prison. THE DESIRE TEST PASSED OVER THIS ENTIRELY and it is the most important letter in the correspondence. Harris had been offended that Wilde's thanks for money and clothes were not elaborate enough. Wilde's answer is a defence of plain speech as the form sincerity actually takes, and it doubles as a statement about his own post-prison prose. The elision drops a paragraph about the driving-tour he declined. The letter continues past the printed page.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The friendship being repaired in the open, and Wilde defining what gratitude and directness now meant to him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 944; printed folio 894 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Frank, I do not know if you are still in Paris or not: if you are would you mind letting me have now my monthly allowance for October. I have no clothes but those you so generously supplied me with last May year, and excellent as they are the strain of seventeen months has severely told on them, and I want to buy some more. If you can do this it would be very good of you. Perhaps before you leave we may see each other, and discuss our Shakespeare - your Shakespeare I should say. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Frank Harris, [end September 1898], Hôtel d'Alsace (MS Hyde) - quoted whole. Seventeen months after Dieppe, and the clothes are the same clothes. Kept entire because the shape of the exile is in it: an allowance asked for by the month, and a joke about authorship in the last line.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What the friendship had become by 1898, in Wilde's own accounting.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1143; printed folio 1097 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Frank, I cannot express to you how deeply touched I am by your letter: it is une vraie poignée de main. I simply long to see you, and to come again in contact with your strong, sane, wonderful personality. … When you return from Monte Carlo please let me know. I long to dine with you. As regards a comedy, my dear Frank, I have lost the mainspring of life and art, la joie de vivre; it is dreadful. I have pleasures, and passions, but the joy of life is gone. I am going under: the morgue yawns for me. I go and look at my zinc-bed there. After all, I had a wonderful life, which is, I fear, over. But I must dine once with you first. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Frank Harris, [end February 1898], Hôtel de Nice (MS Texas), quoted across the page break. The elision drops two paragraphs on the reviewing of The Ballad. ALSO MISSED BY THE DESIRE TEST. Harris was pressing him to write a comedy; the refusal turns into the plainest statement of despair in the late letters, and then swerves back to dinner. 'une vraie poignée de main' is a real handshake.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Wilde told a friend he had left, and that seeing him was still worth staying for.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 1070-1071; printed folios 1024-5 confirmed on the rendered page images.

people.name: W. Morton Fullerton
people.bio: American journalist, Paris correspondent of The Times. In June 1899 Wilde, quite without money, asked him for a loan of 100 francs, to be sent to 'Monsieur Sebastian Melmoth'. Fullerton replied that he was distressed to have left the appeal unanswered so long, and addressed him by the alias without comment.
people.bio_note: WHAT IS NOT ASSERTED: Fullerton's own documented relationships with men, and his later affair with Edith Wharton, are outside this volume; this node does not borrow them. THE THIRD LETTER, at printed 1155, is located and unread. DATES NOT RECORDED and none inferred.

sources.quote: My dear Fullerton, I find myself in very great trouble owing to not getting some money I expected, from America, where it is owing to me. Would it be an inconvenience to you to lend me 100 francs? I receive my quarterly allowance, such as it is, on July 1st, when I will be able to return it to you. At present I am quite without money, and I hope you will not mind my asking you this favour. If you are able to do this would you send it to me, Monsieur Sebastian Melmoth, at the above address? Believe me, truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to W. Morton Fullerton, [June 1899], Hotel Marsollier (MS Harvard) - quoted whole. 'Sebastian Melmoth' is italicised in the printed text: the money has to be addressed to the alias, which is the exile's whole condition in one clause. Eighteen months before his death.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde asking a journalist for a hundred francs, under his assumed name.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1200; printed folio 1154 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Melmoth, I am distressed to have left your touching appeal unanswered for so long. But I have been on conge in the patrie of Stendhal, and had cognisance of your gene only yesterday.
sources.context: Fullerton's reply, 3 June 1899, 35 boulevard des Capucines (MS Clark), quoted by the editors. HIS OWN WORDS, which few people on this map get. He addresses Wilde by the alias without remark - 'My dear Melmoth' - which is what the courtesy of that circle looked like in practice. 'conge' is leave; 'gene' is embarrassment or want.
sources.speaker: W. Morton Fullerton
sources.supports: That the appeal was answered, and how Fullerton addressed him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1200; printed folio 1154 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Galton, Your Tacitus is a charming little book, and your preface, like everything you write, very perfect in its sanity of wise criticism and good English. Many thanks for your gift. I still hope that Tiberius was very wicked, but fear that philology was his only crime. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Arthur Galton, [October 1890], 16 Tite Street (MS Montague) - quoted whole. The book is the Camelot Classics Tacitus of October 1890. THE SAME YEAR Galton received Lionel Johnson's letter about Wilde.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The whole of the correspondence, and that the two men were in contact in 1890.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 477; printed folio 455 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Arthur Galton
people.bio: Writer and editor (1852-1921), who edited a translation of the Tacitus Annals published in the Camelot Classics in 1890. One letter from Wilde survives, thanking him for it.
people.bio_note: ONE LETTER at printed 455, read at the page. DATES 1852-1921 from the editors' note there.

people.name: George Batten
people.bio: Secretary to the Viceroy of India, and the man Mabel Hatch married in 1874 when she was about eighteen - the marriage that gave her the surname she is known by. They had one daughter, the painter and film-maker Lady Cara Harris. He was still living when his wife met Radclyffe Hall in 1907; Hall and Mabel Batten set up house together in Cadogan Square only after his death.
people.bio_note: Dates 1832-1910 are from Wikidata Q76278040 (P569/P570); the Wikipedia article on Mabel Batten gives him no dates at all, and the Wikidata item is sourced only as 'imported from Wikimedia project'. The marriage itself is footnoted on the article to Emily Hamer, Britannia's Glory (2016 edn), p. 94, which was not read. Sally Cline, Radclyffe Hall: A Woman Called John (1999) would be the better underlying source if the repo acquires it.

people.name: Georges
people.bio: A young Parisian whom Wilde called 'a great friend of mine' and referred to by the nickname 'le petit Georges'. In a letter to Reginald Turner postmarked 3 January 1899 Wilde wrote that Georges was then at Nice and that he had promised to go over and see him, describing him as 'like a very handsome Roman boy, dark, and bronze-like, with splendidly chiselled nose and mouth'. Wilde adds that he was visiting Nice 'on speculative business'. No surname, age or dates appear on the page read.
people.bio_note: SECOND PAGE FOUND 2026-08-05 and read at the page: printed 1108, the Kalisaya bar in Paris, December 1898 - 'One beautiful boy of bad character - of the name of Georges - goes there too, but he is so like Antinous, and so smart, that he is allowed to talk to poets.' Verified source: Wilde to Reginald Turner, [Postmark 3 January 1899], Hôtel des Bains, Napoule, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1117 (repo PDF 1163, printed folio 1117 confirmed at the foot of the rendered page image). The paragraph runs over onto printed 1118, where the sentence about his 'speculative business' completes - that completion was not read in the source and is carried as a pointer, not quoted. FURTHER MENTIONS, FINDING-ONLY AND NOT VERIFIED: the OCR mirror's general index carries the entry 'Georges (boy), 1097, 1108, 1117', which is the editors' own judgement that the three mentions are one person; the mirror text at printed 1108 contains a Georges compared to Antinous. Neither printed 1097 nor 1108 was read in the source, so neither is used here, and the identification across pages remains the editors' index claim rather than a verified finding. DATES: NONE RECORDED. Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel does not treat him at all - the only 'Georges' in that book is the Belgian poet Georges Rodenbach, in a footnote about Khnopff. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and none is likely to be: the record preserves a first name (or a trade) in another man's correspondence and no surname to search by.

context_engagements.note: Friendship, recorded without a connection line, from Wilde's side only - Gide's own writing on Wilde has not been consulted and nothing from it is used here.

sources.quote: Cher Monsieur Louÿs, J'accepte avec le plus vif plaisir la gracieuse et charmante invitation que vous et M. Gide ont eu la bonté de m'adresser.
sources.context: Wilde to Pierre Louÿs, 28 November 1891 - the day after Wilde and Gide first met, and the invitation is from the two of them jointly. QUOTED HERE FOR THE EDITORS' NOTE ON THE FACING COLUMN, which is the substance: Gide wrote to Paul Valéry about Wilde that same week; 'according to his letters he saw Wilde almost every day till 15 December, but the pages in his journal covering those days have been torn out.' Who tore them out, and when, is not stated.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The first day of it, and the three weeks that were removed from the record.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 516; printed folio 496 confirmed on the rendered page image.
sources.translation: Dear Monsieur Louÿs, I accept with the keenest pleasure the gracious and charming invitation which you and M. Gide have been kind enough to address to me.

sources.quote: André Gide, one of my old friends here, has written an astonishing play on Saul, whose madness he ascribes to his hopeless love for David, and his wild jealousy of Jonathan: it is to be played at the Théâtre Antoine, but the parts of the lads are to be filled by women, which is, artistically, to be regretted.
sources.context: Wilde in Paris, December 1898, describing Gide's Saül - written in 1898 and not produced until 1922. Seven years after they met, Gide is 'one of my old friends here'. Wilde reads the play's subject without a flicker of euphemism - a king's madness ascribed to hopeless love for a man - and his only complaint is that boys' parts are going to actresses.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That the friendship lasted through the trials and the exile, and how plainly Wilde could describe the play's subject in 1898.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1154; printed folio 1108 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Mon cher André, Je vous remercie beaucoup. Un de mes amis, le rédacteur du Saturday Review, à Londres, vient d'arriver à Paris, et me prend à Cannes avec lui pour un mois. Peut-être là je retrouverai mon âme. J'espère vous voir à mon retour. Tout à vous
sources.context: Wilde to André Gide, [postmark 14 December 1898], Taverne F. Pousset, Paris (MS Doucet) - quoted whole, and written the same day as the letter to Housman on the same page, which reports the same journey in English. To Housman the hope is 'perhaps these may tune my soul to some note of beauty'; to Gide it is 'perhaps there I shall find my soul again', which is a harder thing to say.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The address at 'mon cher André', and what Wilde told him he had lost.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1157; printed folio 1111 confirmed on the rendered page image.
sources.translation: My dear André, Thank you very much. One of my friends, the editor of the Saturday Review in London, has just arrived in Paris, and is taking me to Cannes with him for a month. Perhaps there I shall find my soul again. I hope to see you on my return. All yours

people.name: André Gide
people.bio: French writer (1869-1951), later a Nobel laureate, and the most consequential openly homosexual author in Wilde's French orbit. He met Wilde in Paris on 27 November 1891, when he was twenty-two, and co-hosted with Pierre Louÿs the invitation that produced Wilde's first surviving letter to Louÿs the following day. By his own account he then saw Wilde almost every day until 15 December. The pages of his journal covering those weeks have been torn out. Seven years later Wilde was still writing to him as 'mon cher André' and reading his play about Saul's hopeless love for David.
people.bio_note: THE TORN JOURNAL: the editors record at printed 496 that his letters place him with Wilde almost daily for three weeks and that the journal pages for exactly those days are missing. They are the obvious next sources and nothing from them is asserted. TWO WILDE LETTERS SURVIVE here (printed 1108 and 1111, repo PDF 1154 and 1157), both read at the page, 2026-08-05.

people.name: Maurice Gilbert
people.bio: Member of Wilde's Paris circle of the exile years, on first-name terms ('Maurice') with the whole inner circle. During Wilde's final illness in November 1900 he came to the sickroom almost daily alongside Reggie Turner, though Turner noted he 'does not like being in the room'; at Robert Ross's request he took the (unsuccessful) photograph of Wilde on his deathbed. He was one of the nine named mourners who walked behind the hearse to St Germain des Prés and is listed among the senders of funeral wreaths. The editors' main particulars are sparse: except that his father was English and his mother French, and that he was a young soldier in the marine infantry, nothing is known of him.
bio_sources: Nicholas Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), p. 209 - 'about whom very little is known'
people.bio_note: All facts from the Epilogue of Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000): sickroom attendance from Turner's letters to Ross, pp. 1217-19 (repo PDF 1262-64); photograph, procession roll-call and wreath list from Ross to Adey, 14 Dec. 1900, p. 1222 (PDF 1267). The dossier's 'shared intimate' hypothesis (Wilde/Ross/Douglas) rests on secondary literature not yet read in the source; the planned reads of the letter at printed p. 1084 and the General Index mention pages were not completed (predecessor session cut off) - no romantic or sexual claim about Gilbert appears in any passage transcribed so far. Main-particulars footnote at Complete Letters (2000), p. 1025 n. 4, transcribed by the correspondents pass 2026-08-03. Birth and death dates are not recorded in the edition. DATES: NOT FOUND, AND TWO SOURCES STATE POSITIVELY THAT THE RECORD DOES NOT CARRY THEM. The Complete Letters editors, at the main-particulars footnote already cited above (printed p. 1025 n. 4), write that 'Except that his father was English and his mother French, and that he was a young soldier in the marine infantry, nothing is known of him.' Nicholas Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (Harvard, 2017), printed p. 209 (repo PDF 223, read as a rendered page image so far and the folio confirmed), calls him 'a young man named Maurice Gilbert, a one-time marine infantryman, the son of a French mother and an English father - Wilde called him "all French lily and English rose" - about whom very little is known except what can be gleaned from Wilde's surviving letters'. Also searched without result: every 'Maurice Gilbert' occurrence in the Complete Letters OCR mirror (PDF 602, 1071, 1100, 1119, 1130, 1221, 1252, 1267) and Frankel's index. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted. Note the small discrepancy between the two: the Letters say his father was English and his mother French, Frankel writes 'a French mother and an English father' - the same parentage, stated in the same order, no conflict.

people.name: Sylvie Goddard
people.bio: Wife of James Goddard ('Kit'), and a member of George Ives's household: Cook records that on marrying, Goddard brought her into the house too, and that their daughters were known there as 'the 2 Kit girls'. Her presence makes the household's composition plain - a married couple and their children living inside the domestic circle Ives called 'my little circle in the world'.
people.bio_note: From Cook 2014 printed p. 96 (repo PDF 107, folio confirmed). Cook gives her only as 'his wife Sylvie' - maiden name, dates and marriage date are not stated in the page read. Cook's printed p. 100 reportedly adds that she kept house for Ives and that she and James remained until their deaths, with the daughters staying until the early 1940s (one, Therese, still visiting in 1944); that page is known so far only from the PDF text layer and is a pointer on the marriage record, not yet verified at the rendered page. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED. She is the least documented member of the household in Cook, who says so himself: her domestic labour 'also went largely without comment' (printed p. 102). Searched so far, WITHOUT RESULT: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), repo PDF - every occurrence of the surname in the whole book, plus the endnotes and bibliography for the household chapter; the Ives repo transcripts (ives_diaries_burnet.txt, ives_letters_burnet_collated.txt, ives_letters_burnet_transcription.txt, ives_lewis_correspondence_2026-06.md), which contain no occurrence of any of the household surnames; and the open web, which returned only the Palgrave chapter version of Cook's same text ('George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family') and no dates. Cook is the only scholar to have written this household up and he dates their arrivals, their departures and Ives's will, but never a person: he gives no birth or death date for any member of the household. Unresolved without census, GRO index and probate research on common English surnames. Ives's own proved will (Cook, printed pp. 109-110), which leaves the Adelaide Road house to Bloodworth and Saunders, names Bloodworth an executor and portions the Goddards, is the natural documentary starting point, since a grant of probate fixes addresses and often identifies legatees.

people.name: James Goddard
people.bio: 'Kit' of George Ives's household. Cook (2014) records that he had been a servant at the Ives family seat in Hampshire and moved with George to London; on marrying he brought his wife Sylvie into the household, and their daughters were known as 'the 2 Kit girls'. He and Sylvie remained with Ives until their deaths. Ives called the household 'my little circle in the world'.
bio_sources: Cook, London and the Culture of Homosexuality (2003), pp. 146, 148
people.bio_note: Household role, Hampshire service, marriage to Sylvie and the daughters from Cook 2014, printed p. 96 (repo PDF 107, folio confirmed). The earlier Cook 2003 p. 146 describes him instead as 'the son of one of his father's employees' - the two accounts differ in emphasis; 2014 is the fuller treatment. That the Goddards stayed until their deaths and the daughters until the early 1940s is from Cook 2014 printed p. 100, known so far only from the PDF text layer - verify at the rendered page before quoting. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED. Cook's fullest treatment of Kit runs across printed pp. 96, 98, 100, 102, 109 and 122 (repo PDF 107, 109, 111, 113, 120, 133) and gives no dates: even the sentence that would most invite one - 'James and Sylvie Goddard remained with Ives until their deaths' - names no year. Searched so far, WITHOUT RESULT: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), repo PDF - every occurrence of the surname in the whole book, plus the endnotes and bibliography for the household chapter; the Ives repo transcripts (ives_diaries_burnet.txt, ives_letters_burnet_collated.txt, ives_letters_burnet_transcription.txt, ives_lewis_correspondence_2026-06.md), which contain no occurrence of any of the household surnames; and the open web, which returned only the Palgrave chapter version of Cook's same text ('George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family') and no dates. Cook is the only scholar to have written this household up and he dates their arrivals, their departures and Ives's will, but never a person: he gives no birth or death date for any member of the household. Unresolved without census, GRO index and probate research on common English surnames. Ives's own proved will (Cook, printed pp. 109-110), which leaves the Adelaide Road house to Bloodworth and Saunders, names Bloodworth an executor and portions the Goddards, is the natural documentary starting point, since a grant of probate fixes addresses and often identifies legatees.

people.name: Graham Hill
people.bio: Poet, journalist and playwright; his musical play Havana was a success at the Gaiety in 1908. Five of Wilde's letters to him survive, three of them from 1888, when Hill was about twenty-three and sending Wilde his first book of verse. Wilde read it, criticised one rhyme, praised the touch, teased him about the woman it was dedicated to, and twice asked him to come round. The correspondence resumes in 1891 with the two warmest letters of the five, in which Wilde asks whether he is 'still enamoured of love and poetry' and says he thinks of him often.
people.bio_note: L. love you?' - is about a third party, which is right: the editors' note identifies M. ALL FIVE LETTERS have been read at the page: three at printed 380 (repo PDF 402), then printed 480 (PDF 500) and printed 483 (PDF 503), every folio confirmed on its own page image. Dates 1865-1933 from the editors' note at printed 380.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Hill, Come and have tea on Friday at 5 o'clock if you have nothing to do. So you are a rhymer! We all are when we are young. Believe me truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to Graham Hill, [? 1888], 16 Tite Street (MS Mason) - the first of the three letters printed together on this page.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The invitation, and the terms of the friendship: an established writer amused by a young one.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 402; printed folio 380 confirmed on the rendered page image. Quoted whole.

sources.quote: My dear Graham Hill, I am charmed with your little volume; the triolets, ballades, and rondeaus are very graceful and dainty. I am sorry you have rhymed 'tears' to 'ideas' in your envoy; rhymes of this kind are very wicked, but you certainly have a light touch and a pleasant fancy. The book is very prettily got up, and 'M. L.', whoever she is, should feel quite proud at such an artistic offering. Are you very much in love with M. L.? and does M. L. love you? Come and see me some day. Wednesday afternoon usually finds me in. Truly yours
sources.context: The second letter on the same page, on Hill's Under Her Window (1888). The editors' note 3 identifies 'M. L.' as Matilda (Minnie) Lloyd, whom Hill later married - the line the 2026-08-04 sweep correctly read as being about a third party. It is quoted here in its place in the letter rather than on its own, because on its own it is the only thing anyone has noticed about this correspondence.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde reading a young poet's book closely, praising and correcting it, teasing him about his sweetheart, and asking him to call.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 402; printed folio 380 confirmed on the rendered page image. Quoted whole.

sources.quote: Dear Graham Hill, I don't think that poems are ever really helped by the publication of letters from private friends. An anonymous criticism is always something, or supposed to be something, but personal letters are different. However you are quite at liberty to do as you think best. I hope you will be successful in whatever branch of literature you take up, and am very glad you are turning your attention to prose. Good prose is what we want. How is your journalism progressing? Truly yours
sources.context: The third letter on the same page. Hill had evidently asked to print Wilde's praise; Wilde declines the use and encourages the career in the same breath.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The shape of the friendship - Wilde withholding his name from Hill's publicity while backing his work.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 402; printed folio 380 confirmed on the rendered page image. Quoted whole.

sources.quote: Your paper is charming – it was kind of you to send it to me. I never write for newspapers now, but if I have at any future time something suitable you shall have it. I wish I saw you oftener. Sincerely yours … Write yourself a review of Dorian Gray.
sources.context: Wilde to Graham Hill, [? May 1891], 16 Tite Street (MS Mason) — quoted whole, postscript included. The editors could not identify the paper Hill was writing for, and record that no review of Dorian Gray by him has ever been traced.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Three years on from the first letters, the friendship still running — and Wilde saying plainly that he would like to see more of him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 500; printed folio 480 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Thank you so much for the cutting which amused me very much. How are you getting on? Are you still enamoured of love and poetry? I hope so. They are the only two things in the world that remain. I often think of you, and am sorry we meet so rarely. Sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to Graham Hill, [? Summer 1891], Lyric Club, Piccadilly East (MS Mason) — the last of the five, quoted whole, and the warmest.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The closest thing to a declaration in this correspondence: 'I often think of you, and am sorry we meet so rarely.'
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 503; printed folio 483 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: W. Graham Robertson
people.bio: Artist, illustrator and stage designer (1866-1948), painted by Sargent in 1894 and the owner of an important collection of Blake drawings. His children's play Pinkie and the Fairies was produced by Tree in 1908, and his autobiography Time Was (1931) is a standard source for the period. He was twenty-one when Wilde began writing to him in 1887 and Wilde was thirty-three. Seven of Wilde's letters to him survive, running to 1893, and they are among the most affectionate he wrote to anyone outside the circle this map already draws: 'your narcissus keeps you in my memory'; 'You are made for olive-groves, and for meadows starred with white narcissi'; 'I should have loved to have been with you'. He bought Wilde a drawing of Sarah Bernhardt, illustrated for him, and paid Charles Ricketts, of whom Wilde's first recorded impression is in a letter to Robertson.
people.bio_note: SEVEN LETTERS at repo PDF 359, 369 (two on one page), 412, 420, 432 and 612; FIVE have been read at the page (printed 347, 390, 398, 410, and the two at 347), every folio confirmed on its own page image. TWO remain located but unread: repo PDF 359 (postmark 12 December 1887, the earliest) and 612 (postmark 14 April 1893, sending a first-night stall). DATES: none recorded — the editors give none on the pages read, and none is inferred.

people.name: Walter Grainger
people.bio: A servant at the house in High Street, Oxford, where Lord Alfred Douglas had rooms — 'about sixteen when I knew him,' Wilde swore of 1893 — who waited at table during Wilde's stays and asked Wilde to find him a place; Wilde brought him to 'The Cottage' at Goring as under-butler from June-July 1893 until Wilde left in October. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at Oxford and Goring; the allegations, outside the Central Criminal Court's jurisdiction, were never charged and Grainger never testified. Carson's pursuit of Wilde's answer to 'Did you ever kiss him?' — 'Oh, dear no. He was a peculiarly plain boy' — is recorded by Hyde as the turning point of the libel trial.
bio_sources: Wilde's libel-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 150-151 (djvu OCR)
Wilde's final-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 320 (djvu OCR)
Queensberry's plea, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 343-344 (IIIF page images 2026-08-03)
Hyde, Trials (1948), Introduction pp. 51-52 (the cross-examination climax; djvu OCR)
people.bio_note: The age sixteen is Wilde's own sworn estimate at the libel trial, NOT stated in the plea as printed by Hyde (verified in the source image) — the ROSTER's 'aged 16 (plea)' attribution needs adjusting to '(Wilde's testimony)'.
