The General Index of Complete Letters (2000) has no Grainger entry (verified at the rendered index page, printed p. 1248: the sequence runs 'Grain, J. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED FROM THE SOURCES CONSULTED. He was a servant at a certain house in High Street, Oxford, where Lord Alfred Douglas had rooms' (Hyde, printed p. 149-150 region; located in the IA OCR text, consistent with the in the source reading already recorded above). McKenna's endnotes cite a 'statement of Walter Grainger, 1895, witness statements, private collection' - a document not in public hands and not consulted. SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted.

people.name: John Gray
people.bio: Poet. His Silverpoints (Mathews and Lane, 1893) was designed by Ricketts and initially underwritten by Wilde before the two fell out; in the same year The Blackmailers, a play written in collaboration with his close friend Andre Raffalovich, was produced at the Prince of Wales's Theatre. After the publication of The Picture of Dorian Gray he referred to himself as Dorian and allowed others in the Wilde circle to do so, though the editors find no evidence he was the character's original. He became a Roman Catholic, was ordained priest at thirty-five, and spent his later years in Edinburgh, where Raffalovich built St Peter's Church for him; in 1904 he edited and published Last Letters of Aubrey Beardsley, which were written to Raffalovich.
people.bio_note: All facts from the main-particulars footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 520 n. 3 (repo PDF 540, folio confirmed). Born/died 1866-1934 from the same footnote.

people.name: Frances Gregg
people.bio: American avant-garde writer, for a time H.D.'s lover, who married Louis Wilkinson in April 1912 inside a triangle with John Cowper Powys - Powys being in love with her and unwilling to divorce his own wife. She and Wilkinson had a son and a daughter and divorced in 1923. She was killed with her mother and her daughter Betty in the Plymouth blitz of April 1941. Her memoir The Mystic Leeway was published in 1995.
people.bio_note: Eliot letter of 9 February 1929; Ann Reid to Wilkinson's own Seven Friends (1953) dedication and to Friedman (2002), with her 1932 death to Elwin (1946), p. 207; Diana Bryn to Who Was Who; Joan Lamburn to his Times obituary.

people.name: Radclyffe Hall
people.bio: Novelist and poet, born Marguerite Antonia Radclyffe-Hall on 12 August 1880, best known for The Well of Loneliness (1928), a serious treatment of lesbianism that was prosecuted and banned in England until 1949. The Ransom Center's biographical sketch records that, "[s]elf-identifying as a sexual 'invert,' Hall adopted a masculine appearance and the name John". Her two long partnerships were with the singer Mabel Batten (1856-1916), her first lover, and with Batten's cousin Una Troubridge (1887-1963), from 1915 until Hall's death. Hall belongs to a later generation than Wilde's circle and does not appear anywhere in his Complete Letters; she reaches this map from the Ives side, as a figure of the homophile politics Ives helped begin. Matt Cook records that she and Troubridge "seem to have been considered" for the Order of Chaeronea and that Ives took an interest in the 1928 obscenity case over her novel. She died on 7 October 1943.
people.bio_note: The Order-of-Chaeronea and obscenity-case detail from Matt Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), p. 108, transcribed from the source in the IVES-DOMESTICITIES dossier (long-form research notes, kept in the private research repository) (Passage 26); Cook's double hedge is preserved and no Order-membership or Ives edge is created on it.

sources.quote: Will you come and see me tonight at nine o'clock or any time when you can escape from 'Sir John' - whom by the bye I believe you like much better than yours truly
sources.context: Wilde to Harold Boulton, [? April 1878], Magdalen College (MS Yale). 'much better' is italicised in the printed text. The editors identify 'Sir John' as most probably Sir John Alexander Hanham, ninth Baronet, Magdalen undergraduate 1875-8. He is the rival in the only letter that carries `boulton--wilde`.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That Boulton had a preferred companion, and who the editors think he was.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 93; printed folio 66 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Sir John Alexander Hanham
people.bio: Ninth Baronet, and a Magdalen undergraduate from 1875 to 1878, having succeeded to the baronetcy on his uncle's death in 1877. He is on this map as the third point of a triangle: the 'Sir John' whose company Wilde believed Harold Boulton preferred to his own.
people.bio_note: IDENTIFICATION IS THE EDITORS' AND IS HEDGED - 'most probably Sir John Alexander Hanham' (printed 66, note 2) - and that hedge is kept rather than dropped.

people.name: Richard Reginald Harding
people.bio: Magdalen Commoner 1875-9 and an Oxford friend of Wilde's, addressed in sixteen surviving letters as 'Kitten'. The nickname was not Wilde's invention and was not private to him: it came from a music-hall song about the family's surname — 'Beg your parding, Mrs Harding, / Is my kitting in your garding?' — and his elder brother James was Puss and his sister Amy Miss Puss. The letters run from 1876 to 1879. The tenderest belong to April 1878, when Wilde was ill at Magdalen and Harding stole him flowering branches from the New Buildings: 'I heard your light quick step down the passage this morning… I can bury my face in them and dream how nice it would be to be out again. You are the nicest of kittens.' He joined the London Stock Exchange in 1895 and remained a member until his death.
people.bio_note: SIXTEEN LETTERS at repo PDF 42, 43, 46, 48, 54, 55, 59, 68, 72, 79, 86, 92 (three on one page), 93 and 109. TEN have been read at the page (printed 30, 65 and 66, folios confirmed); the other ten are located, not read, and all are rendered in the session scratchpad. DATES 1857-1932, the full name and the nickname's origin are from the editors' note at printed 15, read at the rendered page 2026-08-05. 'PUSS' IS SETTLED and is NOT another name for Kitten, which was the obvious guess: the editors' note at printed 15 gives him as JAMES HARDING, Reginald's elder brother, with their sister Amy as Miss Puss; the volume's index lists all three separately, and a third letter (printed 21) settles the sex beyond doubt — 'Miss Puss has fallen in my estimation if SHE is fetched with Swan'. Every page in these two correspondences that mentions Frank or the Miles family has now been read at the page - repo PDF 42, 46, 47, 49, 54, 56 and 72, printed 17, 21, 22, 24, 29, 31 and 47 - and the note is not audible in any of them.

sources.quote: Dear Kitten, Have you fallen into a well, or been mislaid anywhere that you never write to me? Or has one of your nine lives gone? Frank Miles and I came down here last week, and have had a very royal time of it sailing. … Frank has done some wonderful sunsets since he came down; he has given me some more of his drawings. … Frank has never fired off a gun in his life (and says he doesn't want to) … But on Friday we go into Connemara to a charming little fishing lodge we have in the mountains where I hope to make him land a salmon and kill a brace of grouse. … Write to me there if your claws have not been clipped. Best love to Puss. I hope he is reading hard. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, Wednesday [? 16 August 1876], Moytura House, Cong, Co. Mayo (MS Hyde) — the house Sir William Wilde built above Lough Corrib. The elisions drop topography and a query about a drawing for Harding's sister. TWO THINGS WORTH NOTING: the cat-naming runs right through it — nine lives, clipped claws, and 'Puss', who is a third friend the letters do not identify; and Frank Miles, who is on this map, is here on holiday with Wilde in 1876, three years before they shared a house.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The earliest register of the friendship — teasing, cat-named, and reproachful about silence — and Wilde and Frank Miles on holiday together in 1876.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 55; printed folio 30 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Boy, Thousand thanks for your letter. Half the pleasure of getting a First is to receive such delightful congratulations. … I came down here Monday and had no idea it was so lovely. A wonderful garden with such white lilies and rose walks; only that there are no serpents or apples it would be quite Paradise. The church is very fine indeed. Frank and his mother, a very good artist, have painted wonderful windows, and frescoed angels on the walls, and one of his sisters has carved the screen and altar. It is simply beautiful and everything done by themselves. These horrid red marks are strawberries, which I am eating in basketfuls, during intervals of lawn tennis, at which I am awfully good. There are four daughters, all very pretty indeed, one of them who is writing at the other side of the table quite lovely. My heart is torn in sunder with admiration for them all, and my health going, so I return to Ireland next week.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, [circa 13 July 1876], Bingham Rectory, Notts (MS Hyde) — written from THE MILES FAMILY HOME. The 'Frank' is Frank Miles, who is on this map and with whom Wilde would share two London houses; the rector was his father. The elision drops a week of London engagements. The letter is the Miles family seen admiringly and collectively — mother, sisters, windows, screen — and the note Croft-Cooke hears is not audible in it. IT RUNS ON PAST THE PAGE BREAK, and the ending is the point: having described Frank's windows and Frank's mother's frescoes, Wilde finishes on Frank's four sisters and says his heart is torn in sunder with admiration for them all.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Harding's congratulations were worth to him, the first Miles-household letter in the correspondence, and the sisters at the end of it.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 46-47; printed folios 21 and 22 both confirmed on the rendered page images.

sources.quote: My dear Kitten, I am very sorry to hear you did not meet the poor Bouncer Boy; see what comes of having rowdy friends fond of practical jokes. I had an awful pencil scrawl from him yesterday, written sitting on the rocks at Lundy. I hope nothing will happen to him. I had a very pleasant time in Lincolnshire … as probably Bouncer will tell you when you see him next (I wrote a full account to him). I examined schools in geography and history, sang glees, ate strawberries and argued fiercely with my poor uncle, who revenged himself on Sunday by preaching on Rome in the morning, and on humility in the evening. Both very 'nasty ones' for me.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, Wednesday [5 July 1876], Magdalen College (MS Hyde), three days after the letter to Ward printed on the same page. The elision drops the weather. Kept because it shows the triangle from Harding's side: Wilde writing to Kitten about Bouncer, and saying he has already written Bouncer a fuller account.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The three of them as a set, and Wilde's solicitude for Ward expressed to Harding.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 43; printed folio 18 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Boy, You are in chapel I suppose with a divine calm in your soul. The doomed one is wretched at failure – and no tea. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, [? April 1878], Magdalen College (MS Hyde) — the first of three letters printed together on this page, and the whole of it.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The register at its lightest: a note across college, imagining where he is.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 92; printed folio 65 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Kitten, Many thanks for your kind note. I have a childish longing for some flowers – I don't care what – only not wallflowers. If you have any spare moments and can get me a few you will be doing as benevolent an action as giving groundsel to a starving canary would be! I am very wretched and ill and as soon as possible I am to be sent away somewhere out of Oxford, so my Greats work has collapsed finally for ever. Only that Tuckwell and William are awfully kind to me I should jump into the muddy Cherwell. Ever yours … Could you steal a branch of that lovely red blossoming tree outside the New Buildings for me? I am sick at heart for want of some freshness and beauty in life.
sources.context: The second letter on the same page, Tuesday [? April 1878], quoted whole including its postscript. Wilde was ill and had been told to leave Oxford. 'William' is probably William Ward, who is also on this map.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The ask — flowers, from him specifically, because he is sick at heart for want of beauty.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 92; printed folio 65 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Kitten, If there is anything that could console me for being ill it is your charming basket of flowers and delightful letter. The roses have quite given me a sense of the swift beauty and light of the spring: they are most exquisite. And I heard your light quick step down the passage this morning and am awfully obliged for your theft of the pink and white blossoms. I can bury my face in them and dream how nice it would be to be out again. You are the nicest of kittens. Ever yours
sources.context: The third letter, [? April 1878], running across the page break and quoted whole. Harding had done what was asked: stolen the branch and sent a basket besides.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The tenderest thing in either Oxford correspondence.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 92-93; printed folios 65 and 66 both confirmed on the rendered page images.

sources.quote: My dear Kitten, I suppose you are reading much too hard ever to write any letter now. It seems a long time since I heard from you, and as for Bouncer I have not heard anything about him for a fortnight. In his last letter he complained terribly that his mother and sisters would not let him read. I hope your people are better, and encourage your industry in every way. I have been waiting for my brother who is on circuit, and for Frank Miles who could not get away from home till we go down to Galway together. We expect them both tomorrow. I am rather tired of sea bathing and lawn tennis and shall be glad to be down for the 12th. After this rain too there will be a lot of fish up. I am just going out to bring an exquisitely pretty girl to afternoon service in the Cathedral. She is just seventeen with the most perfectly beautiful face I ever saw and not a sixpence of money. I will show you her photograph when I see you next.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, Sunday [6 August 1876], 1 Merrion Square North (MS Hyde), quoted whole - written the same day as the Todd letter to Ward, and printed on the facing page to it. The girl is almost certainly Florence Balcombe, who later married Bram Stoker. The two paragraphs are consecutive and untouched: Frank Miles as a travel arrangement, and then the most perfectly beautiful face he ever saw, which belongs to a seventeen-year-old girl.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The clearest single test of the Croft-Cooke claim, and it fails in the space of two paragraphs.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 54; printed folio 29 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Boy, Thanks for your letter: I had made out the facts by a careful study of the statutes going up to town, but it was comforting all the same to have it confirmed by such an authority as the Schools Clerk. I had a delightful time in town with Frank Miles and a lot of friends and came home on Friday. My mother was of course awfully astonished to hear my news and very much disgusted with the wretched stupidity of our college dons, while Mahaffy is raging! I never saw him so indignantly angry; he looks on it almost as an insult to himself. The weather is charming, Florrie more lovely than ever, and I am going
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, Tuesday [15 May 1877], 1 Merrion Square North (MS Hyde). The news is that Wilde had been fined and rusticated for returning to Oxford a month late from Greece; he later told Ricketts he was 'sent down from Oxford for being the first undergraduate to visit Olympia'. The quote breaks where the printed page does. The Florrie is Florence Balcombe. Again the pattern: Frank Miles in a subordinate clause, and the lovely thing in the sentence is a girl.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The last of the seven Miles pages, and the third time a Miles mention sits next to praise of a woman.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 72; printed folio 47 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Kitten, So glad to hear from you again. I have been here fishing for the last three weeks. Jack Barrow and Dick Trench are staying with me, so I find myself far from lonely, which is unfortunate as far as reading goes. … I have become an awful misanthrope however: you won't know me next term. I had two jolly letters yesterday, one from Bouncer who is quill-driving …
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, [August 1877], Illaunroe Lodge, Lough Fee (MS Hyde). The elisions drop a paragraph of salmon and sea-trout counts; the letter runs on past the printed page. 'Bouncer' is William Ward, also on this map, and the two Oxford correspondences touch here. ADDED 2026-08-06: read at the page during the Pater sweep and left unlogged at the time.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The ordinary footing of the friendship between the tender letters - fishing, house guests, and a joke about his own misanthropy.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 86; printed folio 59 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Herbert
people.bio: A young man described in December 1898 simply as Hylton's — 'Hylton is here with his boy Herbert'. Nothing else about him is on record here: not his surname, not his age, not a word of his own.

people.name: Doris Gillian Herring
people.bio: John Fothergill's first wife, whom he met at the Slade School in 1905-06 and married shortly afterwards. Fothergill never once named her - not in his memoirs, not in any surviving letter - and what little is recorded of the marriage comes through Romaine Brooks, who had just finished painting his portrait. After the separation she went to Rome and worked there as an artist until her death in the 1950s.
people.bio_note: NO DATES ARE RECOVERABLE from the sources read: Sox gives no birth or death year, no wedding date and no place, and Wikipedia's article on Fothergill does not mention her or the first marriage at all. The marriage year 'c. 1905-06' is Sox's own relative dating (Romaine Brooks places it just after finishing the 1905 portrait) and is NOT a documented date; a GRO marriage-index search would fix it. That Fothergill never named her is Sox's explicit point and is recorded here as part of the record rather than as a gap in it.

people.name: Charlie Hickey
people.bio: A young man of Lord Alfred Douglas's circle, described by Douglas in his Autobiography (1929) as 'a charming boy about a couple of years younger than myself and well known to Oscar, a son of Colonel Hickey' - which, Douglas having been born in 1870, would place his birth around 1872. He was with Douglas in Paris in May 1895 while Wilde's second trial was proceeding in London, and is the 'Charlie' who 'sends you his best love' in Douglas's letter to Wilde of 15 May 1895, one of only three Douglas-to-Wilde letters recovered. Nearly four years later, in exile at Napoule, Wilde had a presentation copy of The Importance of Being Earnest addressed to him and asked Reggie Turner after him.
people.bio_note: All facts from Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000) with printed folios confirmed. The Douglas Autobiography (1929) description and the 15 May 1895 letter it glosses are p. 649 n. 3 (repo PDF 700); the note prints the Douglas letter in full and appends the Autobiography sentence. The presentation copy and Wilde's enquiry after him are p. 1122 (PDF 1168), in Wilde to Reginald Turner, [postmark 3 February 1899]. NOT read so far (pointers): the remaining General Index locators 811, 830, 837, 878, 1132. DATES: NONE RECORDED. Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. The only quantity in the record is relative and remains an inference that is deliberately not entered: Douglas's Autobiography (1929), as printed in the editors' note at p. 649 n. 3, calls him 'a charming boy about a couple of years younger than myself'. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and no surname search is possible beyond 'a son of Colonel Hickey', which would need an Army List to pursue.

people.name: Harold Holt
people.bio: One of the young men of George Ives's household; Cook identifies him as Ives's grandmother's former secretary, named alongside James Goddard as sharing Ives's rooms at E4 the Albany - and sometimes his bed - from 1894.
bio_sources: Cook, London and the Culture of Homosexuality (2003), pp. 146, 148
people.bio_note: Cook 2003 p. 146 (read in the source 2026-08-03) names the two men sharing Ives's bed as 'James Goddard (Kit)' and 'Harold Holt (Cubby)'. Cook 2014 p. 101 (repo PDF 112, folio confirmed, read in the source 2026-08-03) instead identifies the long-term resident nicknamed Cubby as 'Charles Gee'. Facts from Cook, London and the Culture of Homosexuality (2003), p. 146 (repo PDF 162; printed folio confirmed). DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED, and note that the source position is weaker for him than for the rest of the household. Harold Holt does not appear in Cook 2014 at all - a search of the whole repo PDF returns no occurrence of the name - so the only source for him remains Cook 2003 p. 146, which names him but gives no dates, and Cook 2014 assigns the nickname Cubby to a different man (Charles Gee), the unresolved conflict already recorded above. Searched so far, WITHOUT RESULT: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), repo PDF - every occurrence of the surname in the whole book, plus the endnotes and bibliography for the household chapter; the Ives repo transcripts (ives_diaries_burnet.txt, ives_letters_burnet_collated.txt, ives_letters_burnet_transcription.txt, ives_lewis_correspondence_2026-06.md), which contain no occurrence of any of the household surnames; and the open web, which returned only the Palgrave chapter version of Cook's same text ('George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family') and no dates. Cook is the only scholar to have written this household up and he dates their arrivals, their departures and Ives's will, but never a person: he gives no birth or death date for any member of the household. Unresolved without census, GRO index and probate research on common English surnames. Ives's own proved will (Cook, printed pp. 109-110), which leaves the Adelaide Road house to Bloodworth and Saunders, names Bloodworth an executor and portions the Goddards, is the natural documentary starting point, since a grant of probate fixes addresses and often identifies legatees.

people.name: Winifred Christabel Hopkins
people.bio: Harry Marillier's second wife, married in 1906 - daughter of the artist Arthur Hopkins, and herself the composer of 'The Rose and the Ring'. They had one son.

people.name: Herbert Horne
people.bio: Architect, designer, typographer, poet and art historian of the Century Guild circle, and later the founder of the Museo Horne in Florence. His one volume of poems, Diversi Colores, he printed himself in 1891. Eleven of Wilde's letters to him survive, from 1886 to 1891 - Wilde asking him to dinner alone, praising his verse twice at length, and arguing with him about how cautiously to restore a school building.
people.bio_note: ELEVEN LETTERS at repo PDF 305 (two), 306, 483, 504 and others; SIX READ AT THE PAGE (printed 283 twice, 463 and 484, folios confirmed). DATES NOT RECORDED and none inferred.

sources.quote: Are you doing anything? If not, come in and stay to dinner. No one but myself - so come as you are. Sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to Herbert P. Horne, [8 July 1886], 16 Tite Street (MS Private) - quoted whole, the earliest of the eleven, and the whole of it is an invitation to dinner alone. 'No one but myself' is doing the work; 'come as you are' says how little ceremony was wanted. Wilde was married and living at Tite Street.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: A dinner for two, at no notice.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 305; printed folio 283 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: I fear I have to go out tonight, but I hope to see you soon. Your poems are most charming, and your choice of epithets exquisite and felicitous. You combine very perfectly simplicity and strangeness. I have no doubt you will do very lovely work.
sources.context: Wilde to Herbert P. Horne, [14 July 1886], 16 Tite Street (MS Clark) - quoted whole, six days after the dinner invitation and printed directly beneath it.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The praise that came a week later.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 305; printed folio 283 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Horne, Many thanks, but I am dining out, otherwise I would come with pleasure to hear you read some delicate Herrick-like song, and Lionel read that sonnet on Wormwood that so fascinated me. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Herbert Horne, [postmark 28 January 1891], 16 Tite Street (MS Fales) - quoted whole. Written the same day as the letter to Arthur Clifton on the same printed page.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: An evening of poems among men, declined but wanted.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 483; printed folio 463 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Horne, A thousand thanks. What a lovely little book! And what dainty delightful verse! The notes of passion so vivid and scarlet, and yet conveyed with such subtlety and fine reticence. … and indeed the whole book is full of honey and very sweet to taste, and just touched with that sadness which is inseparable from modern art, and gives a preciousness to beauty, as of a thing one might lose, and so loves overmuch: and you are a perfect player of a little lovely reed. And so, more thanks, and always sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to Herbert P. Horne, [date of receipt 2 July 1891], 16 Tite Street (MS Mason). The book is Diversi Colores, Horne's only volume of poems, printed by himself in 1891. The elision drops the names of four individual poems. NOT TO BE OVER-READ: the editors print the 'marvellous third stanza' Wilde singles out, and it is about a woman's thigh. 'The notes of passion so vivid and scarlet' is a judgement about verse.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The fullest thing Wilde wrote him, and a caution about reading praise of poems as praise of the poet.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 504; printed folio 484 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Horne, I am very glad we are in agreement on this matter. We must not spoil by new gauds the ancient spirit of the place. As for repairs don't you think that these should be done by the Trustees? … The tablet is excellent, so is the wainscote and fireplace idea; beyond that I feel we should not go. … Of course the whole place should be a Chatterton museum. I wish you were here to talk over it. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Herbert P. Horne, [postmark 23 August 1886], 16 Tite Street (MS Simpson). The elisions drop two paragraphs on who should pay for repairs. The scheme is a memorial to Thomas Chatterton, the boy poet who killed himself at seventeen in 1770 and whom Wilde had lectured on. ADDED 2026-08-06 from a folio opened for Otho Lloyd.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The two of them working on a Chatterton memorial together, and Wilde wishing him there.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 307; printed folio 285 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Horne, We must clearly wait till Christmas, as there should be no rash hurry, and I would like to have a long talk with you about the whole matter before any pronunciamento. Believe me, truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to Herbert P. Horne, [postmark 31 August 1886], 16 Tite Street (MS Dugdale) - quoted whole, eight days after the letter above and printed directly beneath it.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde wanting a long talk before anything is announced.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 307; printed folio 285 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Violet Hunt
people.bio: Violet Hunt, later a novelist, was the daughter of the landscape painter Alfred William Hunt and the novelist Margaret Raine Hunt, of Tor Villas, Campden Hill, where Wilde took tea with the family during his Salisbury Street years. In 1880-81 he paid her marked attention - 'the sweetest Violet in England I think her', he wrote to her mother in March 1880 - promised and sent her a poem, and thanked her directly in July 1881 for admiring his Poems. Her autobiography The Flurried Years (1926), quoted by the editors for her reminiscence of the young Wilde at Tor Villas, is the family memoir of the acquaintance.
people.bio_note: Facts from the main-particulars footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 88 n. 4 (repo PDF 113, folio confirmed) and Wilde's letters at pp. 88-9, 93, 94 (to Mrs Alfred Hunt) and 114 (to Violet Hunt). It is confirmed: Sutherland, Stanford Companion to Victorian Fiction (1989), p. 314, also gives 1866. en.wikipedia and Wikidata (Q1677011) give 1862, and en.wikipedia cites Sutherland - the work that contradicts it. Ellmann has them meeting in London 'when she was not yet seventeen' (see the source on hunt--wilde), which fits neither 1866 (she would be about thirteen when the letters begin in March 1880) nor 1862 (about eighteen). Ellmann also puts the meeting in London at the beginning of the 1880s, not Dublin in 1879, and our own verified letters are London from March 1880. LETTER COUNT ESTABLISHED 2026-08-06 from the volume's Index of Recipients (printed 1233): 'Hunt, Violet - 114'.

people.name: Hylton
people.bio: A member of Wilde's Paris circle in December 1898, who arrived at the Hôtel d'Alsace 'with his boy Herbert' and whom Wilde found almost impossible - 'a sort of grown-up man with a hysterical womb', who made scenes with Sir John Ashton 'like a woman with child'.
people.bio_note: found by reading printed 1107 whole after the General Index sent me there for Alphonse. **He is indexed nowhere** - neither in the Index of Recipients nor under his own name in the General Index - and would never have been found by any search.

people.name: Irma Perry
people.bio: Richard Le Gallienne's third wife, married on 27 October 1911, four months after his divorce from Julie Norregaard. Her own previous marriage - to her first cousin, the painter and sculptor Roland Hinton Perry - had been dissolved in 1904. She was with Le Gallienne in Paris from the late 1920s and no separation is recorded before his death at Menton in 1947.

people.name: George Cecil Ives
people.bio: Poet, penologist and pioneering campaigner for homosexual law reform; illegitimate son of Colonel Gordon Maynard Gordon-Ives and, by his own account, the Baroness de Molarti of Spain, raised by his paternal grandmother and living on a private income. Kept a diary from 1886 to 1950 - 122 volumes, around three million words - alongside a forty-five-volume press-cuttings casebook, an archive now split between Yale and the University of Texas at Austin. In about 1893 he founded the Order of Chaeronea, the first homosexual support-and-pressure group in Britain, named for the Theban band slaughtered in 338 BC, and structured it deliberately without hierarchy: any two existing members could invite a third. In October 1894 he published an outspoken justification of same-sex love in the Humanitarian. Lived at 56 St James' Street from July 1891, at Flat E4 the Albany, Piccadilly, from 30 June 1894, from 1897 in his late grandmother's Regent's Park house, and from 1905 at Adelaide Road, Primrose Hill, with an unconventional household of younger working-class men he called his 'children' - a family, in Cook's phrase, connected by co-residence rather than by blood. He was treasurer of the British Society for the Study of Sex Psychology (Edward Carpenter was its life president). Though he identified settledly as homosexual, he also had affairs with women, and considered having a child outside marriage with Matilda 'Tilly' Hayes. His will of 1939, eight typed pages with ten later codicils, left the Adelaide Road house and contents to the two men he was then living with, Harold Bloodworth and Stanley Saunders.
people.bio_note: Born/died and Order founding from the biographical footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 573 n. 3 (repo PDF 625): 'George Cecil Ives (1867-1950). Albany move-in date from p. 592 n. 3 (PDF 644). Parentage, diary scope (1886-1950, 122 vols, c. 3M words), casebook, archive split, Chaeronea-as-first-group, Humanitarian article, and addresses from Cook (2003) pp. 31, 143-8 (repo PDF 47, 159-164). Cook spells the Order 'Chaerona'. Lewis (NHC podcast, repo ASR transcript) notes the Spanish-baroness maternal descent is not borne out by census records. ENRICHED 2026-08-03 from Matt Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), ch. 'George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family': the Regent's Park interval (from 1897), the Order's non-hierarchical two-members-invite-a-third structure, the BSSSP treasurership with Carpenter as life president, the affairs with women and the Tilly Hayes child question, and the 1939 will. PAGINATION - TWO DIFFERENT OFFSETS in this PDF: in the body text printed folio = repo PDF page - 11 (re-confirmed at PDF 108=97, 109=98, 110=99, 111=100, 113=102, 114=103, 115=104, 116=105, 117=106, 118=107, 119=108, 120=109, 121=110), but IN THE BACK-MATTER NOTES printed folio = repo PDF page - 10 (confirmed at PDF 280=270, 281=271, 282=272, 283=273). CHAPTER EXTENT - the Ives chapter runs printed 95-111, NOT 95-123; ch. 5 (Joe Ackerley) begins at printed 112, and the 'Freddie' of printed 113 onward is Ackerley's lover, a different man from the household's Freddie Smith. Cook 2014 spells the Order 'the Order of the Chaeronea' (Cook 2003 has 'Chaerona'). Cook dates the Albany move to 1893 ('two years later' than 1891) against the Complete Letters' 30 June 1894, and dates the will to October 1939 in his text but 1 December 1939 in his endnote 80 - both unresolved. PROVENANCE CAVEAT: Cook's endnotes credit Brian Lewis, by personal communication and with no archival citation, for the Goddard-daughters departure reading (n. 22), the Tilly Hayes identification (n. 61), and the Charles French connection (n. 84).

context_engagements.period: Adelaide Road household, from 1905; departure undated
context_engagements.note: He left to move in with Robert 'Robbie' Ross, whom Cook describes as a good friend of both Ives and Wilde. STRONG CAVEAT: this single sentence is the only mention of Freddie Smith in the whole 336-page book, and Cook cites NOTHING for it - the attached endnote 21 is purely methodological (Gilding, Behlmer, McBride and McCandless, Tosh, on household and family).

sources.quote: Also in the house were Pug and Elephant and other intimate male friends of Ives who became housemates for often extended periods before moving on - often to marry, or in the case of Freddie Smith to move in with Robbie Ross who was a good friend of both Ives and Wilde.
sources.context: Cook, on the turnover of the Adelaide Road household
sources.supports: Freddie Smith's household membership and his departure to live with Robert Ross - the Ives-circle/Wilde-circle bridge.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 111 (printed folio 100 confirmed on the rendered page).

context_engagements.note: A woman with whom Cook says Ives had a long-running 'affair/friendship' across three decades, and with whom he discussed having a child - the 'certain girl' of the 1920 diary entry. She stood third in line to inherit the Adelaide Road house under his 1939 will, after Bloodworth and Saunders and ahead of his kin, and Cook names her among the friendships Ives kept up 'close and open'. Cook's compound 'affair/friendship' is deliberately unresolved and should be preserved rather than collapsed to either term. CAVEAT: Cook's endnote 61 credits the identification of Hayes with the 'certain girl' to Brian Lewis by personal communication, with no archival citation.

sources.quote: This was Matilda (Tilly) Hayes with whom Ives had a long running affair/friendship from the 1910s to the 1940s.
sources.context: Cook, identifying the 'certain girl' with whom Ives had discussed having children in a 1920 diary entry
sources.supports: A named, decades-long relationship with a woman, in Cook's own deliberately unresolved formulation.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 116 (printed folio 105 confirmed on the rendered page).

sources.quote: she attracted me physically (not the romantic love; no girl can win that from me) [...] she said she wanted a baby but only under married conditions.
sources.context: Ives's diary (vol. 76, 14 September 1920, p. 20, per Cook's endnote 62), quoted by Cook as a displayed block quotation; the ellipsis is Cook's own
sources.supports: Ives's own account of the relationship: physical attraction, romantic love explicitly withheld, marriage refused.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 116 (printed folio 105 confirmed on the rendered page).
sources.speaker: George Ives, diary

context_engagements.period: Named in the 1939 will; bequest later revoked
context_engagements.note: Cook reads him as probably working-class and service-sector, and suggests he was 'perhaps a former lover' - but immediately offers the competing reading that French was one of the men Ives called 'Ducks', short for 'lame ducks', men he helped out intermittently but thought hopeless cases. ROSTER CANDIDATE, but any certainty must not exceed Cook's own hedge, which is explicitly speculative; and his endnote 84 credits the connection to Brian Lewis by personal communication, with no archival citation.

sources.quote: Probably working-class, employed in the service sector (which we've already seen had a reputation for attracting queer men), French was perhaps a former lover, though was also one of the men Ives went on to call 'Ducks' (short for 'lame ducks' - men he helped out intermittently but thought hopeless cases).
sources.context: Cook, on a legatee named in Ives's 1939 will as having worked at the Spread Eagle Hotel, Midhurst, and latterly at 1 Greek Street, London W1
sources.supports: Charles French as a possible former lover of Ives - Cook's own speculation, offered alongside a competing non-sexual reading.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 121 (printed folio 110 confirmed on the rendered page).

context_engagements.note: Poet, and named by Cook as a fellow member of the Order of Chaeronea. Not a partner; recorded as an Order-kinship tie, which is the relation Cook argues Ives understood as a form of family. This is a firmer Order-membership attestation than Cook's hedged sentence about Radclyffe Hall and Una, Lady Troubridge (printed 108), who 'seem to have been considered'.

sources.quote: He left the poet and fellow member of the Order of the Chaeronea, Laurence Housman, a ring bearing the numbers 338 (the date of the last battle of the Theban Bands).
sources.context: Cook, on the bequests in Ives's 1939 will beyond his kin and household
sources.supports: Housman's membership of the Order of Chaeronea alongside Ives, and a personal bequest marking it.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 121 (printed folio 110 confirmed on the rendered page).

people.name: Joseph
people.bio: A young man in Paris, described by Wilde in December 1898 as I. D. W. Ashton's 'little friend'. He lived in the same establishment as Ashton and served at table when sober. Wilde's letter has him returning with a black eye and a swollen nose after drink and a political discussion, then vanishing from a Sunday morning until the next day; Wilde calls him 'a little Dionysiac' and blames Ashton's habit of giving good advice for driving him to drink. No surname, age, occupation beyond waiting at table, or later trace appears in the pages read.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Reginald Turner, [postmark 6 December 1898], Hotel d'Alsace, Paris, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1107.

people.name: Charles Kains-Jackson
people.bio: London solicitor specialising in literary matters (1857-1933), and from 1888 to 1894 editor of The Artist and Journal of Home Culture - a magazine which, in the editors' own words, he used in part as a forum for London's homosexual coterie, and to which Lord Alfred Douglas contributed. Wilde consulted him professionally over Salomé in November 1893.
people.bio_note: the volume's Index of Recipients. THE DESCRIPTION OF HIS MAGAZINE IS THE EDITORS' OWN AND IS QUOTED RATHER THAN PARAPHRASED - 'which he used in part as a forum for London's homosexual coterie' (printed 574, note 1). TWO ITEMS at printed 574 and 576; ONE read at the page. HIS OWN CIRCLE - the Uranian poets, and his editorship's place in that literature - lies outside this volume and is not asserted here.

sources.quote: Can you come and see me here tomorrow at eleven. Wish to consult you professionally on Salomé business.
sources.context: Telegram, Wilde to Charles Kains-Jackson, 6 November 1893, 7.32 p.m., St James's Street (MS Clark) - quoted whole. The editors note that on the verso someone has written 'Reply - that C. K.-J. will keep appointment'. THE SALOMÉ BUSINESS is the dispute over whether Douglas's name should appear as translator on the title page; it was settled by dedicating the play to him instead - 'To my friend Lord Alfred Bruce Douglas, the translator of my play' - after Douglas wrote that the difference was 'between a tribute of admiration from an artist and a receipt from a tradesman'.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That Wilde used him as his solicitor at the height of the Salomé dispute.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 626; printed folio 574 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Kernahan, I should have thanked you long ago for sending me your charming fairy tale, but the season with its red roses of pleasure has absorbed me quite, and I have almost forgotten how to write a letter. … But your strength lies not in such fanciful, winsome work. You must deal directly with Life - modern terrible Life - wrestle with it, and force it to yield you its secret. You have the power and the pen. You know what passion is, what passions are; you can give them their red raiment, and make them move before us. You can fashion puppets with bodies of flesh, and souls of turmoil: and so, you must sit down, and do a great thing. It is all in you. Your sincere friend
sources.context: Wilde to Coulson Kernahan, [postmark 20 June 1892], 16 Tite Street (MS British Library). The elision drops three sentences of praise for the tale's symbolism. Included for completeness rather than for what it proves: the 'passion' is the subject Wilde thinks he should be writing about.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Warmth between men, recorded whether or not it amounts to anything.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 548; printed folio 528 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Coulson Kernahan
people.bio: Writer, and a reader for the publisher Ward, Lock. Six of Wilde's letters to him survive, from around 1891 to 1892, mostly on the business of A House of Pomegranates and Lord Arthur Savile's Crime. One of them is not business at all: an unprompted page telling a younger writer that his gift for fairy tales is beneath him and that he should be writing about passion instead.
people.bio_note: SIX LETTERS at repo PDF 459, 493, 494, 507, 541 and 548; ONE read at the page (printed 528, folios confirmed).

people.name: G. H. Kersley
people.bio: George Herbert Kersley, who published five volumes of verse between 1885 and 1897 and also painted. Wilde wrote to him over nearly ten years, from 1885 to 1894, and the seven surviving letters are almost entirely invitations: come to tea, read me one of your poems, come in this evening at nine, come on Tuesday morning and see me. In the preface to his first book Kersley called Wilde 'my noted friend'.
people.bio_note: Whether Kersley ever went is not recorded here. ALL SEVEN LETTERS READ AT THE PAGE: printed 251, 283, 352, 410, 420, 443 and 622-3 (repo PDF 273, 305, 374, 432, 442, 465, 675), every folio confirmed on its own page image, 2026-08-05. Judged against the actual rule all five qualified - they are invitations, reproaches for not visiting, and an offer to find him work - so they were read at the page and added. DATES NOT RECORDED and none inferred; the editors give none.

sources.quote: I am very sorry to hear of your father's death, and hope it will not be any obstacle to your remaining at your work in London. I will come and see you some day and write my name in my book for you, if you tell me when I will find you at home - some afternoon at five - and you will give me a cup of tea, and read me one of your poems. Friday? Would that suit you? I am sure that you will do beautiful work some day. You have the temperament of the artist. Yours sincerely
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [postmark 24 February 1885], 16 Tite Street (MS Rosenbach) - quoted whole, the earliest of the seven. Condolence, an offer to come to him, and a flat statement of belief in him. Wilde was thirty.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: How it started: a death in the family, and Wilde proposing himself for tea.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 273; printed folio 251 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Kersley, I am very pleased that you like my stories. They are studies in prose, put for Romance's sake into a fanciful form: meant partly for children, and partly for those who have kept the childlike faculties of wonder and joy, and who find in simplicity a subtle strangeness. If you come to tea some Wednesday about 5.30 o'clock I will be charmed to write your name in the book. I hope your painting is going on all right. Truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [15 June 1888], 16 Tite Street (F Hyde) - quoted whole. The stories are The Happy Prince and Other Tales, published that May, and the sentence about what they are for is one of the clearest statements Wilde made about them.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The book promised in 1885, three years later, and what Wilde said his stories were for.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 374; printed folio 352 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Kersley, I send you a line for Whitman. I hope you will see him and admire him. Truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [postmark 4 August 1886], Albemarle Club (MS Clark) - quoted whole. WALT WHITMAN IS ON THIS MAP: Wilde had visited him at Camden in 1882 and the map carries the reported parting kiss. Four years later he is handing a young English poet an introduction to him, and the instruction is not to interview him or learn from him but to 'admire him'. Whether Kersley went is not recorded.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde passing a young poet on to Whitman.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 305; printed folio 283 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Kersley, Of course you should have come to see me before you left town. I wanted to hear all about you, and what art you are now devoted to. As for the art of money-making I know nothing about it. I wish I did, but it is not in my temperament. If I see Charlie Hawtrey I will speak to him about you. Are you writing anything now? Sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [postmark 6 August 1889], 16 Tite Street (MS Clark) - quoted whole. The address has moved from 'Dear Mr Kersley' to 'My dear Kersley'. Charles Hawtrey was an actor-manager; Kersley was after work.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Reproach for not calling, and Wilde offering to put a word in for him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 432; printed folio 410 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Kersley, Of course you behaved dreadfully in not coming to see us, but I need hardly tell you you will always be welcome. If you have nothing better to do come in this evening at 9 o'clock or Wednesday afternoons will always find us. It is ages since we met and I want to hear all about you. Truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [postmark 3 January 1890], 16 Tite Street (TS Clark) - quoted whole. Note the pronoun: 'coming to see US', 'will always find US'. This is the Tite Street household, Wilde and Constance, and the invitation is to it.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The warmest of the invitations, and the reproach repeated five months on.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 442; printed folio 420 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Kersley, Kleon might do, till we get something better. I dine out tomorrow, but come on Tuesday morning and see me. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [postmark 1 August 1890], 16 Tite Street (MS Clark) - quoted whole; the whole letter is two sentences. 'Kleon' is italicised in the printed text and appears to be a proposed pen-name or title they had been discussing. The sign-off has reached 'Ever yours' and the signature is 'OSCAR' alone.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Two sentences, and both of them are 'come and see me'.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 465; printed folio 443 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear George, I fear that comic footmen do not come into my scheme of art, and the two minor parts of my play - two young dandies - do not come into the possibility of an offer: they are both cast already. But I am cheered to know that you will at any rate be a part of my play, so that I shall have an opportunity of seeing you. You must not think that I have forgotten you: friends who are also poets are never forgotten: memory keeps them in rose-leaves: but Life - coloured, turbulent Life - rushes like a river between oneself and those whom one likes, too often. Sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [postmark 21 November 1894], 16 Tite Street (MS Hyde) - quoted whole, and the last of the seven. Kersley had asked for a part in An Ideal Husband and was given an understudy. Nine years after the first letter the address has reached 'My dear George'. The closing sentence is Wilde apologising for drift, and it is the best writing in the correspondence.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: How Wilde said sorry for losing touch, five months before the trials.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 675; printed folio 623 (letter begins 622) confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: For the idea of writing simple impressions, I am partly indebted to my noted friend Mr Oscar Wilde, who, I think, agrees with me in only meaning them to appear to the reader short descriptions of any things that have fleeting charms for the poet.
sources.context: Kersley's own words, from the preface to his first book Early Flight (1885), quoted by the editors in their note identifying him. THE ONLY PLACE IN THIS RECORD WHERE KERSLEY SPEAKS. Every other source on this node is Wilde writing to him; this is him writing about Wilde, in public, in the year of the first surviving letter, and claiming him as 'my noted friend'.
sources.speaker: George Herbert Kersley
sources.supports: That the friendship was acknowledged from Kersley's side too, in print.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 273; printed folio 251 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Kate Headley Kirby
people.bio: John Fothergill's second wife, married about 1920, and by his own published account the making of him. Under the two of them the Spread Eagle at Thame became a destination restaurant; An Innkeeper's Diary (1931) credits her by name, down to the trifle. Sox's verdict is that Fothergill married her having 'apparently resolved previous emotional ambivalences', and that 'In many respects, Kate was his salvation'.
people.bio_note: The marriage year is ARITHMETIC, not testimony: Sox says the innkeeping life began when Fothergill was 46 - 1922, he having been born 27 February 1876 - and 'two years after' the marriage, which gives c. 1920. Sox states no wedding date and neither does Wikipedia.

people.name: Joan Lamburn
people.bio: A writer of children's stories, Louis Wilkinson's fourth and last wife, married after his divorce from Diana Bryn. She died in 1956, ten years before he did.
people.bio_note: The fourth marriage is footnoted on the article to Wilkinson's Times obituary. Eliot letter of 9 February 1929; Ann Reid to Wilkinson's own Seven Friends (1953) dedication and to Friedman (2002), with her 1932 death to Elwin (1946), p. 207; Diana Bryn to Who Was Who; Joan Lamburn to his Times obituary.

people.name: Lillie Langtry
people.bio: Emily Charlotte Le Breton of Jersey, 'considered the most beautiful woman of her generation' in the editors' words; she married Edward Langtry in her teens, was brought by him to London, and became a leading Society figure and, as the editors put it, a friend of the Prince of Wales. Painted by Whistler, Poynter, Watts, Burne-Jones, Leighton and particularly Millais, whose portrait The Jersey Lily gave her the nickname; Wilde's friend Frank Miles made many drawings of her. In 1899 she married Hugo Gerald de Bathe.
bio_sources: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 91 n. 2
people.bio_note: All facts from the main-particulars footnote at p. 91 n. 2 (repo PDF 116, folio confirmed).

people.name: Laurence Housman
people.bio: Poet, dramatist, novelist and artist (1865-1959), younger brother of A. E. Housman. He sent Wilde his book of imaginary legends All-Fellows in August 1897, three months after Wilde came out of Reading, and five of Wilde's replies survive, running to the end of 1898. In 1923 he published Echo de Paris, a reconstructed dialogue recording Wilde's conversation in his last years, which remains one of the standard accounts of it. He was a member of the Order of Chaeronea, and when George Ives came to make his will in 1939 he left Housman a ring bearing the numbers 338 - the year of the battle at which the Theban Band was destroyed, and the number the Order took its name and its dating system from. He is on this map for two reasons: that, and the fact that he is the man Wilde told about Raphael and Fortune.
people.bio_note: ALL FIVE LETTERS READ AT THE PAGE: printed 923, 928, 1027, 1111 and 1113 (repo PDF 973, 978, 1073, 1157, 1159), every folio confirmed on its own page image, 2026-08-05. DATES 1865-1959 from the editors' note at printed 923.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Housman, I cannot tell you how gratified and touched I was to receive your charming letter, and the beautiful book that it so gracefully heralded. Your prose is full of cadence and colour, and has a rhythmic music of words that makes that constant appeal to the ear, which, to me, is the very condition of literature. … The whole book, with its studied and imaginative decorations and its links of song, is a very lovely and almost unique work of art. Your title pleases me little, but every one has some secret reason for christening a child: some day you must tell me yours. Ricketts and Shannon, those good kind friends of mine, are coming to see me this month. It would be charming if you came with them. I have lately been reading your brother's lovely lyrical poems, so you see you have both of you given me that rare thing happiness. With renewal of my thanks, believe me truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to Laurence Housman, 9 August 1897, Chalet Bourgeat, Berneval-sur-Mer (MS Bryn Mawr) - the first of the five, written three months after Reading. The book is All-Fellows (1896); the brother's poems are A Shropshire Lad. The elision drops praise of three individual stories. Ricketts and Shannon are both on this map. The editors add that Robert Ross recited Housman's brother's poems to Wilde in prison.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The opening of the friendship, and what counted as happiness to Wilde that summer.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 973; printed folio 923 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Housman, Thank you for your kind letter. I hope some day to see you here, or elsewhere. It is absurd of Ricketts and Shannon not to see the light lyrical beauty of your brother's work … but Shannon is inexcusable: you must get him alone, and read them to him: you can tell him I think your brother's poems exceedingly like his own lithographs! With regard to what you ask me about myself - well, I am occupied in finishing a poem, terribly realistic for me, and drawn from actual experience, a sort of denial of my own philosophy of art in many ways. I hope it is good, but every night I hear cocks crowing in Berneval, so I am afraid I may have denied myself, and would weep bitterly, if I had not wept away all my tears. I will send it to you, if you allow me, when it appears. Believe me truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to Laurence Housman, 22 August 1897, Chalet Bourgeat, Berneval-sur-Mer (MS Bryn Mawr). The poem is The Ballad of Reading Gaol. The elision drops a sentence on why Ricketts might dislike A Shropshire Lad. The cocks crowing are Peter's denial of Christ, and Wilde is applying it to himself.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde telling a near-stranger, unprompted, that he thinks he has betrayed himself.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 978; printed folio 928 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Housman, I am so glad you got the copy I ordered to be sent to you. I was in Naples, so had to deny myself the pleasure of writing your name on the fly-leaf. I thank you very much for all you have said to me about The Ballad: it has greatly touched me. I quite hold with you on all you say about the relation of human suffering to art; as art is the most intense mode of expression, so suffering is the most real mode of life, the one for which we are all ultimately created.
sources.context: Wilde to Laurence Housman, [February-March 1898], Hotel de Nice, Paris (TS Clark). 'I was in Naples' is how Wilde refers, to someone outside the inner circle, to the months he spent living with Douglas at Posillipo. The quote breaks where the printed page does.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The Ballad received, and the nearest thing to a statement of belief in the correspondence.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1073; printed folio 1027 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Housman, Thank you so much, not merely for your kindness, but for your charming letter. Style is certainly part of your character: your soul has beautiful curves and colours. Frank Harris, late of the Saturday Review, a dear good friend of mine, has just arrived, and is taking me tomorrow to a lovely little place near Cannes called Napoule. I am to work there!! And to stay for a month, at the end of which I am to produce a work of art. I hope I shall be able to do something. The high sapphire wall of sea, the gold dust of the sun, the petals and perfumes of southern flowers - perhaps these may tune my soul to some note of beauty. Of course I shall write and let you know my address. Sincerely and affectionately yours
sources.context: Wilde to Laurence Housman, Wednesday, 14 December [1898], Taverne F. Pousset, Paris (MS Somerset) - quoted whole. The address has moved to 'My dear Housman' and the signature to 'Sincerely and affectionately yours'. 'Your kindness' is money. The warmest sentence Wilde wrote him is the second one, and it is a compliment paid to a man's prose style by way of his soul.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The correspondence at its warmest, and the journey to Napoule that produced the next letter.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1157; printed folio 1111 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Housman, After your letter declaring the impossibility of coming here, I am surprised not to find you in the adjacent pinewoods, for these woods change the air to an aromatic: the wind that makes their branches restless is pungent with keen odours: when one walks in their dappled shadows one's feet crush sweetness out of the fallen needles: and the still sweeter sun is as warm as wine, and coloured like an apricot. I think your drawing lovely, so delicate in modulation of curve and line. I am sure Donatello would have liked it, and I wish I had ever written anything that Donatello would have liked. The people here - fisher-folk all - have beautiful eyes, crisp hair of a hyacinth colour, and no morals: an ideal race. I have two special friends, one called Raphael, the other Fortune - both quite perfect, except that they can read and write. How wrong of the young Greek Alexander to be ill: it is mixing up two distinct and separate styles. I think a little want of sympathy would make him well: it has a wonderful effect on invalids. Send him, however, all nice phrases from me. Sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to Laurence Housman, [circa 28 December 1898], Hotel des Bains, Napoule (MS Bryn Mawr) - quoted whole, and the reason this node exists. THE SAME LETTER IS THE SOLE SOURCE FOR TWO OTHER NODES on this map, Raphael and Fortune, where it is cited at this same page. What it shows about Housman is that Wilde picked him to say it to. 'No morals: an ideal race' is not ambiguous, and 'two special friends' who are 'quite perfect' is Wilde being as plain as he was ever going to be in writing again after 1895. He is at this point four months from bankruptcy and two years from death, writing to a man he had met perhaps twice.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's candour about the Napoule fishermen, and the choice of Housman to receive it.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1159; printed folio 1113 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Lawley
people.bio: A soldier - Wilde believed a Third Hussars man - and a fellow prisoner in Reading, remembered by Wilde as "a quiet well-conducted chap in Reading always". In a postscript of June 1897 Wilde recommended him for a place in service, arguing that soldiers make good servants and that this one would make a good groom. **Even his name is uncertain**: the editors of the Complete Letters footnote it "Or possibly Langley", and nothing else about him survives - no first name, no dates, no outcome.
people.bio_note: From a postscript printed on p. 897, read at the rendered page 2026-08-04; surfaced by the mechanical sweep.

people.name: Richard Le Gallienne
people.bio: Poet, critic and man of the nineties, born in Liverpool and for a time reader to John Lane at the Bodley Head - the firm that published Wilde. He was a conspicuous ornament of the period, long-haired and much photographed, and Wilde wrote to him across a decade: fourteen letters survive in the Complete Letters, running from the mid-1880s to the mid-1890s. The warmest is of December 1890, on Le Gallienne's book about Meredith. He married three times, moved to the United States in 1901 and died at Menton in 1947.
people.bio_note: Dates and the fourteen letters from the Complete Letters (letters at PDF pp. 349, 373, 389, 397, 414, 417, 418, 419, 421, 436, 478, 502, 538, 604).

people.name: Vernon Lee
people.bio: Aesthetician, critic, novelist and writer of supernatural tales, born Violet Paget at Chateau St Leonard near Boulogne-sur-Mer on 14 October 1856 and resident for most of her life in Italy, latterly at Il Palmerino, Maiano. She adopted the androgynous pen name "Vernon Lee" in the late 1870s and came to public notice in 1880 with Studies of the Eighteenth Century in Italy. Two long attachments to women structure her life as the Y90s biography records it: the poet Mary Robinson (1857-1944), from 1880 until Robinson's marriage in 1887, and Clementina "Kit" Anstruther-Thomson (1857-1921), her companion and co-author from 1887 to 1900. She met Wilde in London in 1881 at the Robinsons', and appears in the Complete Letters only in the editors' apparatus, which quotes her own letters describing him; there is no correspondence between them in the volume. Amy Levy fell in love with her at Florence in 1886. Lee died at Il Palmerino on 13 February 1935.
people.bio_note: Birth and death dates and places, the pen-name adoption, and both attachments from Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography of Vernon Lee (2018/2019). Dates corroborated by the editors' footnote in Wilde's Complete Letters (2000), p. 229, read at the rendered page image 2026-08-03, which identifies "Violet Paget (1856-1935), who lived mostly in Italy and published many books under the name Vernon Lee".

people.name: Ada Leverson
people.bio: Novelist and parodist, whom Wilde called the Sphinx and addressed as nothing else for five years. Thirty-five of his letters to her survive, running from 1893 to 1897. In May 1895, between the second and third trials, when no hotel in London would take him and his brother's house had become impossible, she and her husband Ernest moved their children out of the nursery floor and put Wilde in it, and kept him there until the day he was convicted. She was among the first people to greet him when he came out of prison two years later, having got up before dawn to do it.
people.bio_note: THIRTY-FIVE LETTERS at repo PDF 621, 622, 640, 645, 667, 670, 677, 680, 682, 695, 696, 698, 699, 700, 701, 895, 921 and 1028. FOUR READ AT THE PAGE - printed 650, 845 and, on the same opening, the Holloway sequence - folios confirmed on the rendered page images, 2026-08-05. The thirty-two unread are largely Yellow Book and Punch business and are located, not read.

sources.quote: Dear Sphinx, Your aphorisms must appear in the second number of the Chameleon: they are exquisite. 'The Priest and the Acolyte' is not by Dorian: though you were right in discerning by internal evidence that the author has a profile. He is an undergraduate of strange beauty. The story is, to my ears, too direct: there is no nuance: it profanes a little by revelation: God and other artists are always a little obscure. Still, it has interesting qualities, and is at moments poisonous: which is something. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Ada Leverson, [early December 1894], Albemarle Club (MS Clark) - quoted whole. The editors identify the anonymous author as John Francis Bloxam, editor of The Chameleon and an undergraduate of Exeter College, and record that the story was attributed to Wilde and that 'much play was made' with it at his trial - along with Wilde's own aphorisms in the same issue and Douglas's poem 'Two Loves'. 'Dorian' here is John Gray, who is on this map. ADDED 2026-08-06 from a folio opened for Adela Schuster; the correspondence is largely unread.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Wilde told her about the story that would be used against him at trial.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 677; printed folio 625 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Sweet Kind Friend, I have no words to thank you for all you do for me, but for you and Ernest Bosie and I have deepest love. I hope to be in better spirits tonight. Your sweetness last night was wonderful. Your flowers are like him - your sending them like yourself. Dear, dear Friend, tonight I see you at 7.45. Ah! you are good and gentle and wonderful. Always devotedly yours
sources.context: Wilde to Ada Leverson, [? early May 1895], [? 146 Oakley Street, Chelsea] (MS Clark) - quoted whole, and written between the second and third trials, in the weeks when the Leversons were sheltering him. THE ADDRESS IS NOT 'DEAR SPHINX' but 'My dear Sweet Kind Friend', the only time in the eighteen letters. The 'him' whose likeness he sees in her flowers is Douglas. Note also what he thanks her for: not the roof, which goes unmentioned, but the sweetness and the flowers.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The warmest thing Wilde wrote her, at the worst moment of his life.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 701; printed folio 650 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Sphinx, I was so charmed with seeing you yesterday morning that I must write a line to tell you how sweet and good it was of you to be of the very first to greet me. When I think that Sphinxes are minions of the moon, and that you got up early before dawn, I am filled with wonder and joy. I often thought of you in the long black days and nights of my prison life, and to find you just as wonderful and dear as ever was no surprise. The beautiful are always beautiful. This is my first day of real liberty, so I try to send you a line, and with kind regards to dear Ernest whom I was pleased to see again, ever affectionately yours … I am staying here as Sebastian Melmoth - not Esquire but Monsieur Sebastien Melmoth. I have thought it better that Robbie should stay here under the name of Reginald Turner, and Reggie under the name of R. B. Ross. It is better that they should not have their own names.
sources.context: Wilde to Ada Leverson, [20 May 1897], Hôtel Sandwich, Dieppe (MS Clark) - quoted whole including the postscript, on his first day out of prison. Two years and a conviction after the previous letter, the friendship is exactly where it was. THE POSTSCRIPT IS THE CIRCLE'S DISCRETION AT ITS MOST LITERAL: Robert Ross and Reginald Turner, both on this map, were travelling under each other's names, and Wilde under a third. He tells her because she is someone who can be told.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That she was among the first to meet him out of prison, and that he trusted her with the aliases.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 895; printed folio 845 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Amy Levy
people.bio: Anglo-Jewish poet and novelist, born Amy Judith Levy in London on 10 November 1861, the second of seven children of a stockbroker; in 1879 she became the second Jewish woman to attend Cambridge and the first at Newnham College. Wilde published her while he edited the Woman's World: her story appeared in the first number, followed by articles on Christina Rossetti's poetry (March 1888) and on women and club life (June 1888), and two poems and a story during 1889. His one surviving letter to her, of October 1887, solicits more of her fiction - "I think your method as admirable as it is unique" - and after her death he printed a tribute to her in the same magazine, judging that she had "ceased to hold the orthodox doctrines of her nation, retaining, however, a strong race feeling"; she is one of the very few women on this map whose tie to Wilde is professional, mutual, and documented in his own hand. At Florence in 1886 she met Vernon Lee and fell in love with her, sending her the sonnet "To Vernon Lee" and the poem "New Love, New Life"; her biographer Linda Hunt Beckman calls these love poems. She took her own life on 10 September 1889, aged twenty-seven.
people.bio_note: NOTE a discrepancy in the Wilde apparatus: the editors' footnote to Wilde's letter to her, Complete Letters (2000), p. 326 (read at the rendered page image 2026-08-03), gives her dates as "(1862-89)" - a year late on the birth. The Woman's World bibliography and the manner of death ("She committed suicide by inhaling fumes of charcoal") are from that same footnote. The Wilde tribute and the quoted sentence from it are Beckman's, who dates the tribute to an 1890 issue of the Woman's World; Wilde's tribute has NOT been read at source so far and the quotation is Beckman quoting Wilde.

people.name: Lionel Johnson
people.bio: Poet and critic (1867-1902), a Winchester and New College man, a friend and great admirer of Walter Pater, and a member of the Rhymers' Club alongside Yeats, Dowson and Symons. Wilde called on him unannounced at Oxford in February 1890 because he admired his poems; two days later Johnson wrote to a friend, 'I am in love with him'. In 1891 he brought his Winchester contemporary Lord Alfred Douglas to Tite Street and introduced them. In 1892 he wrote 'The Destroyer of a Soul', believed addressed to Wilde, which begins 'I hate you with a necessary hate'. He died at thirty-five.
people.bio_note: ALL FOUR PIECES OF EVIDENCE READ AT THE PAGE, printed 423, folio confirmed on the rendered page image, 2026-08-05. NOT RECORDED because it is not in this volume: the text of 'The Destroyer of a Soul' beyond its first line, Johnson's later Catholicism, and his alcoholism. His own Complete Poems (1953) is the obvious next source.

people.name: Martha Lips
people.bio: Robert Sherard's wife, whom he married in 1886. The editors of Wilde's letters describe her only as 'a Polish girl called Martha Lips'. Wilde, writing to Sherard in Paris about two years later, asked after 'your pretty, romantic looking wife with her lovely eyes'.
people.bio_note: Both statements are from the Complete Letters, read at the rendered page: the marriage from the editors' note at printed 347, Wilde's description from the letter at printed 348 (repo PDF 369-370, both folios confirmed). DATES: NONE RECORDED, and almost nothing else is: the record preserves her nationality, her name, the year she married, and one sentence a friend of her husband's wrote about her eyes.

people.name: Pierre Louÿs
people.bio: French poet and novelist (1870-1925). He founded the review La Conque in 1889, at nineteen, and printed Swinburne, Verlaine, Mallarmé, Maeterlinck, Gide and Moréas in it. He met Wilde in Paris in November 1891, went over the French of Salomé line by line, and Wilde dedicated the play to him - 'À mon ami Pierre Louÿs', his name, as Wilde put it, written in gold on purple. Fifteen months later the friendship was over. Seven of Wilde's letters to him survive and they hold the whole arc, from 'Cher Monsieur Louÿs' to 'Mon très cher Ennemi' to the last one, which ends: 'It is new to me to think that friendship is more brittle than love is.'
people.bio_note: FOUR OF SEVEN LETTERS READ AT THE PAGE: printed 496, 506, 528 and 557 (repo PDF 516, 526, 548, 609), every folio confirmed on its own page image, 2026-08-05. THE FIFTH, repo PDF 549, is located but unread; the OCR mirror shows it badly scrambled and it will need the page image. DATES 1870-1925 from the editors' note at printed 496.

sources.quote: Cher Monsieur Louÿs, J'accepte avec le plus vif plaisir la gracieuse et charmante invitation que vous et M. Gide ont eu la bonté de m'adresser. Vous m'indiquerez, n'est-ce-pas, l'endroit et l'heure.
sources.translation: Dear Monsieur Louÿs, I accept with the keenest pleasure the gracious and charming invitation which you and M. Gide have been kind enough to address to me. You will tell me, will you not, the place and the hour.
sources.context: Wilde to Pierre Louÿs, 28 November 1891, 29 boulevard des Capucines - the first of the five, quoted whole. Wilde was thirty-seven, Louÿs twenty-one. THE INVITATION CAME FROM TWO PEOPLE. The editors note that André Gide had met Wilde for the first time the day before, on 27 November, and wrote to Paul Valéry about him that same week; that according to his letters he then saw Wilde almost every day until 15 December; and that the pages of his journal covering those days have been torn out. Gide is not on this map and should be.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The opening of the friendship, and the fact that Gide was there from the first day of it.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 516; printed folio 496 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Mon cher ami, Voilà le drame de Salomé. Ce n'est pas encore fini ou même corrigé, mais ça donne l'idée de la construction, du motif et du mouvement dramatique. Ici et là, il y a des lacunes, mais l'idée du dráme est claire.
sources.translation: My dear friend, Here is the drama of Salomé. It is not yet finished or even corrected, but it gives the idea of the construction, of the motif and of the dramatic movement. Here and there, there are gaps, but the idea of the drama is clear.
sources.context: Wilde to Pierre Louÿs, [December 1891], Paris (MS Clark) - quoted whole, and the address has moved to 'mon cher ami'. This is Wilde handing over the manuscript of Salomé; the editors identify the draft as the third and apparently final one, which carries Louÿs's interlinear corrections. Where the corrections were points of grammar Wilde took them, and most of the rest he deleted or ignored.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The collaboration the dedication was payment for.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 526; printed folio 506 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Mon très cher Ennemi, Pourquoi pas d'adresse sur ta carte? Voilà deux jours que je te cherche!! Enfin, voulez-vous diner avec moi ce soir? Rendez-vous Café Royal, Regent Street, 7.45, habit de matin. Je serai charmé naturellement si Madame vous accompagne. Et j'inviterai John Gray.
sources.translation: My very dear Enemy, Why no address on your card? I have been looking for you these two days!! Well then, will you dine with me this evening? Meet at the Café Royal, Regent Street, 7.45, morning dress. I shall be charmed naturally if Madame accompanies you. And I shall invite John Gray.
sources.context: Wilde to Pierre Louÿs, [June 1892], on Louÿs's first visit to London - quoted whole. Note the pronouns: Wilde opens with the intimate 'ta carte' and 'je te cherche', then switches to the formal 'voulez-vous' for the invitation itself, which is either affection catching itself or the reverse. The 'Madame' is Lucile Delormet, the young woman Louÿs came to London with. JOHN GRAY IS ON THIS MAP.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The friendship at its most familiar - a joke address, two days of looking, and John Gray asked along.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 548; printed folio 528 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Pierre, Is the enclosed really all that you have to say to me in return for my choosing you out of all my friends to whom to dedicate Salomé? I cannot tell you how hurt I am. Those to whom I merely gave copies have written me charming letters coloured with delicate appreciation of my work.
