You alone - you whose name I have written in gold on purple - you say nothing, and I don't understand what your telegram means; some trivial jest I suppose; a drop of froth without wine. How you disappoint me! Had you wired 'Je vous remercie' it would have been enough. It is new to me to think that friendship is more brittle than love is.
sources.context: Wilde to Pierre Louÿs, [postmark 27 February 1893], Torquay - the last of the five, quoted whole, and written in English, which none of the others are. Salomé had been published in Paris the previous week, dedicated 'À mon ami Pierre Louÿs'; Louÿs had answered with a telegram Wilde could not read the tone of. The friendship did not recover. The closing sentence is as near as Wilde comes anywhere in this volume to saying what he thought friendship was, and he says it at the moment of losing one.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The end of it, in Wilde's own hand, and the sentence the whole node is for.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 609; printed folio 557 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Lane, Here is your seat; front row of dress-circle; I think the best in the house. Next you, you will find Pierre Louÿs, the young poet to whom I dedicated Salomé. Pray introduce yourself to him. He is a perfect English scholar. In haste
sources.context: Wilde to John Lane, [? 19 April 1893], Hotel Albemarle - the first night of A Woman of No Importance, quoted whole. IT COMPLICATES THE BREAK, which is why it is here: this is seven weeks after the letter saying friendship is more brittle than love, and Wilde has given Louÿs a front-row seat, seated a publisher beside him and told the publisher to introduce himself. Whatever ended between them had not ended by that evening, or had not finished ending.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That the break was not clean, and that Wilde was still placing him well seven weeks later.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 613; printed folio 561 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Giuseppe Loverde
people.bio: A young seminarist of the Cathedral of Palermo, where he lived with eleven others in rooms beneath the roof. He showed Wilde over the cathedral daily during the eight days Wilde spent at Palermo in April 1900, and told him he had entered the Church because his father was a poor cook with too many mouths to feed. Wilde gave him a book of devotion and some money. The letter states his age.
people.bio_note: THE AGE IS THE FIRST FACT ABOUT THIS RECORD, not a footnote to it: the letter states it, and it is the reason the passage is entered by hand rather than through the ordinary pipeline.

sources.quote: My dear Mahaffy, I am so pleased you like the play, and thank you for your charming letter, all the more flattering to me as it comes not merely from a man of high and distinguished culture, but from one to whom I owe so much personally, from my first and my best teacher, from the scholar who showed me how to love Greek things. Let me sign myself, in affection and admiration, your old pupil and your old friend
sources.context: Wilde to J. P. Mahaffy, [? April 1893], Haymarket Theatre (MS Dublin) - quoted whole. The play is A Woman of No Importance. READ IT AGAINST THE DELETION recorded at printed 28: the thing Wilde thanks him for here, teaching him how to love Greek things, is the thing later editions of Mahaffy's book stopped mentioning, along with Wilde's name. Wilde had two years left before the trials.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Wilde said he owed him, in the words the later editions removed.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 613-614; printed folios 561 and 562 both confirmed on the rendered page images.

sources.quote: I am with that dear Mahaffy every day. He has a charming house by the sea here, on a place called the Hill of Howth … the only place near town with fields of yellow gorse, and stretches of wild myrtle, red heather and ferns. … Mahaffy's book of Travels in Greece will soon be out. I have been correcting his proofs and like it immensely.
sources.context: Wilde to William Ward, Sunday [6 August 1876] (MS Magdalen), aged twenty-one - the same letter as the Todd passage. The elision drops a party to the North of Ireland Wilde missed. THE EDITORS' NOTE ON THIS PAGE is the reason the node exists: Mahaffy thanked 'my old pupil Mr Oscar Wilde of Magdalen College, Oxford' in the preface to Social Life in Greece for improvements 'all through the book', and 'Significantly, in later editions of Social Life both the discussion of Greek homosexuality and the reference to Wilde were dropped.'
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The closeness at the start, against which the deletion has to be read.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 53-54; printed folios 28 and 29 both confirmed on the rendered page images.

people.name: J. P. Mahaffy
people.bio: Classical scholar (1839-1919), Wilde's tutor at Trinity College Dublin and later its Provost. He took Wilde to Greece in 1877, and Wilde corrected the proofs of his Rambles and Studies in Greece and made 'improvements and corrections all through' an earlier book, Social Life in Greece from Homer to Menander (1874), for which Mahaffy thanked him by name in the preface. Social Life contained a discussion of Greek homosexuality. In later editions both that discussion and the thanks to Wilde were removed.
people.bio_note: The editors state it flatly at printed 28: 'Significantly, in later editions of Social Life both the discussion of Greek homosexuality and the reference to Wilde were dropped.' TWO LETTERS at repo PDF 301 and 613-14; the 1893 one is read at the page, the earlier one is located and unread.

people.name: Vladimir Makaroff
people.bio: A Russian emigre who worked in a London bookshop, and the man Evguenia Souline married after the Second World War, when she was well into her forties - three to six years after Radclyffe Hall's death. He outlived her, and it was his sale of his wife's letters from Hall that put the correspondence into the University of Texas collection where it survives.

people.name: Manuele
people.bio: One of three coachmen - cocchieri - who drove Wilde out to Monreale during the eight days he spent at Palermo in April 1900. Wilde named the three to Robert Ross as the most favoured, and said he had loved them all. Manuele is the only one of the three Wilde says he still remembered.

people.name: Harry Marillier
people.bio: Henry Currie Marillier, a Bluecoat Boy (pupil of Christ's Hospital, then still in London) 1875-84, lodged at 13 Salisbury Street, Strand, while Wilde was living there in 1880-81 and, as a boy, brought Wilde his coffee. Classical scholar of Peterhouse, Cambridge, 1884-87; his autumn-1885 letter to Wilde, inviting him to the Cambridge Eumenides, opened the 1885-86 correspondence. He later became an engineer and partner in W. A. S. Benson's metalworks, then a literary and art journalist, editing The Early Work of Aubrey Beardsley (1899) and writing on tapestry.
people.bio_note: All facts from the main-particulars footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 266 n. 3 (repo PDF 288, folio confirmed), plus the coffee/Salisbury Street recollection in Wilde's letter of [Postmark 5 November 1885] at the same page.

people.name: John Marshall
people.bio: Liverpool wine-merchant's son who went up to New College, Oxford, on a Classics scholarship intending Holy Orders, met Ned Warren in his third year (1884), and after Warren's five-year wooing gave up church, a Fellowship path and Liverpool to join him in November 1889 - thereafter co-head of the Lewes House collecting operation, whose eye supplied the classical collections of Boston and, from 1906, the Metropolitan Museum as its Rome-based purchasing agent. He and Warren called each other 'Puppy'; Burdett described the pair 'pacing arm-in-arm on the lawn at Lewes House' as 'replicas of each other'. He married Warren's cousin Mary Bliss on 5 November 1907 - 'Neither love nor sex had anything to do with the union' per Sox - and after her death in 1925 shared his old Rome flat with Warren again. He died there in February 1928 with Warren beside him - his last words, in Warren's account, 'good-bye Puppy' - and is buried at Bagni di Lucca with Mary and Warren, under a plain Grecian urn.
bio_sources: Liverpool family, wine-merchant father: Sox (1991) p. 39 (repo PDF 55, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03)

Liverpool College, Classics scholarship to New College, met Warren 1884 ('It was in his third year at New College (1884) that he met Ned.'), Merton Fellowship path abandoned: Sox p. 40 (PDF 56, rendered 2026-08-03)
Joined Warren: 'By November 1889, "the man of his choice" was at Ned's side.' - Sox p. 44 (PDF 60, rendered 2026-08-03)
Met purchasing agent from Robinson's 1905-06 offer; Rome flat 'made possible by Ned's generosity': Sox pp. 77-78, 107 (PDF 93-94, 123, rendered 2026-08-03)

Died: 'She died there in 1925, and Marshall in Rome in February, 1928.' - Sox p. viii (PDF 12, rendered); Portland newspaper: 'passed away in the latter country in February, 1928' - p. 130 (PDF 146, rendered); Warren's account of the night, pp. 126-127 (PDF 142-143, rendered)

British School at Rome, John Marshall Archive catalogue (archive.bsr.ac.uk, resource 65); Guido Petruccioli, 'Introduction', Ancient Art and its Commerce in Early Twentieth-Century Europe (Archaeopress, 2022), p. 1 - birth year
people.bio_note: Sox states no birth date or year for Marshall in the pages read (text search for '1862' returns nothing); the enlarged Bagni di Lucca monument carries the three names 'with their birth and death dates' (p. 130) but Sox does not print them - born stays null. Death not sharpened past the month: Sox's narration gives 'February, 1928'; Warren's first-person account has Marshall dying at 'five minutes past one' in the night after 'the evening of the 15th'. 'Johnny' is Warren's and the circle's regular name for him; 'Puppy' was mutual (Marshall writes 'Puppy dear' to Warren, pp. 64-65; Warren signs 'Your Puppy', p. 107). (1) The British School at Rome's archival catalogue for the John Marshall Archive - the repository that holds his papers (BSR Archive & Special Collections, ArchivesSpace resource 65, fonds 1900-1928, archive.bsr.ac.uk) - whose biographical note reads 'John Marshall (1862-1928) was a connoisseur of Classical art and a cultivated intellectual.' (2) Guido Petruccioli, 'Introduction', in Ancient Art and its Commerce in Early Twentieth-Century Europe (Archaeopress, 2022), p. 1, read in the publisher's own sample PDF: 'John Marshall (1862-1928) - not to be confused with the homonymous (and far more notorious) American statesman John Marshall (1755-1835) or the British archaeologist John Hubert Marshall (1876-1958) - is known only to a few people.' This closes the gap Sox left: Sox reports that the Bagni di Lucca monument carries 'their birth and death dates' (p. 130) without transcribing them. DEATH-DATE CONFLICT, REPORTED NOT RESOLVED - died stays {y:1928, m:2}: Wikipedia's 'John Marshall (died 1928)' opens '15 February 1928' but attaches no citation to that date (its listed references are Streitmatter, Outlaw Marriages, and De Puma, Etruscan Art in the Metropolitan Museum of Art), so by this module's rule it cannot be entered; Sox's repo text has Warren's first-person account of Marshall retiring on 'the evening of the 15th' and dying at 'five minutes past one' in the night, which points to the small hours of 16 February; BSR and Petruccioli give the year only.

people.name: Charles Spurrier Mason
people.bio: The man with whom Alfred Taylor went through a marriage ceremony in 1893 - Taylor in a wedding dress as the bride, Mason as the bridegroom, an exchange of rings and a wedding breakfast afterwards. Charles Parker gave the ceremony in evidence at the Old Bailey in April 1895; Pierre Louys had reported it to Andre Gide at the time as 'a marriage - a real marriage - between two of them'. Wilde wrote to him from Worthing in August 1894 asking after 'poor Alfred' following the Fitzroy Street raid, and joking, 'I hope marriage has not made you too serious?'
people.bio_note: Dates 1868-1940 from the Complete Letters editors (p. 603 n. 2), who also note Croft-Cooke's suggestion that the marriage was genuine; McKenna calls him 'a twenty-five-year-old male prostitute' at the time of the ceremony, which is consistent with those dates.

people.name: Sidney Mavor
people.bio: 'The only other individual of decent family and upbringing besides Shelley' among the Crown's young men (Hyde): living at 66 St Helen's Gardens, North Kensington, and by 1895 in partnership in a City business. Taylor met him at the Gaiety Theatre in 1892, groomed him for the Kettner's dinner given by Schwabe ('Mr. Wilde likes nice clean boys'), and Wilde sent him a silver cigarette case inscribed 'Sidney from O. W., October, 1892' before an overnight at the Albemarle Hotel. On the stand he repeated his Bow Street denial — no misconduct, no impropriety ever — and the Mavor counts were struck out; Hyde's footnote preserves Douglas's own account of coaching that denial in the Bow Street corridor. Atkins had 'heard him called Jenny Mavor.'
bio_sources: Mavor's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 211-212 (p. 212 read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03)

Hyde, Trials (1948), Introduction pp. 72-73 with n (counts struck out; the corridor story from Douglas's Autobiography, 2nd edn. p. 119; djvu OCR) and pp. 85-86 (Mavor dropped at the final trial; djvu OCR)
Atkins's testimony ('Jenny Mavor'), Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 207 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Ellen Grant's testimony ('Mavor and Mason stayed there for nights with Taylor'), Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 199 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
people.bio_note: No birth/death dates found in sources read so far; the General Index of Complete Letters (2000) has NO Mavor entry (verified at the rendered index page, printed p. 1255, where it would fall between 'Maurice, Dr Oliver' and 'Max'). AGE ON OATH, FOR CONTEXT ONLY: Wilde, cross-examined in April 1895 about Taylor's rooms, put Mavor at 'About twenty-five or twenty-six', which would place his birth about 1869-70 and sits awkwardly with the 1866 of the Find a Grave memorial; McKenna, Secret Life (2008), repo PDF p. 328, has him 'twenty' when Taylor picked him up in late September 1892, which would mean about 1872. SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web.

people.name: Harold Mellor
people.bio: Wealthy English expatriate, and Wilde's host, patron and travelling companion through the exile years 1898-1900. Per the editors of the Complete Letters, 'the neurotic son of a Bolton cotton spinner', left wealthy by his father's death in 1893, who 'spent most of the rest of his life abroad, finally committing suicide in his villa at Cannes'; his aunt Ursula Mellor married the Liberal MP Jacob Bright. Wilde met him at Napoule at Christmas 1898 and stayed at his villa at Gland, Vaud, in March-April 1899 and again in July-August 1900; Mellor also funded Wilde's journey to Italy in 1900 'to the extent of £50'. Wilde recorded Mellor's own queer life in two letters: that he had been 'sent away from Harrow at the age of fourteen for being loved by the captain of the cricket eleven', and that he 'has Greek loves, and is rather ashamed of them'. The Italian servant Eolo travelled with him from at least 1898 until 1900.
bio_sources: Life-dates, family, wealth, expatriation and manner of death: 'Harold Mellor (1868-1925) was the neurotic son of a Bolton cotton spinner. His father died in 1893, leaving him wealthy, and he spent most of the rest of his life abroad, finally committing suicide in his villa at Cannes. His aunt Ursula Mellor married Jacob Bright (1821-99), brother of John Bright and Liberal MP for Manchester 1867-95 with two short intervals.' - Holland & Hart-Davis, editors' footnote, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1112n (repo PDF 1158, printed folio confirmed on rendered page image, 2026-08-03).

The meeting: 'A nice fellow called Harold Mellor, who is staying at Cannes, comes over constantly to see me. He is a nephew of Mrs Jacob Bright's.' - Wilde to Robert Ross, [27 December 1898], Napoule; p. 1112 (repo PDF 1158, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).

Harrow: 'a charming fellow called Harold Mellor (sent away from Harrow at the age of fourteen for being loved by the captain of the cricket eleven) who is staying with his mother near Cannes, and comes over on his bicycle to breakfast every morning' - Wilde to Robert Ross, 2 January 1899, Napoule; p. 1116 (repo PDF 1162, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).

'Greek loves' and the patronage frame: 'I don't like Mellor: he is a silent, dull person, cautious, and economical … has Greek loves, and is rather ashamed of them: has heaps of money, and lives in terror of poverty: so I regard it as a sort of Swiss pension, where there is no weekly bill.' - Wilde to Reginald Turner, [postmark 20 March 1899], Gland; p. 1132 (repo PDF 1178, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).

The 1900 Italy money: 'Mellor, with whom I am now friends (below zero of course) has invited me to go to Italy to the extent of £50!' - Wilde to Robert Ross, [late March 1900], Paris; p. 1177 (repo PDF 1223, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).

The last visit and Mellor's own surviving letter: 'I have been with Harold Mellor at Gland: he is almost as neurasthenic as I am' - Wilde to Ross, [August 1900]; and editors' footnote 1 on the same page: 'A surviving letter from Mellor to Wilde (MS Clark), written from Gland and dated 21 July 1900, runs: "Am much distressed about your illness . . . I hope to be able to receive you on Monday 30 [July]."' - p. 1194 (repo PDF 1240, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).
people.bio_note: Dates: the editors' footnote gives the death year only inside the life-dates (1868-1925); it does not date the suicide separately, and the place is 'his villa at Cannes'. Register: the friendly words are the first-impression ones of December 1898 and January 1899; from printed 1129 onward Wilde's private register toward Mellor is hostile ('very lamentable', 'this loathsome place', 'Gland, which has become intolerable', 'this dreadful place' - three correspondents in one week, March 1899, all p. 1137, repo PDF 1183, folio confirmed). Cross-thread note: p. 1194 carries Wilde's use of 'neurasthenia' as a diagnosis for himself and for Mellor - relevant to the separate sexual-neurasthenia thread, though nothing there ties the term to sexual aetiology.

sources.quote: My dear Harry, I am going down to my publisher to tell him to send you a copy of my little book. It contains some studies in prose: the best I think being the first, though 'The Nightingale and the Rose' is the most elaborate. What a charming time we had at Abbots Hill. I have not enjoyed myself so much for a long time, and I hope that we will see much more of each other, and be often together. We are always at home on Wednesday afternoons, when you will always be le bienvenu. On Friday I am paying a visit in Beaufort Gardens. Will you be in about 5.30? Ouida has just sent me a clever article. Your affectionate friend
sources.context: Wilde to Harry Melvill, [? June 1888], 16 Tite Street (MS Clark) - quoted whole. The book is The Happy Prince and Other Tales. Beaufort Gardens is where Melvill was then living with his parents, so the 'visit' on Friday is to his house. The sign-off is 'Your affectionate friend'.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: A plain wish to see more of someone, and to be often together.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 374; printed folio 352 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Harry Melvill
people.bio: A dandy and, by all accounts, a relentless talker - known to Jacques-Emile Blanche as 'Mr Chatterbox', the model for the central character of Osbert Sitwell's story 'The Machine Breaks Down' and caricatured as Mr Cherry-Marvel in Michael Arlen's The Green Hat. One letter from Wilde survives, from June 1888, after a country-house visit.
people.bio_note: ONE LETTER at repo PDF 374, read at the page (printed 352, folios confirmed). Dates 1861-1936 from the editors' note at printed 352.

sources.quote: Dear Stuart, I will call for you tomorrow at 7 o'clock. We must have a delightful evening. Ask Retté to come, if you think he would like it. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Stuart Merrill, [November-December 1891], 29 boulevard des Capucines (MS Hyde) - quoted whole. 'tomorrow' is italicised in the printed text. This is the Paris winter in which Wilde also met Gide and Louÿs; the same folio carries a long letter in French to Juliette Adam about Dorian Gray and Walter Pater.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The whole of the correspondence, and the Paris circle it sits in.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 520; printed folio 500 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Stuart Merrill
people.bio: American poet who wrote in French and lived in Paris (1863-1915). He met Wilde in 1890 and went over the French of Salomé before Pierre Louÿs did. As manager of the Théâtre de l'Oeuvre he was there when Salomé had its first production, in February 1896 - while Wilde was in Reading Gaol.
people.bio_note: ONE LETTER at printed 500, read at the page. DATES 1863-1915 and the Théâtre de l'Oeuvre from the editors' note there. That was decided from a single reference; the General Index lists him at 500 AND 506n, and the second is his own memoir account of correcting Salomé.

people.name: Mildred Lee
people.bio: Richard Le Gallienne's first wife, who died in 1894 giving birth to their second daughter Maria, who died with her; their elder daughter Hesper Joyce survived. Le Gallienne afterwards carried an urn of her ashes with him everywhere, through his second marriage and beyond - a habit Rupert Brooke satirised in a poem, 'For Mildred's Urn'.

people.name: Frank Miles
people.bio: George Francis ('Frank') Miles, portraitist of Society beauties - the editors note he 'did many drawings' of Lillie Langtry - awarded the Royal Academy's Turner silver medal on 10 December 1879 for a painting of an Ocean Coast. He shared rooms with Wilde at Thames House, 13 Salisbury Street, off the Strand, until August 1880, and then at Keats House, 1 Tite Street, Chelsea; the friendship dates from Wilde's Oxford years, with visits together at Bingham and Moytura in the mid-1870s per the General Index.
bio_sources: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial notes, Complete Letters (2000), p. 78 n. 3, p. 86 n. 2, p. 91 n. 2, p. 94 n. 1; General Index entry, p. 1256
Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 19 n. 1 (dates)
people.bio_note: DATES (added 2026-08-03): born 1852, died 1891, from the editors' first-mention footnote, Complete Letters (2000), printed p. 19 n. 1 (repo PDF 44) - 'George Francis Miles (1852-91), son of the rector, was a popular artist in the early Eighties: his many drawings of Lillie Langtry did much to enhance her popularity. The same footnote is the source for the asylum years, which the bio does not yet carry. All facts from editorial notes: p. 78 n. 3 (Salisbury Street cohabitation to Aug 1880; repo PDF 103), p. 86 n. 2 (Turner medal; PDF 111), p. 91 n. 2 (Langtry drawings; PDF 116), p. 94 n. 1 (Keats House move; PDF 119), General Index p. 1256 (PDF 1301; 'W stays with, 17, 19, 20', Moytura 30-31). NO LETTERS SURVIVE. Established 2026-08-06 from the volume's Index of Recipients: Frank Miles HAS NO ENTRY. Miles (printed 542), a different man.

people.name: Mrs Alexander
people.bio: George Alexander's wife. Wilde sent her his regards in 1894 and, in the last letter he wrote to her husband in July 1900, said he would not forget 'your dear wife's charming and affectionate greeting of me. I know now how to value things like that.' She had greeted him in the street in Paris, five years after the trials. After her husband's knighthood in 1911 she was Lady Alexander, and it is to her that the survival of this correspondence is owed: the editors record that Wilde's letters to Alexander were still in her possession in the 1930s, when A. E. W. Mason worked from them for his life of her husband.
people.bio_note: THE LABEL IS A DESCRIPTOR, NOT A NAME, on the rule set by napoule-fisherman: **no source in this repository gives her given name.** The Complete Letters call her only 'Mrs Aleck' and 'your dear wife'; searches of the letters' full OCR mirror, Ellmann and McKenna return nothing further. Both quotations were read at the rendered page (printed 620 and 1193, folios confirmed). DATES: none recorded. HER TITLE AND HER CUSTODY OF THE LETTERS are from the editors' note at printed 515, read at the rendered page 2026-08-05: the text of one 1892 letter is 'corroborated by a typescript at the Clark Library almost certainly made by Mason direct from Wilde's letters which were still in Lady Alexander's possession in the 1930s'.

people.name: A fisherman, Napoule
people.bio: A fisherman at La Napoule, on the Riviera, to whom Wilde described himself as 'practically engaged' in a letter to Robert Ross of 2 January 1899. The letter calls him 'a fisherman of extraordinary beauty, age eighteen'. Nothing else about him - name, family, how they met, what became of it - appears in the pages read.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, 2 January 1899, Napoule, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1116 (repo PDF 1162, printed folio confirmed on the rendered page image, 2026-08-03; transcription and provenance reused unchanged). He is distinct from the collective mentions on the same tier - 'The fishing population of the Riviera have the same freedom from morals as the Neapolitans have' (Ross, 27 December 1898, printed 1112) and the Napoule fisher-lads (pointer, printed c. 1119, not read) name no individual and stay in the collective context_engagement on wilde.json. DATES: NONE RECORDED. Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel quotes the same sentence at printed p. 245 (repo PDF 259) - 'I am practically engaged to a fisherman of extraordinary beauty, age eighteen' - and gives him no name and no dates either. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and none is likely to be: the record preserves a first name (or a trade) in another man's correspondence and no surname to search by.

sources.quote: My dear Little Nellie, You will be delighted to hear that Constance got through her confinement all right, suffering hardly any pain. The child - an amazing boy! - was born when she was under chloroform, and on coming to she absolutely declined to believe it was born at all! And was only convinced of the fact by the nurse producing a stalward boy, who already knows me quite well. She is very happy and peaceful but cannot see anyone for some days. The doctor has posted a bulletin in the hall to that effect. You must have a little girl and we will make up a match at once. I will let you and Otho, the important uncle and aunt of our son and heir, know how she gets on. I hope you will get through your own confinement as easily as Constance - I am sure you will. It really is very little after all - you must not …
sources.context: Wilde to Nellie Lloyd, [postmark 5 June 1885], 16 Tite Street (MS Holland), written the same day as the telegram to her husband. The letter breaks where the printed page does. 'who already knows me quite well' is italicised in the printed text. Wilde was thirty and had been married eleven months.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde on the birth of his first son, to his sister-in-law, the same morning.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 283; printed folio 261 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Nellie Lloyd
people.bio: Otho Holland Lloyd's wife, and so Constance Wilde's sister-in-law. Wilde wrote to her as 'My dear Little Nellie' on the morning Cyril was born, in a letter that is one of the few places he writes about his own children with unguarded delight.
people.bio_note: DATES NOT RECORDED and none inferred.

people.name: Julie Nørregaard
people.bio: Danish journalist, Richard Le Gallienne's second wife from 1897, and the mother of the actress and director Eva Le Gallienne. She left him in 1903, taking both his daughters to Paris, and divorced him in June 1911, citing his inability to keep a home or pay his debts, his drinking and his womanising.
people.bio_note: Dates 1863-1942 from the Wikipedia article.

people.name: Henning Nyberg
people.bio: A twenty-five-year-old Swede who moved into Townshend House as Charles Ricketts's secretary and companion after Charles Shannon's incapacitating fall of 1929 - the last year or two of Ricketts's life. He brought a gramophone with him, and the two went out to the theatre and the cinema at least three times a week.
people.bio_note: Matt Cook's phrasing is explicitly hedged, 'possibly also sexual partner', and nothing in the passage settles it; Cook's endnote 149 carries his own citation and has not been chased.

sources.quote: Omero has never received your letter. I need not say I have not given him your London address - at least not your real one: he now believes that your real name is Edmondo Gosse, and that your address is the Savile. I also added that some of your more intimate friends prefer to write to you as Reginaldo Turner, Avvocato, The Reform Club: but that I, from old associations, prefer to address you as Sir Wemyss Reid, so I fancy there will be many interesting letters arriving in London.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Rome, April 1900 - quoted whole. Edmund Gosse, Reginald Turner and Wemyss Reid are all real people and all appear elsewhere in this volume; Turner is on this map. The joke only works because concealing a real name from a young man was ordinary practice.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The circle's discretion machinery, seen from the outside.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1228; printed folio 1182 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Omero was with me, and Armando, forgiven for the moment.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Rome, April 1900. The second and last mention: Omero is simply there, in company with Armando.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That the three of them were together.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1230; printed folio 1184 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Omero
people.bio: A young Roman of Wilde's April 1900 circle, present when Wilde and Armando were together, and the subject of a running joke: Wilde had given him a false name and address for Robert Ross, so that Omero believed Ross was really called Edmondo Gosse and lived at the Savile.
people.bio_note: The gap existed because only Armando has his own General Index entry ('Armando (boy), 1182, 1184'); the other two appear inside the same paragraphs and are indexed nowhere. WILDE ALSO CALLS HIM 'HOMER' (noted 2026-08-06): the letter at printed 1181 opens 'Homer talks much - a little too much - of you.

people.name: Oscar Browning
people.bio: Schoolmaster and historian (1837-1923). An Eton master from 1860 to 1875 - George Curzon was his most famous pupil - and thereafter a Cambridge don and celebrated 'character'. Fifteen of Wilde's letters to him survive, beginning in 1879 when Wilde was twenty-four and running through the 1880s. The early ones have Wilde running his errands in London, buying him neckties and hunting Paternoster Row for a bible, and wishing he had been at the theatre with him.
people.bio_note: the volume's Index of Recipients. The editors' note gives only 'Eton master 1860-75' and passes over the rest in silence. FIFTEEN LETTERS at printed 80 (two), 87, 88, 111, 268, 313, 337, 339, 342, 348, 358, 360, 368, 373, 407. THREE READ AT THE PAGE - printed 80 twice and 111.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Browning, I would have been only too happy to have the opportunity of doing any commission for you had I been in town, but I have been away for a week with friends. I shall see about your ties this afternoon. I am perhaps a better judge of neckties than of bibles, but I shall not fail to enquire about the latter. Nothing would please me more than a visit to you: when are your festivities? Very truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to Oscar Browning, [late May 1879], St Stephen's Club (MS Mason) - quoted whole, and the earliest of the fifteen. Wilde was twenty-four and Browning forty-two.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The footing at the start: Wilde running an older man's errands and angling for an invitation.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 105; printed folio 80 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Browning, Your bible and prayer book only exists in a bookseller's Utopia! There is no such thing: I ransacked all Paternoster Row on this wretched rainy day and found nothing that would suit you. … I am afraid you will have to take refuge in an Edition de Luxe of Keble's Christian Year if you want something nice. I am so sorry my search is so unsuccessful. I wish so much you could have been with me last night. Sarah Bernhardt's Phèdre was the most splendid creation I ever witnessed. … It seems so foolish to call French Tragedy stilted: the scene last night was not a bit 'ἐκ δρυός καὶ πέτρης' but the most impassioned human nature.
sources.context: Wilde to Oscar Browning, [3 June 1879], St Stephen's Club (MS Hughan). The elisions drop practical detail about the Bible Society and a paragraph on being in Oxford. The Greek the editors render 'out of oak and stone'. Note the address has moved from 'Dear Mr Browning' to 'My dear Browning' within a fortnight.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: A whole rainy day spent shopping for him, and the wish that he had been there.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 105; printed folio 80 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Browning, If you get the opportunity, and would care for it, I wish you would review my first volume of poems just about to appear: books so often fall into stupid and illiterate hands that I am anxious to be really criticised: ignorant praise or ignorant blame is so insulting. Truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to Oscar Browning, [June 1881], Keats House, Tite Street (MS Dartmouth) - quoted whole. The editors record that Browning did review Poems, in the Academy of 30 July 1881. THE SAME PRINTED PAGE carries Wilde's letter to ROBERT Browning offering him the first copy of the same book - two unrelated Brownings on one folio, which is why the index lists them separately.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde asking him for the review he then wrote.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 136; printed folio 111 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Vincent O'Sullivan, I am delighted to hear from Smithers that there is really some chance of your being at Naples this winter, and look forward with the greatest pleasure, I need hardly say, to seeing you again. I have also heard incidentally of something that happened at the Authors' Club last week: and I cannot express to you adequately how deeply touched I was by the position you took up with regard to me, and by the dignity and, …
sources.context: Wilde to Vincent O'Sullivan, 19 October 1897, Villa Giudice, Posilippo (MS Bodley). The letter breaks where the printed page does. THE SAME FOLIO carries Wilde's rebuke to Sherard for the attack O'Sullivan had stood against.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde thanking a man for defending him in public in 1897, when few would.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1011; printed folio 963 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Vincent O'Sullivan
people.bio: Writer, and author of Aspects of Wilde (1936), a first-hand memoir of the exile years. Two of Wilde's letters to him survive. In October 1897, while Wilde was at Posillipo with Douglas and being attacked in London, O'Sullivan took his side publicly at the Authors' Club - and Wilde wrote to say he could not express adequately how deeply touched he was.
people.bio_note: the volume's Index of Recipients. WHAT THE FOLIO SHOWS, and why he belongs here: printed 963 carries TWO letters of the same week, one rebuking [[sherard]] for attacking Wilde behind his back at the Authors' Club, the other thanking O'Sullivan for the position he took there. TWO LETTERS at printed 963 and 1160; ONE read at the page. HIS MEMOIR is outside this volume and is the obvious next source - he is one of the few witnesses to the last years who wrote at length. DATES NOT RECORDED and none inferred.

sources.quote: Constance had a boy this morning at ten forty-five. She is quite happy and doing well but can not see anyone for some days. She sends her love.
sources.context: Telegram, Wilde to Otho Holland Lloyd, 5 June 1885, Chelsea (MS Holland) - quoted whole. The boy is Cyril Wilde (1885-1915), who was educated at Radley, became a professional soldier and was killed in action in the First World War.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde wiring his brother-in-law within hours of Cyril's birth.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 283; printed folio 261 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Otho, Thank you so much for your lovely present. It will be of great use to me as it is by far the best book on Japanese Art that I know. It really was most kind of you to think of it. I hope little Otho is better and that Nellie is not working herself too hard nursing.
sources.context: Wilde to Otho Holland Lloyd, [postmark 31 August 1886], 16 Tite Street (MS Holland) - quoted whole. The editors note that two books on Japanese art were among those sold at the Tite Street sale in 1895. 'Little Otho' is his nephew; Nellie is Otho's wife.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The ordinary family footing - a present, and asking after a sick nephew.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 307; printed folio 285 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Otho Holland Lloyd
people.bio: Constance Wilde's elder brother, and so Wilde's brother-in-law. Five of Wilde's letters to him survive, from 1885 to 1898 - the first a telegram announcing the birth of Cyril, the last two from the exile. He and his wife Nellie had a son also called Otho.
people.bio_note: the volume's Index of Recipients. FIVE LETTERS at printed 261, 262, 285, 1036 and 1055; TWO read at the page.

people.name: An Egyptian, Café d'Egypte
people.bio: A waiter at the Café d'Egypte in Paris who, Wilde wrote to Leonard Smithers in September 1900, 'occasionally serves me drinks'. Wilde describes him as 'A slim brown Egyptian, rather like a handsome bamboo walking-stick', and says in the same sentence that he does not console him for the loss of a Neapolitan who had gone home. No name, age, dates or further trace appear on the page read.
people.bio_note: Source: Complete Letters (2000), p. 1196 (repo PDF 1242, printed folio 1196 confirmed at the foot of the rendered page image). PROVENANCE CAVEAT, from the editors' own footnote 1 on the same page: 'The text of this incomplete letter is taken from Forty Years in my Bookshop by W. Spencer (1923), corrected and supplemented by the American Art Association catalogue of 1 February 1928.' The heading carries no manuscript line - unlike the Ives letter below it, which is 'MS Texas' - so this text descends from a printed memoir and a saleroom catalogue rather than from a surviving manuscript, and the letter is incomplete. DATES: NONE RECORDED. Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel quotes the same description at printed p. 271 (repo PDF 285) and gives no name or dates. A DISCREPANCY BETWEEN SOURCES: Frankel places the cafe inside the Egyptian pavilion of the 1900 Paris Exposition rather than at a standing 'Cafe d'Egypte'; the two accounts have not been reconciled against the letter. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and none is likely to be: the record preserves a first name (or a trade) in another man's correspondence and no surname to search by.

people.name: Charles Parker
people.bio: A gentleman's valet, out of employment at the beginning of 1893 when Taylor picked him and his brother up at the St James's Restaurant bar; aged 21 by his own sworn statement at the April 1895 trial. The first and most damaging Crown witness: his testimony describes sodomy at the Savoy and continued relations at Chapel Street, Park Walk, Tite Street and St James's Place, alongside his admitted £30 share of a Wood-Allen blackmail. Arrested and discharged in the Fitzroy Street raid of August 1894, he enlisted on 3 September 1894 and was traced to his regiment by Queensberry's solicitor at the end of March 1895. Wilde was convicted on all four Parker counts; from prison Wilde wrote of 'my connection with Charley Parker of which you may read a full account in my trial.'
bio_sources: Charles Parker's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 191-198 (pp. 191, 193, 197 read as IIIF page images 2026-08-03; rest djvu OCR)
Wilde to Robert Ross [1896], Complete Letters (2000), p. 670, with the editors' note 'One of the young men who gave evidence at Wilde's trials' (p. 670 n 1; read at rendered PDF p. 721, 2026-08-03)
people.bio_note: His father was 'a horse dealer' (cross-examination, p. 196). DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED FROM THE SOURCES CONSULTED. The age is now verified in the source rather than from OCR: Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde (Notable British Trials), printed p. 191, opening the prosecution evidence at the first criminal trial - 'CHARLES PARKER, examined by Mr. Read as a page image in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, IA PDF p. 230) and the printed folio 191 confirmed. SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web. The obvious next step is not another book: it is the GRO birth index and the 1881/1891 censuses for a Charles Parker, valet, and his brother William, groom - genealogical work outside what so far could do.

people.name: William Parker
people.bio: A groom, brother of Charles Parker, present at the pick-up in the St James's Restaurant bar and at the Rupert Street dinner where Wilde fed Charles from his own fork and spoon and passed him a preserved cherry mouth-to-mouth. He understood from the outset that the brothers 'were to be treated as women, and that you were to have money for it'; he went twice to Little College Street, shared Taylor's bed with his brother one night — his testimony describes an attempted sodomy by Taylor — then took country work as a groom and 'had nothing more to do with Taylor or with Mr. Wilde.' Taylor was convicted of gross indecency with him (count 9) on 21 May 1895.
bio_sources: William Parker's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 198-199 (p. 199 read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Verdict at Taylor's trial, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 292 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Taylor's account of the brothers staying a week, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 284 (djvu OCR)
people.bio_note: Taylor said he ultimately 'persuaded William Parker to go home to his father' (p. 284, djvu OCR). DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED FROM THE SOURCES CONSULTED. Unlike his brother Charles, William gave no age on oath in the Hyde text: his examination-in-chief opens simply 'WILLIAM PARKER, examined by Mr. I have been employed as a groom' (located in the IA OCR text of Hyde; the neighbouring page carrying Charles's sworn age was verified at the page image, this passage was not). McKenna, Secret Life (2008), repo PDF p. 341, reports only Taylor's guess that the two brothers 'were sixteen or seventeen, or thereabouts' when he met them - a bystander's estimate of two people at once, not an age statement, and nothing is inferred from it. SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted.

people.name: Harold Woodbury Parsons
people.bio: The last and latest of the Lewes House circle - 'among the latter-day group of Ned's boys and.. the most audacious and elusive, and certainly the least likeable' (Sox). Born plain Harold Parsons at Lynn, Massachusetts (he claimed 1883 and a Harvard degree; the birth certificate says 13 July 1882, and he took 'Woodbury' from his brother's name), he was raised by his 'indulgent Woodbury grandfather' on Commonwealth Avenue, Boston. Warren, consulted at a Boston dinner, advised the art-life abroad: from 1906 Parsons studied in Cassel and Dresden, then made Lewes House his English headquarters 'eight months at a time'. Marshall 'came to despise' him. After Warren's and Marshall's deaths he carried the collecting tradition on as European purchasing agent for Cleveland, Kansas City and Omaha, and ended as a celebrated exposer of forgeries - the 'Etruscan' warriors among them - from his base in Rome, where, after a long life 'despite several attempts at suicide', he died in 1968.
bio_sources: Born: 'The birth certificate of Harold Parsons (no middle name) from Lynn says he was born on 13 July 1882, the son of Edward P. and Marcia E. Parsons of 11 Baker Street, Lynn.' - Sox (1991) p. 211 (repo PDF 235, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03); claimed 1883 and the borrowed 'Woodbury', same page

Died: 'When Parsons died in 1968, in Rome, few mourned his passing' - Sox p. ix (PDF 13, rendered 2026-08-03); 'The last of Ned Warren's companions, Harold Woodbury Parsons, died in 1968.' - p. 211 (PDF 235, rendered 2026-08-03)
'Ned's boys' / least likeable / Cellini on his self-invention: Sox p. 211 (PDF 235, rendered 2026-08-03)

Warren's advice and the 1906 start; Lewes House as headquarters 'eight months at a time' (Parsons's 1967 letter to Henry Francis); 'one of Ned's new friends' (Burdett & Goddard, as quoted by Sox): Sox p. 212 (PDF 236, rendered 2026-08-03)
Marshall 'came to despise' him: Sox p. 77 (PDF 93, rendered 2026-08-03)
Cleveland/Kansas City/Omaha; suicide attempts; forgery obsession: Sox p. ix (PDF 13, rendered 2026-08-03)
people.bio_note: Sox gives the death only as the year (1968, in Rome). The forgery-exposure career (Dossena catalogue with Pico Cellini, 1955, p. 124; the Metropolitan's Etruscan warriors, pp. 117ff; Time magazine plate, 24 Feb. 1961, PDF 244 caption) was read at text layer only - pointers, not verified in the source. NULL FINDING for a parsons--warren romantic edge: Sox's characterizations are mentor-protégé and patronage throughout the pages read ('Ned's boys', 'one of Ned's new friends', 'in obvious emulation of Ned Warren'); no romantic or sexual wording anywhere - see the LEWES-HOUSE dossier (long-form research notes, kept in the private research repository). Parsons's own gloss of Warren: 'a belated Greek who seemed to live in the age of Pericles and not to belong to the modern world' (p. 221, text layer - pointer).

sources.quote: Dear Mr Wilde, Accept my best thanks for the magazine and your letter. Your excellent article on the Grosvenor Gallery I read with very great pleasure: it makes me much wish to make your acquaintance, and I hope you will give me an early call on your return to Oxford. I should much like to talk over some of the points with you, though on the whole I think your criticisms very just, and they are certainly very pleasantly expressed. The article shows that you possess some beautiful, and, for your age, quite exceptionally cultivated tastes: and a considerable knowledge too of many beautiful things. I hope you will write a great deal in time to come. Very truly yours
sources.context: Walter Pater to Oscar Wilde, headed 'Bradmore Road. Oxford. July 14' [1877] (MS Texas), quoted whole. It survives inside a letter of Wilde's to William Ward, who had been sent the original and told to return it by registered post; Wilde then thought better of trusting it to the postman and copied it out instead. Wilde's transcription has three small errors, which the editors list. His own comment follows it: 'You won't think me snobbish for sending you this? After all, it IS something to be honestly proud of.' Wilde was twenty-two; the article was his first.
sources.speaker: Walter Pater
sources.supports: The first contact, in Pater's own hand, and what it was worth to Wilde.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 86; printed folio 59 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Walter Pater
people.bio: Fellow and Tutor of Brasenose College, Oxford (1839-94), and the writer whose Studies in the History of the Renaissance (1873) formed the aesthetic creed of Wilde's generation at Oxford. Its six-page 'Conclusion' caused enough of a stir that Pater removed it from the second edition of 1877. In July of that same year he wrote to Wilde, then twenty-two and unknown, to praise an article and ask to meet him. Wilde copied the letter out in full and posted it to a friend, unable to keep it to himself.
people.bio_note: HIS OWN LETTER IS QUOTED AS THE PRIMARY SOURCE and Wilde's transcription is the manuscript; the editors note Wilde got three small words wrong, which is recorded rather than silently corrected.

people.name: Katherine Isabella Pattison
people.bio: Harry Marillier's first wife, married in 1893 - the daughter of John Pattinson, a Newcastle public analyst. They had two daughters. She died in 1901.

sources.quote: My dear Pickering, We are all angry with you for not coming over. When the lilacs blossom and the laburnum hangs its dusty gold over the railings of our London squares we look for our American friends, and so we look for you. Come in the autumn, and we will ask the laburnum to grow honey-coloured for your pleasure. I am charmed you like Dorian Gray. It is my best piece of work, and I hope to make it still better, when it appears in book form. The fatal book that Lord Henry lent Dorian is one of my many unwritten works. Some day I must go through the formality of putting it on paper. My wife and my mother both send you their kindest and most affectionate greetings. So does your sincere friend
sources.context: Wilde to Arthur Howard Pickering, [late July 1890], 16 Tite Street (MS Clark) - quoted whole. Pickering had written from Roxbury on 7 July praising Dorian Gray in Lippincott's. Kept entire partly for the laburnum and partly for the middle paragraph, which is Wilde saying the poisonous yellow book of the novel was never written.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's charm turned on a stranger, and a note on Dorian Gray's unwritten book.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 465; printed folio 443 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Arthur Howard Pickering
people.bio: An American, a friend of the dramatist Clyde Fitch, who wrote to Wilde from Roxbury, Massachusetts in July 1890 praising The Picture of Dorian Gray on its appearance in Lippincott's. Wilde's reply is the only letter between them in this volume.
people.bio_note: ONE LETTER at repo PDF 465, read at the page (printed 443, folios confirmed). DATES NOT RECORDED and none inferred.

people.name: Pietro
people.bio: Italian whom Wilde met at Nice in January 1899, on a three-day trip from La Napoule with Harold Mellor. Wilde described him to Robert Ross as 'a little Italian, Pietro, like a young St John', adding 'One would have followed him into the desert'. No surname, age, occupation, dates or further trace appear in the letter, and nothing else about him was found in the pages read.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, Thursday [? 12 January 1899], Napoule, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1118 (repo PDF 1164, printed folio confirmed on the rendered page image, 2026-08-03; transcription and provenance reused unchanged). DATES: NONE RECORDED. Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel treats the Nice trip at printed p. 245 (repo PDF 259), naming Pietro as 'like a young St John' and adding nothing beyond the letter. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and none is likely to be: the record preserves a first name (or a trade) in another man's correspondence and no surname to search by. [[branca-doro]] - Pietro Branca-d'Oro - is a DIFFERENT man: Palermo and Rome, April 1900, printed 1181, introduced by Wilde as a new addition to his circle. This Pietro is Nice, January 1899, printed 1118.

people.name: H. C. Pollitt
people.bio: Herbert Charles Pollitt, a native of Kendal in Westmorland and an undergraduate at Trinity College, Cambridge, 1889-92, where he made a name as an amateur ballet dancer. He collected Beardsley drawings, which he bought from Wilde's publisher Leonard Smithers. He preferred 'Jerome' to his own Christian names and signed himself so in his letters to Wilde; his Kendal home was called The Green Window. Wilde corresponded with him between November 1898 and January 1899 and appears never to have met him - in January 1899 he was still asking Smithers what Pollitt was like. Wilde sent him inscribed copies of the French translation of The Ballad of Reading Gaol and of The Importance of Being Earnest, and, per the editors, misspelt his surname in all four of the surviving letters.
people.bio_note: All facts from Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000) with printed folios confirmed. Birth and death years, Kendal, Trinity College 1889-92, the amateur ballet dancing, the Beardsley collecting bought from Smithers, the preference for 'Jerome' and the inscribed presentation copies are from the main-particulars footnote at p. 1103 n. 1 (repo PDF 1149). 'Pollitt's Kendal home was called The Green Window' is p. 1107 n. 1 (PDF 1153, transcribed by the earlier record session). The four surviving letters and the misspelling in all of them are p. 1120 n. 2 (PDF 1166); the misspelt envelope address itself is quoted at p. 1116 n. 1 (PDF 1162). The never-met reading rests on Wilde's own question to Smithers at p. 1117 (PDF 1163). Nothing read so far states how or when Wilde and Pollitt were introduced to each other by correspondence; the earlier index locator at printed 1103 is the first letter, and no Pollitt letter to Wilde is printed in this edition.

people.name: Matthew Stewart Prichard
people.bio: Barrister turned aesthete - 'the keenest and most capable of Ned Warren's assistants' and, per the Introduction, 'once considered the most able of Warren's aesthetes'. Born at Brislington near Bristol; Marlborough College, then New College, Oxford, from January 1884, months after Warren's matriculation; called to the bar in 1892, he abandoned the law to join Lewes House as Warren's secretary with George Harding, imposing order on the household, negotiating the Boston Museum's Bartlett Head in Greece, and speaking of Warren as 'a sort of Buddha at whose feet he used to sit'. Sox: 'Prichard clearly loved Warren who was like a father to him' - and names him the member of the brotherhood 'who was as openly misogynistic as Ned'. Viewed by the jealous Marshall as a rival, he left with Richard Fisher for the Boston Museum of Fine Arts in 1901; later a confidant of Isabella Stewart Gardner (285 letters), of Matisse and the Stein circle in Paris, and an internee-champion at Ruhleben in the First World War. He died in 1936; his ashes were scattered in the back garden of the Buckinghamshire house he shared with his brother.
bio_sources: Born: 'Prichard was born on 4 January 1865 in the little village of Brislington just to the east of Bristol. His parents were Charles Henry Prichard and Mattie Stewart.' - Sox (1991) p. 168 (repo PDF 192, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03)

Died: the Walker draft biography 'was written at the instigation of Dame Una Pope-Hennessy after Prichard's death in 1936' - Sox p. 167 (PDF 191, rendered 2026-08-03); burial/ashes at Parslows Hillock, Bucks., with brother Charles Stewart Prichard - p. viii (PDF 12, rendered 2026-08-03)
Marlborough 1878-83, New College January 1884 'only months after Ned Warren's matriculation': Sox p. 169 (PDF 193, rendered 2026-08-03)
Bar 1892, Lincoln's Inn practice; secretaryship with Harding: Sox pp. 170-171 (PDF 194-195, text layer; folio not rendered - finding aid)

'the most individual character' / 'keenest and most capable': Sox p. 167 (PDF 191, rendered); 'like a father' and Buddha: p. 172 (PDF 196, rendered); 'as openly misogynistic as Ned': p. 176 (PDF 200, rendered); Bartlett Head: p. 176 (PDF 200, rendered)
Left with Fisher for Boston, 1901: Sox p. 40 (PDF 56, rendered 2026-08-03); Gardner letters and Matisse/Stein: pp. 167, viii (PDF 191, 12, rendered); Ruhleben: p. 168 (PDF 192, rendered)
people.bio_note: Death is stated by Sox only as the year (1936); the Introduction's 'Seven years later' (than the April 1929 interment) agrees. Sixth of eight children (p. 168). Warren addressed him 'Dear Ducky' in a letter dismissing his Nietzsche-fed individualism (p. 174, text layer - pointer). Full passages and the prichard--warren NULL FINDING (no romantic edge; Sox's characterization is filial/discipleship, with the counter-texture preserved) in the LEWES-HOUSE dossier (long-form research notes, kept in the private research repository).

people.name: Marc-André Raffalovich
people.bio: A rich Russian educated in France and England; poet, whose Tuberose and Meadowsweet Wilde reviewed in the Pall Mall Gazette in March 1885, prompting a printed exchange between them over the scansion of 'tuberose'. Wilde is reported to have quipped that he came to London to found a salon and only succeeded in founding a saloon; the editors record the belief that Raffalovich revenged himself by breaking up Wilde's friendship with John Gray, with whom he remained close friends for the rest of his life. He largely supported Beardsley in the artist's last years, and in his own later years built St Peter's Church, Edinburgh, for Gray.
people.bio_note: All facts from the editorial footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 255 n. 2, running onto p. 256 (repo PDF 277-278, folios confirmed); born/died 1864-1934 from the same footnote. St Peter's Church from p. 520 n. 3 (repo PDF 540). The 1885 tuberose exchange is printed at pp. 255-256.

people.name: Raphael
people.bio: One of the two young men at La Napoule whom Wilde called his 'two special friends' in a letter to Laurence Housman of about 28 December 1898, singling them out from the local fisher-folk. Wilde wrote that both were 'quite perfect, except that they can read and write'. No surname, age, dates or further trace appear in the letter, and nothing else about him was found in the pages read.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Laurence Housman, [Circa 28 December 1898], Hôtel des Bains, Napoule, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1113 (repo PDF 1159, printed folio 1113 confirmed at the foot of the rendered page image). FINDING-ONLY POINTER, NOT VERIFIED: the OCR mirror's general index carries a line reading 'Raphael, 747, 1113'; printed 747 was not read, and at that date it is at least as likely to be the painter as this man. DATES: NONE RECORDED. Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel repeats the Housman letter at printed p. 243 (repo PDF 257) - 'By December 28 he had two boyfriends, one called Raphael, the other Fortuné' - and adds nothing further about either man. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and none is likely to be: the record preserves a first name (or a trade) in another man's correspondence and no surname to search by.

people.name: Ann Reid
people.bio: Writer and novelist, Louis Wilkinson's second wife, married after his 1923 divorce from Frances Gregg. They had a daughter, to whom Wilkinson dedicated Seven Friends (1953). She died in 1932.
people.bio_note: The wedding is UNDATED in everything read; only her 1932 death has a year, sourced on the article to Malcolm Elwin, The Life of Llewelyn Powys (1946), p. 207. The marriage itself is footnoted to Wilkinson's own Seven Friends dedication page and to Friedman (2002), p. 13. Eliot letter of 9 February 1929; Ann Reid to Wilkinson's own Seven Friends (1953) dedication and to Friedman (2002), with her 1932 death to Elwin (1946), p. 207; Diana Bryn to Who Was Who; Joan Lamburn to his Times obituary.

people.name: Adolphe Retté
people.bio: Symbolist poet (1863-1910), and one of the three Frenchmen who went over the French of Salomé before it was printed. In Le Symbolisme, Anecdotes et Souvenirs (1903) he described what he did to it: struck out the over-formal anglicisms, marked corrections in the margin, and made Wilde cut a long list of jewels from Herod's mouth. Wilde asked him to dinner through Stuart Merrill in the winter of 1891.
people.bio_note: The General Index entry reads 'Retté, Adolphe, 500, 506n', and 506n carries a page of his own first-hand account of working on Salomé, plus Merrill corroborating it.

sources.quote: les anglicismes trop formels … J'indiquai quelques corrections en marge du drame. Je fis supprimer à Wilde une trop longue énumeration de pierreries mise dans la bouche d'Hérode. De son côté, Merrill lui proposa quelques retouches. Puis Salomé passa entre les mains de Pierre Louÿs qui modifia également quelques phrases. C'est ce texte qui a été imprimé.
sources.translation: the over-formal anglicisms … I marked some corrections in the margin of the drama. I made Wilde cut a too-long enumeration of jewels put into Herod's mouth. For his part, Merrill proposed some retouches. Then Salomé passed into the hands of Pierre Louÿs, who likewise altered some phrases. It is that text which was printed.
sources.context: Adolphe Retté, Le Symbolisme, Anecdotes et Souvenirs (1903), quoted by the editors in their note on the manuscripts of Salomé. HIS OWN ACCOUNT, thirteen years after the fact. It names the whole chain of hands the play passed through - Retté, then [[merrill]], then [[louys]] - and all three are now on this map. The editors add that three manuscripts survive, all in Wilde's hand and all in French.
sources.speaker: Adolphe Retté
sources.supports: What Retté actually did to Salomé, in his own words.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 526; printed folio 506 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Charles Ricketts
people.bio: Wood-engraver, book designer, publisher, painter, sculptor and stage designer, born in Geneva in 1866 to a French mother and an English father, and from 1882 a student at the City and Guilds Technical Art School in Lambeth, where he met Charles Shannon (1863-1937) and began the partnership that lasted the rest of his life. The two shared every home they had - Kennington Park Road; Whistler's former house in The Vale, Chelsea, from 1888; Beaufort Street from 1894; three years at Spring Terrace, Richmond; a studio-flat at Lansdowne House, Kensington, from 1902; Townshend House by Regent's Park from 1923; and Chilham Keep in Kent, given them for life in 1918 by their patron Edmund Davis - and ran between them the privately printed magazine the Dial (1889-97) and, from 1896, Ricketts's Vale Press, which issued forty-six books in eight years and was named after their first Chelsea home. For Wilde he designed the title-page and binding of The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891), the binding of Intentions and of Lord Arthur Savile's Crime (both 1891), the limited edition of Poems (1892) and the whole of The Sphinx (1894), and with Shannon designed and decorated A House of Pomegranates (1891); he also painted, at Wilde's request, the forged Elizabethan portrait of Willie Hughes for "The Portrait of Mr W. H.", framed in worm-eaten moulding that Shannon pieced together. Wilde met the pair in August 1889 after they sent him the first number of the Dial, called Ricketts "the subtle and fantastic decorator" of his books and nicknamed him "Orchid"; Ricketts destroyed private letters and sections of his journal after Wilde's prosecution, visited him in Reading Gaol, and published recollections of him in 1932. He turned down the directorship of the National Gallery in 1914, was elected RA in 1928, and died of heart failure on 7 October 1931; the collection he and Shannon had built together passed to the Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge.
people.bio_note: Dates from two sources read at the rendered page so far: the editors' identifying footnote in Wilde's Complete Letters (2000), pp. 410-411 n. 3 ("Charles De Sousy Ricketts (1866-1931)"), and Matt Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), printed p. 29 ("Charles Ricketts (1866-1931)"). The precise death - heart failure on 7 October 1931 - is Cook's, printed p. 52. Birthplace, parentage and the Vale Press particulars are from Nicholas Frankel's Y90s biography of Ricketts; the household chronology is Cook's, printed pp. 31-33; the Willie Hughes picture and its frame are from the editors' note at Complete Letters p. 412 n. 2, quoting Ricketts. "Jean Paul Raymond" was the fictional persona under whose name Ricketts published his 1932 Wilde recollections; the Complete Letters general index enters the book as Recollections of Oscar Wilde (index read in the source, printed p. 1261).

context_engagements.period: From August 1889 — Wilde's first recorded impression of him

sources.quote: I saw Mr Ricketts on Saturday, and he is most grateful for your cheque. He seems very cultivated and interesting.
sources.context: Wilde to W. Graham Robertson, [? August 1889], 16 Tite Street (MS Huntington). Robertson had sent Ricketts a cheque; Wilde had evidently delivered the thanks. Within two years Ricketts was designing The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891), the limited Poems (1892), Intentions and Lord Arthur Savile's Crime.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's first recorded impression of Ricketts, a year and a half before Ricketts began designing his books.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 432; printed folio 410 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: In Recollections of Oscar Wilde (1932) Charles Ricketts reported his saying: 'I was sent down from Oxford for being the first undergraduate to visit Olympia'.
sources.context: The editors' note explaining Wilde's rustication in 1877 - he was fined £47.10s, half his Demyship, and sent down for the rest of the academic year for returning a month late from Greece. THE POINT FOR THIS MAP is not the punishment but the transmission: a remark of Wilde's survives because Ricketts wrote it down thirty-five years later. Several of the things this map knows about Wilde's talk reach it the same way, through friends' memoirs, and it is worth marking who the recorders were.
sources.supports: Ricketts as one of the friends through whom Wilde's spoken words survive.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 72; printed folio 47 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Mary Robinson
people.bio: Poet, born 1857. She met Vernon Lee in 1880 and, on the Y90s account, the two developed a romantic friendship that lasted until Robinson's marriage in 1887 to the orientalist James Darmesteter. Lee first visited her in London in 1881, where Robinson introduced her to the Burne-Joneses, Edmund Gosse, the Morrises, the Rossettis and Oscar Wilde; Robinson's own published recollection of visiting "Casa Paget" in Florence is cited by Pulham for the cosmopolitan range of the Paget circle. She died in 1944.
people.bio_note: Dates (1857-1944) and the relationship account from Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography of Vernon Lee (2018/2019).

people.name: James Rennell Rodd
people.bio: Poet and diplomat, later British Ambassador to Italy (1908-19) and first Lord Rennell of Rodd. A friend of Wilde at Oxford, where he won the Newdigate Prize in 1880, two years after Wilde. Wilde wrote the 'envoi' to his Rose Leaf and Apple Leaf (1882) and published, as its dedication, an inscription Rodd had written privately in Wilde's own copy — 'TO OSCAR WILDE— HEART'S BROTHER' — which Rodd found much more effusive than he had intended, and which helped end the friendship.
people.bio_note: Dates 1858-1941 and the biography are from the editors' note 4 at Complete Letters printed 102, folio confirmed on the rendered page image. ONLY ONE LETTER to Rodd survives in the volume, headed 'To Rennell Rodd' at printed 102-103 (the whole of the correspondence, checked by extracting every letter heading in the OCR mirror). It sits in the same register the Complete Letters sweep ruled 'warm, and not desire' for Sherard's dedication. Ellmann's one suggestive line - that the two travelled under false names 'presumably to keep Rodd's friends from suspecting that their intimacy was so constant' (repo PDF 189) - is flagged by Ellmann himself as a presumption, and the editors' own note at printed 101 says the travelling companion was 'almost certainly Rennell Rodd', which is a second hedge on top of the first.

context_engagements.period: Oxford friendship from the late 1870s; the correspondence survives only for 1880

sources.quote: Dear Rennell, My best congratulations. Greats is the only fine school at Oxford, the only sphere of thought where one can be, simultaneously, brilliant and unreasonable, speculative and well-informed, creative as well as critical, and write with all the passion of youth about the truths which belong to the august serenity of old age. I wish you had got a First, that my compeers should not all be sluggish and syllogistic Scotchmen; still, a Second is perhaps for a man of culture a sweeter atmosphere than the chilly Caucasus of an atheistical First. Come back very soon. Truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to Rennell Rodd, circa 4 December 1880, Keats House (MS Private) - the only letter to Rodd in the volume, congratulating him on his Second in Greats, announced in The Times on 4 December 1880.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The entire surviving correspondence, and the extent of the affection in it: 'Dear Rennell' and 'Come back very soon'.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 127-128; printed folios 102 and 103 both confirmed on the rendered page images. The letter runs across the page break and is transcribed whole.

people.name: Edoardo Rolla
people.bio: Young Genoese seaman whom Wilde had written to ahead of his move from Switzerland to Genoa in the first week of April 1899, and hoped to find waiting for him there. Wilde described him to Robert Ross as 'a young lad, by name Edoardo Rolla, one of the sea-farers', with 'fair hair', 'always in dark blue'. No age, dates or other trace appear in the letter, and no record of whether the meeting took place was found in the pages read.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, [early April 1899], Gland, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1140 (repo PDF 1186, printed folio confirmed on the rendered page image). The editors' general index reportedly lists him as 'Rolla, Edoardo (boy)', per the triage's mirror read - finding-only, not verified in the source. DATES: NONE RECORDED. Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel treats him at printed pp. 248 and 250 (repo PDF 262, 264) and indexes him as 'Rolla, Edoardo, 248, 250'; he offers only 'possibly a sailor or fisherman' and no dates. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and none is likely to be: the record preserves a first name (or a trade) in another man's correspondence and no surname to search by.

people.name: Robert Ross
people.bio: Canadian-born literary journalist, art critic and gallery-owner, grandson of Robert Baldwin, first Prime Minister of Upper Canada; brought to England aged two, he went up to King's College, Cambridge, in October 1888 and left abruptly in 1889 after a student-magazine libel, a ducking in the college fountain and a nervous breakdown. He met Wilde in 1886 and lodged with the Wildes at 16 Tite Street through part of 1887; he remained, in the editors' words, 'his most faithful friend until Wilde's death when he became the literary executor to the estate'. In 1893 he and Lord Alfred Douglas were jointly threatened with prosecution over a schoolboy pupil of the Rev. Biscoe Wortham's at Bruges, and Ross spent the following winter out of reach at Davos. By 1897 he shared lodgings with More Adey at 24 Hornton Street, Kensington - by his biographer's account 'not as lovers, but as two bachelor friends' - and later ran the Carfax picture gallery with him. He kept daily attendance through Wilde's final illness, brought the priest who received Wilde into the Catholic Church, was at the bedside at the death on 30 November 1900, hired the Bagneux grave in his own name and moved the remains to Pere Lachaise in 1909. From early 1903 until the autumn of 1913 his life was shared with Frederick 'Freddie' Smith, a clerk of eighteen when they met, whom he employed as his secretary and with whom he openly set up house at 15 Vicarage Gardens, Kensington, from 1906. He published Wilde's De Profundis in 1905, cleared the estate of bankruptcy, became art critic and then art editor of the Morning Post, and was passed over for the directorship of the Tate. From 1911 Douglas and T. W. H. Crosland ran a campaign of surveillance and criminal accusation against him that produced the 1913 Ransome libel trial, Ross's own eight-day prosecution of Douglas at the Old Bailey, and the 1914 conspiracy proceedings; he was cleared, and afterwards lived quietly in rooms at 40 Half Moon Street, mentoring younger writers including Siegfried Sassoon and, through Sassoon, Wilfred Owen. He died there of heart failure on 5 October 1918, aged forty-nine.
people.bio_note: Born/died, Canadian origin, Baldwin descent, Cambridge dates, 1886 meeting, 'most faithful friend' and executorship from the biographical footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 360 n. 1 (repo PDF 382; the footnote cites Margery Ross, Robert Ross: Friend of Friends, 1952, and Maureen Borland, Wilde's Devoted Friend, 1990). Hornton Street lodgings shared with Adey from the editorial note at p. 781 n. 2 (PDF 832); Carfax partnership from p. 577 n. 2 (PDF 629). Final illness, priest, deathbed and 'the grave is at Bagneux, in a temporary concession hired in my name' from Ross to More Adey, 14 Dec. 1900, Epilogue pp. 1219-22 (PDF 1264-67); 1909 removal to Père Lachaise from the editorial matter at p. 1230 (PDF 1275). ENRICHED 2026-08-03 from Jonathan Fryer, Robbie Ross: Oscar Wilde's Devoted Friend (2000), repo PDF at docs/research/queer-history/victorian/ross/sources/. Cambridge arrival and abrupt departure, the ducking and breakdown: printed pp. 26-27, 33-35, 38-39. 1886 meeting and the 1887 Tite Street lodging: pp. 18, 21. Dansey/Bruges near-prosecution and Davos: pp. 78-81, 84, 237. Hornton Street with Adey and the 'not as lovers' formula: p. 66. Freddie Smith - meeting early 1903, ages, the secretaryship as cover: p. 177; move to 15 Vicarage Gardens: p. 192; 'his lover': p. 193; still flourishing at Lower Grosvenor Gardens: p. 214; ended autumn 1913: p. 230. Douglas's plea of justification and the Old Bailey trial from 19 November 1914: pp. 237-238. Half Moon Street from early summer 1914 and judgement in Ross's favour with costs: p. 243. Death on 5 October 1918 'aged just forty-nine' of heart failure: p. 258. Morning Post art editorship and the Tate directorship: index at printed pp. 199, 212-14, 251. VERIFICATION STATE: pp. 18, 21, 33, 42, 66, 108, 176, 177, 192, 193, 198, 214, 230, 237, 238, 243, 258 were with the printed folio confirmed on each; pp. 26-27, 34-35, 38-39, 78-81, 84, 149, 199, 212-13, 251 are index or OCR-text-layer locations NOT yet verified in the source. Full passages and the pagination box in the ROSS-FRYER dossier (long-form research notes, kept in the private research repository).

people.name: William Rothenstein
people.bio: Painter and lithographer (1872-1945), later Principal of the Royal College of Art. Sixteen of Wilde's letters to him survive, from 1893 to 1899. He was one of the friends who came out to Berneval to see Wilde after prison, and he drew the hotel at Napoule on a postcard Wilde sent his publisher.
people.bio_note: SIXTEEN LETTERS at repo PDF 523, 551, 614, 616, 643, 653, 941, 954, 975 and others; TWO read at the page (printed 562 and 1024, folios confirmed).

sources.quote: My dear Will, I have always been fond of you, and your art is always dear to me. I had been told that you wanted to take sides - that was all - and foolish as it is to take sides in a one-sided quarrel, or attack rather, still charming people are foolish often. So I did not go to see you in Paris. But when I saw you in St James's Street, I had to jump from my hansom and shake hands with my friend. When I go to Paris I shall wait your coming, and we shall be merry, as of old, at Sylvain's. Always affectionately yours
sources.context: Wilde to William Rothenstein, [? April-May 1893], Hotel Albemarle (MS Rothenstein) - quoted whole. A quarrel patched up: Wilde had heard Rothenstein was siding against him in something, stayed away in Paris, then saw him in the street and could not keep it up. The editors record that Rothenstein's son thought the quarrel concerned his father's continued friendship with Whistler.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde jumping out of a cab to end a coldness he had been maintaining on principle.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 614; printed folio 562 confirmed on the rendered page image.
