sources.quote: My dear Will, I cannot tell you how touched I am by your letter, and by all you say of my poem. Why on earth don't you write literary criticisms for papers? I wish The Ballad had fallen into your hands. No one has said things so sympathiques, so full of delicate insight, so large, from the point of view of art, as you. Your letter has given me more pleasure, more pride, than anything has done since the poem appeared. Yes: it is something to have made a 'sonnet out of skilly' (Cunninghame Graham will explain to you what skilly is. You must never know by personal experience). And I do think the whole affair 'realised', and that is triumph. I hope you will be in Paris some time this spring, and come and see me. I see by the papers that you are still making mortals immortal, and I wish you were working for a Paris newspaper, that I could see your work making kiosques lovely. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to William Rothenstein, [late February 1898], Hôtel de Nice (MS Rothenstein) - quoted whole, and found on the same printed page as the Harris letter above during the re-triage. Skilly was the thin gruel served in prison; the parenthesis - 'You must never know by personal experience' - is Wilde wishing a friend clear of what he had been through.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What one friend's letter about The Ballad was worth to him, and the wish that Rothenstein never learn what skilly is.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1070; printed folio 1024 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Salvatore
people.bio: One of three coachmen - cocchieri - who drove Wilde out to Monreale during the eight days he spent at Palermo in April 1900. Wilde named the three to Robert Ross as the most favoured, and said he had loved them all. Salvatore is named as one of the three most favoured.

people.name: Stanley Saunders
people.bio: 'Elephant' of George Ives's household, a later addition who jointly inherited the Adelaide Road house with 'Pug' (Harold Bloodworth). Cook describes him as an apparently lovable but difficult alcoholic; his drinking eventually drove the Goddard daughters out of the house, and Ives - a teetotaller for whom the drinking was itself a source of angst - kept him nonetheless.
people.bio_note: From Cook 2014 printed p. 96 (repo PDF 107, folio confirmed), where the surname is printed 'Stanley Suanders' - evidently a typo for Saunders, the spelling used elsewhere and in this roster; recorded here rather than silently corrected. The account of the daughters leaving and Ives choosing Elephant is from Cook 2014 printed p. 100, known so far only from the PDF text layer - verify at the rendered page before quoting. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED. Cook names him only at printed pp. 96 and 109 (repo PDF 107, 120), and at 96 the surname is printed 'Stanley Suanders' - the typo already recorded above. Searched so far, WITHOUT RESULT: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), repo PDF - every occurrence of the surname in the whole book, plus the endnotes and bibliography for the household chapter; the Ives repo transcripts (ives_diaries_burnet.txt, ives_letters_burnet_collated.txt, ives_letters_burnet_transcription.txt, ives_lewis_correspondence_2026-06.md), which contain no occurrence of any of the household surnames; and the open web, which returned only the Palgrave chapter version of Cook's same text ('George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family') and no dates. Cook is the only scholar to have written this household up and he dates their arrivals, their departures and Ives's will, but never a person: he gives no birth or death date for any member of the household. Unresolved without census, GRO index and probate research on common English surnames. Ives's own proved will (Cook, printed pp. 109-110), which leaves the Adelaide Road house to Bloodworth and Saunders, names Bloodworth an executor and portions the Goddards, is the natural documentary starting point, since a grant of probate fixes addresses and often identifies legatees.

people.name: Ernest Scarfe
people.bio: A valet's son and sometime valet, 'a young man of about twenty' by Wilde's sworn estimate, who went out to the Australian gold-diggings in 1893 — meeting Lord Douglas of Hawick, Bosie's elder brother, on the voyage — and returned to a clerkship in St Paul's Churchyard. He knew Taylor from the Knightsbridge Skating Rink; Taylor introduced him to Wilde at 10 St James's Place, where the waiter counted five or six visits, and he dined alone with Wilde and received the customary £4 cigarette case, last dining with him at the Avondale Hotel in February 1895. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at St James's Place (Oct 1893-Apr 1894); Scarfe was never called and no charge was ever laid; a begging letter from 'Ernesto' that Wilde mentions to Douglas in mid-1894 is tentatively identified with him by the Letters editors.
bio_sources: Wilde's libel-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 148-149, 152 (djvu OCR)
Taylor's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 286 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Thomas Price's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 205-206 (djvu OCR)
Hyde, Trials (1948), Introduction p. 47 n (the Hawick voyage acquaintance, 1893; djvu OCR)
Queensberry's plea, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 343 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 598 n 2 ('Possibly Ernest Scarfe, a valet'; read at rendered PDF p. 650, 2026-08-03)
people.bio_note: DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED FROM THE SOURCES CONSULTED. The Complete Letters editors do not identify him beyond a hesitant footnote: the recipient of an 1894 letter is glossed 'Possibly Ernest Scarfe, a valet (see Trials, pp.148-9)' - located in the OCR mirror at repo PDF 650 (printed folio around 598, NOT confirmed in the source) - and the General Index entry is the cross-reference 'Ernesto see Scarfe, Ernest'. SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted.

sources.quote: Dear Miss Schuster, I was so sorry I could not come down yesterday: but I will try and come down for the afternoon next Sunday: I was so pleased at all you said of the Woman of No Importance. My new play the Ideal Husband - to be brought out in January - I like less - there is no one like myself in it - horrid objective creations of serious folk. However it has some dramatic scenes in it. Sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to Adela Schuster, [? December 1894], 16 Tite Street (MS Hyde) - quoted whole. Four months before the trials. 'there is no one like myself in it' is Wilde on An Ideal Husband, and is as good a statement of his own measure of a play as he gives anywhere.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The friendship at its ordinary footing, months before she gave him £1,000.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 677; printed folio 625 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Adela Schuster
people.bio: A friend of Wilde's of the Tite Street years, known in the circle as 'Miss Tiny'. Two of Wilde's letters to her survive, both from December 1894. She is remembered chiefly for what she did the following spring: she gave Wilde £1,000 before the trials, at a point when almost nobody would be seen helping him.
people.bio_note: the volume's Index of Recipients. TWO LETTERS at printed 621 and 625; ONE read at the page. DATES NOT RECORDED and none inferred.

people.name: Maurice Schwabe
people.bio: The circle's connective figure and its most protected name: nephew by marriage of Sir Frank Lockwood, the Solicitor-General who prosecuted Wilde's final trial. Schwabe introduced Wilde to Taylor (Wilde's and Taylor's concurring sworn testimony), introduced Atkins to Taylor, and gave the Kettner's dinner at which Mavor met Wilde; Atkins placed him, 'a man of about twenty-two years of age,' in Wilde's bed in Paris in November 1892. At the trials his name was written on paper and passed to counsel rather than spoken; Wilde testified in April 1895 that Schwabe had been out of England for about two years, and he was never called.
bio_sources: Atkins's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 206-207 (p. 207 read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Hyde's footnote identifying Schwabe, Trials (1948), p. 137 n (djvu OCR)
Wilde's re-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 158 with Hyde's note 'Schwabe' (djvu OCR)
Taylor's cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 283 ('That is the person you say introduced Wilde to you?—Yes.'; djvu OCR)
Queensberry's plea of justification, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 342 ('Maurice Salis Schwabe'; IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
State Library of New South Wales, collection-item description for Lord Alfred Douglas, 'My darling pretty boy', letter to Maurice Schwabe, 1893 (Mitchell Library, Safe 1/2c) - birth and death years
people.bio_note: The General Index of Complete Letters (2000) contains NO Schwabe entry — verified at the rendered index page (printed p. 1263, where the entry would fall between Schreiner and Schuster) — so no editorial 'main particulars' footnote exists there to cite. (The deeper catalogue record at collection.sl.nsw.gov.au returned HTTP 403 and was not read.) SEARCHED WITHOUT RESULT: McKenna, Secret Life (2008), repo PDF pp. 327-333, 547, 568, 586, 604 - the fullest narrative treatment in the repo, and it gives no dates; Laura Lee's blog posts under her 'Maurice Schwabe' category and her book page - no dates, and she notes that Schwabe 'did not leave any autobiographies or a large cache of his correspondence in an archive'; the Complete Letters OCR mirror, which contains no occurrence of the name at all, consistent with the earlier finding that the General Index has no Schwabe entry.

people.name: A 'Sea-God', Naples
people.bio: A young man Wilde met during a three-day stop at Naples on his Italian journey of April 1900, and with whom, in his own words to Robert Ross, he 'fell in love'. Wilde calls him a Sea-God and says he was at the Regia Marina School - the Italian naval school - 'instead of being with Triton'. No name, age, dates or further trace appear on the page read.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, 16 April [1900], c/o Cook & Son, Piazza di Spagna, Rome, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1179 (repo PDF 1225, printed folio 1179 confirmed at the foot of the rendered page image). What IS verified in the source: the editors' footnote 2 on the same page reads 'Easter Day 1900 was on 15 April', and Wilde places his Vatican appearance 'yesterday', which is consistent with the mirror's 16 April heading.

people.name: Charles Shannon
people.bio: Painter and lithographer, born on 20 April 1863, the second son of a Lincolnshire country rector, and from 1881 a student at the City and Guilds Technical Art School in Lambeth, where he met Charles Ricketts (1866-1931); the two began a partnership and a shared household that lasted until Ricketts's death and never once involved living apart. Shannon was the painter of the pair and one of the first British artists after Whistler to take up lithography as an art rather than a trade, teaching himself from a printer's handbook and contributing to L'Estampe Originale in Paris; he co-founded and co-edited the Dial with Ricketts (1889-97), was art editor of the Pageant (1896-97), and became an Associate of the Royal Academy in 1911 and a full Academician in 1920. For Wilde he designed the bindings of Lady Windermere's Fan (1893), A Woman of No Importance (1894), The Importance of Being Earnest (1899) and An Ideal Husband (1899), and with Ricketts designed and decorated A House of Pomegranates (1891); Wilde nicknamed him "Marigold" and called him "the drawer of dreams", and Max Beerbohm later dubbed the two of them "the ladies of the Vale". Shannon had affairs with women, sat more than once on the edge of marrying one of his models, and did neither; his biographers divide over what to make of it, and no statement by him about his life with Ricketts in the language of sexual identity survives. In 1929 he fell while hanging a picture, suffered brain damage from which he never recovered, was nursed by Ricketts and then, after Ricketts's death, by paid nurses in Kew, and died in 1937; the collection the two men had built together passed to the Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge.
people.bio_note: Birth date (20 April 1863) and birthplace from Koenraad Claes's Y90s biography of Shannon - which gives the town as Quarrington "in the East Midlands"; "Lincolnshire" follows McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008 edn), PDF p. 190, read at the rendered page. Death year (1937) from two sources read at the rendered page: the editors' identifying footnote in Wilde's Complete Letters (2000), pp. 410-411 n. 3 ("Charles Hazlewood Shannon (1863-1937)"), and Matt Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), printed p. 29. CONFLICT to resolve: Claes gives ARA 1911 and RA 1920; the Wilde editors' footnote gives "Shannon in 1921". Career detail from Claes; the household chronology, the nursing and the Kew arrangement from Cook, printed pp. 31-33 and 52; the Wilde bindings from Complete Letters p. 411 n. 3; "Marigold" and "the ladies of the Vale" from McKenna, PDF p. 190, read in the source.

people.name: Edward Shelley
people.bio: Clerk at Wilde's publishers Elkin Mathews & John Lane (the Bodley Head) from 1891 — 'of decent family and upbringing' in Hyde's phrase — whom Wilde invited to dine at the Albemarle Hotel in February 1892; his testimony describes kisses, embraces and two nights in Wilde's bed, resisted, with no completed act. Wilde sent him inscribed books ('To one I like well') and theatre tickets, seating Pierre Louÿs beside him at the Lady Windermere's Fan first night; Shelley quarrelled with Wilde at the Savoy in March 1893 and broke off the acquaintance by letter. He testified at both criminal trials; the count concerning him was withdrawn for want of corroboration, and the editors of the Letters record that after the trials he joined the Grenadier Guards and served in the Boer War.
bio_sources: Shelley's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 212-214 and 296-297 (pp. 212-213 read as IIIF page images 2026-08-03)
Withdrawal of the count, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 305-307 (djvu OCR)

Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 529 n 2 ('Edward Shelley (1874-1915). A young employee of Elkin Mathews and John Lane...'; read at rendered PDF p. 549, 2026-08-03) and p. 530 (Grenadier Guards / Boer War; read at rendered PDF p. 550)
Wilde to Pierre Louÿs [mid-June 1892], Complete Letters (2000), p. 529 ('Vous serez à côté d'Edouard Shelley'; read at rendered page)
people.bio_note: The djvu OCR of Hyde gives 'In 1893 they were publishing a book' — the page image reads 1892 (verified 2026-08-03). Neil McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF p. 350, writes that 'Edward Shelley was deeply confused about his sexuality and eventually married.' NO WIFE IS NAMED, no date, no place, and the sentence is UNFOOTNOTED - McKenna's notes apparatus was searched and the only Shelley entry there attaches to a different quotation. The clause also sits inside a speculative passage about which of Wilde's partners preferred which sexual role, which is the least evidentially careful register McKenna writes in; the adjacent clauses are hedged ('seems to have hankered after') and this one is not, which is a stylistic difference rather than a documentary one. Read it as 'McKenna says he eventually married', not as an established marriage. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: McKenna cites 'witness statements, private collection' for Shelley elsewhere and may have had material not in public hands; failing that, the GRO marriage index for a man born 1874 and dead 1915, cross-referenced with the Grenadier Guards service the Complete Letters editors note at p. 530.

people.name: Robert Harborough Sherard
people.bio: Journalist and biographer, great-grandson of Wordsworth, born Robert Harborough Sherard Kennedy and known from youth by the middle name alone. He met Wilde in Paris in early 1883 and was still writing about him half a century later: four books, beginning with Oscar Wilde: the Story of an Unhappy Friendship (1902) and ending with Bernard Shaw, Frank Harris and Oscar Wilde (1937), besides biographies of Zola, Daudet and Maupassant. Thirteen of Wilde's letters to him survive, from 1883 to 1898, including three from Holloway between the trials and one from Reading Gaol. He fought duels in Paris on Wilde's behalf; he also denounced the Naples reunion with Douglas in 1897, and Wilde answered him coldly. The last letter sends him a copy of the Ballad 'in memory of our long friendship'.
people.bio_note: DATES 1861-1943 and the biography are from the editors' note at Complete Letters printed 205, folio confirmed on the rendered page image. THE THIRTEEN LETTERS are at repo PDF 227, 232-3, 369, 524, 530, 676, 693-4, 695, 696, 713, 1011 and 1072. ALL THIRTEEN have now been read at the page (printed 205, 210-11, 347-8, 504, 510, 624, 642-3, 644, 645, 662, 963, 1026), every folio confirmed on its own page image. HIS WIFE: the editors' note at printed 347 records that he married a Polish woman, Martha Lips, in 1886; she is now a node under the spouse rule. A CORRECTION TO THIS PROJECT'S OWN RECORD: the 2026-08-04 sweep cited the dedication letter at printed 202 - that is the Mary Anderson letter about The Duchess of Padua - and quoted it from 'how could I refuse' onward, omitting 'Your letter was as loveable as yourself' and the 'moonlit meanderings'.

people.name: Frederick 'Freddie' Smith
people.bio: Robert Ross's companion for a decade. Fryer records that Ross met him early in 1903, when Smith was an eighteen-year-old clerk and Ross almost twice his age; he became Ross's secretary, a position that also served as cover, and in 1906 moved into 15 Vicarage Gardens over his family's objections. He acted on the amateur stage as 'F. Stanley Smith'. The relationship ended in the autumn of 1913, and in 1914 he was named in Lord Alfred Douglas's plea of justification, where witnesses testified to having seen Ross embrace him.
people.bio_note: All facts from Jonathan Fryer, Robbie Ross (2000), transcribed and verified at rendered pages. Birth and death dates are not given by Fryer: he states only that Smith was eighteen early in 1903, which would place his birth about 1884-85 - an inference, deliberately not entered in the born field. NOTE ON HIS ORIGINS: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), printed p. 100, states that Smith left George Ives's household to move in with Ross. Cook cites nothing for it - the sentence carries no note marker, and the nearest endnote (21, printed p. 271) is methodological literature on household and family. Fryer, who documents Smith abundantly, never mentions Ives in connection with him, and the dates sit awkwardly (Cook puts the Adelaide Road household from 1905; Fryer has Smith with Ross from early 1903). DATES: NONE RECORDED; CONFIRMED AGAIN so far. Fryer's first-mention passage, printed p. 177 (repo PDF 199), is as close as the biography comes: 'early in 1903, he met a young man with whom he entered into a relationship quite unlike his other brief encounters with boys. Every later mention (printed pp. 192, 193, 198, 200, 207, 214, 230, 237, 238; repo PDF 214, 215, 220, 222, 229, 236, 252, 259, 260 - Fryer's second-half offset is printed = PDF minus 22) is narrative and dateless. Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF, contains no Freddie Smith at all - every 'Freddie' there is Freddie Manners-Sutton, the Crosland prosecutor, a different man entirely, and the two should not be conflated. Also searched: the Complete Letters mirror and Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014). No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted; the age eighteen in early 1903 would put his birth about 1884-85 and is still not entered.

people.name: Leonard Smithers
people.bio: Publisher, bookseller and pornographer, who issued The Ballad of Reading Gaol and both of Wilde's last plays in book form when no respectable house would touch his name. One hundred and eight of Wilde's letters to him survive - more than to anyone else in this volume except Douglas and Ross - and they are overwhelmingly about proofs, print runs and money. He died bankrupt in 1907.
people.bio_note: ONE HUNDRED AND EIGHT LETTERS at repo PDF 972, 977, 983, 987, 992, 999, 1000, 1006, 1010 and many more; FOUR read at the page (printed 1006, 1098, 1111 and 1141, folios confirmed) and both are quoted whole below because both are three lines long. DATES NOT RECORDED and none inferred. THE REMAINING HUNDRED-AND-SIX are located, not read, and are a large outstanding item for anyone continuing this work. Only 4 of 108 have been read at the page. The first pass filtered for desire and so treated this correspondence as business; on the warmth test it is not - 'I miss you very much' (printed ~1101), 'It was a great delight seeing you' (printed 1025), 'my life here is too lonely. I wish you would' (printed 1141).

sources.quote: Could you lend me or send me £10? I am in great straits, and have been ill in bed for some time. Please try to do this, as I have no money. Do please tell me if I am to have proofs of my play, and when. I have been expecting to see you for days.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [postmark 18 October 1898], Paris - quoted whole. The editors note the text comes from a 1927 auction catalogue. The play is The Importance of Being Earnest, then going through the press.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The two subjects of this correspondence in four sentences: money, and proofs.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1144; printed folio 1098 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: This is to show you where the poet is now living. I sent you the proofs days ago. Pray acknowledge them. The landscape and figures are by Conder: the hotel by Rothenstein.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [circa 18 December 1898], Hôtel des Bains, Napoule (MS Texas) - a postcard, quoted whole. The last sentence is a joke about a picture postcard of the hotel, crediting the view to two real painters, one of whom is on this map.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde still making jokes about attribution while asking to be paid attention to.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1157; printed folio 1111 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Smithers, … The £10 arrived safe - many thanks. Of course it was a blow not getting the £20, but I do hope you will send the balance soon. I now want to get back to Paris - my life here is too lonely. … Is there really any chance of your coming out here? I wish you would. I am at Santa Margherita, Ligure, Genoa, where please write and send the DC: the only consolation I have as I do not love the lad Edoardo Rolla as much as I did. Yours
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [? 8 April 1899], Genoa (MS Simpson) - the same letter that is cited on the Rolla connection, kept here for the other half of it. 'my life here is too lonely' and 'Is there really any chance of your coming out here? I wish you would' are addressed to Smithers, and they are not business. THE DESIRE TEST WOULD HAVE FILED THIS UNDER ROLLA ONLY.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That Wilde wanted his publisher's company, not only his cheques.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1187; printed folio 1141 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Smithers, We have waited for you for hours. Surely you have not left Paris? It seems impossible, as the city wears its wonted air of joy. Please see about the leaflet, and the Author's Edition with a cover by Ricketts - a new colour and a remarque in gold. The DT, by the influence of Reggie Turner, has been forced to notice the book, but grudgingly and badly. Do send me all the papers that have notices tomorrow. I have hopes of the Academy. Will you kindly send me six copies of the Second Edition. It was a great delight seeing you, and I must thank you for all your kindness to me. Maurice sends his kindest regards. We met by chance this morning, and I hope to see him again this evening. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [postmark 25 February 1898], Hôtel de Nice (MS Clark) - quoted whole. The book is The Ballad; the DT is the Daily Telegraph, where Reginald Turner then worked; the Maurice is Maurice Gilbert. Both Turner and Gilbert are on this map. ADDED 2026-08-06: read at the page during the Harris re-triage and left unlogged. IT IS EVIDENCE AGAINST THE 'BUSINESS CORRESPONDENCE' READING of this node's first pass - proofs and print runs, and then 'It was a great delight seeing you'.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That Wilde waited hours for him and was glad to have seen him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1071; printed folio 1025 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: You say in your last letter that you object to being 'Reynolds-ised', but I think you might have remembered that you were writing to a confirmed 'Smithersist'. The observation was quite unnecessary. I saw the other day in the museum here the bust of a young man of grave, somewhat severe beauty, and the most delicate refinement of type, rather like a young Oxonian of a very charming kind, the expression a mixture of pride and ennui. On referring to the catalogue I found it was the Emperor Heliogabalus; it was most curious and has filled me with a desire to write his life. Of course I shall publish it with you. His marriage with the moon, just referred to in Dorian Gray, would make a beautiful chapter of coloured words.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, Wednesday [27 October 1897], Villa Giudice, Posillipo (MS Harrow) - quoted across the page break. TWO THINGS. First, 'a confirmed Smithersist' is Wilde joking that he is devoted to his publisher, which is not the language of a purely commercial relation. Second, and larger: the bust he takes for a charming young Oxonian turns out to be HELIOGABALUS, the boy-emperor remembered for wearing women's dress, for taking a man as husband, and for asking his physicians to give him a woman's body - and Wilde's response is to want to write his life and publish it with Smithers. The book was never written. ADDED 2026-08-06: the passage was read at the page earlier but broke across a folio and was left unlogged until the second half was read.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde in exile proposing to write the life of Heliogabalus - and calling himself a confirmed Smithersist.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 1020-1021; printed folios 972 and 973 both confirmed on the rendered page images.

people.name: Evguenia Souline
people.bio: Russian émigrée nurse, born 5 January 1904, and the woman to whom Radclyffe Hall wrote the letters collected as Your John. Almost everything known about her early life comes through Hall's letters rather than from her own papers: her editor records that we do not know where or to whom she was born, that Souline is not a Russian name, that no patronymic and no father's name is ever given, and that the recurring details are White Russian origins and being a general's daughter - which would make her father an officer of the Russian Imperial Army. Uprooted at seventeen by the revolution, she lived among the Russian exiles in Paris "basically without family, without status, and without financial reserves", and worked as a private nurse at the American Hospital at Neuilly. In 1934 Hall, at the spa of Bagnoles-de-l'Orne and unable to nurse Una Troubridge through a bout of gastroenteritis, sent to the American Hospital for a nurse; Souline was the nurse who came. The attachment that followed lasted until Hall's death in 1943. Her own side of the correspondence does not survive: of nine years of letters to Hall, one, from 1939, is extant. She died in 1958, a date her editor gives with a question mark.
people.bio_note: Birth date, the circumstances of the meeting, the nursing post and the evidentiary situation from Joanne Glasgow's introduction to Your John (1997), printed pp. 1-3, read at rendered page images 2026-08-04 (printed folio 2 confirmed in the running head). The death year is from the Library of Congress cataloguing-in-publication data printed in the same volume, which gives "Souline, Evguenia, 1904-1958?" - **the question mark is the cataloguer's and the year should be treated as uncertain**. Souline does not appear in Wilde's Complete Letters and has no Wikipedia article; no Wikidata entity was matched, so she has no portrait on the map, which is itself the pattern the README describes - the record thins for people without property or status.

people.name: Harry Stafford
people.bio: New Jersey farm boy and, from 1876, the companion of Whitman's Camden years. He was eighteen and working as an errand boy at the Camden New Republic when Whitman, fifty-seven and still recovering from the stroke of 1873, came in to work on the Centennial Leaves of Grass. His parents George and Susan Stafford were tenant farmers at White Horse Farm near Kirkwood, and it was there, beside Timber Creek, that Whitman took the sun-and-mud cures he wrote up in Specimen Days. The two shared a top-floor bedroom at the farm; travelling, Whitman called him 'my nephew' and insisted on a shared bed. Whitman gave him a friendship ring, which Stafford returned more than once in the course of a quarrelsome attachment. He drifted between jobs, went back to the farm, and married Eva Westcott - in 1883 by the Whitman Archive's note on the letters, in 1884 by Kantrowitz's reference entry, a conflict left standing. Whitman left him the silver watch he had originally meant for Peter Doyle.

people.name: Bram Stoker
people.bio: A young Irish civil servant with literary and dramatic interests when he married Florence Balcombe at St Anne's Church, Dublin, on 4 December 1878. Wilde had courted Balcombe for the two years before the engagement, and the parting letters he wrote her are the reason both she and Stoker appear on this map.
people.bio_note: Everything above comes from ONE editorial footnote - Holland and Hart-Davis's note to Wilde's parting letters to Balcombe, Complete Letters (2000), p. 72 n. 1, which gives the wedding date, the church, the husband and his dates.

sources.quote: I send you a copy of my Ballad, which I hope you will accept with the author's compliments … The copy is of the first edition, which, I am glad to say, has now some interest for the bibliophile, and fetches a high price in London: it was exhausted on the day of issue. The poem has been a great success, I am glad to say, and the Press has not boycotted it after all.
sources.context: Wilde to Rowland Strong, Tuesday [February-March 1898], Hôtel de Nice (TS Clark). The editors note the text is supported by an entry in a 1911 bookseller's catalogue. The elision is the editors' own, marking a cut in their copy-text rather than one made here.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's own account of how The Ballad had done, sent to a journalist.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1073; printed folio 1027 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: I cannot tell you what pleasure your letter gave me, I wish my poem had fallen into your hands for review. Though I have had some most sympathetic and intellectual criticisms, nothing that has been said about The Ballad has touched me, or encouraged me, as much as your letter … In the meanwhile, have you any money to spare? If you have it would be very kind of you if you would lend me fifty francs. I am quite sans le sou, and awaiting money from my absurd publisher …
sources.context: Wilde to Rowland Strong, [February-March 1898], Hôtel de Nice (TS Clark). The elisions are the editors'. THE JOIN IS THE POINT: the warmest sentence in the letter and the request for fifty francs are two paragraphs apart, and by 1898 the two things travel together in almost every letter Wilde writes.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What a good review was worth to him, and what he needed in the same breath.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1073; printed folio 1027 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Rowland Strong
people.bio: A Paris-based English journalist of the exile years, correspondent for the Observer and the New York Times, who in September 1898 published Esterhazy's confession that he had written the bordereau at the heart of the Dreyfus affair. Two of Wilde's letters to him survive, both from the spring of 1898, both about The Ballad of Reading Gaol.
people.bio_note: TWO LETTERS at repo PDF 1073, both read at the page (printed 1027, folios confirmed). THE DREYFUS CONNECTION is from the editors' note and is context only; nothing about Wilde's part in it is asserted here.

sources.quote: Dear Bouncer, I am very glad you like Aurora Leigh. I think it simply 'intense' in every way. I am deep in a review of Symonds's last book whenever I can get time and the weather is too bright for fishing.
sources.context: Wilde to William Ward, [postmark 28 August 1876], Illaunroe Lodge, Connemara (MS Magdalen). The editors identify the book as Symonds's Studies of the Greek Poets and state that Wilde's review was never published. Wilde was twenty-one and had taken his First that July. The same week's letters contain the Todd passage.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That Wilde was reading Symonds closely at twenty-one, and that what he wrote about him did not survive into print.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 56; printed folio 31 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: John Addington Symonds
people.bio: Writer and cultural historian (1840-93), author of Studies of the Greek Poets and, privately, of A Problem in Greek Ethics - one of the earliest sustained defences of homosexuality written in English. In the summer of 1876 Wilde, then twenty-one, was writing a review of Studies of the Greek Poets between fishing trips in Connemara. The review was never published.
people.bio_note: THE EVIDENCE IS ONE SENTENCE, read at the page, plus the editors' identification of the book and their statement that the review went unpublished. WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS FIRMER: the review text itself, which has not been consulted, and Symonds's own Memoirs and letters, which are outside this volume.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Symons, We have no day just at present, as my wife is going away for a fortnight, but I hope you will come and dine with us some night. It was a great pleasure meeting you, as I had admired your work for a long time. I …
sources.context: Wilde to Arthur Symons, [postmark 22 October 1890], 16 Tite Street (MS Berg). The letter breaks where the printed page does. This is the two of them having just met.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The beginning of the acquaintance.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 477; printed folio 455 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Arthur Symons
people.bio: Poet and critic (1865-1945), a leading figure of the 1890s and author of The Symbolist Movement in Literature. Two of Wilde's letters to him survive. He wrote an admiring notice of The Ballad of Reading Gaol in 1898 which Wilde called 'admirably written, and most intellectual and artistic in its mode of approval'.
people.bio_note: the volume's Index of Recipients. TWO LETTERS at printed 354 and 455; ONE read at the page.

people.name: Herbert Tankard
people.bio: A pageboy at the Savoy Hotel, named in the Marquess of Queensberry's 1895 plea of justification. Queensberry's solicitors traced him after he had moved to Calais. He was never called and gave no evidence: the allegation exists only as a clause in the plea, and nothing of his own account survives.
people.bio_note: Read at the rendered page: Holland, The Real Trial of Oscar Wilde, Appendix A, printed 289 (repo PDF 337, folio confirmed on the page image). Holland's index entry reads 'Tankard, Herbert (Savoy pageboy), tracked down by Russell, xxiv; cited in Q's plea, 289'; the introduction at repo PDF 28-29 describes Russell's agents reaching 'a pageboy from the Savoy who had since moved to Calais'. DATES: none recorded; no age is stated anywhere on the page read, and none is inferred.

people.name: Alfred Taylor
people.bio: Marlborough-educated son of a cocoa manufacturer who came into a fortune of £45,000 on coming of age in 1883 and thereafter 'lived a life of pleasure' (his own testimony), keeping perfumed, permanently curtained rooms at 13 Little College Street and later 3 Chapel Street where he introduced young men — the Parkers, Wood, Mavor, Atkins, Scarfe — to one another and to Wilde, who was brought to him by Maurice Schwabe in 1892. Arrested in the Fitzroy Street raid of 12 August 1894 and discharged; arrested again in April 1895, he refused to turn Queen's Evidence against Wilde, was convicted on 21 May 1895 of gross indecency with Charles and William Parker, and was sentenced with Wilde on 25 May to two years' hard labour, Mr Justice Wills declaring it impossible to doubt he had 'kept a kind of male brothel.' The Letters editors give his full name as Alfred Waterhouse Somerset Taylor, born circa 1862, and record that after his release he lived in Canada and the USA.
bio_sources: Taylor's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 242 (age 33; Marlborough; £45,000; djvu OCR, folio '2A2' visible) and p. 286 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Mr Justice Wills's sentence, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 339 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Verdict, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 292 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)

Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 603 n 2 (born circa 1862; Fitzroy Street raid 12 Aug 1894; refused Queen's Evidence; Canada and the USA; read at rendered PDF p. 655, 2026-08-03)
people.bio_note: DEATH DATE: NOT FOUND, AND POSITIVELY RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED. Searched so far: the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror (the only 'Alfred Taylor' occurrences are pp. 603 and 679n plus the General Index line 'Taylor, Alfred, 603, 679n' - there is no editorial main-particulars footnote carrying dates); McKenna, Secret Life (2008) repo PDF (extensive on Taylor, silent on his dates and on his later life); Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, read in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238) - the trial record carries his sworn age, not a date; and the open web. The specialist compilations agree the death is unrecorded: Zagria's 'A Gender Variance Who's Who' heads its entry 'Alfred Taylor (1862 - ?) aristocrat, procurer, waiter' and states 'On release Taylor emigrated to the United States where nothing is known of him except that in the 1920s he was working as a waiter in Chicago, for by chance he served Alfred Douglas, Wilde's old lover, who was visiting the city' (zagria.blogspot.com, January 2010, citing Croft-Cooke, Feasting with Panthers (1968), and Ellmann, Oscar Wilde (1988)); a second web page repeats the same Chicago sentence and nothing further. NO WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: the en.wikipedia 'Alfred Taylor (British Army officer)' (Q4723503) is Captain Alfred James 'Bulala' Taylor, 1861-1941, an Anglo-Irish officer of the Scramble for Africa and the Second Boer War, tried for war crimes - not Wilde's co-defendant.

people.name: Harry Thomas
people.bio: E. P. Warren's 'young and handsome protege' and private secretary, who gave Lewes House as his Harvard address in 1903-04. In 1906 Warren paraded him around Boston and Fewacres, and some saw him as 'Ned's new boy friend' - which John Marshall, already bitter about Harold Parsons, swallowed badly. Thomas married Nan Devey the year after Marshall married, stayed in Warren's service to the end, and was one of the few at the Golders Green chapel.
people.bio_note: Sox p. 77 rendered 2026-08-03 for the quotation; p. 79 (the Harvard address), p. 78 (the Devey marriage), p. 21 (the jealousies list), p. 129 (those Warren loved and 'wanted to possess') and p. vii (Golders Green) read in the text layer and carried as context rather than as quotations.

sources.quote: He saw me so I went round to speak to him for a few minutes. He told me that he and Foster Harter had been fishing in Donegal and that he was going to fish South now. … He (Todd) looked awfully nervous and uncomfortable. I thought of Mark.
sources.context: Wilde to William Ward, Sunday [6 August 1876] (MS Magdalen). What Wilde did on seeing them: he went round to the box and made conversation, and Todd talked about fishing. The elision drops the judgement, which is quoted in full on the connection.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's own conduct on the night - he went over, and he noticed the discomfort.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 53-54; printed folios 28 and 29 both confirmed on the rendered page images.

people.name: Charles John Todd
people.bio: A Magdalen undergraduate of Wilde's own years (1874-7) who took orders and served as Chaplain to the Royal Navy from 1881 to 1909, dying at eighty-five. He is on this map for one evening in Dublin in the summer of 1876, when Wilde walked into a theatre at ten o'clock and found him sitting at the back of a private box with a Magdalen chorister. Wilde wrote about it to William Ward, decided in Todd's favour, and asked Ward to tell nobody.
people.bio_note: THE ONLY EVIDENCE IS WILDE'S LETTER, read at the page. His later life is from the editors' note and nothing in it is connected to this evening.

people.name: Una Troubridge
people.bio: Sculptor, translator and diarist, born Margot Elena Gertrude Taylor on 8 March 1887 and generally known as Una Vincenzo. She trained at the Royal College of Art, sculpted a bust of Nijinsky in his role as the faun (1912), and later became the principal English translator of Colette. She married the naval officer Sir Ernest Troubridge in 1908 and had a daughter, Andrea, in 1910; the Ransom Center's sketch records that the Troubridges "were separated by 1919 because of Una's relationship with Radclyffe Hall". She was Mabel Batten's cousin, met Hall in 1915, and was her partner until Hall's death in 1943, afterwards writing The Life and Death of Radclyffe Hall (1961). Her diaries run to 131 volumes at the Ransom Center. She does not appear in Wilde's Complete Letters. She died in Rome on 24 September 1963.
people.bio_note: Cook (2014, p. 108) names her with Hall among women who "seem to have been considered" for the Order of Chaeronea - a hedge too weak to carry an Ives edge.

people.name: Reggie Turner
people.bio: An old friend of Robert Ross who, in Ross's words, 'had been very kind to Mr Wilde since his release', and the constant presence of Wilde's last weeks at the Hôtel d'Alsace: he sent Ross daily bulletins, was with Wilde 'the whole of the last week of his life', slept at the hotel to give the 4 a.m. remedies, restrained him in delirium, held the ice-bag, and told the doctor he would be responsible for any expenses. He and Ross were, per the editors' plate caption, 'the two friends who were with Oscar on the day he died' (30 November 1900); he walked in the funeral procession and sent a wreath. Wilde's register toward him stayed teasing-affectionate to the end - 'You dear little Jew, don't you think that's enough?' during the ice-bag nursing, and the Rome 1900 photograph sent to Turner inscribed 'A young unmitred Bishop in partibus'. The 1898-99 letters show the ordinary setting of the friendship: Wilde's standing sign-off to him was 'Ever affectionately yours' (p. 1118), and Turner is the correspondent to whom Wilde reports other men's boys, other men's infatuations and a blackmail arrest in a shared idiom that assumes no explanation (pp. 1107-08, 1122). Looking back on Berneval in September 1897 Wilde counted what each friend had given him: Ross a week, Fothergill six days, 'Reggie gave me three days' (p. 942).
people.bio_note: DATES (added 2026-08-03): born 1869, died 1938, from the editors' first-mention footnote to 'To Reginald Turner', Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), printed p. 592 n. 1 (repo PDF 644) - '1869-1938. The footnote gives years only; no month or day, so none is recorded. All facts from Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000): 'an old friend of mine who had been very kind to Mr Wilde since his release' and 'the whole of the last week' from Ross to Adela Schuster, 14 Dec. 1900, pp. 1227-28 (repo PDF 1272-73); night-nursing, delirium restraint, ice-bag, expenses and the 'dear little Jew' remark from Turner's own letters to Ross, [November 1900], pp. 1217-18 (PDF 1262-63); deathbed-presence caption to plate 84 and the Rome inscription caption to plate 89 from the unpaginated plate section (PDF 600-601); procession and wreath from p. 1222 (PDF 1267).

people.name: A valet, Cannes
people.bio: A young manservant Wilde saw at the Bataille des Fleurs at Cannes on 1 February 1899, riding on the box of his employer's carriage beside the coachman, wreathed in flowers. Wilde described him to Robert Ross the next day as 'a very handsome boy' and answered the tableau with a phrase — 'Imperial, Neronian Rome'. Nothing else about him survives: not his name, not his age, and no suggestion the two ever spoke.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, 2 February 1899, Napoule, Complete Letters printed 1121 (repo PDF 1167, folio confirmed on the rendered page image). A CITATION CORRECTION: the 2026-08-04 sweep placed this passage at 'printed ~p. 1119'. It is printed 1121; the OCR mirror's page attribution drifts by a page or two here and the folio was confirmed from the page itself.

people.name: A boy in grey velvet, Paris
people.bio: A young man Wilde was seen with outside a small café behind the Madeleine in Paris in late March 1900, eight months before his death. He is known from a single sentence of Wilde's own, written to Robert Ross: Ross's brother Aleck walked past and saw them together. Wilde describes him as 'a beautiful boy in grey velvet - half rough, all Hylas' - 'rough' being the period word for a working-class young man, and Hylas the youth Herakles loved and lost. No name, age or occupation is recorded, and nothing else about him survives.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, Thursday [Late March 1900], Grand Cafe, 14 boulevard des Capucines, Paris; Complete Letters printed 1177 (repo PDF 1223), read on the rendered page 2026-08-04. The editors' footnote 3 to that page explains Wilde's joke about Aleck's eye: 'Aleck Ross had lost the sight of one eye in early youth.'

people.name: Renée Vivien
people.bio: Symbolist poet writing in French, 1877-1909, English by birth, a central figure of Natalie Barney's Paris circle and, in Sarah Parker's phrase, "one of Barney's former lovers" by the time Olive Custance visited Paris around 1901. Custance befriended her there. Barney's memoir Souvenirs Indiscrets (1960) records, as reported by Parker, a plan to gather Barney, Vivien and Custance into a recreated Sapphic community at Mytilene, an endeavour "stymied by Vivien's jealousy". Vivien's roman a clef A Woman Appeared to Me (1904) fictionalises Custance as the "little English poetess Dagmar". She does not appear anywhere in Wilde's Complete Letters; her connection to this web runs entirely through Barney and Custance.

people.name: Walter
people.bio: A youth whom Wilde, writing to Robert Ross in January 1899, named as the object of I. D. W. Ashton's 'absurd love' - the one thing about Ashton he could not forgive. Wilde describes him as 'a plain, crooked, ugly, and tedious youth'. Nothing else is recorded: no surname, no age, no occupation, no trace beyond the single sentence.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, Thursday [? 12 January 1899], Hotel des Bains, Napoule, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1118 - the editors' own query mark on the date is preserved.

people.name: William Ward
people.bio: William Welsford Ward (1854-1932), Wilde's closest Oxford friend and the man he wrote to more often than anyone else in his twenties. He came to Magdalen from Radley as a Classical Demy in 1873, took a First in Mods and a Second in Greats, and went down at the end of 1876 to follow his father as a solicitor in Bristol, where he became a considerable public figure. His nickname 'Bouncer' came from a comic Oxford novel of 1873; Wilde's own was 'Hosky'. Wilde scratched a drawing inscribed 'Little Mr Bouncer' on the window of the room the two of them occupied in succession, and it survived until a college party smashed it in the 1960s. Ward wrote a short 'Oxford Reminiscence' of Wilde, published in 1954.
people.bio_note: TWENTY-TWO LETTERS at repo PDF 39, 43, 45, 47, 49, 50, 52, 56 (two), 60, 62, 63, 66, 82, 84, 87, 88, 91, 96, 97, 102 and 137. FIFTEEN have been read at the page (printed 20, 38, 64, 69, 70 and the four-double-sheet letter at printed 38-9, folios confirmed); the other sixteen are located, not read, and all are rendered and waiting in the session scratchpad. DATES: NONE RECORDED — his years are probably in the editors' note at the first letter (repo PDF 39), which has not been read; nothing is inferred here. THE LETTER TO READ NEXT is repo PDF 63, which the editors describe as 'a letter of four double sheets' — by far the longest of the twenty-two, and the likeliest to carry more than news. THE ARC IS NOW BRACKETED: the earliest letter (printed 15, March 1876) signs off 'Your affectionate friend' and the last (printed 112, mid-1881) 'Ever affectionately yours', so the register at both ends is on the record even though thirteen letters in the middle remain unread. TWO MORE CANDIDATES THIS TURNED UP, neither on the map: JOHN ADDINGTON SYMONDS, whose Studies of the Greek Poets Wilde was reviewing in August 1876 (printed 31) and who is a central figure in the period's homosexual writing; and WALTER PATER, whose first letter to Wilde is printed whole at printed 59. Every page in these two correspondences that mentions Frank or the Miles family has now been read at the page - repo PDF 42, 46, 47, 49, 54, 56 and 72, printed 17, 21, 22, 24, 29, 31 and 47 - and the note is not audible in any of them.

sources.quote: I heard once from the Kitten about a gummy hat-box he says he left in his little room. I was too much ashamed to ask Mrs Brewer about it, so I suppose the poor Kitten has to go to church in a frock coat and pot-hat. … I hope you will write soon. Your affectionate friend
sources.context: The close of Wilde's letter to William Ward, Monday [20 March 1876], Magdalen College (MS Magdalen) — the earliest of the twenty-two. The elision drops reading plans and college news. Kept because it shows the three of them in one frame: Wilde writing to Ward about Harding, and signing himself Ward's affectionate friend.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The earliest surviving sign-off to Ward — 'Your affectionate friend' — and the Ward/Harding/Wilde triangle in one letter.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 40; printed folio 15 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Boy, I know you will be glad to hear I have got my First all right. … Of course I knew I had got a First, so swaggered horribly. … Altogether I swaggered horribly, but am really pleased with myself. My poor mother is in great delight and I was overwhelmed with telegrams on Thursday from everyone I know. My father would have been so pleased about it. I think God has dealt very hardly with us. It has robbed me of any real pleasure in my First, and I have not sufficient faith in Providence to believe it is all for the best — I know it is not. I feel an awful dread of going home to our old house, with everything filled with memories.
sources.context: Wilde to William Ward, [postmark 10 July 1876], 4 Albert Street, London (MS Magdalen). Sir William Wilde had died on 19 April, three months earlier. The elisions drop the examiners' viva and a list of people met. Wilde was twenty-one.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The First and the grief in the same breath — what Wilde told Ward that he told almost nobody.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 45; printed folio 20 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Boy, I confess not to be a worshipper at the Temple of Reason. I think man's reason the most misleading and thwarting guide that the sun looks upon, except perhaps the reason of woman. Faith is, I think, a bright lantern for the feet, though of course an exotic plant in man's mind, and requiring continual cultivation. … About Newman I think that his higher emotions revolted against Rome but that he was swept on by Logic to accept it as the only rational form of Christianity. His life is a terrible tragedy. I fear he is a very unhappy man.
sources.context: Wilde to William Ward, Wednesday [26 July 1876], 1 Merrion Square North (MS Magdalen). The elision drops a long passage on his mother's beliefs and on Schopenhauer. This is the intellectual register of the friendship, which is most of what it consists of: two undergraduates arguing about faith and reason. The same letter's opening asks after 'the King's Close Cats' — Harding's family, whose surname produced the whole cat-naming.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Wilde and Ward actually talked about — faith, Newman, reason — which is the friendship's substance and is not romantic.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 50; printed folio 25 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Bouncer, I am very glad you like Aurora Leigh. I think it simply 'intense' in every way. I am deep in a review of Symonds's last book whenever I can get time and the weather is too bright for fishing. … I hope next year that you and the Kitten will come and stay a (lunar) month with me. I am sure you would like this wild mountainous country, close to the Atlantic and teeming with sport of all kinds. … Write like a good boy to Moytura House, Cong, County Mayo, as I will be leaving here this week. With kind regards to your mother and sisters, ever yours … I have Frank Miles with me. He is delighted with all.
sources.context: Wilde to William Ward, [postmark 28 August 1876], Illaunroe Lodge, Connemara (MS Magdalen). The elision drops fishing and shooting counts. TWO THINGS THE FILTER SHOULD FIND HERE. The invitation is to both men together — 'you and the Kitten'. And the Frank Miles sentence is a POSTSCRIPT, added after the signature: Croft-Cooke, quoted on the Miles connection, reads the Miles mentions in the Ward and Harding letters as the one place an 'alien note' enters them, so where and how Miles appears is worth recording exactly. Here he appears last, in five words, after Wilde has signed off. The Symonds under review is John Addington Symonds, Studies of the Greek Poets, and Wilde's review was never published.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde inviting Ward and Harding together for a month, and the exact placement of a Frank Miles mention — the thing Croft-Cooke says the charge lives in.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 56; printed folio 31 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Bouncer, I am in terrible dread of reading a pathetic account in Reynolds' Police News of 'the death by starvation of a young man on Lundy Island'. The idea of you forgetting your food. I hope you got it safe. … [and, from the letter of August 1877:] After all I can't trust my letter from Pater to the mercies of the postman, but I send you a copy … You won't think me snobbish for sending you this? After all, it is something to be honestly proud of.
sources.context: Two letters joined here because they show the same thing: what Wilde brought to Ward first. The first is [2 July 1876], The Vicarage, West Ashby (MS Magdalen), fussing over whether Ward had eaten. The second is [August 1877] and encloses a full copy of Walter Pater's first letter to Wilde — 'it makes me much wish to make your acquaintance' — which Wilde would not trust to the post in the original. He was twenty-two. THE PATER LETTER IS PRINTED IN FULL ON THE SAME PAGE and Pater is not on this map.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The confidence in the friendship — solicitude about his meals, and the proudest letter of his young life sent to Ward before anyone else.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 43 and 86; printed folios 18 and 59 both confirmed on the rendered page images. The two letters are quoted together and the join is marked; each is separately locatable at its own folio.

sources.quote: However I think you are an awful cynic about women – a Passionless Sphinx of Society – (sounds rather abusive!) I hope some day to hear you raving about pretty lips and blue eyes. Ever yours
sources.context: The close of Wilde's letter to William Ward, [postmark 3 January 1877], 1 Merrion Square North (MS Magdalen). Recorded because of what it says about Ward rather than about Wilde: it is a friend teasing him, at twenty-one or so, for showing no interest in women. Nothing else read so far follows it up, and no inference is drawn here — it is one joke in one letter, and it is on the page.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's own observation that Ward was indifferent to women, and his wish that he would not be.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 63; printed folio 38 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear old Boy, You are the best of fellows to telegraph your congratulations: there were none I valued more. It is too delightful altogether this display of fireworks at the end of my career. I cannot understand my First except for the essays which I was fairly good in. I got a very complimentary viva voce. The dons are 'astonied' beyond words — the Bad Boy doing so well in the end! … Then I rowed to Pangbourne with Frank Miles in a birchbark canoe! and shot rapids and did wonders everywhere — it was delightful. I cannot, I am afraid, yacht with you. … Dear old boy, I wish I could see you again. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to William Ward, [circa 24 July 1878], Magdalen College (MS Magdalen), on his First in Greats. The elisions drop college gossip and a paragraph on his lawsuit. The Frank Miles here is the Frank Miles on this map, whom Wilde would live with from the following year.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Ward's congratulations were worth to him, and the plain wish to see him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 97; printed folio 70 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Boy, Why don't you write to me? I don't know what has become of you. As for me I am ruined. The law suit is going against me and I am afraid I will have to pay costs, which means leaving Oxford and doing some horrid work to earn bread. The world is too much for me. However, I have seen Greece and had some golden days of youth. I go back to Oxford immediately for viva voce and then think of rowing up the river to town with Frank Miles. Will you come? Yours
sources.context: Wilde to William Ward, Thursday [? 11 July 1878], St Stephen's Club, Westminster (MS Magdalen) — quoted whole. The lawsuit concerned house property inherited from his father and was heard in Dublin that week. Frank Miles is on this map.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde at his lowest before the First was announced, asking Ward why he does not write and whether he will come.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 96; printed folio 69 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Will, My volume is out: I wish you could review it: no one is more qualified to be a critic than you with your keen insight and exquisite taste. I wish in any case you would let me know what you think of it. But I am very anxious to be read, and a review in a Bristol paper might cause a sale in that lovely old town. Ever affectionately yours
sources.context: Wilde to William Ward, [June-July 1881], Keats House, Tite Street (MS Magdalen) — the last of the twenty-two, quoted whole, sent with his first volume of Poems. He wrote to Matthew Arnold the same week about the same book; the letter to Ward asks for a review and the letter to Arnold asks for nothing.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The close of the correspondence, five years on and still affectionate — and Wilde's estimate of Ward's judgement.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 137; printed folio 112 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: I want to ask your opinion on this psychological question. In our friend Todd's ethical barometer, at what height is his moral quicksilver? Last night I strolled into the theatre about ten o'clock and to my surprise saw Todd and young Ward the quire boy in a private box together, Todd very much in the background. He saw me so I went round to speak to him for a few minutes. He told me that he and Foster Harter had been fishing in Donegal and that he was going to fish South now. I wonder what young Ward is doing with him. Myself I believe Todd is extremely moral and only mentally spoons the boy, but I think he is foolish to go about with one, if he is bringing this boy about with him. You are the only one I would tell about it, as you have a philosophical mind, but don't tell anyone about it like a good boy - it would do neither us nor Todd any good. He (Todd) looked awfully nervous and uncomfortable. I thought of Mark. I hope nothing is wrong with your people or yourself that you don't write. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to William Ward, Sunday [6 August 1876], 1 Merrion Square North (MS Magdalen), quoted unbroken from where the subject is raised to the signature; the elision drops only the letter's earlier news of Mahaffy, Howth and Wilde's poems. THE MOST IMPORTANT ITEM IN EITHER OXFORD CORRESPONDENCE, and it has nothing to do with Frank Miles. Wilde is twenty-one. The editors identify Todd as Charles John Todd (1854-1939), a Magdalen undergraduate of Wilde's own years who became Chaplain to the Royal Navy from 1881 to 1909, and 'young Ward the quire boy' as Eric Richard Ward, a Magdalen chorister 1874-8 and no relation to the recipient. 'Spoons' is period slang for courting or being sentimentally in love; 'mentally' is Wilde drawing the line he thinks Todd has not crossed. WHAT THE LETTER SHOWS is the machinery of discretion already fully assembled around a twenty-one-year-old: a thing seen, a judgement withheld, one confidant chosen for having 'a philosophical mind', and an explicit instruction to say nothing because exposure would damage the teller as much as the man told of - 'it would do neither us nor Todd any good'. The 'us' is doing a great deal of work.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Wilde could say to Ward and to nobody else, and the earliest recorded instance of him handling a suspected attachment between men.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 53-54; printed folios 28 and 29 both confirmed on the rendered page images.

sources.quote: I have had a delightful week here. The garden and house are very beautiful. I never saw such lilies - white and red and golden. Nearly all the family are good artists. Mrs Miles is really wonderful. I suppose you remember my showing you her drawings in Ruskin's School at Oxford when we went there to your sister. Mr Miles pere is a very advanced Anglican and a great friend of Newman, Pusey, Manning, Gladstone and all English theologians. He is very clever and interesting: I have learned a lot from him. … I make myself as charming as ever and am much admired. Have had some good arguments with Dean Miles who was a great friend of Newman, Pusey and Manning at Oxford and a very advanced Anglican. Write me a line soon like a good boy. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to William Ward, Monday [postmark 17 July 1876], Bingham (MS Magdalen) - the Miles family home, where Wilde spent a week that July. The elision drops a book recommendation and a garden party. Kept because it is one of the seven Miles pages Croft-Cooke's claim depends on, and the Miles who interests Wilde here is Frank's father.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: A week inside the Miles household, written up entirely in terms of the parents.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 47; printed folio 22 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Edward Perry Warren
people.bio: Boston paper-fortune heir turned expatriate collector of classical antiquities - the great supplier of the Boston Museum of Fine Arts - and 'master of Lewes House' in Lewes, East Sussex, where from 1890 he 'collected art and young men' and tried to forge his secretaries into a 'brotherhood of aesthetes'. Born at Waltham, Massachusetts, 'in the year Lincoln was elected President'; at New College, Oxford, he met John Marshall in 1884 - 'the love of his life' per Sox - whom he wooed by letter for five years and whose forty-year partnership anchored the enterprise. Author of A Tale of Pausanian Love, the privately printed fairy tale The Prince Who Did Not Exist (1900, dedicated to Mary Bliss), and A Defence of Uranian Love, written and rewritten in his garden office at 'Thebes'. Died in London on 28 December 1928 after an abdominal operation, ten months after Marshall; cremated at Golders Green on 1 January 1929; his ashes were placed in the Marshalls' tomb at Bagni di Lucca on 5 April 1929, next to 'his beloved "Puppy"'.
bio_sources: Born: 'Born at Waltham, Massachusetts near Boston in the year Lincoln was elected President (1860)' - Sox (1991) p. 3 (repo PDF 19, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03)

Died: 'Ned was dead on 28 December 1928. After an abdominal operation, he entered the Cambridge House Nursing Home at Dorset Square in London where he died.' - Sox p. 129 (PDF 145, rendered 2026-08-03)
Cremation 1 Jan 1929, ashes to Bagni di Lucca 5 Apr 1929, 'collected art and young men', 'brotherhood of aesthetes', 'his beloved Puppy': Sox pp. vii-viii (PDF 11-12, rendered 2026-08-03)
Lewes House lease April 1890 (first seen Oct 1889): Sox p. 44 (PDF 60, rendered 2026-08-03)

Works: A Tale of Pausanian Love, Sox pp. 38, 44 (PDF 54, 60, rendered); The Prince Who Did Not Exist, p. 75 (PDF 91, rendered); Defence of Uranian Love at 'Thebes', pp. 153-154 (PDF 177 text layer; title italicized in Fothergill's letter at p. 154, PDF 178, rendered)
people.bio_note: Sox gives the birth year only as '(1860)' inside the Lincoln's-election phrase; no month or day in pages read. Oxford matriculation 1883 is implied, not stated ('In January 1884, Prichard entered New College only months after Ned Warren's matriculation', p. 169, rendered). (Cumberland Mills paper), p. 3.

people.name: Arthur George Bainbridge West
people.bio: E. P. Warren's first choice of life-companion, before John Marshall. On a trip to Wiesbaden and Rome in 1889 Warren confided his wish to share his life with 'an alter ego'; West, long set on Holy Orders, was not happy with the possible implications and declined. Warren remained devoted to him regardless, becoming godfather to his sons; West's son Charles Murray West later ran Warren's house in Maine and inherited it.
people.bio_note: Sox pp. 38-39, read as rendered page images 2026-08-03.

people.name: Eva Westcott
people.bio: Harry Stafford's wife, married in 1883 or 1884 - the sources disagree - and still married to him in November 1884, when Whitman was addressing letters to 'Harry and Eva Stafford' jointly. Stafford was the New Jersey farm boy Whitman gave a friendship ring to and shared a bed with; he married Eva Westcott and stayed married, and outlived Whitman by twenty-six years.

people.name: Walt Whitman
people.bio: American poet, author of Leaves of Grass (first published 1855; its 1882 eighth edition was withdrawn by its publishers on a threatened prosecution for indecency). By 1882 he was living in Camden, New Jersey, across the Delaware from Philadelphia, partly paralysed since 1873. During the American lecture tour of 1882 Wilde visited him there twice - on 18 January, taken by the Philadelphia publisher J. M. Stoddart at Whitman's written invitation, and again in early May - and Wilde's one surviving letter to him (postmarked 1 March 1882) relays Swinburne's admiration and declares an intent to visit again before leaving America. Whitman kept that letter until 1888, when he handed it to Horace Traubel, whose Camden conversation records preserve Whitman's side of the acquaintance.
people.bio_note: Dates (1819-92), Camden residence, the 18 January visit with Stoddart, and the Leaves of Grass withdrawal are from the biographical footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 144 n. 1 (repo PDF 167, printed folio confirmed). Letter postmark and closing from pp. 144-5 (repo PDF 167-168, same session). Second visit 'early in May' 1882: Ellmann, 'Oscar Meets Walt', NYRB 3 Dec. 1987 (read at article page). 1888 letter handover: Traubel, With Walt Whitman in Camden, vol. 2, pp. 287-8 (IA withwaltwhitmani0002unse_c4l4, IIIF page images).

people.name: Oscar Wilde
people.bio: Dublin-born writer; born 16 October 1854 at 21 Westland Row, educated at Trinity College Dublin and Magdalen College, Oxford. Married Constance Lloyd on 29 May 1884; two sons, Cyril (b. 1885) and Vyvyan (b. 1886). Convicted 25 May 1895 and sentenced to two years' hard labour following the three trials of that spring; released 19 May 1897 and lived thereafter in France and Italy. Died 30 November 1900 at the Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris, of cerebral meningitis; buried at Bagneux, moved to Père Lachaise in 1909.
people.bio_note: All facts from the Chronological Table, Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), pp. viii-xii (repo PDF 8-12).

sources.quote: My life cannot be patched up. There is a doom on it. Neither to myself, nor others, am I any longer a joy. I am now simply an ordinary pauper of a rather low order: the fact that I am also a pathological problem in the eyes of German scientists is only interesting to German scientists: and even in their works I am tabulated, and come under the law of averages! Quantum mutatus!
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, Saturday [11 December 1897], Villa Giudice, Posilippo (MS Hyde). 'averages' is italicised in the printed text; the Latin is Virgil, 'How changed from what he once was'. THE GERMAN SCIENTISTS are the sexologists - Krafft-Ebing's Psychopathia Sexualis and its successors, in which the Wilde trials had become standard case material within two years. Wilde is describing his own conversion into a data point, and the sting he picks out is not being called pathological but being TABULATED: made ordinary, averaged, one of a class. No specific work is named on the page and none is inferred here.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's own awareness that he had become a case study in the medical literature of homosexuality, in his lifetime.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1054; printed folio 1006 confirmed on the rendered page image.

people.name: Louis Wilkinson
people.bio: Louis Umfreville Wilkinson, a Radley schoolboy when he opened a correspondence with Wilde in the winter of 1898. To get into correspondence he invented an 'Ipswich Dramatic Society' and its wish to dramatise The Picture of Dorian Gray; the editors identify a second invention, his claim to have been at the first night of Lady Windermere's Fan, as made for the same purpose. A third claim was not invented but misattributed: it was his father, not he, who had known Edward FitzGerald, the two being neighbours in Suffolk. He and Wilde never met. Wilde, writing to Reggie Turner in January 1899, described him as 'a Radley schoolboy, aged seventeen'. He went up to Oxford, published many novels and other books under the name Louis Marlow, and in Seven Friends (1953) printed many of Wilde's letters to him, there confessing the Ipswich fabrication. His first letter to Wilde and some of the subsequent ones are in the Hyde Collection.
people.bio_note: All facts from Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000) with printed folios confirmed. Birth and death years, the Radley schooling, the Ipswich Dramatic Society fabrication, the pen-name Louis Marlow, Seven Friends (1953), the Hyde Collection provenance and the flat statement that the two never met are from the main-particulars footnote at p. 1109 n. 1 (the note begins on 1109 and concludes at the foot of 1110; repo PDF 1155-56, transcribed by the earlier record session). The Lady Windermere's Fan invention is p. 1127 n. 2 (PDF 1173). The FitzGerald correction is p. 1133 n. 1 (PDF 1179). The age is Wilde's own contemporaneous statement to Reginald Turner at p. 1118 (PDF 1164) and is consistent with the 1881 birth year. NOT read so far (pointers): the correspondence tail at printed 1136, 1159n, 1168, 1170-71 (Paris invitation) and 1171, and the funeral-wreath mention at approximately printed 1224.

people.name: Alfred Wood
people.bio: An out-of-work clerk who lived three weeks in Taylor's one-bed rooms in January 1893 and was sent to Wilde at the Café Royal by Lord Alfred Douglas's telegram from Salisbury; his testimony describes an act of 'the grossest indecency' at 16 Tite Street, and Wilde was convicted on that count. In a suit of clothes Douglas gave him at Oxford he found Wilde's letters to Douglas — the seed of the Allen-Cliburn blackmail affair — and left for America in spring 1893 with £35 from Wilde; back in London by 1894, he took £175 from a £300-£400 extortion worked with Allen on a gentleman caught with Charles Parker. In De Profundis Wilde described blackmail as the 'sole source of income' of 'people like Alfred Wood.'
bio_sources: Wood's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 201-205 (p. 202 read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03; rest djvu OCR)
Wilde's libel-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 134-135 (djvu OCR)
Verdict on count 13, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 337 (djvu OCR)
Wilde, De Profundis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 761, with the editors' note 'A blackmailer who gave evidence at Wilde's trials' (p. 761 n 1; read at rendered PDF p. 812, 2026-08-03)
