sources.quote: old man i got your kind and welcom letter last week and was glad to hear from you my loving old friend i love to hear from you and to know that you ar well and i would Com up to see you But i cant get of a day now for we ar so Bisse now husking corn i went with some Boys up the Pond to day and i seen your old Chir floting down the stream … i think of you old man think of the times down on the Crieek. … i love you Walt and all ways will so may god Bless you is my prayer from of your frend Edward P Cattell
sources.context: Cattell to Whitman, 21 October 1877, headed only 'Sunday 21th'. **The spelling and capitalisation are Cattell's own** and are preserved here as the archive preserves them; he was a farm labourer and wrote as he could. The elisions drop his news of George Stafford and Herbert Gilchrist and his hope of coming to Camden. Recorded in full register rather than trimmed to the declaration, because trimming it to 'i love you Walt' would tidy away the husking and the floating chair, which are the texture of the thing.
sources.supports: Cattell's own voice - the only substantial thing of his that survives, and the other half of the self-reported class.

null_findings.finding: NO DATES EXIST FOR CATTELL in anything consulted, and this is a finding rather than a gap in the search. Stafford and Doyle each have a signed reference entry with birth and death years in its title; Cattell has none, and the nearest the record comes is Whitman's own note that he was 'about 25 or 6' in 1876. He is a farm labourer, and the apparatus that records dates - articles, entries, obituaries, portraits - tracks property. The `born` and `died` fields are therefore null by evidence, not by oversight. The diary and commonplace-book entries the archive quotes ('the hour (night, June 19, '76, Ed & I.) at the front gate by the road'; 'Sept meetings Ed C by the pond at Kirkwood moonlight nights') are in the Feinberg Collection at the Library of Congress and were NOT consulted at the manuscript - they are quoted here only as the archive quotes them, and remain the obvious next step.

phases.note: Acquaintance and courtship: first met London, June 1881 ('I can't help liking him' - Constance to Otho, 7 June 1881, quoted p. 221 n. 1).

Marriage: honeymoon Paris (Hotel Wagram, June 1884); two sons; passionate letter of 16 Dec 1884; by 1893 much apart (Constance in Rome/with the boys while Wilde at Babbacombe, p. 555) - but only three letters to her survive, the rest destroyed after her death (p. 241 n. 6).

relationships.summary: Wilde's wife. Constance Mary Lloyd (1858–1898), daughter of Horace Lloyd QC, met Wilde in London in June 1881, accepted him in Dublin in November 1883, and married him at St James's Church, Sussex Gardens, on 29 May 1884. Two sons, Cyril (b. 1885) and Vyvyan (b. 1886). Only three of Wilde's letters to her survive - a passionate one of December 1884 and two pencilled notes from the 1895 catastrophe; the rest were destroyed after her death. She visited him in Reading Gaol on 19 February 1896 to tell him of his mother's death - their last meeting - kept his allowance, took the name Holland, withheld the children, and died at Genoa on 7 April 1898; Wilde telegraphed 'Am in great grief' and visited her grave in 1899.

sources.quote: My dearest Otho, Prepare yourself for an astounding piece of news! I am engaged to Oscar Wilde and perfectly and insanely happy.
sources.context: Constance Lloyd to her brother Otho Holland Lloyd, 26 November 1883, 1 Ely Place, Dublin. Editors' n. 1 at p. 221 gives her main particulars: "Constance Mary Lloyd (1858–98) was the daughter of Horace Lloyd, QC (1828–74)", and that she "had first met Wilde in London two years earlier" (her letter of 7 June 1881 quoted there).

sources.quote: My children are taken from me by an order of the court. I am legally no longer their father. I have no right to speak to them. If I try to communicate with them I can be put into prison for contempt of court. My wife also is of course wounded with me for what she considers a breach of faith on my part. On Monday I sign here a deed of separation of the most painfully stringent kind and of the most humiliating conditions. If I try to communicate with my wife against her will, or without her leave, I lose my wretched £150 a year at once. My life is to be ruled after a pattern of respectability.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 13 May [1897], HM Prison, Reading - written days before release, describing the deed of separation he was about to sign.

relationships.date_label: August–September 1894, Worthing and Brighton
relationships.summary: Wilde and Douglas met Alphonse Conway launching boats on Worthing beach in August 1894; for six weeks he was Wilde's companion, lunching and dining with the family, and receiving a cigarette case, photograph, book, walking-stick, and a blue serge suit before a twenty-four-hour Brighton trip (~27 September, adjoining rooms). Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at Worthing and the Albion Hotel; the charge was never brought to trial and Conway never gave evidence, though he was seen outside the Court in May 1895.

disputed.disputed_by: Wilde's sworn denials at the libel trial ('It is not true that I met him by appointment one evening and took him on the road to Lancing, kissing him and indulging in familiarities on the way') and at the final trial

relationships.date_label: fellow prisoners in Reading; staying with Wilde at Berneval-sur-Mer and introduced to Wilde's friends in June 1897
relationships.summary: Arthur Cruttenden was a saddler who had served time in Reading with Wilde. In June 1897, barely a month out of prison himself, Wilde had him to stay at Berneval, set about finding someone who could put him back into trade, and wrote to Reggie Turner twice in one day to introduce him - the second time to add that he sang and wrote songs, and to ask Turner to receive him as a friend rather than a case.

sources.quote: Dear Reggie, I write to you a little line to present Arthur Cruttenden to you. He will tell you all the Berneval news. He really is a nice simple fellow, and a good musician, I find. He sings, and writes songs. I hope you will be able to see him as a friend of mine. He is very sensitive to kindness.
sources.context: The second of two letters Wilde wrote to Reggie Turner on 16 June 1897, this one at 1.15 p.m. from the Café Suisse, Dieppe. The first, earlier the same day from Berneval, calls Cruttenden "a very simple nice fellow" who "has been gentle and unassuming and grateful", and sets out the plan to get him back into business as a saddler. Both are printed on the same page.
sources.supports: Wilde's personal regard for him, and the deliberate attempt to place him socially rather than charitably.

relationships.date_label: correspondence from June 1901; eloped 4 March 1902; separated 1913; attachment maintained until her death, 1944
relationships.summary: The courtship began with Custance's admiring letter to Douglas in June 1901 and ran on role-play correspondence — Fairy Prince for Douglas, Princess and boyish Page for Custance — plus secret meetings, several in the upper room of Robert Ross's Carfax gallery. Douglas abandoned an American heiress-hunt for her; Custance jilted her fiancé George Montagu and eloped with Douglas on 4 March 1902, honeymooning at the Hôtel Rastadt, Paris; their son Raymond was born 17 November 1902. Strained by litigation, money trouble, and the custody fight for Raymond, the couple separated in 1913 but never divorced; from 1932 Custance lived near Douglas in Hove, seeing him nearly every day until she died in 1944.

sources.quote: Custance wrote to Douglas in June 1901, praising the “fairy land” of his poems and signing herself as “Opal” (which, as Patricia Pulham notes, refers not only to her debut volume but also to her changeable, flirtatious personality). The two poets began to correspond, playfully using the personas of Fairy Prince for Douglas, and Princess and boyish Page for Custance; alternating these masculine and feminine identities allowed Custance to negotiate Douglas’s bisexual desires.
sources.context: Parker's scholarly biography of Custance on Yellow Nineties 2.0, paragraph on the Douglas courtship; the same paragraph notes the match was opposed by Custance's parents.
sources.supports: Courtship by correspondence begins June 1901; the Prince/Princess/Page personas; Custance's 'Opal' signature.
sources.provenance: https://1890s.ca/custance_bio/ fetched (curl) and read in full 2026-08-03; quote extracted byte-exact from the downloaded HTML, line-wrap whitespace normalized.

sources.quote: The couple eloped on 4 March 1902 and honeymooned in Paris. This was a particularly busy year for Custance as her second volume Rainbows was published in 1902 (again by The Bodley Head) and she gave birth to a son Raymond on 17 November 1902.

sources.quote: My own Prince, The little heart is sweet and I shall wear it even when you have forgotten all about me and married the beautiful rich princess who will give you all those lovely things you ought to have. I miss you more than I can ever say for I love you beyond everything in the world and I think we shall never be happy together again. Write to me soon and tell me you love your little Page, and that one day you will come back to ‘him’, my Prince, my Prince.
sources.context: Olive Custance to Lord Alfred Douglas, autumn 1901, thanking him for a heart-shaped locket containing a strand of his hair before he sailed for America. The Prince/Page address is theirs, and it runs both ways: Murray quotes Douglas asking her, 'Why can't you dress up as a boy and come with me?' and later, 'how could I after I have known the dear little page?' Murray's own reading on the same page: 'Both had a strongly homosexual nature so the masculine side of Olive attracted Douglas while the feminine side of him attracted her.' They married at St George's, Hanover Square, on 4 March 1902.
sources.supports: Courtship-letter texture; elopement details; separation and later relations.

sources.quote: Thus, on 4 March 1902, Lord Alfred Douglas and Olive Custance became man and wife at St George's, Hanover Square. Douglas was accompanied by his sister, Lady Edith Fox-Pitt, and the other witness was a friend called Cecil Hayes. … Another person was present at the wedding. From the back of the church Robert Ross watched.
sources.context: Murray on the elopement: Olive was staying with the family of her fiance George Montagu that weekend while Douglas obtained a special licence; she told her maid what she intended and arrived at the church with her bags packed. Lady Queensberry followed the service in her prayer book at home. The elision drops Lady Queensberry's message to her son and the note that her own marriage to Douglas's father had taken place in the same church; the sentences after the quote are Murray's own gloss on what Ross felt, not evidence.

relationships.date_label: Paris, c. 1901; contact sustained after Custance's return to London that year
relationships.summary: Olive Custance met Renee Vivien in Paris around 1901 through Natalie Barney, whose former lover Vivien was, and the two became friends. Vivien's roman a clef A Woman Appeared to Me (1904) fictionalises Custance as the 'little English poetess Dagmar', and Sarah Parker reads the novel as suggesting the two had a brief love affair - the sole basis for that claim in anything read here. Custance kept up contact with Vivien as well as Barney after moving back to London in 1901, the year before she eloped with Lord Alfred Douglas.

sources.quote: However, Vivien’s roman à clef A Woman Appeared to Me (1904) fictionalises Custance as the “little English poetess Dagmar” and suggests that she and Custance enjoyed a brief love affair.
sources.context: Sarah Parker's Y90s biography of Olive Custance, following the Mytilene sentence. Note the verb: the novel 'suggests', it does not attest. Parker's peer-reviewed 2011 article files the Barney and Vivien connections together as 'rumoured entanglements' (Wickes 1977: 58-60; Souhami 2004).
sources.supports: The affair claim, at exactly the strength the source gives it; and the Dagmar identification.

sources.quote: “Should one be afraid of love?” she asked, so simply that I drew back from the kiss she offered. … My little virgin with the short curls had stayed away for many days. … She stopped, then with a trembling sigh: “The Prince I waited for has come to me . .”
sources.context: A Woman Appeared to Me, chapters XVII-XVIII: the narrator and Dagmar
sources.supports: What the novel actually depicts, against which Parker's 'brief love affair' has to be read: an offered kiss refused, Dagmar described as a virgin, and her engagement announced.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 94 rendered and; folio 52 at the foot. Three passages from the same and facing pages, joined by ellipses. This is Foster's 1976 English, NOT Vivien's French - the 1904 French wording is still unverified, and the phrasing here is the translator's.

sources.quote: « Faut-il craindre l’amour ? » demanda-t-elle, si simplement que, devant le baiser qu’elle m’offrait, je reculai.. Je reculai comme un être que la démence a frappé à demi recule devant le meurtre conçu en une heure insensée. … La vierge aux boucles légères s’éloigna pendant de longs jours.
sources.context: Renée Vivien, Une femme m'apparut… (1904), chapters XVII-XVIII: the narrator and Dagmar
sources.supports: The same passage in Vivien's own French, which is what the claim turns on. It confirms the substance - the offered kiss is refused, and Dagmar is 'la vierge' at this point - while showing that Foster's English overstates the possessiveness: Vivien writes 'La vierge aux boucles légères', the virgin with the light curls, where Foster gives 'My little virgin with the short curls', adding a possessive and a diminutive and changing the adjective. Foster likewise renders 'le Prince inconnu' as 'the Unknown Lover'. The narrative facts are Vivien's; some of the colouring is the translator's.
sources.provenance: Read from the BnF Partenariats EPUB of the Gallica 1904 digitisation, in the repo. EPUB has no pagination, so cited by chapter. Confirmed to be the first edition by the Vally/Lorély test - Vally 153 occurrences, Lorély none.
sources.translation: 'Must one fear love?' she asked, so simply that, faced with the kiss she was offering me, I drew back… I drew back as a creature half-struck by madness draws back from a murder conceived in an insane hour. … The virgin with the light curls kept away for long days.
sources.translation_note: **A published English version exists and differs**: Foster gives 'My little virgin with the short curls', adding a possessive and a diminutive and changing the adjective, and renders 'le Prince inconnu' as 'the Unknown Lover'. The literal reading is given here precisely because that difference is what this quotation was entered to show.

disputed.claim: That Olive Custance and Renee Vivien had a brief love affair in or around 1901.
disputed.asserted_by: Sarah Parker's Y90s biography of Custance, reading Vivien's roman a clef A Woman Appeared to Me (1904), in which Custance appears as 'the little English poetess Dagmar'; Parker's verb is 'suggests'.
disputed.disputed_by: Nobody, in anything read so far - no source contests it. It is recorded as uncorroborated because nothing independent supports it, not because it was challenged.
disputed.grounds: A single scholar's inference from a single work of fiction written by one of the two parties three years after the fact. THE FICTION HAS NOW BEEN READ (2026-08-04), and it does not depict the affair Parker's word points to. The narrator desires Dagmar and declares love, but when Dagmar offers a kiss the narrator draws back from it; Dagmar is called 'my little virgin'; she then announces her 'Prince' and marries. The novel closes with San Giovanni relaying Dagmar's question whether the narrator resents her, 'that she couldn't cure you by loving you with the terrific ardor you demanded of her' (p. 58). So on its own terms the book depicts an unconsummated courtship declined by both parties in turn, not a love affair. Gayle Rubin, introducing the translation, reads it the same way: the narrator 'attempts to console herself with Dagmar'. The French of the first edition has now been read too, and it holds: 'devant le baiser qu’elle m’offrait, je reculai'. Parker's reading is not unreasonable - the erotic charge is real and sustained - but the text does not carry it as far as 'enjoyed a brief love affair', and this remains a novel either way. Parker's own peer-reviewed article (2011, p. 1) puts the Barney and Vivien connections in the register of 'rumoured entanglements'. The friendship and sustained contact are separately documented and not in question.

relationships.date_label: accepted him in 1887; m. August 1888; ended by his death, 19 October 1894
relationships.summary: Mary Robinson accepted James Darmesteter in 1887, over the objections of both families, and married him in August 1888, moving to Paris. It ended her eight-year partnership with Vernon Lee, who broke down at the announcement and was depressed for a long time after the wedding; Kit Anstruther-Thomson took Robinson's place as Lee's companion the same year. Darmesteter died in 1894 after a short illness. Five years later Robinson - by then Mme Darmesteter - and Lee were still writing to each other, and arranging through discreet intermediaries to return each other's old love letters.

sources.context: Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography of Vernon Lee, in the paragraph on Lee's emergence in 1880. The following sentences record Robinson's account of the visitors to 'Casa Paget' and Lee's return visit to London in 1881, at which she met Wilde.

relationships.date_label: Three days at Genoa, on Wilde's journey from the Riviera into Switzerland, recounted in a letter postmarked 20 March 1899 from Gland. The letter dates neither the stop nor the days; the February 1899 placing of that journey is an itinerary inference, not read in the source.
relationships.summary: On his way from the Riviera to Harold Mellor's villa at Gland, Wilde broke his journey at Genoa and met a young Florentine actor named Didaco, with whom he spent three days. He reported it to Reginald Turner in a letter postmarked 20 March 1899 - a named, dated, first-person-attested liaison of the exile years, and one of the few for which Wilde records the other man's name. Nothing further about Didaco survives in the correspondence read: the letter ends on the following printed page with no second mention.

sources.quote: On my way I stopped at Genoa, where I met a beautiful young actor, a Florentine, whom I wildly loved. He has the strange name of Didaco. He had the look of Romeo, without Romeo's sadness: a face chiselled for high romance. We spent three days together.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Turner, [postmark 20 March 1899], Gland, Switzerland - the closing paragraph on the printed page; the letter continues onto printed 1133 and ends there without returning to Didaco.
sources.supports: The whole of the record: Wilde's account of meeting Didaco at Genoa, of loving him, and of three days spent together

CORROBORATION: Cook returns to this in Queer Domesticities (2014) p. 99, where the sexual relationship is stated in his own voice as settled background - the anecdote turns on his refusing a *third* man, not on the fact of the pair.
relationships.date_label: Oct. 1893 (introduced at Wilde's Savoy dinner, 15 Oct.) - mid-1890s; the Albany night(s) undated by Cook, necessarily after 30 June 1894 (E4 move-in). Attachment ended when 'Douglas turned on Wilde' (Ives marked him 'traitor' in the diary; undated).
relationships.summary: A brief liaison within the Wilde circle: Wilde brought Ives and Douglas together at a Savoy dinner on 15 October 1893 (recorded in Ives's diary), and Douglas visited and spent at least one night at Ives's chambers at E4 the Albany, where Ives refused to allow a third man to join them - 'it wouldn't do in the Albany'. Ives's diary records that he repeatedly warned Douglas over his recklessness while having 'no objection to the thing itself', and after Douglas turned on Wilde, Ives wrote 'traitor' against his name.

sources.quote: I warned Lord A more than once that he was indulging in homosexuality to a reckless and highly dangerous degree. For tho' I had no objection to the thing itself we were all afraid he would get arrested any day.

sources.supports: PROMOTED TO LEAD by the Q2 quality pass 2026-08-03: the only passage on this edge in which a participant speaks, and the most explicit characterization available of what Ives thought he was doing with Douglas. The clause that carries it is 'I had no objection to the thing itself' - Ives conceding the sex and objecting only to the risk of arrest, which is as close to a plain statement of a sexual relationship as either man left. Ives's diary, undated entry, as quoted by Cook (2003); Cook prints no more of it than this, so the fuller text remains a target in the Ives papers and in Kaplan (2005).

relationships.certainty_reasoning: MCKENNA read in the source, 2026-08-03 - this record's basis changed. (2) The dating is corrected: McKenna places the meeting in 1893, with Wilde's involvement with Walter Grainger as the time-marker, not before or around Douglas's 1891 introduction to Wilde as this record previously framed it. Against McKenna stand two biographers read in full who never assert it - see the disputed block.
relationships.date_label: co-present in Wilde's circle by mid-1892; alleged early-1890s intimacy; friendly until c. 1912; open enmity from 1913 until Ross's death (1918)
relationships.summary: Douglas and Ross were fellow intimates of Wilde from 1892 and remained on good terms long after Wilde's death: Custance and Douglas courted in the upper room of Ross's Carfax gallery with his consent, and Ross stood at the back of the church at their 1902 wedding. McKenna and others have alleged a brief affair between the two around Douglas's entry into the circle; no primary evidence for it was reachable so far, and the Letters apparatus records only the Lionel Johnson introduction of 1891. From the Ransome libel trial of 1913 — brought over a book Douglas said was written 'at the instigation of' Ross — the friendship collapsed into open war: Douglas libelled Ross in deliberately actionable terms ('a notorious sodomite', among others) until Ross prosecuted him at the Old Bailey, where an eight-day trial ended without a verdict; the enmity ran until Ross's death in 1918.

disputed.claim: That the Douglas-Ross connection was sexual or romantic, as distinct from a close friendship.
disputed.asserted_by: Neil McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde, PDF p. 378, read in the source 2026-08-03: 'some sort of relationship ensued, sexual as well as emotional'. His own characterization; the Douglas quotation he adduces attests devotion and admiration only.
disputed.disputed_by: Two biographers read in full, by informative silence. Douglas Murray, Bosie (2020 edn): 388 Ross occurrences across 103 pages, every pre-1900 one read in context, never asserts or rejects an affair; at the point where it would belong he writes friendship. Jonathan Fryer, Robbie Ross (2000), Ross's own biographer: asserts nothing romantic, and his index subheadings for Douglas are 'battle against Ross' and 'and the Dansey affair'. Fryer states negatives explicitly when he means them - he writes that Ross and More Adey shared lodgings 'not as lovers, but as two bachelor friends' - which is what makes his silence here carry weight.
disputed.grounds: One asserting biographer against two silent ones, with the single piece of participant testimony falling short of the claim. Fryer does record that Ross named Douglas among the three most important men in his life (p. 198) - importance, in indirect speech, not romance.

sources.quote: While Oscar was busy with Walter Grainger, Bosie was having his own sexual adventures. Earlier in the year he had met Robbie Ross, and some sort of relationship ensued, sexual as well as emotional. 'Ross was by way of being devoted to me in those days,' Bosie recalled in his Autobiography:
sources.context: McKenna, in the chapter on the summer of 1893; 'earlier in the year' places the meeting in 1893, with Wilde's involvement with Walter Grainger as the time-marker. The colon introduces the Douglas quotation carried in the next source.
sources.supports: The assertion at issue: McKenna states a Douglas-Ross relationship 'sexual as well as emotional'. Note it is McKenna's own characterization, and that he dates the meeting to 1893 - not, as this record previously framed it, to before or around Douglas's 1891 introduction to Wilde.

sources.quote: If I had followed his example and kept the letters he wrote to me, I could have showed that he professed devotion and admiration for me in as extravagant terms as those used by Oscar.
sources.context: Lord Alfred Douglas, Autobiography, quoted by McKenna immediately after the sentence above
sources.supports: Douglas's own words - the only participant testimony on this pair. They attest devotion and admiration professed by Ross, not a sexual relationship; the sexual reading is McKenna's addition.

sources.quote: My dearest Bobbie, Bosie has insisted on stopping here for sandwiches. He is quite like a narcissus – so white and gold. I will come either Wednesday or Thursday night to your rooms. Send me a line. Bosie is so tired: he lies like a hyacinth on the sofa, and I worship him. You dear boy. Ever yours OSCAR
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, [? May–June 1892], Royal Palace Hotel, Kensington. Editors' note 1 at the page: 'This letter cannot be dated exactly, but it seems likely to have been written fairly soon after May 1892 (see p.461).' Earliest read evidence of Douglas and Ross sharing Wilde's intimate orbit — evidence of co-presence, not of relations between the two.
sources.supports: By mid-1892 Wilde writes to Ross about Bosie in terms assuming familiarity; the two men are co-members of the inner circle.

sources.quote: I subsequently discovered that Robert Ross during the marriage ceremony was in the church in the background. I had taken him into my confidence because, as I have already said, Olive and I used to meet occasionally at his little picture shop in Ryder Street. For some extraordinary reason Ross always seemed to resent my marriage. All the same, I continued to be on good terms with him for several years after it took place, and he professed to be devoted to Olive, and made every effort to ingratiate himself with her.
sources.context: Douglas on his 4 March 1902 wedding; p. 197 (image-verified) has the pre-wedding meeting 'in the upper room of Robert Ross's little picture shop, "Carfax," in Ryder Street, with his consent.' Partisan retrospect written mid-hatred (1929): the 'resentment' gloss is Douglas's reading, not evidence of Ross's state of mind.
sources.supports: Friendly relations at and 'for several years after' the 1902 wedding; Ross hosted the couple's secret meetings and attended the ceremony.
sources.provenance: IA autobiographyofl0000doug leaf 226, IIIF page image read 2026-08-03; printed folio 198 confirmed (Carfax sentence verified at leaf 225, folio 197).

sources.quote: This is what happened to me in 1913. I had long ceased to have any connection with the Wilde gang or cult. … Yet when I appealed to the courts for protection against a malicious statement made in a book at the instigation of the late Robert Ross (who hated me and had sworn to revenge himself on me because I declined to go on associating with him) to the effect that I was responsible for the ruin of Oscar Wilde, the courts, instead of protecting me as they should have done, allowed me to be flung to the wolves.
sources.context: Douglas on the Ransome libel trial (1913), which he lost; his aftermath campaign is described at pp. 42-43 (image-verified, in the dossier): 'I swore the day after the Ransome trial that I would never rest till I had publicly exposed Ross … I libelled Ross and at last forced him to take criminal proceedings against me', with the libels listed at p. 43 ('a notorious sodomite', etc.) and 'The trial lasted eight days at the Old Bailey.' All of it Douglas's partisan telling.
sources.supports: The break dated to 1913 (Ransome trial) — with Douglas himself placing the estrangement earlier ('because I declined to go on associating with him'); Douglas's belief that Ross instigated the Ransome book.
sources.provenance: IA autobiographyofl0000doug leaf 51, IIIF page image read 2026-08-03; printed folio 33 confirmed (campaign passages verified at leaves 60-61, folios 42-43).

sources.quote: Friendship with Wilde meant that Douglas began to move in a new circle of people. … Of them, perhaps the most important was Robert Ross. … Whether or not he was 'the first boy Oscar ever had', he was certainly devoted to Wilde, and when he was ousted as Wilde's lover by a series of attractive young men, he grew bitter. When Douglas first got to know him, though, Ross was an amusing and appealing personality. The two quickly became friends, as did More Adey who shared rooms with Ross.
sources.context: Murray's full account of how Douglas came to know Ross, in the chapter on Douglas's entry into Wilde's circle (1891-92). This is the passage where a Douglas-Ross affair would have to appear if Murray held one; it does not. The elisions drop only Murray's characterisation of the circle ('cultured, usually witty and sometimes talented') and Ross's Canadian birth, 1886 meeting with Wilde and King's, Cambridge years. Murray's account of Ross being displaced is about WILDE's affections, not Douglas's.
sources.supports: Non-corroboration of the alleged early-1890s Douglas-Ross affair by a named biographer who can be read in the source: Murray's account of their meeting is friendship formed inside Wilde's circle, with the rivalry running through Wilde rather than between the two men.
