NO PRINTED FOLIO EXISTS: the file is an ebook conversion with no page numbers, no running heads and an unpaginated Contents, so the offset is n/a and the locator is the PDF page, marked 'PDF p.' - see the pagination note in the DOUGLAS-MURRAY dossier (long-form research notes, kept in the private research repository).

sources.quote: Ross had known a pupil there, Philip Danney, since the lad was fourteen. Danney was now sixteen and Ross invited him to 'stay' with him in London. A smitten Ross communicated the boy's presence in London to Douglas, who was still in Goring with Wilde.
sources.context: Autumn 1893, from a letter of Max Beerbohm to Reginald Turner. The school was the Reverend Biscale Hale Wortham's at Bruges. Murray continues on the next PDF page: Douglas's 'response was to rush to London, seduce the boy and take him back to Goring', and quotes Oscar Browning's summary - 'On Saturday the boy slept with Douglas, on Sunday he slept with Oscar.' Danney's father went to the police and then dropped it 'when he realised that although Ross and Douglas would be sentenced to two years each, his own son would spend six months in prison'; Ross hid in Davos and Douglas left for Egypt. Ages are stated exactly as Murray states them (README register rule).
sources.supports: The closest thing in Murray to intimacy between the two men in the alleged period - and it runs through a third person, not between them: Ross passes the boy's whereabouts to Douglas, and the two are jointly exposed to prosecution. Evidence of shared sexual milieu, not of a relationship.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 68 and 69 of Murray_2020_Bosie, both; no printed folios (ebook conversion). The quoted sentences are contiguous on PDF p. 68; the continuation quoted in the context line is at PDF p. 69.

sources.quote: I agree with you that it is better that we should keep apart. I don't consider that you have ever been a real friend of mine, in the sense that More and others have been my friends. And I may tell you frankly that I don't think your character has improved with age.
sources.context: Douglas to Ross, c. early 1909, the closing paragraph of the letter breaking off relations - written after Ross declined Olive Custance's attempts to bring the two men to lunch. The paragraph before it, quoted by Murray on the same page, contains the sentence Murray calls 'actionable in itself': 'I do not care to meet those who are engaged in active propaganda of every kind of wickedness from anarchy to sodomy.' Ross's solicitor Sir George Lewis advised him against proceeding. Murray notes the reference to More Adey 'would soon be proved sadly misguided'.
sources.supports: Douglas's own retrospective denial, in 1909 and in his own hand, that Ross had ever been a real friend - dating the break four years before the Ransome trial and locating it in Douglas's post-conversion turn against homosexuality rather than in 1913.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 170 of Murray_2020_Bosie; no printed folio (ebook conversion).
sources.speaker: Lord Alfred Douglas

sources.quote: Relations between Bosie and Robbie were deteriorating fast. Though Robbie once said that the three most important men in his life had been Oscar Wilde, Bosie Douglas and Freddie Smith, by the end of 1907, relations with Bosie were distinctly frosty.
sources.context: Fryer at the November 1907 dinner Ross gave for Vyvyan Holland's twenty-first birthday, to which Douglas was not invited. Reported in indirect speech with no note number at the sentence; Fryer identifies no source for Ross's remark.
sources.supports: A reported first-person statement by Ross placing Douglas beside his two documented lovers - Wilde and Freddie Smith - as the three most important men in his life. The claim reported is IMPORTANCE, not romance, and it is unsourced on the page: a lead toward a Douglas-Ross intimacy, not evidence of one.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 220 of Fryer_2000_Robbie-Ross (docs/research/queer-history/victorian/ross/sources/), printed folio 198 confirmed on the rendered page. Offset is +22 in this half of the scan and +14 in the first half - see the pagination box in the ROSS-FRYER dossier (long-form research notes, kept in the private research repository).

sources.quote: Adey became more than just a friend and collaborator to Robbie, as the two of them shared lodgings for several years at 24 Hornton Street, Kensington, not as lovers, but as two bachelor friends with a common interest in art, literature, companionship, gossip and sitting around in armchairs for hours on end smoking cigarettes.
sources.context: Fryer's introduction of the Hornton Street household, spring 1892. Filed here as the calibration case: this is what it looks like when Fryer wants to rule a relationship out, and he does it in the same sentence that establishes the cohabitation. He never does anything comparable - in either direction - for Douglas and Ross.
sources.supports: Non-corroboration calibrated: Fryer's readiness to state a negative explicitly is what makes his silence on a Douglas-Ross affair informative rather than merely incurious.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 80, printed folio 66 confirmed on the rendered page.

null_findings.finding: COMPLETE SCAN of all 304 pages: eleven sentences contain both a Douglas token (Bosie/Douglas) and an intimacy token (lover/affair/slept with/sexual/seduced/in love with). NONE asserts a Ross-Douglas relationship. All eleven are false positives: 'the two lovers' means Wilde and Bosie (p. idx105); 'affair' means 'matter' (the Dansey affair, the Salome Row); Drumlanrig and Rosebery; Bosie's 'sexual interest in young women'; Crosland's attack ON Ross as a 'seducer of young boys'; and two index pages. The strongest single datum runs the other way: Douglas's own solicitors tried to get a Pentonville prisoner to state he had had sexual relations with Ross. Fryer - the biographer with the best access to Ross's papers and every incentive to know - never makes the claim. This confirms the absence the pointer was raised to test.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Murray quotes in the source, in the Foreword to the 2020 edition, letters written by Douglas to Schwabe in 1893 that surfaced in an Australian archive after the 2000 publication: Douglas addresses Schwabe as his 'darling pretty boy' and calls himself Schwabe's 'loving boy-wife'. Murray's 2000 text had already read the pair that way by inference ('It is fairly easy to guess what Douglas's relationship with Schwabe had been'), and Murray revisits the inference in 2020 in light of the letters.
relationships.date_label: friends 'for some years' before 1892; the surviving letters written 1893; Schwabe staying with Douglas several months after Douglas's March 1902 wedding
relationships.summary: Maurice Schwabe was Douglas's friend before he was Wilde's: Murray has Douglas introducing him to Wilde's circle out of his own Oxford set, and reads their relationship as sexual. Letters from Douglas to Schwabe of 1893, unknown when the biography was first published in 2000 and quoted in the Foreword to the 2020 edition, address Schwabe as 'My darling pretty boy' and sign Douglas as his 'loving boy-wife'. Schwabe, returned from Australia, was staying with Douglas several months after Douglas's marriage to Olive Custance in March 1902 - which is what makes Murray, re-reading, 'wonder' whether his own account of Douglas's later life was too clean.

sources.quote: Since the publication of this book some missing letters from Bosie to Maurice Schwabe have surfaced in an Australian archive. Written in 1893, Bosie addresses Schwabe as 'My darling pretty boy', continuing, 'I really love you far more than any other boy in the world and shall always be your loving boy-wife, or your "little bitch" if you prefer it.'
sources.context: Foreword to the 2020 Edition, in the paragraph where Murray revises his 2000 view of Douglas's later sexuality; the preceding sentence is 'it does seem unlikely that there was no gay feeling in Bosie in later life', and the following sentences record that Schwabe, back from Australia, stayed with Douglas several months after Douglas's wedding, and that Murray, re-reading, 'wonder[s]'.
sources.supports: First-person letters by Douglas, quoted in the source by his biographer, addressing Schwabe in explicitly amorous and self-feminising terms - the class-deciding evidence for this edge.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 20 of Murray_2020_Bosie (docs/research/queer-history/victorian/douglas/sources/). NO PRINTED FOLIO EXISTS: the repo file is an ebook conversion with no page numbers, no running heads and an unpaginated Contents; the offset is n/a and the locator is therefore the PDF page, marked 'PDF p.' so it cannot be mistaken for a printed folio.

sources.quote: When he met Olive his homosexual activities were suspended but he did not drop his old friends. Only a few months after his marriage he told his wife in a letter that Maurice Schwabe was staying with him, and he stayed in touch with Reginald Turner, Max Beerbohm and More Adey.
sources.context: Murray's 2000 text, opening the section on the first years of Douglas's marriage to Olive Custance (married March 1902); Murray's endnote 47 hangs on the Schwabe clause, i.e. the statement rests on Douglas's own letter to his wife. This is the fact Murray returns to in the 2020 Foreword when he writes that, re-reading, he 'wonder[s]'.
sources.supports: That Douglas himself, in a letter to his wife a few months after the March 1902 wedding, reported Schwabe staying with him - the participant-sourced basis for this edge's end date.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 143 of Murray_2020_Bosie (docs/research/queer-history/victorian/douglas/sources/). NO PRINTED FOLIO EXISTS on the page (ebook conversion); locator is the PDF page, marked 'PDF p.'. Murray's superscript endnote marker 47, printed after 'staying with him,', is dropped from the transcription; nothing else altered.

sources.quote: Douglas introduced some of his Oxford friends to Wilde's circle, and one in particular made an impact: Maurice Schwabe had been a friend of Douglas for some years though his introduction to Wilde was unfortunate. … It is fairly easy to guess what Douglas's relationship with Schwabe had been, and that Wilde and Douglas were in the habit of swapping their young men.
sources.context: Murray's 2000 text, in the chapter on Douglas's entry into Wilde's circle; the elided sentences concern Schwabe's later role as 'a millstone around Wilde's neck' at the trials. Written before the Australian letters surfaced, so the reading is Murray's inference, not his evidence.
sources.supports: The precedence of the friendship (Schwabe was Douglas's friend first, 'for some years' before Wilde), and Murray's own reading of it as sexual - stated as inference.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 53; no printed folio on the page (ebook conversion - see the pagination note in the DOUGLAS-MURRAY dossier (long-form research notes, kept in the private research repository)). One elision, marked. evidence_date carries the date of the event described - Douglas bringing Schwabe into Wilde's circle, the friendship already some years old - not Murray's publication year, so the card sorts with the events rather than at the end of the run.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Editors' note (p. 646 n. 1) records that the Holloway/Courtfield letter texts are retranslations whose wording may be distorted 'but their substance need not be doubted.'

start.label: introduced by Lionel Johnson, 1891 (editors: most likely beginning of July); Wilde dated the friendship proper from May 1892

end.label: contact until Wilde's death; Douglas chief mourner at the funeral, 3 December 1900

phases.note: Acquaintance: four meetings in ~18 months by Wilde's own count (quoted p. 461).

Intimacy: 'I worship him' (to Ross, spring 1892); Babbacombe menage early 1893; Savoy/St James's Place routine 1893 (De Profundis, p. 686); quarrel-reconciliation cycle incl. Egypt separation winter 1893-94 ('our love has passed through. estrangement', pp. 577-8).

Post-release: correspondence resumed within a fortnight; reunion at Rouen 28-29 August 1897; Naples together from late September (cohabitation end-date and allowance crisis at pp. 979-996 not yet transcribed - pointer).

Paris years: intermittent contact ('Oscar has only seen Douglas once' - Ross, April 1898, p. 1054 n. 2); Douglas arrived the day after Wilde's death and followed the coffin, 3 December 1900 (p. 1222).

relationships.summary: The central relationship of the circle. Douglas (b. 1870), third son of the Marquess of Queensberry, was brought to Wilde at Tite Street by Lionel Johnson in 1891; Wilde dated the friendship proper from Douglas's blackmail appeal of May 1892. The surviving letters run from 'Dearest Bosie' (Nov 1892) through the Hyacinthus letter (Jan 1893, later used for blackmail and read at the trials), the crisis letters of 1893-95, De Profundis (1897), and the post-prison reunion at Rouen and Naples (Aug-Sep 1897). Queensberry's card of 18 February 1895 and the collapse of Wilde's libel suit led to Wilde's conviction; the relationship survived in attenuated form until Wilde's death in Paris, where Douglas was chief mourner.

sources.quote: Love me always, love me always. You have been the supreme, the perfect love of my life; there can be no other.
sources.context: Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas, [20 May 1895], [? 2 Courtfield Gardens], on bail between the trials, written the day the verdicts were ordered to be rendered separately; the letter closes 'O sweetest of all boys, most loved of all loves' and is signed OSCAR. Editors' n. 1 refers this text's provenance to their note on p. 646 - like the Holloway letters it survives as a retranslation whose wording may be distorted, 'but their substance need not be doubted'.
sources.supports: Wilde naming the relationship in the plainest terms the correspondence contains - Douglas as 'the supreme, the perfect love of my life; there can be no other' - written between the trials
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 703, printed folio 652 confirmed on the rendered page; the letter opens on printed 651 (PDF 702, folio confirmed). Contiguous sentences, no elision.

sources.quote: It was in the year 1891 that there entered Wilde's life the man who was to be in some sense his inspiration and in every sense his evil genius. Lord Alfred Bruce Douglas, the third son of the eighth Marquess of Queensberry, had been born in 1870, educated at Winchester and was now a second-year undergraduate at Magdalen College, Oxford. Lionel Johnson, a Winchester contemporary and Oxford friend, brought him to see Wilde at Tite Street.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial headnote on the first Wilde–Douglas meeting; the same note quotes Wilde to More Adey, 7 April 1897: "The friendship began in May 1892 by his brother appealing to me in a very pathetic letter to help him in terrible trouble with people who were blackmailing him. I hardly knew him at the time. I had known him eighteen months, but had only seen him four times in that space." ! Corrected 2026-08-05: this was tagged as a period voice, which attributed the editors' own headnote to Wilde himself and printed it under his name. It is Holland and Hart-Davis writing about him - the giveaway is in the quotation, which speaks of "Wilde's life" in the third person.
sources.supports: Meeting 1891 (editors: most likely ~beginning of July); introduction by Lionel Johnson; Douglas's parentage and birth year; Wilde's own May-1892 dating of the friendship.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 481 (printed p. 461, folio checked)

sources.quote: My dearest Bobbie, Bosie has insisted on stopping here for sandwiches. He is quite like a narcissus – so white and gold. … Bosie is so tired: he lies like a hyacinth on the sofa, and I worship him.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, [? May–June 1892], Royal Palace Hotel, Kensington; editors' n. 1 dates it "fairly soon after May 1892".
sources.supports: Earliest surviving intimate register about Douglas, told to a third party (Ross), spring 1892.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 546 (printed p. 526, folio checked)

sources.quote: My Own Boy, Your sonnet is quite lovely, and it is a marvel that those red rose-leaf lips of yours should have been made no less for music of song than for madness of kisses. Your slim gilt soul walks between passion and poetry. I know Hyacinthus, whom Apollo loved so madly, was you in Greek days. … Always, with undying love, yours OSCAR
sources.context: Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas, [? January 1893], [Babbacombe Cliff] — the 'Hyacinthus' letter; editors' n. 1: "This letter … was later stolen, used as material for the attempted blackmail of Wilde, and finally read out in court during the Queensberry and later trials."
sources.supports: Explicit love-letter register in Wilde's own hand; the letter itself became trial evidence.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 564 (printed p. 544, folio checked)

sources.quote: Dear Lady Queensberry, You have on more than one occasion consulted me about Bosie. Let me write to you now about him. … I like to think myself his greatest friend – he, at any rate, makes me think so – so I write to you quite frankly to ask you to send him abroad to better surroundings.
sources.context: Wilde to Lady Queensberry (Douglas's mother), [8 November 1893], 16 Tite Street; the letter urges sending Douglas to Egypt. Editors' n. 1: "This letter certainly helped to send him abroad for some months."
sources.supports: Wilde intimate enough with Douglas's mother to be consulted about him; the late-1893 crisis and engineered Egypt separation.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 627 (printed p. 575, folio checked)

sources.quote: I am happy in the knowledge that we are friends again, and that our love has passed through the shadow and the night of estrangement and sorrow and come out rose-crowned as of old. Let us always be infinitely dear to each other, as indeed we have been always.
sources.context: Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas, [Circa 20 December 1893], 10 & 11 St James's Place; Douglas had gone to Cairo on 2 December (editors' n. 3).
sources.supports: "Our love" in Wilde's own words; the quarrel-and-reconciliation pattern across the Egypt separation.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 629 (printed p. 577, folio checked)

sources.quote: My dearest boy, This is to assure you of my immortal, my eternal love for you. Tomorrow all will be over. If prison and dishonour be my destiny, think that my love for you and this idea, this still more divine belief, that you love me in return will sustain me in my unhappiness and will make me capable, I hope, of bearing my grief most patiently.
sources.context: Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas, Monday Evening [29 April 1895], HM Prison, Holloway, on the eve of the first Crown trial. Editors' n. 1 warns the text is a retranslation (via the Mercure de France affair) whose wording may be distorted "but their substance need not be doubted"; the same note records Douglas's statement that he later destroyed 150 of Wilde's letters.
sources.supports: Mutual love asserted at the moment of catastrophe ('that you love me in return').
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 697 (printed p. 646, folio checked)

sources.quote: My darling Oscar, Have just arrived here. It seems too dreadful to be here without you, but I hope you will join me next week. … Do keep up your spirits, my dearest darling. I continue to think of you day and night, and send you all my love. I am always your own loving and devoted boy BOSIE
sources.context: Lord Alfred Douglas to Wilde, Wednesday, 15 May 1895, Hôtel des Deux Mondes, Paris — printed by the editors in n. 3, who introduce it as "One of the only three letters from Douglas to Wilde which have been recovered (MS Clark)". Wilde was then on bail between the trials.
sources.supports: Reciprocity in Douglas's own voice during the trials — first-person evidence from the second participant.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 700 (printed p. 649, folio checked)
sources.speaker: Lord Alfred Douglas

sources.quote: Dear Bosie, After long and fruitless waiting I have determined to write to you myself, as much for your sake as for mine … Our ill-fated and most lamentable friendship has ended in ruin and public infamy for me, yet the memory of our ancient affection is often with me, and the thought that loathing, bitterness and contempt should for ever take that place in my heart once held by love is very sad to me …
sources.context: Opening of Wilde's prison letter to Douglas (De Profundis), [January–March 1897], HM Prison, Reading; the letter runs to p. 780. Editors' caution (p. 684 n. 1): "Wilde's indictments of Douglas in this letter need to be approached with caution. While some are undoubtedly valid, others, in the light of later research, seem both unfair to Douglas and inaccurate if taken entirely at face value."
sources.supports: Wilde's own retrospective naming of the relationship ('that place in my heart once held by love'); the prison rupture. Also p. 686 (read): the 1893 daily-inseparability routine ('We did not separate as a rule till after midnight').
sources.provenance: repo PDF pp. 734-7 (printed pp. 683-6, folios checked)

sources.quote: Everyone is furious with me for going back to you, but they don't understand us. I feel that it is only with you that I can do anything at all. Do remake my ruined life for me, and then our friendship and love will have a different meaning to the world. I wish that when we met at Rouen we had not parted at all. … But we love each other.
sources.context: Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas, Tuesday, 7.30 [? 31 August 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe — after their reunion meeting at Rouen. Editors' n. 1 (p. 933): "This fateful meeting seems to have taken place on 28–9 August. In his Autobiography Douglas wrote: 'Poor Oscar cried when I met him at the station. We walked about all day arm in arm, or hand in hand, and were perfectly happy.'"
sources.supports: The post-prison reunion decision against the circle's opposition; Rouen meeting 28-29 Aug 1897; corroborated to Ross, 4 Sept 1897 (p. 934, read): "Yes: I saw Bosie, and of course I love him as I always did, with a sense of tragedy and ruin."
sources.provenance: repo PDF pp. 982-4 (printed pp. 932-4, folios checked)

sources.quote: You tell me that you, and Bobbie, on being asked whether Bosie was 'a disreputable person' felt bound at once to say yes: and that you declared that my wife was acting 'strictly within her legal rights according to the agreement' in depriving me of my allowance, because I have the pleasure of Bosie's companionship, the only companionship in the world open to me.
sources.context: Wilde to More Adey, postmark 21 November 1897, Villa Giudice, Posilippo - written while living with Douglas at Naples, after Constance stopped the allowance.
sources.supports: Cohabitation at Naples from late September 1897 and its end when Constance's allowance and Lady Queensberry's terms cut the money off - pages not yet transcribed.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1037, printed folio 989 read off the rendered page - NOT p. 991; the volume's PDF/printed offset is not constant.

sources.quote: On Sunday, the next day, Alfred Douglas arrived, and various people whom I do not know called. … On Monday morning at 9 o'clock, the funeral started from the hotel – we all walked to the Church of St Germain des Prés behind the hearse – Alfred Douglas, Reggie Turner and myself, Dupoirier, the proprietor of the hotel … the second [coach contained] Alfred Douglas, Turner, the proprietor of the hotel, and myself … Wreaths came from, or at the request of, the following: Alfred Douglas, More Adey, Reginald Turner …
sources.context: Robert Ross's account of Wilde's death and funeral (funeral Monday 3 December 1900, per n. 1; Wilde died 30 November 1900). The letter's heading falls on a preceding page not read so far; the narrator is identified as Ross by p. 1222 n. 2.
sources.supports: Contact until death: Douglas came at once, walked behind the hearse and rode in the second coach, and sent a wreath.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 1267 (printed p. 1222, folio checked)
sources.speaker: Robert Ross

sources.quote: Douglas's candour in days when such acts could still condemn a man to prison is some proof of the truth of his statement, and his coyness is understandable.
sources.context: Murray's own comment on the passage of Douglas's memoir he has just quoted, in which Douglas describes what did and did not take place between him and Wilde on the first night, probably January 1892, at Tite Street. Douglas's account states that sodomy never took place, that Wilde 'treated me as an older boy treats a younger one at school', and names one specific act; Douglas adds that he never liked it, only consented to oblige Wilde, and that Wilde 'very soon cut it out altogether'. Douglas was 21. The full passage is transcribed in the DOUGLAS-MURRAY dossier (long-form research notes, kept in the private research repository); only Murray's framing sentence is carried here.
sources.supports: Douglas's own first-person account of the sexual relationship with Wilde, its specific and limited content, and its brevity - independent corroboration, from Douglas's side, of an edge otherwise carried by Wilde's letters.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 52 of Murray_2020_Bosie (docs/research/queer-history/victorian/douglas/sources/). NO PRINTED FOLIO EXISTS: the file is an ebook conversion with no page numbers and an unpaginated Contents, so the printed-to-PDF offset is n/a and the locator is the PDF page, marked 'PDF p.' - see the pagination note in the DOUGLAS-MURRAY dossier (long-form research notes, kept in the private research repository).

sources.quote: The sexual relationship between Wilde and Douglas was short-lived, but it was replaced in both by a taste for rent boys.
sources.context: Murray on spring 1893, in the paragraph where the blackmail over the 'Hyacinthus' letter begins; the preceding sentence distinguishes 'the romantic love for Douglas' from 'the sexual encounters with rent boys' as the two sides of Wilde's life.
sources.supports: The biographer's dating of the sexual phase as brief, with the romantic attachment outlasting it - the shape our date fields already carry (1891/92 start, contact to 1900).
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 60 of Murray_2020_Bosie (docs/research/queer-history/victorian/douglas/sources/). NO PRINTED FOLIO EXISTS: the file is an ebook conversion with no page numbers and an unpaginated Contents, so the printed-to-PDF offset is n/a and the locator is the PDF page, marked 'PDF p.' - see the pagination note in the DOUGLAS-MURRAY dossier (long-form research notes, kept in the private research repository).

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Murray states in passing that the blackmailers into whose hands Wilde's letters to Douglas fell were men 'with whom they had slept' - 'they' being Wilde and Douglas, the subject of the sentence. That is a single secondary source, asserting in the plural and without a footnote at the point of assertion, and no first-person evidence is offered for the Douglas half of the claim; Wood's own sworn testimony (which carries the wilde--wood edge) concerns Wilde.
relationships.date_label: acquaintance by late 1892 - early 1893; the blackmail from April 1893
relationships.summary: Alfred Wood was an out-of-work clerk from Oxford, who had worked as a valet in Douglas's Oxford rooms; Douglas befriended him and gave him several old suits, and Wilde's letters to Douglas reached the blackmailers from there - Murray thinks by theft from the rooms rather than by the pockets, as Wood claimed. Murray, describing the moment the two halves of Wilde's life converged, calls Wood one of the blackmailers 'with whom they had slept' - the only statement in the book that Douglas's relations with Wood were sexual, and one made in passing and in the plural.

disputed.claim: That Douglas, as well as Wilde, had sexual relations with Alfred Wood.
disputed.asserted_by: Douglas Murray, Bosie (2020 edn), PDF p. 60 - in a subordinate clause, unfootnoted at that point, and phrased as a class statement about 'blackmailers like Wood'.
disputed.disputed_by: Not rebutted in any source read so far. But nothing corroborates it: Wood's sworn testimony at the 1895 trials describes acts with Wilde, not with Douglas; Douglas was never charged; and the Complete Letters apparatus records only that Douglas gave Wood clothes and introduced him to Wilde by telegram.
disputed.grounds: Single secondary source; assertion made in passing and in the plural rather than itemised; no first-person or testimonial evidence for the Douglas half.

sources.quote: Wilde and Douglas were treading a dangerous path. Douglas had befriended a young and unemployed clerk from Oxford called Alfred Wood, who proved to be less than honest, and when letters from Wilde to Douglas turned up in the hands of blackmailers like Wood with whom they had slept, the two sides of Wilde's homosexual life came together: the romantic love for Douglas and the sexual encounters with rent boys.
sources.context: Murray's chapter on 1893, immediately after Wilde's Savoy letter to Douglas ('you must not make scenes with me') and the appearance of the first blackmailer with the stolen 'Hyacinthus' letter on 21 April 1893.
sources.supports: The whole of the claim: that Douglas befriended Wood, and Murray's assertion that Wilde and Douglas had both slept with him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 60 of Murray_2020_Bosie; no printed folio on the page - the file is an ebook conversion with no pagination (see the pagination note in the DOUGLAS-MURRAY dossier (long-form research notes, kept in the private research repository)), so the locator is the PDF page.

sources.quote: Douglas had given the unemployed clerk several of his old suits, and Wood claimed that he had found the letters in the pockets. Wood was in league with two other blackmailers, Allen and Clibborn, and it is highly improbable that Douglas would have been so careless. A likely explanation is that Wood simply stole the letters from Douglas's rooms at Oxford, where he had worked as a valet.
sources.context: Murray on the first criminal trial, where the prosecution laid emphasis on Wilde's letters to Douglas, 'which had been "found" by Alfred Wood' - Murray's scare quotes are his own. Later on the same page: the foreman of the jury asked the judge why no warrant had been issued for the arrest of Lord Alfred Douglas, and 'The judge said that something more than intimacy would have to be proved if a charge were to be made.'
sources.supports: The documented, non-sexual connection between the two men - Wood worked as a valet in Douglas's Oxford rooms, and the old suits Douglas gave him carried Wilde's letters to Douglas into a blackmailer's hands.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 95 of Murray_2020_Bosie; no printed folio on the page (ebook conversion).

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The evidence read so far is Wilde's own twelve letters to Dowson (the primary source for this pair) plus Dowson's own words about Wilde as printed by Frankel from the Flower-Maas edition - so BOTH participants are on record, which is rare here. That clears the README's bar twice over: the ardour is legible as ardour without the coding hypothesis, AND a scholarly source reads it that way (McKenna: 'their friendship suddenly seemed to deepen into love'). Frankel - the specialist monograph for exactly these years, and the most recent scholarship in the corpus - reads it flatly as 'frank and unguarded friendship' and never suggests otherwise; Dowson's own surviving words about Wilde are admiring, wry and entirely non-romantic; Dowson's documented sexual interest was in women, and by both Sox's and Frankel's accounts he tried to steer Wilde toward women; and the ardent lines are a handful within a correspondence that is otherwise practical (poems, absinthe, a translation, a debt). Sox prints it in an agentless passive with an endnote (n. 12) that names no describer and merely cross-refers to Wilde's own 16 June letter, which does not contain it; the phrase appears nowhere in the Complete Letters, so it is not Wilde's; and McKenna, the only other corpus source to use it, cites Sox p. 141 for it, closing the loop.
relationships.date_label: Acquainted from 1890; Dowson visited Wilde at Oakley Street between the trials, spring 1895. The letters that carry the ardour are Berneval/Dieppe, June-August 1897, concentrated in the fortnight 16-30 June; Dowson returned to England in mid-July 1897. Four further letters from Naples, October 1897, are practical. Wilde's last word on Dowson is his letter of condolence to Smithers, circa 24 February 1900.
relationships.summary: Dowson met Wilde in 1890 through the London literary world and, with Robert Sherard, called on him at Oakley Street between the trials in 1895 - one of very few who did. In the summer of 1897 he was living at Arques-la-Bataille near Dieppe and became the closest daily companion of Wilde's first free months, dining at Berneval on 3 June and thereafter meeting almost constantly at the Cafe Suisse in Dieppe. Wilde's letters over the following fortnight turn markedly warm: he tells Dowson there is 'a fatality about our being together', asks why he is 'so persistently and perversely wonderful', watches for the green costume that suits his 'dark hyacinth locks', calls his absence the one imperfection in an otherwise perfect day, and signs himself 'Tout a toi'. Dowson's own letters of the same weeks are affectionate but unromantic - he found Wilde's 'enormous joy in life' hard to match - and he is reported to have tried to interest Wilde in women; Wilde later told Fothergill they had quarrelled and that Dowson had cut off his long curls to spite him. The friendship survived it in a lower key, and when Dowson died in February 1900 Wilde asked Smithers to lay flowers on his grave.

sources.quote: There is a fatality about our being together that is astounding – or rather quite probable. Had I stayed at Arques I should have given up all hopes of ever separating from you. Why are you so persistently and perversely wonderful? … I suppose I shall see you in ten minutes from this. I am looking out for the green costume that goes so well with your dark hyacinth locks. … Now I am alive, and all is perfect, except your absence. Tout à toi
sources.context: Wilde to Ernest Dowson, [? 16 June 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe (MS Maguire); signed SEBASTIAN MELMOTH. Elisions drop the servant anecdote, the paragraph on Thompson and Socrates, the line 'Come with vine-leaves in your hair' (the editors gloss it to Ibsen's Hedda Gabler), and the first half of the Pernod sentence. Full letter in the dossier. 'Hyacinth' is Wilde's Douglas register: cf. Wilde to Douglas, 'Hyacinthus, whom Apollo loved so madly, was you in Greek days' (Complete Letters p. 544, cited at Frankel p. 328 n. 30).
sources.supports: Wilde's own most explicit statement of attachment to Dowson: inseparability, a compliment on Dowson's hair in the mythological register he used for Douglas, absence as the single flaw in the day, and 'Tout à toi'. This is also the letter Sox is quoting for both 'the green costume' and 'dark hyacinth locks'.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 951, printed folio 901 confirmed on the rendered page. Three elisions marked with spaced ellipses; nothing omitted alters the sense of what is quoted. The editors reproduce a photograph of Dowson in the unfoliated plate section (repo PDF 600, plate 85) captioned with the first sentence of this passage.

sources.quote: My dear Ernest, Do come here at once: Monsieur Meyer is presiding over a morning meal of absinthe, and we want you. I am a wreck of course, but la belle soeur is like the moon. You were wonderful and charming all last night. Ever yours OSCAR
sources.context: Wilde to Ernest Dowson, [? 24 June 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe (MS Maguire) - the entire letter. Line breaks between the three sentences run together here.
sources.supports: The register at its warmest outside the 16 June letter, and the daily rhythm of the Dieppe weeks
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 957, printed folio 907 confirmed on the rendered page.

sources.quote: Dear Ernest, I must see you: so I propose to breakfast at St Martin L'Eglise tomorrow at 11.30 and you must come: take a voiture and be there. I want to have a poet to talk to, as I have had lots of bad news since you left me. Do try, like a good chap, to be there, and wear a blue tie. I want to be consoled.
sources.context: Postcard, Wilde to Ernest Dowson, Monday [postmark 28 June 1897], [postmark Dieppe] (MS Maguire); signed SEBASTIAN MELMOTH. Italics on 'must', 'voiture' and 'blue' in the original. The 'bad news' is his solicitor's resignation and the cancellation of Douglas's visit (Frankel, p. 116).
sources.supports: Summons and dependence: Wilde asking to be consoled, and prescribing what Dowson is to wear - the second such instruction in a week
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 958, printed folio 908 confirmed on the rendered page.

sources.quote: Dear Ernest, I write a little line, whose only excuse is its entire illegibility, to tell you how charming you are (at Berneval) and how much I like your friend, and mine, the dear Achille. … You and Achille and Achille's friend and I must all be at Berneval together. I am making arrangements. Give to Achille my sincere friendship: you have it, and other things, always.
sources.context: Wilde to Ernest Dowson, Wednesday 6.30 [? 30 June 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe (MS Maguire); signed S. M. The letter runs over the printed 908/909 page break. 'Achille' is glossed by the editors as presumably Achille Fromentin. The elision drops the paragraph praising Dowson's 'lovely lyrics' and a passage about a costermonger. The closing clause is addressed to Dowson though its sentence is nominally about Achille.
sources.supports: The only line in the twelve letters that gestures at something withheld from the page ('and other things, always'), and the plan to gather the four of them at Berneval
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 958-959, printed folios 908 and 909 both confirmed on the rendered pages. One elision marked with a spaced ellipsis; full letter in the dossier.

sources.quote: Dowson was described as Wilde's 'first hyacinth since Douglas: But this flower was wilting, and had not much longer to live'. Despite the wilting, Wilde looked for 'the green costume' which went well with Dowson's 'dark hyacinth locks'. Fothergill commented that Dowson was in love with the owner of the Café Royal, but was 'faithful only after his fashion'. Although Dowson was in the house he did not appear. Wilde said they had quarrelled and Dowson, to spite him, 'had had all his long curls cut'.
sources.context: Sox, in the chapter 'Two Loves Have I', on the guests at Wilde's Chalet Bourgeat during Fothergill's own stay - 'Of the other guests at Chalet Bourgeat at this time, Fothergill mentioned seeing only two: Leonard Smithers … [and] the English poet Ernest Dowson' (p. 140). Sox's Part V note-head states that unnoted quotations in the section are from Fothergill's unpublished memoir, so the chain for the quarrel and the cut curls is Wilde -> Fothergill's memoir -> Sox. Endnote markers (nn. 12-13) omitted. CAUTION, and the reason this quote sits fifth rather than first: the 'first hyacinth' phrase is unattributed. Sox's n. 12 (printed p. 271) reads only 'Also see Hart-Davis, Selected Letters, pp. 290-1' - a cross-reference to Wilde's own 16 June letter, which does not contain the phrase. It is not Wilde's; McKenna, the only other corpus source to use it, cites Sox p. 141 for it. Whose words they are is a live open question. Note too the chronology tension: the Letters editors have Dowson back in England from mid-July (p. 924 n. 1), while Fothergill's undated visit falls in Wilde's last month at Berneval.
sources.supports: The only romantic characterization of the pair in the literature, and its unresolved attribution; Fothergill's counter-observation that Dowson's own attachment lay elsewhere; and the quarrel in which Dowson cut off the curls Wilde had admired - the evidential basis for outcome 'unreciprocated'
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 157, printed folio 141 confirmed on the rendered page; the setting sentence from repo PDF 156, printed folio 140 confirmed. Endnote 12 read on the rendered page at repo PDF 303, printed folio 271 confirmed, and the superscript markers on p. 141 checked in a 4x zoom render. Sox's index (printed p. 282) lists Dowson at p. 141 only, and a full-text search of the file confirms this is his sole treatment.

sources.quote: For his part, Dowson was impressed by Wilde's "enormous joy in life just at this moment" and "had some difficulty in suppressing my own sourness" as a result. His first impression was that Wilde had changed a great deal for the better: "he seems of much broader sympathies, much more human and simple. . His delight in the country, in walking, in the simplicities of life is enchanting." … "His gorgeous spirits cheered me mightily," Dowson wrote of Wilde at this time
sources.context: Frankel quoting Dowson's own letters of summer 1897, from Letters of Ernest Dowson, ed. Desmond Flower and Henry Maas (Fairleigh Dickinson UP, 1968), pp. 384 and 387 - his notes 64, 65 and 68 at printed pp. 324-325. The elision drops Frankel's intervening paragraph on the brothel story and the absinthe. Frankel's own reading of the pair, on the same page and the one before, is 'frank and unguarded friendship' and Dowson as 'one of his closest confidantes' (p. 113).
sources.supports: The second participant's own testimony - the counter-weight that keeps this edge below a relationship class. Dowson's register toward Wilde is admiring and wry, never romantic.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 128, printed folio 114 confirmed on the rendered page. Frankel's printed-to-PDF offset established so far as a constant PDF - 14, holding across body and notes (see DOWSON_dossier.md). Frankel p. 113 read at repo PDF 127, folio confirmed. One elision marked with a spaced ellipsis; Frankel's own internal ellipsis inside the Dowson quotation is his.

sources.quote: They met frequently, and their friendship suddenly seemed to deepen into love. It is unlikely that the relationship was ever sexual, but there may have been drunken embraces and declarations of undying love.
sources.context: McKenna on the June 1897 Dieppe weeks, immediately before he quotes the 'fatality about our being together' letter. This is the one scholarly reading in the corpus that names the connection as love, and it is explicitly speculative ('seemed', 'may have been'); works.json records that McKenna is never a sufficient basis on his own. The file carries no printed folios, so the locator is a PDF page.
sources.supports: The scholarly-reading half of the README's attraction-expressed bar - and, by its own hedging, the reason the class stays at attraction-expressed rather than rising higher
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 665; no printed folio or running head appears on the rendered page, consistent with the pagination warning on mckenna-2008 in works.json. McKenna's source note for the adjoining 'first hyacinth since Douglas' phrase, at repo PDF 852, reads 'Sox, Bachelors of Art, page 141'.

sources.quote: My dear Smithers, I am greatly distressed to hear of Ernest's death: how sudden it must have been! Poor wounded wonderful fellow that he was, a tragic reproduction of all tragic poetry, like a symbol, or a scene. I hope bay-leaves will be laid on his tomb, and rue, and myrtle too, for he knew what love is. He was a sweet singer … If he is not yet laid to rest or unrest, do put some flowers for me on his grave.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [circa 24 February 1900], Paris - written the day after Dowson died, and Wilde's last word on him. Addressed to a third party, so it is Wilde's own testimony but not part of the correspondence between the two men. The elision drops the simile comparing Dowson's note to birdsong in Shakespeare's day. The editors' footnote on the same page gives the death and burial particulars.
sources.supports: The close of the connection in Wilde's own voice; 'he knew what love is' is elegiac and unspecific - Wilde does not say for whom
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1219, printed folio 1173 confirmed on the rendered page. One elision marked with a spaced ellipsis; full passage in the dossier.

relationships.date_label: met on a Washington horsecar one stormy winter evening, 1865 by the scholarship and 1866 by Doyle's own reckoning; closest through the Washington years to about 1873, renewed in the mid-1880s when Doyle moved to Philadelphia, and running until Whitman's death on 26 March 1892
relationships.summary: Peter Doyle was twenty-one and conducting a Pennsylvania Avenue horsecar on a stormy night when Walt Whitman, forty-five, boarded as its only passenger with a blanket round his shoulders. By Doyle's account they understood one another before either had spoken much. They spent the Washington years riding the streetcars, eating fruit at Center Market and walking the Potomac by moonlight - Whitman reciting Shakespeare's sonnets, Doyle telling limericks - and Whitman was taken into Doyle's family. Whitman's stroke in 1873 and his move to Camden put a river and a state between them and the intensity cooled; Harry Stafford filled some of the gap in New Jersey. Doyle moved to Philadelphia in the mid-1880s and visited weekly until the nurses of Whitman's last years crowded him out. He came to the funeral. In 1897 he let Bucke print Whitman's letters to him, which is the only reason the relationship is documented at all; his own letters to Whitman largely are not.

sources.quote: You ask where I first met him? It is a curious story. We felt to each other at once. I was a conductor. The night was very stormy,—he had been over to see Burroughs before he came down to take the car—the storm was awful. Walt had his blanket—it was thrown round his shoulders—he seemed like an old sea-captain. He was the only passenger, it was a lonely night, so I thought I would go in and talk with him. Something in me made me do it and something in him drew me that way. He used to say there was something in me had the same effect on him. Anyway, I went into the car. We were familiar at once—I put my hand on his knee—we understood. He did not get out at the end of the trip—in fact went all the way back with me. I think the year of this was 1866. From that time on we were the biggest sort of friends.
sources.context: Doyle, interviewed by Richard Maurice Bucke and printed verbatim in Bucke's introduction under its own running head, 'INTERVIEW WITH PETER DOYLE'. This is the only substantial first-person account Doyle left of the relationship, and the source every later account of the meeting quotes. Note his own hedge on the year: the scholarship dates the meeting to 1865, Doyle says he thinks it was 1866. Henry James, reviewing the book in 1898, called this interview the most charming passage in the volume.
sources.supports: The meeting, in the other participant's own words - and the class, since it puts Doyle's voice beside Whitman's rather than leaving the edge resting on Whitman alone.
sources.provenance: Read as a rendered page image from the archive.org scan (calamusseriesofl00whitrich, scan n36) 2026-08-04; printed folio 23 confirmed on the image, with the running head 'INTERVIEW WITH PETER DOYLE'. Scan = printed + 13 at this point. The IA OCR text was used only to locate the passage.
sources.speaker: Peter Doyle, interviewed by R. M. Bucke

sources.quote: New York, Friday, 25 Sept., 1868. Dear Boy. I received your second letter yesterday—it is a real comfort to me to get such letters from you, dear friend. Every word does me good. … I put down off hand and write all about myself and my doings, etc., because I suppose that will be really what my dear comrade wants most to hear while we are separated.
sources.context: The first letter Bucke prints, opening the section headed 'LETTERS OF 1868'. The salutation is the volume's standard: Whitman writes to Doyle as 'Dear Boy', 'Dear Boy and Comrade' and 'Dear Pete' across the run. The elision drops two sentences about a newspaper and the timing of the post. Small capitals in the printed salutation normalised.
sources.supports: Whitman's own register toward Doyle at the start of the correspondence - 'dear friend', 'my dear comrade' - and the fact of a sustained private correspondence.
sources.provenance: Read as a rendered page image from the archive.org scan (calamusseriesofl00whitrich, scan n48) 2026-08-04; printed folio 35 confirmed on the image, with the running head 'LETTERS OF 1868'. Scan = printed + 13 at this point. The IA OCR text was used only to locate the passage.
sources.speaker: Walt Whitman, letter to Peter Doyle

sources.quote: The romantic friendship that Walt Whitman shared with Peter Doyle embodied the "love of comrades" celebrated in Whitman's "Calamus" poems. Their thirty-year friendship (1865–1892) left a legacy of loving letters from the older man to his younger companion which are invaluable reference points for the student seeking to understand Whitman's emotional and sexual nature.
sources.context: The opening of Martin G. Murray's reference entry on Doyle, the standard short account and by the author of the fullest published biography of him. Recorded as the second-hand layer: it names the relationship 'romantic friendship' and points the reader at the letters for the sexual question without answering it. Murray also supplies the detail that Doyle was twenty-one and Whitman forty-five at the meeting, and that Doyle is buried in Congressional Cemetery.
sources.supports: The scholarly characterisation of the relationship, and its span - corroboration, not the basis of the class.
sources.provenance: https://whitmanarchive.org/item/encyclopedia_entry3 read in full 2026-08-04 in a real browser - the site sits behind Cloudflare and returns 403 to curl and to plain fetching, so an automated retrieval will falsely report it unavailable. Curly quotation marks around 'love of comrades' and 'Calamus' are the source's; the en dash in the date range is as printed.
sources.speaker: Martin G. Murray

null_findings.finding: ASYMMETRY WORTH KNOWING BEFORE ANYONE HUNTS FOR MORE. The volume is Whitman's letters TO Doyle plus Bucke's interview OF Doyle; **Doyle's own letters to Whitman are not in it**. Doyle kept Whitman's and gave them to Bucke in 1880; the reverse run largely does not survive, so apart from the interview this relationship is documented in one direction, like hall--souline. A few Doyle-to-Whitman letters are held elsewhere and are transcribed on the Whitman Archive (e.g. item nyp.00304, Doyle to Whitman, 5-6 October 1868) - not consulted here, and the obvious next step if this edge is ever deepened.

She did not marry again, kept his name, was hidden with her sister at Aurillac when war came in 1939, and died there in 1944 at eighty-six.

relationships.date_label: fellow prisoners in Reading; Wilde released 19 May 1897, Elvin due out 6 November 1897, and the letter arranging his money is of 30 October 1897
relationships.summary: Harry Elvin was a soldier of twenty serving time in Reading Gaol while Wilde was there, and the man Wilde liked best of anyone he met inside. They walked together and talked. Six months after his own release, from a rented villa outside Naples and with no money of his own, Wilde wrote to Reggie Turner to borrow £2.10 so that a letter containing it would be waiting for Elvin at the Post Office on the day he came out - because he had promised, and because "he would be greatly disappointed not to hear from me".

sources.quote: I now want you to do me a favour. I want you to lend me £2.10. I have one friend left in Reading, the one I liked best; a very handsome young soldier of twenty years of age – Harry Elvin. I promised him I would leave a letter at the Post Office for him and he would be greatly disappointed not to hear from me, as we always walked together, and had long chats. So will you put PO orders into the enclosed letter for £2.10. and I will pay you as soon as I get some money from America. … H. E. comes out on November 6th, so the letter should be sent off at once.
sources.context: Wilde to Reggie Turner, postmark 30 October 1897, from the Villa Giudice, Posilippo, where he was living with Douglas and effectively penniless - the same letter frets about syndicating The Ballad of Reading Gaol in America. The elision drops one sentence repaying an earlier loan of Turner's.
sources.supports: Preference, physical admiration, the habit of walking together, and money Wilde did not have - all of it in Wilde's own hand.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 1024 read as a rendered page image 2026-08-04; printed folio 976 confirmed at the foot of the image. Located first in the complete OCR mirror, which locates only. Superscript note markers omitted as typography.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde

relationships.summary: Eolo was an Italian boy whom Harold Mellor's household acquired by purchase - 200 lire, paid to his father - and who was with Mellor on the Riviera in 1898-99 and in Paris in September 1900. Wilde met him when the two bicycled over to Napoule, recorded the purchase, recorded that Mellor was bored by him, and twenty months later described him as Mellor's 'slave, who like all slaves is most tyrannical'.

sources.quote: Sometimes a very pretty, slim, fair-haired Italian boy bicycles over with him. His name is Eolo; his father, who sold him to Harold for 200 lire, having christened all his children – seventeen in number – out of the Mythological Dictionary. Harold is a nice fellow, but his boy bores him. It is dreadfully sad.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 2 January 1899, Napoule - immediately after the sentences on Mellor's Harrow expulsion and daily bicycle visits. 'Eolo' and 'Mythological Dictionary' are italicised in the original.
sources.supports: What the correspondence records of Eolo's position in Mellor's household: the purchase from his father for 200 lire, his name, and Mellor's boredom with him
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1162, printed folio 1116 confirmed on rendered page. Contiguous run from a page transcribed in full in the dossier (M3); no elision inside this quote.

sources.quote: He is now in Paris with his slave Eolo, who like all slaves is most tyrannical.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Saturday, 1 September [1900], Paris, reporting on Mellor after the 'Mellor cure' at Gland; the next sentence begins 'He and I, however, are great' and completes on printed 1195 with 'friends.'
sources.supports: The same relation twenty months later, in Wilde's plain word - Eolo still described as Mellor's property

relationships.date_label: One evening, August 1876
relationships.summary: Wilde walked into a Dublin theatre at ten o'clock one night in August 1876 and saw Charles Todd, a Magdalen undergraduate, sitting at the back of a private box with Eric Ward, a Magdalen chorister. He wrote about it to William Ward, said he thought Todd 'only mentally spoons the boy', and asked him to keep it quiet.
relationships.certainty_reasoning: THE AGE GAP IS THE FIRST FACT ABOUT THIS EDGE, not a footnote to it: an undergraduate of about twenty-two and a schoolboy chorister.

sources.quote: I want to ask your opinion on this psychological question. In our friend Todd's ethical barometer, at what height is his moral quicksilver? Last night I strolled into the theatre about ten o'clock and to my surprise saw Todd and young Ward the quire boy in a private box together, Todd very much in the background. He saw me so I went round to speak to him for a few minutes. He told me that he and Foster Harter had been fishing in Donegal and that he was going to fish South now. I wonder what young Ward is doing with him. Myself I believe Todd is extremely moral and only mentally spoons the boy, but I think he is foolish to go about with one, if he is bringing this boy about with him. You are the only one I would tell about it, as you have a philosophical mind, but don't tell anyone about it like a good boy - it would do neither us nor Todd any good. He (Todd) looked awfully nervous and uncomfortable. I thought of Mark.
sources.context: Wilde to William Ward, Sunday [6 August 1876], 1 Merrion Square North (MS Magdalen), quoted unbroken from where the subject is raised to where it is dropped. Wilde was twenty-one. The editors identify Charles John Todd (1854-1939), Magdalen undergraduate 1874-7 and later Chaplain to the Royal Navy, and Eric Richard Ward, Magdalen chorister 1874-8 and no relation to the recipient. The 'us' in the last clause is doing a great deal of work: Wilde is aware that reporting this would damage him too.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The whole of the evidence for this connection, and the earliest recorded instance of Wilde handling a suspected attachment between men.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 53-54; printed folios 28 and 29 both confirmed on the rendered page images.
