relationships.date_label: c. 1892-1901 and after
relationships.summary: Prichard and Richard Fisher paired off inside the Lewes House household. Fothergill's memoir dates it to Prichard's jealousy of Fothergill and Marshall, after which he took 'little Fisher' with him to the North Room and was never seen in the upper rooms again, nor went riding. Sox counts the pairing among the jealousies that ran through Warren's relationships. In 1901 the two left together for the Boston Museum of Fine Arts, a departure Warren took as a betrayal.

sources.quote: As we shall see, such jealousies and potential rivalries were to be a feature of many of Ned's relationships: Marshall's betrayal of Ned to marry Ned's cousin; Matt Prichard's alliance with Richard Fisher; Fothergill's homosexual and bisexual romances and eventual marriage; Ned's infatuation with Thomas and Thomas's marriage.
sources.context: Sox on how Warren's A Tale of Pausanian Love 'uncannily foretells future difficulties among Warren, Marshall and Thomas'; the list is Sox's own catalogue of the relationship-strains around Warren.
sources.supports: Sox's 'alliance' wording for the Prichard-Fisher pairing, listed among the bonds that stirred jealousies around Warren
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 37, printed folio 21 confirmed on rendered page.

relationships.date_label: Stated in a letter the editors date [Circa 28 December 1898] from the Hôtel des Bains, Napoule. The letter does not say when the friendship began and no later letter read returns to it; the single-month span is the date of the evidence, not a claim about duration.
relationships.summary: In the same December 1898 letter to Laurence Housman that names Raphael, Wilde named Fortuné as the second of his two special friends among the Napoule fisher-folk - 'both quite perfect, except that they can read and write'. That sentence is the whole of the record for him: no surname, no age, no occupation stated, no second mention anywhere in the correspondence read.

sources.quote: The people here – fisher-folk all – have beautiful eyes, crisp hair of a hyacinth colour, and no morals: an ideal race. I have two special friends, one called Raphael, the other Fortuné – both quite perfect, except that they can read and write.
sources.context: Wilde to Laurence Housman, [Circa 28 December 1898], Hôtel des Bains, Napoule - the third paragraph of a four-paragraph letter that opens on the pinewoods and thanks Housman for a drawing.
sources.supports: The whole of the record for Fortuné: named as the second of Wilde's two special friends among the Napoule fisher-folk, called quite perfect, with no outcome recorded
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1159, printed folio 1113 confirmed at the foot of the rendered page.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The sharpest detail, that the marriage went unconsummated, is Romaine Brooks's recollection reported by Sox: second-hand, decades after, and recorded as hers.
relationships.date_label: c. 1905-06; ended in separation, date unrecorded
relationships.summary: Fothergill met Doris Gillian Herring at the Slade and married her at about the time Romaine Brooks finished his portrait in 1905 - soon after John Marshall, his rival for E. P. Warren's attention, had married. Brooks recalled that he 'was married briefly to a woman who refused to consummate their marriage'. He left her; she went to Rome and painted there for the rest of her life, and he never wrote her name down again.

sources.quote: There he met his first wife, Doris Gillian Herring. She is never spoken of by name in Fothergill's memoirs or in any of his surviving letters. Romaine Brooks mentioned that after she had finished Fothergill's portrait in 1905, Fothergill 'was married briefly to a woman who refused to consummate their marriage'.
sources.context: Sox on Fothergill's Slade years and the aftermath of Marshall's marriage. The single-quoted words are Romaine Brooks's, quoted by Sox.
sources.supports: The first marriage, the wife's name, where they met, and Sox's point that Fothergill never named her.
sources.provenance: David Sox, Bachelors of Art (1991), read in the repo TEXT MIRROR of the PDF on 2026-08-05, not at a rendered page image. The locator is the repo PDF page; the printed folio was not confirmed on an image for this passage, which is a weaker provenance than the rest of this module's Sox citations and is flagged as such.

order_hint.why: Sox gives no wedding date; Romaine Brooks places the marriage just after she finished Fothergill's portrait in 1905, so it is read here against that year and not against a documented one.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Wikipedia carries the same, naming her and not the first wife.
relationships.date_label: c. 1920; still married at his death, 26 April 1957
relationships.summary: Fothergill married Kate Headley Kirby about 1920 and two years later took on the Spread Eagle at Thame. She ran it with him and he credited her in print; the inn made his name, and its collapse ended it. They were still married when he died in 1957.

sources.quote: two years after he had apparently resolved previous emotional ambivalences by marrying Kate Headley Kirby. In many respects, Kate was his salvation
sources.context: Sox on Fothergill's turn to innkeeping at forty-six. The index entry reads 'Kirby, Kate Headley (see Fothergill), 159, 162'.
sources.supports: The second marriage, the wife's name, and its dating relative to the Spread Eagle.
sources.provenance: David Sox, Bachelors of Art (1991), read in the repo TEXT MIRROR of the PDF on 2026-08-05, not at a rendered page image. The locator is the repo PDF page; the printed folio was not confirmed on an image for this passage, which is a weaker provenance than the rest of this module's Sox citations and is flagged as such.

order_hint.why: Sox dates the marriage only as two years before Fothergill took up innkeeping at forty-six, which computes to about 1920 on his 1876 birth. No wedding date is stated anywhere read.

sources.quote: Under Fothergill's and his wife Kate's management, the Spread Eagle became a destination restaurant.
sources.context: Wikipedia, 'John Fothergill (innkeeper)'. The article separately records that Fothergill, in his 1931 An Innkeeper's Diary, credited his wife Kate with making the trifle on a regular basis - i.e. his own published testimony to the marriage.
sources.supports: Independent naming of Kate as Fothergill's wife and co-manager.
sources.provenance: Plain-text extract of the article fetched through the MediaWiki API and read 2026-08-05; quotation sliced from that extract. Reference-marker brackets omitted as typography.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: This edge was deferred pending Part V ch. 3-4 (printed 145-166); those chapters were read so far and carry strong texture but no explicit statement of romance or sex. What Sox gives: 'taken up with Warren in Rome' (p. 142) and 'taken up with Ned and Marshall' (p. 151); his own sentence that Fothergill's longing for 'something like a gentleman protector' 'certainly appeared to be fulfilled in Ned' (p. 150); Fothergill's memoir on the arrangement - 'could I ever be worth his keeping me? At once he said he'd give me £300 a year' (p. 151) - and on his feelings ('He became to me. part of my being. I seem to live as one with him', p. 150); Sox's verdict counting Fothergill among the four men Warren loved and 'wanted to possess' (p. 129); and, on Fothergill's marriage soon after Marshall's, that he 'followed his rival to the altar' (p. 155) - 'rival' being the strongest romantic-parallel word applied to the pair. Against that: every explicit sentence describes employment, patronage, nursing and discipleship, and the protective moustache advice (p. 142) is framed as collecting-security. Proposed 'alleged' with a disputed{} block per the mandate for thin characterization; 'romantic-nonsexual' was considered and rejected as overstating what Sox asserts. Single source (Sox), drawing on Fothergill's unpublished 1954 memoir.
relationships.date_label: Taken up with Warren in Rome from 1899 (Caffè Greco, via John Marshall); a Lewes House secretary-collector on Warren's £300 a year; left for Leipzig and the Slade School (enrolled 1905-06) after the 1904-6 'bad years'. The tie persisted: Fothergill's memoir epigraph addresses Warren 'at Lewes House, c.1905', and at Warren's Golders Green cremation in January 1929 Fothergill could recall no mourners in the chapel 'save Harry Thomas and myself'.
relationships.summary: Returning to Rome in 1899, the 23-year-old Fothergill met John Marshall at the Caffè Greco and 'became one of Ned's Lewes House collectors' - fulfilling, Sox writes, his earlier longing for 'something like a gentleman protector.. support, direction and place', which 'certainly appeared to be fulfilled in Ned'. Warren descended on his typhoid sickbed 'complete with a valet and a German doctor' and, when Fothergill confessed his inheritance half spent - 'could I ever be worth his keeping me?' - settled £300 a year on him; aware of Fothergill's prior 'friendships with one or two boys', Warren also had him grow a moustache so as not to give the police 'an excuse for suppressing us'. Sox stops short of calling the bond romantic, but counts Fothergill among the four men Warren loved and 'wanted to possess', and remarks of Fothergill's 1906 marriage, soon after Marshall's, that he 'followed his rival to the altar'. Fothergill left for the Slade c. 1905; he was one of the two mourners he could remember in the chapel at Warren's cremation.

disputed.claim: that the Warren-Fothergill bond was a romantic or kept-companion attachment, over and above secretarial employment and patronage
disputed.asserted_by: No single sentence of Sox's - the reading is a composite of his framings: 'taken up with Warren in Rome' (p. 142); the 'gentleman protector' longing 'certainly appeared to be fulfilled in Ned' (p. 150); Fothergill's 'could I ever be worth his keeping me?' with the £300 settlement (p. 151); 'More than loving Marshall, Harry, Matt and Fothergill, he wanted to possess them' (p. 129); Marshall as Fothergill's 'rival' (p. 155); the Introduction's Warren who 'collected art and young men' (p. viii)
disputed.disputed_by: Nothing read contests a close bond; the reservation is evidential - nowhere in the pages read does Sox assert a romance or sexual relationship between them, and every explicit description is of employment, patronage, nursing and discipleship
disputed.grounds: Single-source (Sox 1991, itself built on Fothergill's unfinished 1954 memoir, which Sox flags as gappy: 'Apparently, he did not want to tell us about certain aspects of his life', p. 133); classification rests on implication, so 'alleged' with this block per the module's thin-characterization rule

sources.quote: After he had taken up with Warren in Rome, Warren was well aware that a year before, Fothergill had had 'friendships with one or two boys'. Warren thought this might 'endanger the collecting for America by giving the police an excuse for suppressing us'. So Warren suggested that Fothergill should grow a moustache - 'a very fine masculine mass of it'.
sources.context: Sox, on Warren's management of Fothergill after Fothergill joined him in Rome
sources.supports: Warren's knowledge of Fothergill's private conduct and his intervention in it - the closest the record comes to characterizing the terms on which they lived, and evidence of criminal-law pressure shaping the household's self-presentation.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 158 (printed folio 142 confirmed on the rendered page).

sources.quote: Fothergill's earlier expressed longing for 'something like a gentleman protector - someone who would give me support, direction and place' certainly appeared to be fulfilled in Ned. His feelings for Ned were strong: 'He became to me, as to the others, part of my being - or at least so far as my tyrannies and unsympathetic impetuousness allowed me to imitate his god-like love and tolerance . . He has become more than a part of me, for I seem to live as one with him, a would-be memorial to him.'
sources.context: Sox introducing Fothergill's memoir observations on the Lewes House community, 'the most incisive of any which survive'. The 'gentleman protector' longing is the same memoir passage that frames the 1897 Wilde episode (see fothergill--wilde). Inner first-person text: Fothergill memoir, as printed in Sox 1991, p. 150; the '. ' is as printed.
sources.supports: Sox's own sentence that the protector-longing 'certainly appeared to be fulfilled in Ned'; Fothergill's devotional language for Warren
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 174, printed folio 150 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: At last, Fothergill felt he had to 'face the problem that had long been on my mind and after all Ned's generosity and loving care of me, I had to come out with it. I imagined that he must be assuming that I was rich. But my £4000 had now half gone. Was I going to tell him that I couldn't go on with him? Or could I ever be worth his keeping me? At once he said he'd give me £300 a year and my mind was fresh to convalesce with.'
sources.context: During Fothergill's typhoid convalescence in the Orsini palace at Lecce, where Warren had 'suddenly arrived complete with a valet and a German doctor' (p. 150). Later on the same page: 'Romaine Brooks was not the only one to notice a change in Fothergill once he had taken up with Ned and Marshall.' Chain: Fothergill memoir, as printed in Sox 1991, p. 151. Episode undated in the pages read (early Lewes House years).
sources.supports: The material arrangement in Fothergill's own words - 'worth his keeping me', the £300 a year - and 'Ned's generosity and loving care'
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 175, printed folio 151 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: Fothergill said that Ned asked him why he wanted to get married in the first place, to which Fothergill replied 'with my usual bravura that it was the only experience I hadn't enjoyed'. … With hindsight, it is interesting to note how soon after Marshall's marriage, Fothergill followed his rival to the altar.
sources.context: On Fothergill's brief marriage to Doris Gillian Herring, met at the Slade (enrolled 1905-06); Romaine Brooks: 'married briefly to a woman who refused to consummate their marriage'. 'His rival' - Sox's word - casts Fothergill and Marshall as rivals in relation to Warren. Elided: Marshall's 1913 notebook note that he met Fothergill's wife once. Same page: 'Fothergill had reacted against Ned's misogyny, but his own sexual ambiguities were far from resolved.'
sources.supports: Sox's 'his rival' framing - the strongest romantic-parallel wording applied to this pair in the pages read
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 179, printed folio 155 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: Ned, however, carried that a step further: if falling in love was confused with his collecting then Marshall and the others were, in a sense, an extension of his obsession to collect. More than loving Marshall, Harry, Matt and Fothergill, he wanted to possess them.
sources.context: Sox's summary verdict on Warren's attachments, following Marshall's death and Kenneth Clark's why-do-men-collect / why-do-they-fall-in-love comparison ('poignantly aimed at Ned'). 'Harry' = Harry Thomas; 'Matt' = Matthew Prichard.
sources.supports: Sox counting Fothergill among the four men Warren loved and 'wanted to possess'
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 145, printed folio 129 confirmed on rendered page.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Sox's account - built on Fothergill's unfinished, previously unpublished 81-page memoir (written 1954; Sox himself flags it as 'highly disorganized' with 'few dates given', p. 133) and corroborated by the 'architect' references in Wilde's letters to Ross - has the 21-year-old Fothergill visiting Wilde alone at Berneval in summer 1897, where Wilde 'liked him and declared to him' the 'Two loves have I' couplet, casting dark-haired Fothergill as the love 'of comfort' against golden-haired Douglas's 'despair'; the book's jacket glosses the episode as Wilde at one time having Fothergill in mind 'to replace Lord Alfred Douglas in his affections'. Divergence from the roster-owner summary, following Sox: Sox never uses a 'kept man' framing and narrates no explicit sexual proposition - the nearest is Fothergill's confessed longing for 'a gentleman protector' and the visit being coordinated through Ross ('send over the architect'); the classification rests on the declaration-plus-decline shape.
relationships.date_label: Single visit to Wilde at Berneval, summer 1897: anticipated in Wilde's letters to Ross from 1 June ('send over the architect'); Sox: 'We do not know exactly when Fothergill appeared'; Wilde's 21 Sept. 1897 letter places Fothergill's six days ('Rowland a sextette of suns') within his last month there. Fothergill dropped the correspondence after returning to England (undated by Sox).
relationships.summary: After his May 1897 release Wilde settled at Berneval near Dieppe, and the 21-year-old Fothergill - 'the architect' of Wilde's letters to Ross - visited him there alone, for what Wilde's 21 September letter counts as a 'sextette of suns' in his final month there. Wilde met his boat at Dieppe and, troubled over the estranged Douglas, declared Fothergill his love 'of comfort' against Douglas's golden-haired 'despair'. Fothergill reflected that he could not have 'given much comfort'; back in England, where any association with Wilde was toxic, he answered Wilde's 'charming letters' by writing that it was not 'politic' to go on, and later - by then taken up with Warren in Rome - passed Wilde by at Aragno's cafe without approaching him, a decision his sons say he regretted to the end of his life.

sources.quote: Fothergill – as usual – was looking for something but could not find what it was, or, as we will see, perhaps was afraid to commit himself: 'I had all the time a secret longing for a perfect friend, a thing which I couldn't define – something like a gentleman protector – someone who would give me support, direction and place, for I had no thought of helping myself or how I could, but went on complacently spending my capital.'
sources.context: Sox introducing Fothergill on the eve of the Berneval episode; the inner first-person sentence is Fothergill's unpublished memoir. this stated longing is the implicit basis of the 'prospective companion' framing.
sources.supports: Fothergill's own wish for 'a gentleman protector' - the motive side of the arrangement-texture; his wish, not an arrangement Sox attributes to Ross or Wilde.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 154-155 (printed folios 138-139 confirmed); passage runs over the page break. Transcribed in FOTHERGILL_dossier.md, promoted to the record 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: I have seen the terrain. It is the best here, and the only one left. I must build a house. … I want to live here. Do think over this, and send me over the architect. Monsieur Bonnet is excellent, and is ready to carry out my ideas. I want a little chalet of wood and plastered walls, the wooden beams showing … So your architect has me waiting for him, as he is waiting for me.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 1 June 1897 — a running journal-letter written over two days from Berneval-sur-Mer, a fortnight after his release. Fothergill was then a student at the London School of Architecture, and this is the first of the summons: Wilde has found a plot, wants a chalet on it, and wants Ross to send Fothergill over. The editors identify 'the architect' as him in a footnote on the page. The elisions drop the costings and the description of the plaster diapering.
sources.supports: Wilde asking for Fothergill by function, before the visit — the beginning of the approach that Sox documents from Fothergill's side.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 919 read as a rendered page image 2026-08-04; printed folio 869 confirmed at the foot of the image. Located in the complete OCR mirror, which locates only. Superscript note markers omitted as typography. The letter's date line, 'Tuesday morning [1 June 1897], 9.30', sits on the preceding page, printed 868, also read at the image.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde

sources.quote: Fothergill's visit has gone heretofore unrecorded although Rupert Hart-Davis's edition of selected letters of Oscar Wilde contains veiled references to it: 1 June 1897, Wilde wrote to Ross that he wanted to continue to live at Berneval and 'send over the architect [Fothergill]'. … On 20 July, again to Ross, Wilde said he 'expected Ross on August the First: also, the architect'.
sources.context: The square-bracketed '[Fothergill]' gloss is Sox's own. Elided middle sentence (5 June, Wilde to Ross on visitor expenses at the Hotel de la Plage): 'Architects, on the other hand, are taken at a reduction. I have special terms for architects.' Sox's endnote markers (nn. 7-9) omitted.
sources.supports: The visit is documented in Wilde's letters to Ross; Wilde anticipated 'the architect' at Berneval from 1 June through the summer of 1897
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 155, printed folio 139 confirmed on rendered page. Line-break hyphenation 'con-tains' silently joined; one sentence elided with spaced ellipsis, full passage in dossier.

sources.quote: Architects, on the other hand, are taken at a reduction. I have special terms for architects. But seriously, Robbie, if anyone stayed with me, of course they would pay their pension at the hotel. They would have to: except architects. A modern architect, like modern architecture, doesn't pay. But then I only know one architect, and you are hiding him somewhere from me. I am beginning to believe that he is as extinct as the Dado, of which now only fossil remains are found, chiefly in the vicinity of Brompton, where they are sometimes discovered by workmen excavating.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Saturday 5 June 1897, from the Hotel de la Plage, Berneval-sur-Mer — four days after the first summons, in a comic tariff for visitors ('Sphinxes pay a hundred per cent more than anyone else. They always did in ancient Egypt'). The joke is the complaint: the one architect he knows is being kept from him. The editors footnote 'architects' straight back to the Fothergill note at p. 913. Sox quotes the first two sentences of this and elides the rest; it is given here whole, because the elision removes the point. Italics on *pension* are the volume's.
sources.supports: Wilde pressing for Fothergill a second time in five days, and doing it as a joke against Ross for withholding him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 934 read as a rendered page image 2026-08-04; printed folio 884 confirmed at the foot of the image, and footnote 1 on that page reads in full 'See note 2, p.913.' The letter's heading, 'To Robert Ross … Saturday, 5 June [1897] [Hotel de la Plage, Berneval-sur-Mer]', is on an earlier page. Superscript note markers omitted; one sentence on Lincrusta-Walton elided at the close.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde

sources.quote: Dear Robbie, What delightful news! I will expect you on August 1st. Bring dear More, if he can come. If not, bring the architect of the moon. I have a lot of work on hand for you to do: literary work of course.
sources.context: A postcard, Wilde to Robert Ross, postmark 19 July 1897, from Berneval. 'The architect of the moon' is Wilde's name for Fothergill and is used as though Ross needs no explanation of it. The bargaining order is worth noting: More Adey first, Fothergill as the alternative.
sources.supports: The nickname in Wilde's own hand, and the second summons.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 963 read as a rendered page image 2026-08-04; printed folio 913 confirmed at the foot of the image. Located in the complete OCR mirror, which locates only. Superscript note markers omitted as typography.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde

sources.quote: From the railings of the boat, as she got to Dieppe harbour, I looked down upon what must be a great man standing alone and looking up. I had seen a photograph of this beautiful looking man and here was a huge and fat person in white flannels with a comical little red beret on top of it all. Rather vulgar I thought. My heart sank, but his sweet kindness put me right quickly.
sources.context: Fothergill's memoir on his arrival at Dieppe, Wilde waiting at the harbour ('Fothergill described his arrival at Dieppe:'). He had been primed with a photograph beforehand - the memoir does not say by whom.

order_hint.why: Sox says outright "We do not know exactly when Fothergill appeared". Wilde's letter of 21 September counts the six days as falling inside his last month at Berneval, which he left in mid-September, so the visit sits in August or early September.

sources.supports: The meeting first-person: Wilde met his boat; the photograph seen beforehand (the logistics side of the arrangement-texture); the deflation-then-warmth of the first impression.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 155-156 (printed folios 139-140 confirmed); the memoir block continues on p. 140 (cathedral, cab to the Chalet Bourgeat, shared cafe expenses). Transcribed in FOTHERGILL_dossier.md, promoted to the record 2026-08-03.
sources.speaker: John Fothergill, memoir (1954)

sources.quote: Both Smithers and Fothergill knew Wilde was troubled about Bosie Douglas who was either unwilling to see him or prevented by Ross. Fothergill said Wilde liked him and declared to him: 'Two loves have I: the one of comfort; the other of despair. The one has black; the other golden hair.' Fothergill commented: 'I don't think I could have given much comfort. I was too concentrated on myself. I've ever been incapable of sympathy, even with this sad thing.'
sources.context: At Berneval, with Leonard Smithers the only other guest named as present in this stretch; the chapter title 'Two Loves Have I' is this declaration (Wilde reworking Shakespeare's Sonnet 144, dark-haired Fothergill as 'comfort' against Douglas's golden hair). Fothergill's first-person sentences are from his unpublished memoir.

order_hint.why: The same undated visit as the arrival above; placed with it.

sources.supports: The approach: Wilde's declaration casting Fothergill as the replacement love 'of comfort'; Fothergill's retrospective refusal of the role
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 157, printed folio 141 confirmed on rendered page. Fothergill's quoted sentences: Fothergill memoir, as printed in Sox 1991, p. 141.

sources.quote: I cannot live without the atmosphere of Love: I must love and be loved, whatever price I pay for it. I could have lived all my life with you, but you have other claims on you – claims you are too sweet a fellow to disregard – and all you could give me was a week of companionship. Reggie gave me three days, and Rowland a sextette of suns, but for the last month at Berneval I was so lonely that I was on the brink of killing myself. The world shuts its gateway against me, and the door of Love lies open.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 21 September 1897, from the Hôtel Royal des Étrangers, Naples — the letter explaining why he had gone back to Douglas. Fothergill's visit is counted here, in days, against the loneliness that followed it: six suns, between Ross's week and Turner's three days. This is the passage the edge's date_label already used to place the visit, now recorded as a quotation in its own right.
sources.supports: The length of Fothergill's visit, in Wilde's own reckoning, and what it weighed against — the fullest thing Wilde wrote about him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 990 read as a rendered page image 2026-08-04; printed folio 942 confirmed at the foot of the image. Located in the complete OCR mirror, which locates only. Superscript note markers omitted as typography.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde

sources.quote: We do not know exactly when Fothergill appeared and from his memoirs it seems he visited Wilde alone. … on 21 September, Wilde wrote to Ross that despite several visits by friends to Berneval he was so lonely that he was on the brink of killing himself: in the last month there, Reggie Turner had given him three days, and 'Rowland a sextette of suns'.
sources.context: 'Rowland' = Fothergill (Sox p. 133: called Rowland by some friends, Roland or Ronald by others). The elision skips the first half of the second sentence, on the Wilde-Douglas Naples reunion. The 'sextette of suns' - six days - places the visit in Wilde's last month at Berneval.
sources.supports: Sox's own hedge on the exact visit date; Fothergill came alone; a six-day stay in Wilde's final Berneval month per Wilde's 21 Sept. 1897 letter as quoted by Sox
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 155, printed folio 139 confirmed on rendered page. Elision is mid-sentence (from 'Between 28 and 29 August' to 'and on 21 September'); full passage in dossier. Endnote markers (nn. 10-11) omitted.

sources.quote: When Fothergill returned home he received 'some charming letters with his lovely handwriting', but admitted that the feeling against Wilde and any knowledge of him was then so strong in England that he decided 'to drop him': 'I actually wrote that it was not "politic" to go on with it. What an awful expression!' Wilde replied saying he didn't know what Fothergill meant by 'politic'.
sources.context: Immediately following: 'For Fothergill it was finished, but he said he had assimilated Wilde's manner - even his ponderous intonation "so far as my voice allowed".' The inner first-person sentences are Fothergill memoir text; runs over the printed 141/142 page break at 'he | didn't'.

order_hint.why: Undated in Sox. The visit had ended before Wilde's letter of 21 September and this exchange followed Fothergill's return to England, so it belongs to the autumn.

sources.supports: The decline made effective: Fothergill ended the correspondence by letter as not 'politic' after returning to England; Wilde's baffled reply
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 157-158, printed folios 141-142 confirmed on rendered pages. Fothergill's quoted words: Fothergill memoir, as printed in Sox 1991, pp. 141-142.

sources.quote: Wilde's list of recipients for copies of The Ballad (MS Clark) reads: 'Oswald Sickert, Stanley Makower, Robbie, Reggie, More, Rowland Fothergill, Nelson, …
sources.context: The editors quoting Wilde's own manuscript list, in a note to his letter to Leonard Smithers of 9 February 1898 (postmark 11 February) from Naples, which is itself about getting the addresses right for presentation copies. Fothergill is sixth on it, among Ross, Turner and More Adey — the inner circle — and ahead of Major Nelson, the governor of Reading. This is the act the inscription recorded in the note above belongs to: 'To Rowland Fothergill, the Architect of the Moon, with the compliments of the author O. W.' The list is quoted only as far as the page reproduces it before the note runs on.
sources.supports: That five months after the visit, and after Fothergill had written to break it off, Wilde still put him on the short list of people to receive the Ballad.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 1060 read as a rendered page image 2026-08-04; printed folio 1012 confirmed at the foot of the image. The note continues past the page break, so the quotation is elided where the printed page ends.
sources.speaker: Merlin Holland and Rupert Hart-Davis, eds.

sources.quote: John Rowland Fothergill (1876–1957) had studied at the Slade and was a friend of Ross, Rothenstein and other artists. At this time he was a student at the London School of Architecture, and his copy of The Ballad of Reading Gaol (now in the possession of his son) is inscribed 'To Rowland Fothergill, the Architect of the Moon, with the compliments of the author O. W.' He later spent twelve years as an archaeologist, helping his American friend Edward Perry Warren (1864–1928) to form the collection of classical antiquities in the Boston Museum of Fine Arts, and finally achieved fame as an innkeeper in England.
sources.context: The editors' identifying note on Fothergill, and the closest thing in this volume to a letter from Wilde to him: **the inscription is Wilde's own words, written to Fothergill**, in a presentation copy of the Ballad still held by his son. It also supplies his dates, and the link to Edward Perry Warren, who is on this map in his own right — Fothergill spent twelve years helping Warren assemble the Boston antiquities. The note is modern voice: the editors are writing, and the period phrase sits inside their sentence.

order_hint.why: The note itself is undated editorial apparatus. It is placed at the inscription it records, which belongs to February 1898 - the month Wilde drew up his list of presentation copies of the Ballad, on which Fothergill appears (printed 1012, immediately above).

sources.supports: Fothergill's dates; that Wilde inscribed a book to him under the nickname; and the Warren connection.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 963 read as a rendered page image 2026-08-04; printed folio 913 confirmed at the foot of the image. Located in the complete OCR mirror, which locates only. Superscript note markers omitted as typography.

sources.quote: If you see Rowland, the architect of the moon, please tell him to come over to Paris at once. You should come to take care of him of course.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Wednesday 24 [actually 25] May 1898, from Paris — eight months after Naples, and a year after the Berneval summons. The same nickname, and the same request, now to a different city. The joke in the second sentence is that Fothergill needs a chaperone. (The same letter opens with 'my sweet Maurice, our sweet Maurice' — see gilbert--wilde.)
sources.supports: That Wilde was still asking for Fothergill a year after Berneval, and still by the nickname.

sources.quote: Your story of dear Rowland is charming. How dangerous it is to be called 'John' is the moral. Anything may happen to a person called John.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, [late March 1900], from the Grand Café, Paris — seven months before Wilde's death, and the last mention of Fothergill in the correspondence. 'Dear Rowland': the affection survives, at a distance, as gossip enjoyed. The editors identify him in the footnote. The same page carries the boy in grey velvet seen behind the Madeleine.
sources.supports: That Fothergill remained a figure of affection in Wilde's letters to the end, years after the visit and after the correspondence between them had lapsed.

sources.quote: He sat so still, looking at nothing, and had that same, sad friendless face … I wondered - should I go over to him or, would it once more be that awful word "politic", and a betrayal of my duty to Ned's work? I had to decide for this. I passed on, and never saw him again, but my tragic picture of it all sickens me still.
sources.context: Fothergill's memoir, as printed by Sox: seeing Wilde alone outside Aragno's Café on the Via del Corso in Rome, after Fothergill had taken up with Warren. Sox introduces it as what Fothergill called 'the tragedy', and adds that the feeling stayed with him to the end of his life and that both his sons say he regretted the decision.

order_hint.why: Undated in Sox. Wilde writes in the letter of late March 1900 above that he hopes "to be in Rome in about ten days"; he died that November, so the sighting falls in the months between.

sources.supports: Fothergill in his own words on the end of the connection - the decision not to approach Wilde, and the lifelong regret.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 158 (printed folio 142 confirmed on the rendered page).
sources.speaker: John Fothergill, memoir (1954)

null_findings.finding: **NO LETTERS FROM WILDE TO FOTHERGILL SURVIVE IN THIS EDITION**, and the six records added above are the whole of what does. Checked three ways: every `To <Name>` letter heading in the volume was extracted mechanically (514 recipients, 1,441 letters) and Fothergill is not among them; the Index of Recipients has no entry for him; and the General Index entry — 'Fothergill, John Rowland, 913, 1177; the Architect of the Moon, 913, 1075; starts Carfax Gallery, 374n; wanted at Berneval, 869; gave W a sexette of suns, 942' — lists mentions only. His name variants were searched as well: 'Roland' and 'Ronald' return only Roland Atwood, Lord Ronald Gower, Ronald Powers and Madame Roland. That letters existed is not in doubt — Fothergill told Sox's source he received 'some charming letters with his lovely handwriting' after returning home (see the Sox quotations below) — they simply are not in Holland and Hart-Davis. **CAUTION for anyone extending this**: 'Rowland' in this volume is usually **Rowland Strong**, a journalist and an entirely different man (printed 941 n. 1, and pp. 989, 1073, 1110, 1144, 1267). Fothergill is the Rowland of pp. 869, 913, 942, 1075 and 1177, and the editors footnote each one back to the note at p. 913. There is also a passing record at printed 1012, where 'Rowland Fothergill' appears on Wilde's own list of people to receive a copy of The Ballad, and a note at printed 977 quoting Fothergill's memoir An Innkeeper's Diary on a dinner party — neither bears on this relationship and neither is recorded above.

relationships.sources_order_note: Chronological, and THE ORDER IS PRODUCED BY THE DATA: the panel sorts on `evidence_date`, falling back to `order_hint` (see byEvidenceDate in circle.js), treats a missing month as 0, and drops records with neither to the end. Hand-sorting the array does nothing on its own; the array is kept in the same order only so that records sharing a date break in narrative order. **Five records here are undated in their sources and carry `order_hint` rather than an invented `evidence_date`** - the visit and the 'Two loves have I' declaration, the 'politic' exchange, the identifying note, and the sighting in Rome. Each states what its placement rests on, and the card says on its face that it is a placement. evidence_date is a claim about when something happened; order_hint is a claim about where it reads best.

relationships.date_label: Palermo, April 1900
relationships.summary: Wilde named Francesco to Robert Ross as one of the three most favoured of the Monreale coachmen, and said 'I loved them all'.

sources.quote: Monreale you have heard of, with its cloisters and cathedral. We often drove there, the cocchieri most dainty finely-carved boys. In them, not in the Sicilian horses, is race seen. The most favoured were Manuele, Francesco, and Salvatore. I loved them all, but only remember Manuele.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 16 April [1900], c/o Cook & Son, Piazza di Spagna, Rome (MS Clark), quoted across the page break. 'cocchieri' are coachmen. Wilde had spent eight days at Palermo and drove out to Monreale repeatedly. Seven months before his death.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: SECOND PAGE ADDED 2026-08-05: printed 1108, read at the page, puts the same boy in Paris three weeks earlier - 'One beautiful boy of bad character - of the name of Georges … so like Antinous'.
relationships.date_label: The intended meeting at Nice, announced in a letter postmarked 3 January 1899 from Napoule, for a trip 'tomorrow'. The friendship itself predates the letter - Wilde calls him a great friend and places him as a Paris boy - but no earlier date was verified in the source.
relationships.summary: From Napoule at the start of January 1899, Wilde told Reginald Turner that Harold Mellor was arriving that day and that the two of them were going to Nice the next day, where a great friend of his, a Paris boy he called 'le petit Georges', was then staying and whom he had promised to see. The letter gives four clauses of physical description and says Georges was at Nice on speculative business. Nothing read records whether the meeting took place.

sources.quote: Kalisaya, the American Bar near the Crédit Lyonnais, is now the literary resort of myself and my friends: and we all gather there at five o'clock - Moréas, and La Jeunesse, and all the young poets. One beautiful boy of bad character - of the name of Georges - goes there too, but he is so like Antinous, and so smart, that he is allowed to talk to poets.
sources.context: Wilde in Paris, December 1898, three weeks before the Nice letter. THE EDITORS INDEX THIS AS THE SAME BOY: their entry reads 'Georges (boy), 1097, 1108, 1117' - confirmed on the rendered index page - and printed 1117 is the 'le petit Georges' letter that this connection already rests on. INDEX SLIP WORTH RECORDING: the 1097 in that string is wrong. Printed 1097 carries only the letter to MONSIEUR Georges, the proprietor of L'Écu, whom Wilde thanks for a week's lodging and whose wife and parents he sends compliments to; he has his own index entry at the same page. A future sweep chasing 'Georges' should not merge them. Antinous was the boy the emperor Hadrian loved and deified after his death, and in Wilde's vocabulary the comparison is never neutral.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: That Wilde knew him in Paris before Nice, and how he described him to a correspondent other than Turner.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1154; printed folio 1108 confirmed on the rendered page image. The editors' index entry confirmed on the rendered page image of PDF 1292. Both read 2026-08-05.

sources.quote: My friend, my new friend, Harold Mellor comes here today to stay at the hotel, and tomorrow we go to Nice, for the day. A great friend of mine, a Paris boy called le petit Georges, is now at Nice, and I have promised to run over and see him. He is like a very handsome Roman boy, dark, and bronze-like, with splendidly chiselled nose and mouth, and the tents of midnight are folded in his eyes; moons hide in their curtains. He is visiting Nice on speculative business.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Turner, [Postmark 3 January 1899], Hôtel des Bains, Napoule - the second paragraph of the letter, following the weather. 'le petit Georges' is italicised on the page. The paragraph continues past the last sentence quoted here onto printed 1118.
sources.supports: The whole of the verified record: an existing friendship, a promised meeting at Nice, Wilde's description of him, and the statement that he was at Nice on speculative business; no outcome recorded
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1163, printed folio 1117 confirmed at the foot of the rendered page.

sources.quote: A great friend of mine, a Paris boy called le petit Georges, is now at Nice, and I have promised to run over and see him. He is like a very handsome Roman boy, dark, and bronze-like, with splendidly chiselled nose and mouth, and the tents of midnight are folded in his eyes; moons hide in their curtains. He is visiting Nice on speculative business. It is beautiful, and encouraging, to find people who can combine romance with business – blend them indeed, and make them one.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Turner, postmark 3 January 1899, Hotel des Bains, Napoule. The sentence begun on p. 1117 completes on p. 1118.
sources.supports: How Wilde glosses Georges's 'speculative business' at Nice - the sentence completes on the following page and bears directly on how the connection should be read
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 1163-1164, printed folios 1117 and 1118 read off the rendered pages; 'le petit Georges' is italic in the printed text.

relationships.date_label: First mention in the letters 25 February 1898, already on meeting terms ('We met by chance this morning'); the concentrated run of affectionate references falls 3-9 March 1898; the association lasted to Wilde's death - Gilbert attended the sickroom, took the deathbed photograph at Ross's request, and walked in the funeral procession, 30 November 1900.
relationships.summary: Maurice Gilbert, a young soldier of the marine infantry with an English father and a French mother, was part of Wilde's Paris household of the exile years. Through the spring of 1898 Wilde's letters to his publisher Leonard Smithers report him as a daily fixture - a nightly bezique opponent whose running score Wilde keeps for Smithers, a dinner companion at a two-franc restaurant, the man who takes the cheque to the bank and writes out the signatures Wilde is too tired to write - in a register that keeps sliding from domestic to amorous: Gilbert's 'beaux yeux', a heart 'unfortunately lost' on a side-bet, a friend who 'grows dearer to me daily' and is 'sweeter than ever'. The editors' own note calls him one of Wilde's closest and most devoted friends of the last years, and he was present through the final illness, took the deathbed photograph and walked behind the hearse in November 1900.

sources.quote: Maurice took it to the bank, so I dare say it was on account of his beaux yeux. He grows dearer to me daily, and we now dine at a restaurant for two francs!
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, Saturday [postmark 5 March 1898], on café paper, Paris; the 'it' is Smithers's cheque, which 'with reckless confidence, the banker cashed'. 'beaux yeux' italic in the original. The same letter ends: 'Maurice says he is too old to play marbles, and I am too young to begin, so we bezique our youthful lives away.'
sources.supports: Wilde's plainest first-person statement of the attachment - 'He grows dearer to me daily' - set in the daily domestic texture (the bank errand, the two-franc dinners)
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1077, printed folio 1031 confirmed on the rendered page.

sources.quote: Maurice Gilbert, one of Wilde's closest and most devoted friends during these last years. Except that his father was English and his mother French, and that he was a young soldier in the marine infantry, nothing is known of him.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, main-particulars footnote (n. 4) on the first appearance of 'Maurice' in the text, keyed to Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [postmark 25 February 1898].
sources.supports: Gilbert's identity and the editors' own characterization of the friendship; the sum of what the editors say is knowable about him
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1071, printed folio 1025 confirmed on the rendered page. Whole footnote, both sentences.

sources.quote: Maurice and I are exactly quits now – twenty-six games each – but I have unfortunately lost my heart, which I carefully staked on a separate game.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [postmark 4 March 1898], Hôtel de Nice, Paris; the sentence closes the letter, which runs over the printed 1030/1031 page break, and the running bezique score is a standing joke in the sequence (the previous day: 'as he has youth, and I have only genius, it is only natural that he should beat me').
sources.supports: The amorous turn inside the comic bezique register - Wilde's own 'lost my heart', staked on a side-game
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1077, printed folio 1031 confirmed on the rendered page; the letter opens on printed 1030 (PDF 1076, folio confirmed). En-dashes as printed.

sources.quote: Without my morning letter from you life would be dreadful – is dreadful – except for Maurice, who is sweeter than ever.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, Wednesday [postmark 9 March 1898], Paris; opening sentence of the letter. The preceding day's letter (printed 1034, same page) reports 'Maurice is quite well. I am now two games behind. I wish you could make him your agent here at a salary of £400 a year.'
sources.supports: Gilbert as the single exemption from Wilde's misery in this stretch - 'sweeter than ever'
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1080, printed folio 1034 confirmed on the rendered page. En-dashes as printed.

sources.quote: My dear Maurice, Bosie and I are at Nogent. Do come down either tonight or tomorrow early. I have taught them how to make oeufs à l'aurore. Ever yours O.
sources.context: Petit Bleu, Wilde to Maurice Gilbert, [Postmark 18 June 1898], [Nogent-sur-Marne]
sources.supports: The General Index lead, now read. It widens the affectionate run by a note rather than changing its character: Gilbert summoned to join a household Wilde is already sharing with Douglas, in the domestic register of who is cooking. Nothing here strengthens a romantic reading.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 1130 rendered and; folio 1084 printed at the foot. 'early' and 'oeufs à l'aurore' are italic in the printing.

sources.quote: My dear Robbie, No cheque this morning, but instead my sweet Maurice, our sweet Maurice, looking quite charming and as delightful as ever. He seemed a little tired, but of course that was the journey. He was full of affectionate memories of you and Reggie, and is quite devoted to you both.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 24 [actually 25] May 1898, from Paris. Read while clearing the pointer that named this page for its editorial footnote. Worth noting for the shape of this relationship: Gilbert is 'my sweet Maurice' and 'our sweet Maurice' in the same breath - the affection is real and is also shared openly with Ross and Turner, which is why this edge does not read as exclusive. The same page carries Wilde joking that he means to write a novel called The Boy-Snatcher of Clements Inn, Clements Inn being where Gilbert had been lodging with Reggie Turner.
sources.supports: Wilde's own register about Gilbert in a letter to a third party - affectionate, possessive and communal at once.

Printed p. 1073 n. 2 reads in full: 'See p.878. Reggie Turner lived at 2 Clements Inn, where Maurice Gilbert had been staying with him.' relationships.certainty_reasoning: Cook states the marriage as fact in passing while describing the Ives household; no date, place or maiden name is given on the page read.
relationships.date_label: Married before the household years; date not stated in the source read
relationships.summary: James Goddard married Sylvie and brought her into George Ives's household, where they raised two daughters known as 'the 2 Kit girls'. Cook records that Ives's relationships with the men of the house began possibly sexually before settling into something he framed as paternal - and that the households's men, Goddard among them, married without leaving it.

sources.quote: 'Kit' (James Goddard) had been a servant at the Ives' family seat in Hampshire and then moved with George to London. When he married he bought his wife Sylvie into the household too; 'the 2 Kit girls' were their daughters.
sources.context: Cook's roll-call of the Ives household. 'bought' is printed thus in the source, evidently for 'brought'; transcribed as printed.
sources.supports: The marriage, Sylvie's entry into the household, and the two daughters
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 107 (printed folio 96 confirmed on the rendered page).

sources.quote: Kit and his wife Sylvie kept house for Ives in a relatively familiar – though rapidly diminishing – tradition of live-in domestic service. … James and Sylvie Goddard remained with Ives until their deaths; their daughters until the early 1940s.
sources.context: Cook on the Adelaide Road household. The same page adds that the daughters left to open a shop with money Ives had settled on their father, and that Therese was still visiting in 1944, when Ives called her 'the youngest of my adopted family - and she is 47!' (which would put her birth about 1897).
sources.supports: Cook reportedly records that Sylvie kept house for Ives, that she and James remained until their deaths, and that the daughters stayed until the early 1940s - one, Therese, still visiting in 1944. Known so far only from the PDF text layer; verify at the rendered page before quoting.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 111, printed folio 100 confirmed in the running head on the rendered page ('100 Queer Domesticities').

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Cook states plainly that Ives shared his bed with James Goddard ('Kit') at the Albany, which is more explicit than the household-membership evidence behind the Bloodworth record. It stays 'alleged' on the single-source rule: Cook (2003) is the only work read that attests it, and bed-sharing in a shared bachelor household is not by itself a statement of sexual relations. CORROBORATION: Cook returns to this household at much greater length in Queer Domesticities (2014), where he states that the Adelaide Road relationships 'possibly started sexually' before settling into something platonic, with bed-sharing continuing throughout. Cook's account of the Ives household is drawn from Ives's own 122-volume diary and his endnotes cite it by volume and date; the tier follows whose testimony underlies the claim, not whether our record happens to carry a direct quotation rather than the historian's summary of the same diary.

relationships.date_label: Albany period, from 1894; Kit later at Adelaide Road
relationships.summary: One of the two young men of George Ives's Albany household - the circle of working-class and dependent young men he called his 'children' - with whom Cook records Ives sharing his bed.

disputed.claim: That the bed-sharing recorded by Cook was a sexual or romantic relationship.
disputed.asserted_by: Cook, London and the Culture of Homosexuality (2003), p. 146, as read by the editor
disputed.disputed_by: Single-source and uncorroborated in the works read; Cook himself does not characterize it as sexual
disputed.grounds: Cook's sentence attests shared sleeping arrangements in Ives's household, not sexual relations; Ives's diaries (Harry Ransom Center) and Kaplan (2005) are the verification targets.

sources.quote: Using pet names for his co-residents, he wrote: 'Kit has been with me some 35 years. His wife over 20. Pug 9 or 10. [...] and the 2 Kit girls all their lives'. 'Kit' (James Goddard) had been a servant at the Ives' family seat in Hampshire and then moved with George to London.
sources.context: Cook's opening to the Ives chapter, quoting the roll call Ives made in his diary in 1917 of his 'family' home at Adelaide Road; Cook's endnote 1 cites Diary vol. 70, 21 May 1917, p. 118. The '[..]' is Cook's own elision inside Ives's sentence.
sources.supports: Goddard in Ives's own words, and the plainest first-hand statement of what this bond was: Ives counts Kit first in the roll call of his household and measures the attachment in decades - 'some 35 years' by 1917, which reaches back past the Albany to Ives's father's estate in Hampshire. It is a claim of family rather than of service or of sex; Cook notes on the same page that Ives called the group 'my little circle in the world'. Ives's diary, vol. 70, 21 May 1917, as quoted by Cook.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pp. 106-107 (printed folios 95 and 96 confirmed on the rendered pages; the quotation runs across the page break, breaking at 'has been with me some / 35 years').

sources.quote: Ives shared his new home, and sometimes his bed, with James Goddard (Kit), the son of one of his father's employees, and Harold Holt (Cubby), his grandmother's former secretary.
sources.context: Cook, on Ives's household at E4 the Albany

sources.quote: Kit brought his wife and children to live there for a while, and in 1909, Harold Bloodworth, a teenage footballer, moved in and stayed until Ives' death in 1950.
sources.context: Cook on Ives's move to Adelaide Road, Primrose Hill, in 1905 - the household intimacy outlasting Kit Goddard's marriage.
sources.supports: Cook records that Kit later brought his wife and children to live at Adelaide Road for a time - the household intimacy outlasting his marriage. Transcription pending.

sources.context: Cook's summary characterization of the Adelaide Road household relationships

sources.quote: The men thus shifted from (possible) lovers to sons and, in bed, to comrades.

sources.context: Cook, on the Albany chambers and their live-in servant provision

relationships.date_label: Letters from December 1887 to April 1893
relationships.summary: Seven letters over five and a half years, warming from 'Dear Mr Robertson' to 'My dear Graham' and from 'Very truly yours' to 'am always yours'. Wilde asks when he will see him again, is sorry when he goes away, calls twice in three days to catch him, tells him he is made for olive-groves and meadows of white narcissi, and says he should have loved to have been with him. Robertson was twenty-one when it began and Wilde thirty-three.
relationships.certainty_reasoning: OUTCOME is 'unknown' because Robertson's side does not survive in this volume; he lived to 1948 and wrote a memoir, Time Was (1931), which has not been consulted and is the obvious next source.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Robertson, I am so sorry but neither my wife or I ever go to dances: I am not sure whether we are too old or too young, but we never tread measures now. Pray thank your mother for her kindness all the same: I hope to have the pleasure of introducing my wife to her some day. When shall I see you again? The star-child is lovely: it is clear you have seen him: of course he is not an ordinary baby. We are always at home on Thursday. Very truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to W. Graham Robertson, [postmark 12 December 1887], 16 Tite Street (MS Huntington) — the earliest of the seven, quoted whole. Robertson had illustrated 'The Star-Child', which Wilde published in A House of Pomegranates (1891). Kept entire because it holds both halves of the case: 'When shall I see you again?' and the wife.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The start of the correspondence, on formal terms, already eager.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 359; printed folio 337 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Thank you so much for the drawings. They are a real source of delight to me. By the time you return I hope to have finished the story. I wish I could draw like you, for I like lines better than words, and colours more than sentences. However, I console myself by trying now and then to put 'The Universe' into a sonnet. Some day you must do a design for the sonnet: a young man looking into a strange crystal that mirrors all the world. Poetry should be like a crystal, it should make life more beautiful and less real. I am sorry you are going away, but your narcissus keeps you in my memory. What do you allow your friends to call you? 'W'? or 'Graham'? I like my friends to call me
sources.context: Wilde to W. Graham Robertson, [? early 1888], 16 Tite Street (MS Huntington) — quoted whole. The letter breaks off exactly as shown; the signature 'OSCAR' answers his own question. The design he asks for is a young man looking into a crystal.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The move onto first-name terms, and the narcissus that keeps him in mind.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 369; printed folio 347 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Graham, Come and dine here on Wednesday night at 7.30. I have asked Arthur Clifton. We will see Dr Cupid when you come back. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to W. Graham Robertson, [postmark 28 January 1889], 16 Tite Street (MS Huntington) — quoted whole.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Dinner at Tite Street, and a play promised for his return.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 412; printed folio 390 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Do you really live at Sandhills, Witley? Surely not Sandhills! You are made for olive-groves, and for meadows starred with white narcissi. I am sure this letter will be returned to me by the post office. I have written to you at Rutland Gate to tell you how sorry I am you have missed Paris, and how much more sorry I am that I did not keep you to your promise. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at both places; the allegation was never charged and Grainger never gave evidence. Carson's pressing of Wilde's flippant answer — that he never kissed Grainger because he was 'a peculiarly plain boy' — is recorded by Hyde as the climax of the cross-examination.

relationships.date_label: Close friends by 1892-93 (The Blackmailers, written together, produced June 1893); 'remained close friends for the rest of his life' (both died 1934); later years together in Edinburgh, where Raffalovich built St Peter's Church for Gray.
relationships.summary: Gray and Raffalovich were close by 1892-93, when they wrote The Blackmailers together (Prince of Wales's Theatre, June 1893) - the editors call Raffalovich Gray's 'close friend' and record the belief that he 'revenged himself' on Wilde by breaking up Wilde's friendship with Gray, 'with whom Raffalovich remained close friends for the rest of his life'. The bond ran unbroken to their deaths in the same year, 1934: Gray became a Roman Catholic priest, Raffalovich built St Peter's Church, Edinburgh, for him, and Gray's edition of Beardsley's last letters (1904) was of letters written to Raffalovich. relationships.summary: Gray was publicly tied to Wilde by February 1892, when the Daily Telegraph called him Wilde's 'protege' - a label Wilde corrected in print while praising Gray's 'perfected mode of expression'. In June 1892 Wilde personally undertook the production costs of Gray's Silverpoints (Mathews and Lane, 1893), and after The Picture of Dorian Gray appeared, Gray 'referred to himself as Dorian and allowed others in the Wilde circle to do so', though the editors find no evidence he was the character's original. The two fell out - the editors record the belief that Raffalovich broke the friendship up - but in De Profundis Wilde still ranked the friendship among those where 'my real life, my higher life' had been. Whether the bond was sexual rests on secondary claims not verified so far.

relationships.date_label: met at Bagnoles-de-l'Orne in the summer of 1934, when Souline came from the American Hospital in Paris as Hall's private nurse; the correspondence runs from July 1934 until Hall's death on 7 October 1943
relationships.summary: In 1934 Radclyffe Hall, fifty-four and between books, went to the Normandy spa of Bagnoles-de-l'Orne to treat an old riding injury. Una Troubridge, her partner since 1915, fell ill there, and Hall sent to the American Hospital in Paris for a private nurse. The nurse was Evguenia Souline, a Russian émigrée in her thirtieth year. What began with a few stolen kisses at the spa became a nine-year attachment conducted very largely by post - Hall wrote at first in letter-and-response intervals, then every two days, then daily and sometimes twice - and it did not displace Troubridge, who remained. Hall's editor calls the arrangement that followed "an imperfect, stormy triangle" and lets it stand as one. The letters were published in 1997 as Your John; Souline's replies were not kept, and one survives.

sources.quote: But in 1934 everything changed. … At Una's urging, therefore, they went to Bagnoles-de l'Orne, a spa in Normandy where John had once been treated for the same injury. relationships.date_label: met 1915; partners until Hall's death on 7 October 1943
relationships.summary: Una Troubridge, a sculptor and translator and Mabel Batten's cousin, met Radclyffe Hall in 1915 and the two became lifelong partners. Troubridge's marriage to the naval officer Sir Ernest Troubridge ended in separation by 1919, the Ransom Center's sketch states, because of the relationship with Hall. The partnership lasted until Hall's death in 1943 and survived Hall's long affair with the Russian nurse Evguenia Souline in her last nine years, which the same sketch records Troubridge as tolerating despite the unhappiness it caused her. Troubridge afterwards wrote The Life and Death of Radclyffe Hall (1961) and left 131 volumes of diaries.

sources.quote: Life with John was by no means always easy, but her variety was infinite and it was always interesting. That is why when at last her overtaxed body gave out and she could drive it no longer and she went to God for rest, I found that I had lost my occupation as well as my infinitely beloved companion.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Cook states plainly that Ives shared his bed with Harold Holt ('Cubby') at the Albany, which is more explicit than the household-membership evidence behind the Bloodworth record. It stays 'alleged' on the single-source rule: Cook (2003) is the only work read that attests it, and bed-sharing in a shared bachelor household is not by itself a statement of sexual relations. CORROBORATION: Cook returns to this household at much greater length in Queer Domesticities (2014), where he states that the Adelaide Road relationships 'possibly started sexually' before settling into something platonic, with bed-sharing continuing throughout. Cook's account of the Ives household is drawn from Ives's own 122-volume diary and his endnotes cite it by volume and date; the tier follows whose testimony underlies the claim, not whether our record happens to carry a direct quotation rather than the historian's summary of the same diary.

sources.quote: When Pug and another long term resident Cubby (Charles Gee) were both away he wrote in his diary: 'I feel sad. I love those two, deeply, tenderly [...] Love's quite different from passion [...] to sleep side by side with one's comrade is beyond all worlds beautiful. Not exciting, but oh such a protection and sympathy, of healing to the heart's many wounds'.
sources.context: Cook quoting Ives's diary (vol. 76, 20 January 1921, p. 25, per Cook's endnote 35) on Pug and Cubby being away; the ellipses are Cook's own
sources.supports: PROMOTED TO LEAD and QUOTE EXTENDED by the Q2 quality pass 2026-08-03. This is the only passage on this edge in which a participant speaks: Ives's diary, vol. 76, 20 January 1921, as quoted by Cook. The record previously led with Cook's narration and stopped this quotation at 'beyond all worlds beautiful', cutting the clause where Ives says what the bond gave him - 'Not exciting, but oh such a protection and sympathy, of healing to the heart's many wounds'. Ives names love, disclaims passion, and locates the value in comfort; that is the most explicit account of this relationship in his own words that survives in the sources read. THE CRUX OF THE CUBBY IDENTITY CONFLICT: Cook 2014 glosses Cubby as 'Charles Gee', where Cook 2003 p. 146 (quoted above in this record) glosses Cubby as 'Harold Holt'. Same author; neither statement carries a source note; the name 'Holt' does not appear anywhere in the 2014 book. Recorded so the conflict is visible in the record itself. Not resolved here - awaits a decision. Also carries Ives's own declaration of love for the two men and his explicit separation of love from passion.

sources.quote: He referred to his housemates affectionately but patronisingly with infantilising nicknames (Cubby, Pug, Kit, Elephant - Therese was Chooki) and also frequently as his 'children'. … 'My children all laugh at me', he complained, 'but they have not the responsibility of running a house with six or eight people in it; all to be milked for'.
sources.context: Cook, at printed 100, listing the pet names Ives used for the Adelaide Road household and then quoting Ives's diary (vol. 85, 1 August 1923, p. 46, per Cook's endnote 27). Elided between the two sentences: Cook's report that Ives was their 'old bird' and that they teased him to his face for being 'a stingy old b'.
sources.supports: The closest this record can come to Ives characterizing Saunders in his own voice, and the limit is worth stating exactly. Cook records that 'Elephant' was a name Ives himself used, and Ives's diary then names the household collectively as 'my children' - so the relationship Ives claimed with the men he lived with is paternal, proprietary and affectionate at once. But the naming is collective: Ives nowhere names Saunders or 'Elephant' in any first-person passage Cook prints, and Cook never dates Elephant's arrival, so whether Saunders was among the 'six or eight people' of the 1923 entry is not established. Ives's testimony reaching us through Cook, from Diary vol. 85. See the documented-absence note in the pointer entry below.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: One documented passionate kiss - Wilde kissed Ives 'passionately' goodbye at the New Travellers' Club, the word being Cook's in the source quotation from the Ives diary - inside a close, teasing friendship that ran from the early 1890s to Wilde's last months (surviving letters to Ives from Oct. 1893 to Sept. 1900, plus prison messages via Sherard). No source read asserts sexual relations; the editorial note that Ives's anonymous A Book of Chains (1897) held 'poems bearing directly on his feelings for Wilde in prison' supports a romantic charge on Ives's side.
relationships.date_label: Met early 1890s (Cook: 'shortly after' Ives's July 1891 move to St James'; Lewis podcast: 'in about 1893'); kiss undated (New Travellers' Club period); friendship to Wilde's death, Nov. 1900.
relationships.summary: Ives met Wilde in early-1890s London and was drawn into his club and cafe circle; at the New Travellers' Club Wilde once kissed him 'passionately' goodbye (Ives's diary, via Cook). The friendship survived Wilde's imprisonment - Wilde sent word from Reading that he was 'greatly touched' by Ives's wish to visit, and Ives's anonymous 1897 A Book of Chains carried poems on his feelings for Wilde in prison - and continued through the Paris exile, where Wilde teased Ives's 'silly mania for secrecy' and called him 'a great baby', writing to him warmly until three months before his death.

sources.quote: It is a pleasure to me to see you. … I like to talk to you about literature, life, the progress of thought, its power to touch the world, its practical energy - subjects of no interest to others than ourselves.
sources.context: Wilde to Ives, 12 February [Postmark 1900], Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris - the same letter as the 'silly mania for secrecy' passage below, five paragraphs further on, where Wilde answers Ives's request that they meet somewhere out of sight
sources.supports: Wilde in his own hand, writing to Ives, saying plainly what the friendship was: a pleasure, and a private subject-matter shared by the two of them and nobody else. Wilde is refusing Ives's insistence on hidden meeting-places, so the sentence doubles as his statement that this bond needs no concealment - the sharpest first-hand characterization of the Ives-Wilde relationship in the record, and unmediated, unlike the diary-quoting passages below.

sources.quote: Yes: I have no doubt we shall win, but the road is long, and red with monstrous martyrdoms. Nothing but the repeal of the Criminal Law Amendment Act would do any good.

relationships.date_label: fellow prisoners in Reading; the recommendation is of June 1897
relationships.summary: Lawley - or possibly Langley; the editors of Wilde's letters could not settle it - was a soldier who served time in Reading with Wilde and struck him as quiet and well conducted. In a postscript to a long, raw letter written a month after his release, Wilde put in a word to get him a place as a groom. That postscript is the whole of him.

sources.quote: With regard to Lawley. All soldiers are neat, and smart, and make capital servants. He would be a good groom; he is, I believe, a Third Hussars man. He was a quiet well-conducted chap in Reading always.
sources.context: A postscript, printed in italic beneath Wilde's signature, to a long letter of June 1897 whose main body is about a brother prisoner released on 4 June and about the writer's own hurt feelings. The editors' footnote to the name reads, in full, "Or possibly Langley." Wilde signs the letter itself "your sincere friend and admirer".
sources.supports: That the man existed, that Wilde thought well of him, and how little else the record kept.

relationships.date_label: fourteen letters survive across roughly a decade; the letter that carries the class is postmarked 1 December 1890
relationships.summary: Wilde wrote to Richard Le Gallienne over about ten years, mostly about books. In December 1890, thanking him for his study of Meredith, the register changed: he asked when they could meet, named what was between them as friendship and love, and finished on his laurels being too thick to kiss beneath. Le Gallienne's replies are not in the volume, so what came of it is not on the record.

sources.quote: I want so much to see you: when can that be? Friendship and love like ours need not meetings, but they are delightful. I hope your laurels are not too thick across your brow for me to kiss your eyelids. Always yours OSCAR
sources.context: The close of Wilde's letter to Le Gallienne postmarked 1 December 1890, from 16 Tite Street, praising his George Meredith: Some Characteristics, published a fortnight before. The preceding paragraph is literary criticism of the ordinary extravagant kind; the last paragraph is not.
sources.supports: The class, and the direction - this is Wilde writing, and only Wilde.

relationships.date_label: met at Florence, 1886; the poems and letters follow; Levy died in 1889
relationships.summary: Amy Levy met Vernon Lee at Florence in 1886 and fell in love with her. She sent Lee love poems - the sonnet 'To Vernon Lee', set on Bellosguardo, and 'New Love, New Life' - and expressed her admiration in letters; the friendship also brought her into Lee's circle, notably the poet Dorothy Blomfield. Nothing in the sources read records reciprocation by Lee, and Levy's biographer describes a woman who never had a requited attachment to any of the women she loved. Levy died by suicide in 1889, three years after the Florence meeting. The two women's other point of contact is Wilde himself, who was publishing Levy in the Woman's World across exactly these years.

sources.quote: Levy’s visit to Florence in 1886 was pivotal because she met Violet Paget (Vernon Lee), an important figure in the aesthetic movement of the fin de siècle. The love poems Levy sent to Lee (e.g., “To Vernon Lee” and “New Love, New Life”) are revealing, and in letters Levy expressed her admiration. The friendship enabled Levy to become intimate with Lee’s circle of friends, particularly the poet Dorothy Blomfield.
sources.context: Linda Hunt Beckman - Levy's biographer (Amy Levy: Her Life and Letters, 2000) - in the Shalvi/Hyman Encyclopedia of Jewish Women. 'The love poems Levy sent to Lee' is a biographer's characterisation resting on Levy's own poems and letters, which Beckman edited.
sources.supports: That Levy sent Lee love poems and expressed admiration in letters: the desire, and its direction.
sources.provenance: https://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/levy-amy fetched (curl) and read in full 2026-08-03; quote sliced byte-exact from the downloaded HTML, then whitespace artifacts introduced by stripping inline markup (spaces around quotation marks, italic titles and punctuation) normalized to the printed reading.

sources.quote: Levy’s sexual orientation remains a point of contention among scholars. She was, it seems, a platonic lesbian, who never experienced a requited love attachment with any of the women to whom she was attracted. In 1886, while Levy stayed in Florence, she met and became infatuated with Vernon Lee (Violet Piaget), a novelist and essayist, to whom she dedicated one of her best sonnets.
sources.context: Andrzej Diniejko's Victorian Web biography. The page then prints 'To Vernon Lee' in full. 'Violet Piaget' is Diniejko's misspelling of Paget. Note the scholarly caveat in the first sentence, which is why it is quoted rather than elided.
sources.supports: The one-sidedness (outcome = unreciprocated), the 1886 Florence meeting, and the dedication of the sonnet.

relationships.date_label: met 1880; attachment lasting until Robinson's marriage in 1887
relationships.summary: Vernon Lee met the poet Mary Robinson in 1880, the year Lee came to public notice with Studies of the Eighteenth Century in Italy, and the two formed what Pulham calls a romantic friendship. Robinson visited Lee's home in Florence and Lee returned the visit in London in 1881, where Robinson introduced her to the Burne-Joneses, Gosse, the Morrises, the Rossettis and Oscar Wilde - which is how Lee entered the London circle this map charts. The attachment ended with Robinson's marriage in 1887 to the orientalist James Darmesteter; Kit Anstruther-Thomson replaced her as Lee's companion that same year.

sources.quote: It is also in 1880 that Lee first met the poet Mary Robinson (1857-1944) with whom she developed a romantic friendship that lasted until Mary married in 1887.
sources.context: Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography of Vernon Lee, in the paragraph on Lee's emergence in 1880. The following sentences record Robinson's account of the visitors to 'Casa Paget' and Lee's return visit to London in 1881, at which she met Wilde.
sources.supports: The relationship, its character as Pulham states it, and both its start and end dates.

sources.quote: In 1881, Lee in turn visited Mary in London. Here she met many of the Robinsons’ friends and acquaintances including the Burne-Joneses, Edmund Gosse (1849-1928), the Morrises, the Rossettis, and Oscar Wilde (1854-1900).
sources.context: Pulham, immediately following. This is the sentence that puts Lee in the Wilde circle and puts Robinson at the door of it: the introductions are Robinson's.
sources.supports: That the connection to Wilde's London circle ran through Robinson - relevant to why both women are on this roster.

sources.quote: Lee and Robinson met in Florence on 16 October 1880 at a party at Maria Spartali Stillman's and they became steadfast friends and romantic partners for almost eight years – a romantic friendship to which their letters testify (Selected Letters of Vernon Lee, Vols. I and II); and Lee took on the role in Mary's life of a strong companion who at times was both nurturing and domineering. … Lee suffered a long period of depression after the marriage took place in August 1888.
sources.context: The editors' biographical note on Mary Robinson in the standard scholarly edition of Lee's correspondence. It states the relationship's character, its exact beginning and its length without hedging, and cites the letters themselves in Vols. I and II. The elision drops the account of Robinson's proposal to James Darmesteter in 1887 and the two families' objections. Note that the edition names the correspondence as the evidence but places it in volumes this project does not hold - Vol. III, the volume on disk, begins in 1890, after the attachment ended.
sources.supports: The standard edition stating the relationship as romantic, dating its start exactly, giving its length, and recording Lee's depression after the marriage.
