sources.quote: I am going to have a dedication. I don't put any initials or name. I simply say: When I came out of prison / some met me with garments and with spices, / and others with wise counsel. / You met me with love. Please let me see it in some nice type. I think it a beautiful and simple dedication. I hope you do too.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [October 1897], Villa Giudice, Posillipo - quoted whole from where the dedication is raised. THE DEDICATION IS TO ROSS AND IT WAS NEVER PRINTED. The editors' footnote is unambiguous: 'These words were addressed to Robbie Ross, but they did not appear in The Ballad.' Wilde is explicit that the name is to be withheld - 'I don't put any initials or name' - so what he proposed was an unsigned declaration that only its addressee would recognise, and even that was dropped. A SECOND, PUBLISHED dedication went instead to C. T. W., the hanged trooper. NOTE ALSO THE SETTING: Wilde was at Posillipo living with Douglas as he wrote this. CORRECTED 2026-08-06 - an earlier note of mine filed this phrase as Wilde writing to Smithers about Smithers, because the line sits in a letter to Smithers and the page-break hid the footnote. Re-reading the following folio settled it.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: A dedication of love to Ross, composed, shown to the publisher, and then suppressed.

relationships.date_label: late 1893 – February 1895 (acquaintance); Oct 1893 – Apr 1894 (plea allegation)
relationships.summary: Ernest Scarfe, a young valet-turned-clerk who had been to the Australian gold-diggings — meeting Lord Douglas of Hawick on the voyage out in 1893 — knew Taylor from the Knightsbridge Skating Rink and was introduced by him to Wilde at 10 St James's Place. He visited repeatedly, dined alone with Wilde, and received the customary cigarette case; the acquaintance ran to a dinner at the Avondale in February 1895. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at St James's Place; Scarfe was never called and the allegation never charged.

sources.quote: You knew a man named Ernest Scarfe?—Yes. He was introduced to me by Taylor. He is a young man of about twenty, of no occupation. Atkins testified to finding the twenty-two-year-old Schwabe in bed with Wilde at 29 Boulevard des Capucines in November 1892 — testimony from a witness whose credibility was destroyed at the same trial. The plea's Schwabe clause alleges solicitation only, and Schwabe, abroad, was never called.

relationships.date_label: During a three-day stop at Naples on the Italian journey Wilde made with Harold Mellor in April 1900, before they reached Rome on Holy Thursday. The reporting letter is dated 16 April 1900 by the editors' heading - located in the OCR mirror, not read in the source; the editors' footnote on the page read gives Easter Day 1900 as 15 April, and Wilde dates his Vatican appearance 'yesterday'.
relationships.summary: Travelling up through Italy with Harold Mellor in April 1900, Wilde stopped three days at Naples and wrote to Robert Ross that he had fallen in love with a Sea-God, joking that the young man was for some extraordinary reason at the Regia Marina School instead of being with Triton. In the same breath he notes that most of his Naples friends are in prison. Nothing further about the young man appears in the pages read: no name, no age, no outcome.

sources.quote: At Naples we stopped three days. Most of my friends are, as you know, in prison, but I met some of nice memory, and fell in love with a Sea-God, who for some extraordinary reason is at the Regia Marina School, instead of being with Triton.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 16 April [1900], from Rome - a travel narrative running from Palermo through Naples to the Easter pilgrimage at the Vatican. 'H. M.' in the next paragraph is Harold Mellor, his travelling companion.
sources.supports: The whole of the record: Wilde's own statement that he fell in love, the young man's institution, and the absence of any recorded outcome
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1225, printed folio 1179 confirmed at the foot of the rendered page. The letter's heading (recipient, date, address) stands on an earlier printed page not read and is mirror-derived; the page read carries the editors' footnote 'Easter Day 1900 was on 15 April'.

relationships.date_label: February 1892 – March 1893 (acquaintance broken off by Shelley's letter)
relationships.summary: Edward Shelley, a clerk at Wilde's publishers the Bodley Head, dined with Wilde at the Albemarle Hotel in February 1892; his testimony describes being kissed and embraced, objecting, and nonetheless staying the night in Wilde's bed, with 'a repetition of the previous night's performance' the next day. He received inscribed books and letters, quarrelled with Wilde at the Savoy in March 1893, and broke off the acquaintance. The count concerning him was withdrawn from the jury for lack of corroboration at the final trial.

disputed.claim: that Wilde committed sexual acts (sodomy solicited; gross indecency and indecent assault committed) with Edward Shelley at the Albemarle Hotel, February-May 1892
disputed.asserted_by: Queensberry's plea of justification (filed 30 March 1895); Crown indictment count 25 in Regina v. Wilde (1895); Shelley's testimony as to kisses, embraces and a shared bed
disputed.disputed_by: Shelley's own cross-examination (no 'actual improprieties'; 'attempts … on two occasions'); Wilde's sworn denials at all three trials; Mr Justice Wills's withdrawal of the count for want of corroboration; the jury's formal not-guilty on the Shelley count (25 May 1895)
disputed.grounds: the only first-person account stops short of completed acts and the witness resisted; the trial judge held the evidence legally uncorroborated (Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 306-307, 337)

sources.quote: Mr. Wilde said, "Will you come into my bedroom?" I did not know what he meant. As I went into the room Mr. Wilde kissed me. He also put his arms round me. I had been taking a lot of wine. I felt insulted, degraded, and objected vigorously. Mr. Wilde said he was sorry and that he had drunk too much wine. I stayed the night and shared his bed. Mr. Wilde saw me next day and again kissed me and there was a repetition of the previous night's performance.

After that visit I wrote to Mr. Wilde saying that I would not see him again. I think now that attempts at improprieties took place on two occasions. On the first occasion I was not quite sober. relationships.date_label: Met in Paris, early 1883; letters to February 1898
relationships.summary: Fifteen years, and the arc is legible in the letters. In 1883 Wilde accepted the dedication of Sherard's poems — 'one whom I love so much as I love you' — thought of him 'wandering in violet valleys with your honey-coloured hair', and closed a letter 'confidence in our love'. From Holloway in 1895, with almost everyone gone, he wrote 'your chivalrous friendship — your fine, chivalrous friendship — is worth more than all the money in the world'; from Reading in 1896, 'you are one of the few people I would like to see'. Then in 1897 Sherard denounced the reunion with Douglas and Wilde answered coldly. The last letter, in 1898, sends him a book 'in memory of our long friendship' because he would not come in person.
relationships.certainty_reasoning: WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: no source says the attachment was sexual, and Wilde names the thing friendship every time he names it — 'the mirror of perfect friendship' (1883), 'your chivalrous friendship' (1895), 'our uninterrupted friendship, of twelve years' standing' (1896), 'an old and noble friendship' (1898). OUTCOME is 'unknown' because Sherard's side of the correspondence is not in this volume. The two scholarly readings that carried the earlier class still stand in the record - Ellmann on 'young, blond, and idolatrous', McKenna on Sherard being 'obsessed by him' - and both now read as corroboration rather than as the whole case. NOTE ON THE 1897 QUARREL (printed 963, already cited above): an earlier pass had it, and on 2026-08-06 I re-added it from the page without checking, which the duplicate validator caught.

sources.quote: Dear Robert, Your letter was as loveable as yourself, and this is my first moment after channel-crossings, train-catchings, and my natural rage at the charges for extra luggage from Paris, for sitting down to tell you what pleasure it gave me, and what memories of moonlit meanderings, and sunset strolls, the mere sight of your handwriting brought. As for the dedication of your poems, I accept it: how could I refuse a gift so musical in its beauty, and fashioned by one whom I love so much as I love you? … That is, I think, what we are seeking, and that you should seek it with me, you who are yourself so dear to me, gives me faith in our futures, confidence in our love.
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, postmark 17 May 1883, 8 Mount Street, Grosvenor Square, London (MS Clark). The elision drops nothing between the two paragraphs but the paragraph break. The editors' note 2 gives the dedication itself, to Whispers (1884): 'To Oscar Wilde, Poet and Friend, Affectionately and admiringly Dedicated'.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The warmest surviving language between them, in Wilde's own hand, including the letter's actual close — 'confidence in our love'.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 232-233; printed folios 210 and 211 both confirmed on the rendered page images. The letter runs across the page break and ENDS on 211 - an earlier version of this record stopped it at 'purified but consumed' on 210, missing the close. The elision drops the two middle paragraphs on friendship and art, which are quoted separately below. This also corrects the 2026-08-04 sweep's citation of printed 202.

sources.quote: To me the mirror of perfect friendship can never be dulled by any treachery, however mean, or disloyalty, however base. … That is what I think true friendship should be, like that men could make their lives: but friendship is a fire where what is not flawless shrinks into grey ashes, and where what is imperfect is not purified but consumed.
sources.context: The same letter, immediately after the dedication paragraph. It is quoted here because it is the counter-evidence on the same page: Wilde names the thing three times, and the word he uses is friendship.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's own framing of the attachment, against which the affectionate language has to be read.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 232; printed folio 210 confirmed on the rendered page image. The ellipsis drops a paragraph on art and beauty.

sources.quote: That Wilde put up with him at all was due to Sherard's possession of three compensatory merits: he was young, blond, and idolatrous. Not precisely handsome, he was 'beau laid.'
sources.context: Ellmann on why Wilde tolerated Sherard, whom he has just described as uncomprehending. This is the biographer's reading, not either man's statement.
sources.supports: A scholar attributing Wilde's interest in Sherard partly to youth and looks — one of the two readings this connection's class rests on.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 305. **PAGINATION WARNING: this file carries NO printed folios** - checked at PDF 200, 305, 306 and 400, where the text layer begins and ends in running prose - so the locator is written 'PDF p.' and must be re-anchored to a paginated copy before publication, exactly as with murray-2020.

sources.quote: Sherard was not so much devoted to Oscar as obsessed by him. It was an obsession that was to last to the end of his life.
sources.context: McKenna on Sherard's attachment to Wilde. Located in the repo PDF's text layer; NOT yet read at the rendered page.
sources.supports: The second of the two scholarly readings — and the one that makes the attachment asymmetric.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 74, located in the text layer 2026-08-05 and quoted from it. NOT read at the rendered page and NOT folio-confirmed, so it is marked unverified rather than dressed up: it is here because the disputed block cites it, and it should be read at the page before it is relied on.

sources.quote: My dear Robert, I cannot tell you how your letters have cheered and comforted me in this awful, terrible position in which I am placed, and how glad I am that Sarah, and Goncourt, and other artists are sympathising with me. Pray assure Louÿs, Stuart Merrill, Moréas, and all others how touched – touched beyond words – I am. … Ever, with deepest affection and gratitude
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, 13 April 1895, HM Prison, Holloway (MS Clark) — written between the collapse of the libel action and the first criminal trial, when most of his acquaintance had dropped him. The elision drops the request that Sherard ask Sarah Bernhardt to buy Salomé, and the sum Wilde needed; it is money business, not the two of them.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Sherard was to Wilde at the worst moment of his life, in Wilde's own hand — and how Wilde signed off to him from prison.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 693-694; printed folios 642 and 643 both confirmed on the rendered page images. The letter runs across the page break.

sources.quote: My dear Robert, You good, daring reckless friend! I was delighted to get your letter, with all its wonderful news. For myself, I am ill – apathetic. Slowly life creeps out of me. Nothing but Alfred Douglas's daily visits quicken me into life, and even him I only see under humiliating and tragic conditions. Don't fight more than six duels a week! I suppose Sarah is hopeless; but your chivalrous friendship – your fine, chivalrous friendship – is worth more than all the money in the world. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, 16 April 1895, HM Prison, Holloway (MS Du Cann), three days after the letter above. Quoted whole: nothing in it is off the subject of the two of them. 'Don't fight more than six duels a week' is not a joke at random — Sherard had been challenging Wilde's detractors in Paris.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The warmest surviving statement of what the attachment was — and Wilde's own word for it, said twice: friendship.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 695; printed folio 644 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Robert, Your letters are charming, they are iridescent, and everything you see or hear seems to become touched with colour, and tinged with joy. I think of you often, wandering in violet valleys with your honey-coloured hair, and meditating on the influence of paradoxes on the pastoral mind. But you should be here … My book you will have next week: it is a great pleasure to give it to anyone so sympathetic as you. Poet to poet I give you my work because your joy in it makes it more dear to me. Who is your young man who likes what I said of the primrose?
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, [May-June 1883], London (MS Clark). The elision drops a paragraph of London gossip and self-description. THIS IS THE PHYSICAL ADMIRATION the classification turns on: Wilde thinking of Sherard often, and picturing his hair.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde dwelling on Sherard's appearance — the one thing the record needed to carry an arrow, and the reason this connection is attraction-expressed rather than uncorroborated.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 233; printed folio 211 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Robert, The Governor has told me that you have written to ask to see me. It is most kind and affectionate of you, but an order has already been sent to More Adey and Arthur Clifton … I often think of you and of our uninterrupted friendship, of twelve years' standing, and while I bitterly regret the sorrow that I have brought on you and others of my friends, I remember with pride and gratitude your chivalry and courage on my behalf. Should the end of my terrible punishment ever come, you are one of the few people I would like to see, and be with from time to time. Please remember me very kindly to George Ives. I was greatly touched at hearing of his desire to come and see me. In the terrible solitude and silence in which one lives a message or a memory means a great deal. … I was so disappointed at not seeing you that I have been allowed as a favour to write this letter to you.
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, Wednesday [26 August 1896], HM Prison, Reading (MS Hyde). Sherard had applied to visit and been shut out by the two-visitor rule. The elisions drop the visiting-order mechanics and a paragraph routing correspondence through More Adey. NOTE the George Ives paragraph: Ives is on this map, and this is Wilde asking to be remembered to him from prison, through Sherard.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's own dating of the friendship, his account of what Sherard had done for him, and the Ives link.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 713; printed folio 662 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: When you wish to talk morality – always an amusement – and to attack me behind my back, don't, like a good fellow, talk so loud, as the reverberation reaches from the [Authors'] Club to Naples; also, it is easy – far too easy – for you to find an audience that does not contain any friends of mine; before them, play Tartuffe in the style of Termagant to your heart's content; but when you do it in the presence of friends of mine, you expose yourself to rebuke and contempt, and of course I hear all about it.
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, [circa 16 October 1897], Naples — the whole of the surviving fragment, taken by the editors from Sherard's own Story of an Unhappy Friendship. Sherard had been denouncing Wilde's reunion with Lord Alfred Douglas at Naples. THE RECORD IS NOT ALL WARMTH and this is why it is here.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The rupture — Sherard attacking Wilde publicly, and Wilde's cold answer.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1011; printed folio 963 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: … I am sending you a copy of my Ballad – first edition – which I hope you will accept in memory of our long friendship. I had hoped to give it to you personally, but I know you are very busy, tho' I am sorry you are too busy to come and see me or to let me know where you are to be seen …
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, [? end February 1898], Paris — the last surviving letter to him, four months after the rebuke, and printed by the editors from Sherard's own book. The ellipses are the editors' own, marking a fragment. The editors add that the surviving copy (Hyde Collection) is inscribed 'Robert Harborough Sherard: in memory of an old and noble friendship: from the author Oscar Wilde'.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The reconciliation, and its distance — a book sent because the man would not come.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1072; printed folio 1026 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Robert, Many thanks for your letter. Sarah, of course, did not keep her appointment – she never does. Thank Hugues Rebell very much from me. I need not say how deeply touched I am by any kindness from an artist. Dear old Robert. Ever affectionately yours
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, 20 April 1895, HM Prison, Holloway (MS Clark) — the third and last of the Holloway letters, quoted whole. 'Sarah' is Bernhardt: the editors record that Sherard was chasing her round Paris on Wilde's behalf, that she wept at his plight, promised a loan, made a series of appointments with Sherard, kept none of them and sent nothing. That errand is the 'chivalry and courage' Wilde thanks him for from Reading a year later.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The close of the Holloway sequence, and how Wilde signed off to him: 'Dear old Robert. Ever affectionately yours.'
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 696; printed folio 645 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Robert, If you send me your play I will forward it to Wilson Barrett. His address changes every week as he is on tour. I have been so busy that your letter escaped me. I hope you are well; that you are brilliant your letters and stories in the Table assure me. You certainly have the clever touch and caustic satire of the man of the world. How is your pretty, romantic looking wife with her lovely eyes? No one plays dominoes with me now. I hope you will come over to London soon. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, [? 1888], 16 Tite Street (MS Clark) — quoted whole, and the domestic one of the thirteen. Sherard was in Paris writing anonymous 'Romances of the Table'; the editors' note records that he had married a Polish woman, Martha Lips, in 1886. 'No one plays dominoes with me now' is the whole of what Wilde says about missing him, and is the reason this letter is here.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The friendship in its ordinary years: Wilde reading his journalism, asking after his wife, and saying he is missed.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 369-370; printed folios 347 and 348 both confirmed on the rendered page images. The letter runs across the page break.

sources.quote: Dear Robert, Just enter on page one: 'Son père, Sir William Wilde, était archéologue très célèbre et homme de lettres, et du côté de sa mère il est le petit-neveu de l'étrange romancier Maturin, l'ami de Goethe, de Byron, et de Scott; l'auteur de Melmoth, that strange and wonderful book that so thrilled Balzac and Baudelaire, and was a part of the romantic movement in France in 1830.' … Do dine tonight, will you? Come at 6.30. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, [December 1891], Paris (MS Koch). Sherard was writing a long French article on Wilde for Le Gaulois and had sent it for approval; the editors note that all Wilde's suggestions were incorporated. The elision drops two further corrections to the copy. Kept for the last line and for what the letter is: Wilde dictating his own public image to a friend who accepted every word of it.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The working intimacy — Wilde editing Sherard's account of him, and asking him to dinner the same evening.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 524; printed folio 504 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Dear Robert, I am so pleased you are all right. Never mind about the brute. You have asserted yourself like a brave gentleman. Ever
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, [? early 1892], Lyric Club (MS Montague) — quoted whole. It follows a duel Sherard fought in Paris. THE OTHER SIDE OF THE CORRESPONDENCE IS IN THE EDITORS' NOTE, and is the only statement from Sherard's own hand anywhere in this record: he describes Wilde talking his alarmed relation out of going to the police, which 'would have put me under taboo in Paris for the rest of my days', and then writing to approve his conduct — 'I do not think that any of his letters ever gave me so much pleasure.'
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's approval after the duel, and — through the note — what Sherard said his letters meant to him, which nothing else here supplies.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 530; printed folio 510 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Robert, If McClure wishes me to be interviewed he must pay me. I dislike the tone of his letter, and I never allow myself to be interviewed. For you, as we are old friends and I appreciate and admire you, I don't mind allowing an interview: but McClure, after his letter, must understand that I must be paid … Besides, I am sick of my name in the papers. It was charming seeing you so well and so delightful the other night. Truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, [postmark 30 November 1894], Albemarle Club (MS Clark). The elision drops the fee arithmetic. Six months before the trials.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde making an exception to a standing rule for Sherard, and saying why: 'as we are old friends and I appreciate and admire you'.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 676; printed folio 624 confirmed on the rendered page image.

relationships.date_label: m. 1883 or 1884 (sources conflict); still married November 1884
relationships.summary: Harry Stafford married Eva Westcott in 1883 or 1884 - the Whitman Archive's note on the letters says one year, its encyclopedia entry the other - after drifting between jobs and returning to the family farm. Whitman kept writing to them, addressing the two of them together as late as 18 November 1884. The marriage and the attachment to Whitman are not alternatives, and this map does not treat them as such.

sources.supports: That Harry Stafford married Eva Westcott, given as 1884 by Kantrowitz's encyclopedia entry and as 1883 by the correspondent note the Whitman Archive attaches to Stafford's letters - a conflict the Archive itself carries. Corroborated by the Archive's own item title for a letter of 18 November 1884, 'Walt Whitman to Harry and Eva Stafford' (whitmanarchive.org/item/loc.04000), in which Whitman addresses the two of them as a couple.
sources.provenance: NOT TRANSCRIBED. The Whitman Archive sits behind a Cloudflare challenge and returns HTTP 403 to curl and to plain fetching; a direct re-fetch was attempted and blocked on 2026-08-05. The marriage and the 1883/1884 conflict were already recorded on data/people/stafford.json from a reading of Kantrowitz's entry in a real browser on 2026-08-04. Rather than rebuild a quotation out of search-result fragments, this stays a pointer until someone reads the page in a browser again.

relationships.date_label: met in 1876 at the Camden New Republic, Stafford eighteen and Whitman fifty-seven; closest through the Timber Creek years to about 1884, when Stafford married; the two remained in contact until Whitman's death in 1892
relationships.summary: Harry Stafford was an errand boy of eighteen when Whitman met him in a Camden newspaper office in 1876. He took the poet home to his parents' tenant farm at Kirkwood, where Whitman spent the next several summers bathing in Timber Creek and wrestling saplings back to health, and where the two shared a top-floor bedroom. It was a quarrelsome, unequal, much-interrupted attachment - Whitman gave Stafford a friendship ring and Stafford gave it back more than once - and it is the relationship early Whitman scholarship most successfully ignored, because Traubel's first six volumes never mention his name. Whitman's friend John Burroughs, less discreetly, complained that the two 'cut up like two boys'.

sources.quote: Dear Friend— You know how I left you at the station to-day. I have thought of it and cannot get it off my mind, so I have come up to ask your forgiveness. I know how I have served you on many occasions before. I know that it is my falt and not yours. Can you forgive me and take me back and love me the same I will try by the grace of God to do better. I cannot give you up, and it makes me feel so bad to think how we have spent the last day or two; and all for my temper. … Cant you take me back and love me the same. Your lovin but bad tempered Harry.
sources.context: Stafford to Whitman, dated by Miller to 1 May 1877, after a quarrel at the station. Stafford was eighteen. The elision drops one sentence about his temper sending him to prison. **The spelling is Stafford's** - 'falt', 'Cant', 'lovin' - and the archive flags each instance in its markup. The letter is written on the back of someone else's letter to Whitman, which is its own small fact about who had paper. This is the fullest surviving statement from Stafford's side.
sources.supports: The younger participant's own words - the asking-back, the 'I cannot give you up', and the register of the whole attachment.
sources.provenance: https://whitmanarchive.org/item/loc.03964 read in full in a browser 2026-08-04. **The site sits behind Cloudflare and returns 403 to curl and to plain fetching**; it was read in a real browser. An automated retrieval will falsely report it unavailable. Transcribed from the archive's text; the archive's invisible sic markers were dropped and the writer's spelling kept.
sources.speaker: Harry Stafford, letter to Walt Whitman

sources.quote: Dear Hank— Yours of 9th rec'd—am a little surprised you take to L of G so quickly—I guess it is because the last five years had been preparing & fixing the ground, more & more & more—& now that the seed is dropt in it sprouts quickly … Hank, I am still feeling under the weather—My appetite is fair, (when I can get what I like)—& sleep middling, but I am as weak as a cat … (Hank, you do not appreciate your mother—there is not a nobler woman in Jersey)— Your Walt
sources.context: Whitman to Stafford, 11 February 1881, from Camden, five years into the acquaintance; the envelope is addressed to 'Harry Lamb Stafford | Kirkwood | Glendale | New Jersey'. Whitman had given him a copy of Leaves of Grass four days earlier. The register is the ordinary one of this correspondence - domestic, instructive, unguarded about his own body - and it is worth recording precisely because it is not ardent: the attachment ran mostly at this temperature.
sources.supports: The sustained private correspondence and its everyday register.
sources.provenance: https://whitmanarchive.org/item/nyp.00423 read in full in a browser 2026-08-04. The archive's transcription derives from Miller's Correspondence, p. 211; original in the Berg Collection, New York Public Library. **The site sits behind Cloudflare and returns 403 to curl and to plain fetching**; it was read in a real browser. An automated retrieval will falsely report it unavailable.
sources.speaker: Walt Whitman, letter to Harry Stafford

sources.quote: Stafford and Whitman slept together in the same top floor bedroom, and when they traveled together Whitman referred to him as "my nephew" and insisted that they be accommodated in the same bed. … Despite the frolicking, the relationship was a stormy one. They quarreled frequently, and several times Stafford returned a friendship ring given to him by Whitman. … The nature of their bond remains mysterious, and critics have interpreted it as everything from asexual and paternal to erotic and promiscuous.
sources.context: Arnie Kantrowitz's reference entry on Stafford. Recorded as the second-hand layer, and kept at length because its last sentence is the honest state of the scholarship. The elisions drop Burroughs's complaint that the two 'cut up like two boys' and Stafford's own 'something wanting to compleete [sic] our friendship', which Kantrowitz glosses 'perhaps meaning sexual relations'. Kantrowitz also records that Whitman met a Stafford farm hand, Ed Cattell, at the creek and kept those meetings secret from Stafford - see cattell--whitman.
sources.supports: The shared bed, the ring, the quarrels - and that the sexual question is contested among specialists rather than settled.

An automated retrieval will falsely report it unavailable. Curly quotation marks around 'my nephew' are the source's; the parenthetical page citations to Miller's Correspondence are omitted.

Stafford's marriage to Eva Westcott is given as **1884** by Kantrowitz's encyclopedia entry and as **1883** by the correspondent note the Whitman Archive attaches to Stafford's letters - two statements on the same site. Neither is followed here; the bio and date_label carry both. ALSO NOTED, as a caution for any older secondary source on Whitman's circle: the archive states Stafford's name appears **nowhere in the first six volumes** of Traubel's With Walt Whitman in Camden, and only in the last three, published in the 1990s. An absence in Traubel is not evidence of absence in Whitman's life.

relationships.date_label: Alleged March 1893, at the Savoy Hotel — plea only

disputed.claim: that Wilde took indecent liberties with Herbert Tankard at the Savoy Hotel in March 1893
disputed.asserted_by: Queensberry's plea of justification (filed 30 March 1895)
disputed.grounds: The allegation stands in the plea alone. Tankard was traced to Calais by Queensberry's solicitors but never called, gave no evidence at any of the three proceedings, and left no account of his own; no indictment count concerned him. `disputed_by` is null because there is nothing on the other side either - unlike Scarfe, Wilde was never asked about Tankard in the witness box, so the record holds an untested allegation and no denial. The clause is also the weakest on its page: where Parker, Scarfe and Grainger are alleged to have been solicited 'to commit sodomy and other acts of gross indecency', Tankard's alleges only 'indecent liberties'.

relationships.summary: A clause in the Marquess of Queensberry's 1895 plea of justification alleging that Wilde took indecent liberties with Herbert Tankard, a Savoy pageboy, in March 1893. Tankard was traced to Calais by Queensberry's solicitors but never called, and gave no evidence. Nothing corroborates the allegation and nothing of Tankard's own account survives.

sources.quote: And that the said Oscar Fingal O'fflahertie Wills Wilde in the said month of March in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and ninety-three at the said Savoy Hotel did take indecent liberties with one Herbert Tankard.
sources.context: The Marquess of Queensberry's plea of justification, printed as Appendix A. The clause immediately follows those naming Charles Parker and Ernest Scarfe, and is followed by the one naming Walter Grainger.
sources.supports: The allegation itself, in the plea's own words — the whole of the record for this connection.

relationships.date_label: January 1893 (three weeks' cohabitation; acquaintance possibly from May 1892 per Taylor)
relationships.summary: Alfred Wood, an out-of-work clerk, lived at Taylor's one-bed rooms at 13 Little College Street for about three weeks in January 1893, sharing the room and — on the arithmetic of his own testimony that the rooms held 'only one bed' — the bed. He dated his first acts of indecency to going to College Street without naming a partner. Taylor said they had met earlier, in May 1892 at Atkins's rooms. The procuring-Wood counts against Taylor ended in a directed not-guilty; no count alleged acts between the two men.

disputed.claim: that sexual relations occurred between Taylor and Wood at 13 Little College Street, January 1893
disputed.asserted_by: the implication of Wood's own sworn testimony (a single bed shared for three weeks; first acts of indecency dated to 'when I went to College Street' — Hyde pp. 201, 205)
disputed.disputed_by: no direct attestation by any witness; no charge concerning acts between Taylor and Wood; the counts charging Taylor with procuring Wood for Wilde ended in a directed verdict of Not Guilty (Hyde pp. 292-293)
disputed.grounds: testimony implies but never states acts with Taylor himself; classification per the single-source/contested rule

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Every word of feeling in this record is on Warren's side and is reported by Sox - 'infatuation', loved, 'wanted to possess'. What was seen from outside is carefully hedged in the source itself: SOME SAW Thomas as 'Ned's new boy friend', which records a perception and not a fact, and the quotation marks are Sox's.
relationships.summary: Harry Thomas came to Warren as protege and private secretary, giving Lewes House as his Harvard address in 1903-04. By 1906 Warren was parading him around Boston and Fewacres and some read him as 'Ned's new boy friend'; Marshall was bitterly jealous. Sox counts Warren's infatuation with Thomas among the strains that ran through his relationships, and counts Thomas among those Warren loved and wanted to possess. Thomas married Nan Devey the year after Marshall married, and stayed in Warren's service until Warren died.

sources.quote: In 1906, Ned paraded his young and handsome protégé, Harry, around Boston and Fewacres. This was especially hard for Marshall to swallow as some saw Harry as 'Ned's new boy friend'.
sources.context: On the growing 1906-07 alienation between Warren and Marshall; the preceding sentences: Marshall despised Harold Parsons and 'of the other, Harry Thomas, he was bitterly jealous'.
sources.supports: The contemporary perception of Thomas as 'Ned's new boy friend' and Marshall's jealousy
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 93, printed folio 77 confirmed on rendered page.

relationships.date_label: Seen once, at Cannes, 1 February 1899
relationships.summary: Wilde saw him at the Bataille des Fleurs at Cannes and wrote about him to Robert Ross the following day — 'a very handsome boy, all wreathed with flowers' — answering the sight with 'Imperial, Neronian Rome'. One sighting, admiringly described; no contact of any kind is recorded.

sources.quote: Today, for the first time, rain – quite an Irish day. Yesterday was lovely. I went to Cannes to see the Bataille des Fleurs. The loveliest carriage – all yellow roses, the horses with traces and harness of violets – was occupied by an evil-looking old man, English: on the box, beside the coachman, sat his valet, a very handsome boy, all wreathed with flowers. I murmured 'Imperial, Neronian Rome'.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 2 February 1899, Napoule (MS Clark). The Bataille des Fleurs is the flower-battle carnival at Cannes; Wilde had gone over for the day from Napoule, where he was staying with Frank Harris.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The whole of the record for this connection: Wilde's sighting, his description of the young man as very handsome, and the frame he put round it.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1167; printed folio 1121 confirmed on the rendered page image. The sweep cited this as 'printed ~1119', which the page image corrects.

relationships.date_label: A single evening or afternoon, Paris, late March 1900
relationships.summary: Wilde was seen in a boy's company outside a cafe behind the Madeleine by Aleck Ross, and wrote about it to Aleck's brother Robbie the same week. The encounter is known only from Wilde's own sentence, and his framing of it - 'half rough, all Hylas' - is the whole of the evidence for reading it as more than company.

sources.quote: Only an hour after I, with 'waving hands' like Tennyson's Vivien, had evolved a new evangel of morals, dear Aleck passed before the little cafe behind the Madeleine, and saw me with a beautiful boy in grey velvet - half rough, all Hylas. Alas, the eye he turned on me was not the sightless one. His smile was terrible. It was like one of Besant's novels. I really felt it very much. At luncheon I had been singularly ethical. I am always ethical at the Cafe de la Paix.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Thursday [Late March 1900], Grand Cafe, 14 boulevard des Capucines, Paris. 'Aleck' is Ross's brother; the editors' note explains the joke - he had lost the sight of one eye in early youth, so the eye he turned on Wilde was the seeing one.
sources.supports: The encounter, in Wilde's own words, and his framing of the boy.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1223, printed folio 1177 read on the rendered page 2026-08-04. 'cafe' is italicised in the printed text; accents normalised here.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Warren made the proposition; Sox reports West's refusal in terms of his discomfort with 'the possible implications', which is a refusal of the thing proposed and is recorded as such.
relationships.summary: On an 1889 trip to Wiesbaden and Rome, Warren told A. G. B. West that he wanted to share his life with 'an alter ego'. West, who had long intended to take Holy Orders, was not happy with the possible implications of such a relationship, and declined. Warren stayed devoted to him anyway - godfather to his sons, and in the end it was West's son who ran and inherited Warren's Maine house. The wooing of John Marshall followed.

sources.quote: During that trip Ned confided in West his desire to share his life with 'an alter ego'. … When stated that way, West was not happy with the possible implications of such a relationship.
sources.context: The 1889 Wiesbaden-Rome trip; between the sentences, Warren's worry about his companion 'seeming to be a rich man travelling with a friend when he was in reality accepting both salary and hospitality'.
sources.supports: The declined alter-ego proposition that preceded the Marshall wooing
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 54, printed folio 38 confirmed on rendered page.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: (a) The kiss: 'The kiss of Walt Whitman is still on my lips' is transcribed from Richard Ellmann's 'Oscar Meets Walt' (NYRB, 3 Dec. 1987), read at the article page so far; Ellmann's prose attributes it as what Wilde 'would later tell George Ives' and places it at the parting of the second (early-May 1882) visit. The deeper traditional chain - Ives's diary, commonly printed in the source in McKenna 2003 and in Ellmann's 1988 biography - was NOT verified so far (both lending-only); the article's footnote text was unreachable.
relationships.date_label: Two Camden visits, 1882: 18 Jan. (at Whitman's written invitation, taken by Stoddart) and 'early in May' (Ellmann; Stoddart absent) - the reported parting kiss attaches to the second; Wilde's letter between them postmarked 1 Mar. 1882.
relationships.summary: On his American lecture tour Wilde twice spent an afternoon with Whitman in Camden - 18 January 1882 (elderberry wine downstairs, then milk punch and two hours' talk in the third-floor 'den') and again in early May. Whitman told the Philadelphia Press next day that they were on 'thee and thou' terms, that Wilde laid his hand on his knee, and that he 'seemed to me like a great big, splendid boy'; Wilde wrote him 'Before I leave America I must see you again. There is no one in this wide great world of America whom I love and honour so much', and later told George Ives that 'The kiss of Walt Whitman is still on my lips' (per Ellmann). Whitman kept the letter, and in 1888 gave it to Traubel with the verdict: 'both of us friends according each other a mutual respect.'

sources.quote: My dear dear Walt, Swinburne has just written to me to say as follows … There! You see how you remain in our hearts, and how simply and grandly Swinburne speaks of you, knowing you to be simple and grand yourself. … Before I leave America I must see you again. There is no one in this wide great world of America whom I love and honour so much. With warm affection, and honourable admiration
sources.context: Wilde to Walt Whitman, [Postmark 1 March 1882], [Postmark Chicago]; the letter relays Swinburne's admiration of Whitman and closes with Wilde's own declaration
sources.supports: Wilde's side after the January Camden visit: love-and-honour declaration and stated intent to visit again before leaving America
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 167-168, printed folios 144 and 145 confirmed on rendered pages. Elisions skip the body of the quoted Swinburne letter and the request that Whitman send Swinburne his Essay on Poetry; fuller text in dossier.

sources.quote: The great American poet (1819–92) was now living in Camden, New Jersey, a suburb of Philadelphia across the Delaware, where Wilde had been taken by Stoddart to see him on 18 January.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note on the letter to Whitman; first sentence of the note
sources.supports: The first Camden visit: 18 January 1882, Wilde taken by J. M. Stoddart. (The visit was at Whitman's invitation: 'I go to see Walt Whitman, at his invitation, tomorrow', Wilde to Mrs George Lewis, [17 January 1882], p. 128 - transcribed in dossier.)
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 167, printed folio 144 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: "Wilde and I drank a bottle of wine down stairs," he continued, "and when we came up here, where we could be on 'thee and thou' terms, one of the first things I said was that I should call him 'Oscar;' 'I like that so much,' he answered, laying his hand on my knee. He seemed to me like a great big, splendid boy," said Whitman, stroking his silvery beard. "He is so frank and outspoken, and manly. I don't see why such mocking things are written of him."
sources.context: Whitman interviewed at home by the Philadelphia Press the evening of the first visit; earlier in the piece: 'we had a jolly good time … I think him genuine, honest and manly'
sources.supports: Whitman's own next-day account of the first visit: first-name intimacy on 'thee and thou' terms, Wilde's hand on his knee, 'a great big, splendid boy'
sources.provenance: Whitman Archive item med.00534 ('Our transcription is based on a digital image of a microfilm copy of an original issue'), read in full via Wayback capture 20260113032354 of whitmanarchive.org/item/med.00534, page text extracted 2026-08-03. Exact against the Archive transcription; microfilm image not read. Fuller passage in dossier.
sources.speaker: Walt Whitman, interviewed by the Philadelphia Press

sources.quote: W. gave me the Wilde letter. I thought he might say more about it. He said little: only this: "It seems all straight and honest to me. I have been told a thousand times what Wilde is but I do not see why Wilde is not what he is and I am not what I am with both of us friends according each other a mutual respect. There is no parade in this note: it wears the simplest clothes—has no sunflower in its button hole—has in fact a cast of virgin simplicity, sincerity. Read it for yourself: see if the letter does not bear me out." He said nothing while I read.
sources.context: Traubel's entry for Sunday 9 September 1888: Whitman hands over Wilde's 1882 letter, kept six years; the envelope endorsed in his blue pencil 'from Oscar Wilde early in '82' (p. 288)
sources.supports: Whitman's side, six years on: he preserved the letter and framed the bond as 'both of us friends according each other a mutual respect'
sources.provenance: IA withwaltwhitmani0002unse_c4l4 (Rowman & Littlefield 1961 reprint; original copyright 1908), IIIF page images leaves 317-318, printed folios 287-288 and entry head 'Sunday, September, 9th, 1888.' confirmed on rendered pages. Found via djvu.txt; transcription verified against the page images.

sources.quote: He promised to see Whitman again, and did so early in May. This time Stoddart was not present, and the two could talk more freely. Their conversation has not survived, but their parting has. Wilde would later tell George Ives, a proselytizer for sexual deviation in the Nineties, that Whitman had made no effort to conceal his homosexuality from him, as he would do with John Addington Symonds. "The kiss of Walt Whitman," Wilde said, "is still on my lips."
sources.context: Ellmann on the second Camden visit and its parting; the passage carries his footnote marker 8, whose text is not retrievable on the article page
sources.supports: The second visit ('early in May' 1882) and the reported parting kiss, with the attribution chain as Ellmann prints it: Wilde said it later to George Ives. Deeper chain (Ives diary; in the source prints in McKenna 2003 / Ellmann 1988 bio) unverified so far - see dossier pointer.
sources.provenance: nybooks.com/articles/1987/12/03/oscar-meets-walt/ HTML curl-fetched 2026-08-03; passage read directly in the raw extracted page text (article free on the site). Exact as the article prints it, ending before the footnote marker.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The editors state it flatly in the main-particulars footnote: Wilkinson invented an 'Ipswich Dramatic Society' and its wish to dramatise The Picture of Dorian Gray 'so as to get into correspondence with Wilde, whom he never met' (p. 1109 n. 1). AGE, STATED AS THE RECORD STATES IT: the editors give his dates as 1881-1966 and say he 'was at this time a Radley schoolboy' (p. 1109 n. 1); Wilde, describing the correspondence to Reginald Turner on 3 January 1899, calls him 'a Radley schoolboy, aged seventeen' (p. 1118). DIRECTION is Wilde's, and rests on documented acts rather than on tone: Wilde asks for a photograph in his first letter (p. 1109), asks again when a promised enclosure proved missing from the envelope (p. 1113), comments on the photographs when they arrive (p. 1122), reports to Turner that the boy sends them constantly (p. 1118), and asks Robert Ross to go to Radley and see him (p. 1127). OUTCOME is unknown, and cannot be otherwise: no meeting took place, no Wilkinson letter survives in this edition, and the boy's own account came fifty-four years later in Seven Friends (1953), unread here. WEIGH THIS AGAINST THE EDGE: the initiative in the whole affair was Wilkinson's, not Wilde's - he manufactured a theatrical society and, per the editors, at least one further false claim to attract Wilde's attention (p. 1127 n. 2), so the approach that started it ran the other way. QUOTE DEBT ON THIS EDGE, recorded 2026-08-05: nine of its eleven sources were logged by the earlier conservative method and several are far too short to be read - one is the eleven characters 'My dear Boy' (printed 1133), where the whole letter should stand. They are to be re-read at the page and extended during the sweep, per CONTRIBUTING.md.
relationships.date_label: First surviving Wilde letter [postmark 14 December 1898] (p. 1109) to the letter of [postmark 15 July 1900] (p. 1192), four months before Wilde's death. The end date was previously pinned at March 1899, the last letter then read; the General Index leads were followed on 2026-08-04 and the correspondence runs a year and a third longer than the record showed. Wilkinson is also among the senders of funeral wreaths in Ross's post-mortem account (p. 1222).
relationships.summary: In the winter of 1898 a seventeen-year-old Radley schoolboy named Louis Wilkinson wrote to Wilde in exile, having invented an Ipswich Dramatic Society and its wish to stage The Picture of Dorian Gray in order to have a reason to write. Wilde, who was forty-four, answered, granted the imaginary society four performances, asked who was to play Dorian - he should be beautiful - and closed by asking for the boy's photograph. Over the next four months Wilde asked for the photograph twice more, discussed the ones that arrived, praised and criticised the verse Wilkinson sent him, recommended his own 'The Portrait of Mr W. H.' when the boy said he loved Shakespeare's sonnets, told Reggie Turner and Robert Ross about him, and asked Ross to go down to Radley and look at him. The salutation moved from 'Dear Mr Wilkinson' to 'My dear Boy' and the signature from 'Sincerely yours' to 'Affectionately yours'. They never met. Wilkinson went up to Oxford, became the novelist Louis Marlow, sent a wreath to Wilde's funeral in 1900, and in 1953 printed the letters in Seven Friends, where he confessed that the dramatic society had never existed.

sources.quote: Louis Umfreville Wilkinson (1881–1966) was at this time a Radley schoolboy. … In his Seven Friends (1953) he quotes many of Wilde's letters to him, and confessed that he invented an 'Ipswich Dramatic Society' and its wish to dramatise The Picture of Dorian Gray, so as to get into correspondence with Wilde, whom he never met.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, main-particulars footnote (n. 1) on Wilkinson's first appearance, keyed to Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [postmark 14 December 1898]. The note begins at the foot of printed 1109 and concludes at the foot of 1110. The elision drops one sentence stating that he published many novels and other books under the name Louis Marlow; a closing sentence not quoted records that his first letter to Wilde and some of the subsequent ones are in the Hyde Collection. Seven Friends italic in the original.
sources.supports: THE CLASS-DECIDING FACT - 'whom he never met' - together with his dates, his being a Radley schoolboy at the time, the pen-name, the 1953 memoir, and the fabricated Ipswich Dramatic Society that opened the correspondence
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 1155-56, printed folios 1109 and 1110 both confirmed on the rendered pages; carried forward with its original provenance. En-dash in the date range as printed.

sources.quote: I am in constant correspondence now with a Radley schoolboy, aged seventeen.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Turner, [postmark 3 January 1899], Hotel des Bains, Napoule; opening sentence of the paragraph in which Wilde tells Turner about the correspondence. Heading as printed: 'To Reginald Turner / MS Hyde'. The three sentences that follow, not transcribed here, report that the boy sends his photograph constantly and praise it, report that he reads nothing but Wilde's books and wishes to follow in Wilde's footsteps, and record Wilde's reply that they lead to terrible places. The letter is signed 'Ever affectionately yours OSCAR'.
sources.supports: Wilkinson's age at the time of the correspondence, in Wilde's own contemporaneous words and exactly as the record states it - seventeen; and the fact that Wilde described the correspondence to a third party as constant
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1164, printed folio 1118 confirmed on the rendered page. Single sentence, complete.

sources.quote: Wilkinson had invented this, like the dramatisation of Dorian Gray, to attract Wilde's attention.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note (n. 2) at printed 1127, keyed to Wilde to Robert Ross, Saturday [25 February 1899], in which Wilde urges Ross, if he is down at Oxford, to go to Radley and see Wilkinson, reporting the boy's claims that he had known FitzGerald and had been at the first night of Lady Windermere's Fan - the latter being the claim this note corrects. Dorian Gray italic in the original.
sources.supports: That the fabrications continued past the opening gambit, and that the initiative in the acquaintance was Wilkinson's; also that Wilde was recommending him to Ross in person
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1173, printed folio 1127 confirmed on the rendered page. Whole footnote.

sources.quote: It was not Louis Wilkinson but his father who had known FitzGerald. They were neighbours in Suffolk.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note (n. 1) at printed 1133, keyed to Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [postmark 20 March 1899]. The elided opening of the note corrects Wilde's attribution of the Omar Khayyam manuscript to a kinsman, Sir Ralph Ouseley, naming Sir William Ouseley (1767-1842) instead.
sources.supports: A correction to the 1127 n. 2 picture of wholesale invention - the FitzGerald connection was real but paternal, so not every claim Wilkinson made was manufactured
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1179, printed folio 1133 confirmed on the rendered page. Final two sentences of the footnote, quoted complete; the preceding sentences concern the manuscript's provenance.

sources.quote: My dear Boy
sources.context: Salutation of Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [postmark 20 March 1899], Gland, Switzerland; heading as printed 'To Louis Wilkinson / MS Wilkinson', signed 'Affectionately yours OSCAR'. Recorded as the endpoint of a documented four-month register shift, each element read in the source so far or the last: [postmark 14 December 1898] p. 1109 opens 'Dear Mr Wilkinson' and signs 'Sincerely yours'; 28 December [1898] p. 1113 opens 'Dear Mr Wilkinson' and signs 'Sincerely yours'; [postmark 3 February 1899] pp. 1122-23 opens 'Dear Mr Wilkinson' and signs 'Your friend'; this letter opens 'My dear Boy' and signs 'Affectionately yours'. 'My dear Boy' is the salutation Wilde also used to Lord Alfred Douglas.
sources.supports: The escalation of address across the correspondence, as a matter of documented salutation and signature rather than of interpretation
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1179, printed folio 1133 confirmed on the rendered page. The earlier salutations and signatures were read at repo PDF 1155 (folio 1109, predecessor session), 1159 (folio 1113), and 1168-69 (folios 1122 and 1123).

sources.quote: I am in constant correspondence now with a Radley schoolboy, aged seventeen. His photograph, which he has sent me, and sends me constantly, is most beautiful. He seems to read nothing but my books, and says his one desire is to 'follow in my footsteps'! But I have told him that they lead to terrible places. … My Radley boy is called Louis Wilkinson – a horrid name – but his photograph is most interesting, and his poetry passionate and incoherent. He seems a most astonishing boy. He has dramatised Dorian Gray!
sources.context: Two passages printed on the same page, from different letters: the first is Wilde to Reginald Turner (postmark 3 January 1899), the second Wilde to Robert Ross (Thursday [? 12 January 1899]). Wilkinson is named only in the second.
sources.supports: The documented acts on which direction rests - three photograph requests, the comments on the photographs when they came, and the reports to Turner and Ross; recorded as description because the addressee was seventeen
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1164, printed folio 1118 read off the rendered page. The ellipsis spans the end of the Turner letter and the opening of the Ross letter, both on this folio - it is not an elision inside a single letter.

sources.quote:
Dear Boy, Come and see me next week. I can get you a room in my hotel.
I am not going to write to you any more: I want to see you. I have waited long enough. [Signature cut away.]
sources.context: Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [Postmark 15 July 1900], Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris
sources.supports: The last surviving letter of the run, and the most direct: an invitation to Paris with a room offered in his own hotel, and the correspondence itself set aside in favour of meeting.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 1238 rendered at 2.6x and; folio 1192 printed at the foot of that page, giving offset +46 here. Located first in the OCR mirror, then confirmed on the rendered page.

sources.quote: Je suis très malade. Ne venez pas cette semaine. Je vous écrirai.
sources.context: Telegram, Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [July 1900 - a few days later], Paris
sources.supports: How the correspondence ends: the invitation of 15 July is withdrawn a few days later on grounds of illness, with a promise to write that is the last thing in the run.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 1239; folio 1193 printed at the foot.
sources.translation: I am very ill. Do not come this week. I will write to you.

sources.quote: I fear you would not like my hotel. I live there because I have no money ever. It is an absurd place: it is not a background: the only thing really nice in the whole hotel is your own photograph: but one cannot, or one should not, play Narcissus to a photograph: even water is horribly treacherous: the eyes of one who loves one are the only mirror.
sources.context: Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, postmark 4 January 1900, from the Hôtel d'Alsace. The photograph is the one Wilkinson had sent him, which Wilde had already reported to Ross (printed 1118). The letter opens 'My dear Boy'. Wilde is dead within the year.
sources.supports: Wilde's own words placing Wilkinson's photograph at the centre of his room and his attention - the desire, expressed obliquely and unmistakably.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 1215 read as a rendered page image 2026-08-04; printed folio 1169 confirmed at the foot of the image.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde

sources.quote: Also, do come to Paris. I am ill and unhappy. The touch of your hand might heal me. Always affectionately yours

sources.quote: Dear Mr Wilkinson, Thank you so much for your long and interesting letter. I envy you going to Oxford: it is the most flower-like time of one's life. One sees the shadow of things in silver mirrors. Later on, one sees the Gorgon's head, and one suffers, because it does not turn one to stone. I am on the Riviera, in blue and gold weather, the sun warm as wine, and apricot-coloured. The little hotel where I am staying is right on the Golfe de Juan, and all round are pine-woods with their pungent breath: the wind growing aromatic as it moves through the branches: one's feet crushing sweetness out of the fallen needles: I wish you were here. In your second letter you tell me that you enclose your photograph for me, but no photograph was in the envelope. Your thoughts must have been in the crystal of the moon. Call them back, and let me have your portrait. Sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, 28 December [1898], Hôtel des Bains, Napoule (MS Hyde) - quoted whole. Wilkinson was seventeen and the two never met. NOTE WHAT WILDE DOES HERE: the identical landscape - pine-woods, pungent breath, feet crushing sweetness out of fallen needles - appears in the letter to Laurence Housman written the same day and printed on the same opening. To Housman it ends in the fisher-boys; to this schoolboy it ends 'I wish you were here' and a second request for his photograph. ADDED 2026-08-05 during the page sweep: this letter was read at the page but never logged, and the connection carried ten sources without it.

relationships.date_label: January – spring 1893 (Wood left for America with Wilde's £35)
relationships.summary: Douglas telegraphed Wilde from Salisbury to look after Alfred Wood, an out-of-work clerk then living at Taylor's; Wilde met him at the Café Royal, dined him in a private room at the Florence, and took him home to 16 Tite Street, where Wood's testimony describes an act of gross indecency. Wood had found letters from Wilde to Douglas in a suit Douglas gave him; in spring 1893 Wilde gave him £30 plus £5 and Wood left for America. Wilde was convicted on the Tite Street count at the final trial.

sources.quote: When did you first know Wilde?—About a month after I made the acquaintance of Taylor. How did you come to know Wilde?—I was introduced to him by a gentleman at the Café Royal. Who was the gentleman?—Must I give the name? Yes.—Lord Alfred Douglas. What took place when you were introduced to Wilde?—I was introduced by telegram. By Mr. Justice Charles—You would have led anyone to believe that you were personally introduced?—In consequence of the telegram I went to the Café Royal at nine o'clock one evening. Mr. Wilde was sitting down. He spoke to me first. He asked "Are you Alfred Wood?" I said, "Yes." Then he offered me something to drink and I had something; and then he invited me to go round to the Florence in Rupert Street to dinner. I went with him and we dined in a private room. Examination continued—What kind of meal was it?—Very nice, one of the best to be got. What wine did you have?—Champagne. After dinner I went with Mr. Wilde to 16 Tite Street. There was nobody in the house to my knowledge. Mr. Wilde let himself in with a latchkey.
sources.context: Alfred Wood's examination-in-chief by Mr. Avory, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895, with an interjection from the bench by Mr. Justice Charles. Wood had just testified that in January 1893 he was out of work and went to live at Taylor's Little College Street rooms for about three weeks. The page ends on 'latchkey'; what follows on p. 202 is the act evidence quoted below.
sources.supports: How the two men met, in the participant's own sworn words: Douglas's telegram introduction, Wilde waiting at the Café Royal and opening with 'Are you Alfred Wood?', the drink, the private room at the Florence, and the walk back to 16 Tite Street. The plainest first-hand characterization of the connection, chosen in preference to the act evidence that follows it.

ives-diary.title: Diary (George Ives Papers, Harry Ransom Center, University of Texas at Austin)
ives-diary.note: Manuscript Collection MS-02138, eadid 00060; Series III. Diaries, 1886-1949, 122 volumes, open for research. Most volumes carry daily entries from 20 December 1886 to 16 November 1949 - **note the diaries END in November 1949, not 1950**, though Ives lived to 4 June 1950. Repo transcript covers 21 and 23 Nov 1906 only (transcription by Brian Lewis, personal communication). Other diary passages must be quoted via the secondary work that prints them (Cook, Kaplan, Stokes, Lewis), cited at that work's page. TARGETING (finding aid read 2026-08-05): **Cook's volume numbers ARE the Center's volume numbers** - his endnote 62 cites vol. 76 for 14 September 1920, and the container list gives v.76 as 2 September - 24 October 1920 - so every diary citation in Cook's endnotes (printed 125-131) converts directly into a requestable container. Bloodworth's 1909 arrival falls in v.51-55 (6 November 1907 - 14 June 1911); the 1939 will falls in v.104 (28 March 1939 - 18 March 1940) on either of Cook's two conflicting dates for it, October or 1 December 1939. Volumes 1-60 are bound in groups of five and 'bound very tightly and require special care when opening', which constrains reproduction. Ives INDEXED every volume from vol. 13 on, each index pointing to that volume's own page numbers - so the cheap way into an undated question is the index pages, not the volumes. Ives also wrote in several codes; see 'A Catalogue of the George Ives Collection', an appendix to the inventory. The address book (box 5, folder 8) 'provides cross references to his diaries'.

troubridge-diaries-hrc.title: Diaries (Radclyffe Hall and Una Vincenzo, Lady Troubridge Collection, Harry Ransom Center)
troubridge-diaries-hrc.note: Unpublished; cite by entry date. Manuscript Collection MS-01793, eadid 00163. **131 volumes is the COMBINED total across two series, not Series II alone** (an earlier note here double-counted): Series II holds the 60-volume set running 27 December 1930 to 21 June 1943, containers 26.1-32.4; Series III holds 71 further volumes, 11 December 1943 to 21 January 1951, boxes 38-45 (formerly numbered 1-8, which is where the stray '8 boxes' came from). THE TWO SERIES ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE: the Series III volumes were written as letters to Hall AFTER her death on 7 October 1943, so they evidence Troubridge's grief and the estate, not the partnership in life. Note also that the diaries begin only in December 1930, fifteen years into a partnership that started in 1915 - they cannot speak to its first half at all. Supplemented by daybooks for 1934, 1935, 1941 and 1942 (Container 33.1 onward). Condition: 'Some materials in Series I. and II. are extensively water damaged, suffering rust and mold.' Access: open, but researchers must create an online account. Same repository as ives-diary - a natural add-on to the Ives fellowship trip. TARGETING (finding aid read 2026-08-05): Vol. 1 (Container 26.1) opens the diary and states its purpose; Vol. 22, 14 June - 9 October 1934 (Container 28.3) covers the start of the Souline affair, Hall's letters to Souline beginning July 1934; Vol. 60, 6 February - 21 June 1943 (Container 32.4) is the last before Hall's death. Troubridge's own 68 letters to Souline, 1934-1942, are Container 50.5-6. **Not itemised in the container list but described in the scope note, and the single most relevant document to this pair**: a letter 'To the Executors of my Will', written by Troubridge February 1944 and revised September 1944, 'regarding the nature of Troubridge and Hall's relationship with Souline and instructions for the destruction of Troubridge's diaries'. Container 36.1 is the likeliest home; ask the Center to locate it by name.

works._voice_note: Quotes carry a per-quote `voice`: 'period' when the text is ENTIRELY in the words of someone alive in the world this map describes (a letter, a diary, sworn testimony, a contemporary memoir or interview), 'modern' when a historian, biographer or editor is writing about them. It is deliberately per-quote, not per-work: Holland & Hart-Davis's footnotes are modern prose inside a primary volume, while a Douglas or Langtry letter printed inside one of those same footnotes is still a period voice. Mixed text - a biographer's sentence with a period phrase quoted inside it - counts as modern, because it is not entirely the period voice. The panel sets period quotes between large quotation marks; modern ones keep a plain rule.
works._evidence_date_note: A source's `evidence_date` is the date of the THING BEING EVIDENCED - when the letter was written, the testimony sworn, the meeting held - never the publication year of the book it is quoted from. A 1985 biography describing an 1908 holiday carries 1908. The panel orders a connection's sources by this field, so a publication year files modern commentary among the contemporary record. Where a card evidences no dated event at all - historiography, a statement about how a claim is treated in scholarship - leave it null; undated cards sort to the end.

vivien-une-femme-1905-repo.author: Renée Vivien
vivien-une-femme-1905-repo.title: Une femme m'apparut…
vivien-une-femme-1905-repo.short_cite: Vivien, Une femme m'apparut… (1905 nouvelle édition)
vivien-une-femme-1905-repo.note:
208 pp, text-layered and the layer is good (French accents intact). It IS the French - but it is the 1905 rewrite, NOT the 1904 first edition, and the book says so itself: the title page at PDF p. 19, read as a page image 2026-08-04, reads 'Une Femme m'apparut. / NOUVELLE ÉDITION / PARIS / ALPHONSE LEMERRE, ÉDITEUR / 23-31, PASSAGE CHOISEUL / M DCCCCV'. A HardPress reprint of a Boston Public Library copy digitised by the Internet Archive; the '1877' in the filename is Vivien's birth year, not an edition date.
The cast confirms it independently: Lorély (165 occurrences), Ione, Nedda, Doriane, Undine, San Giovanni - and no Dagmar in any spelling. Lorély is the 1905's replacement for the 1904's Vally, so her presence is positive evidence for the rewrite rather than mere absence of Dagmar. NOTE FOR SEARCHING: 'Lorély' carries an acute accent and an unaccented grep for 'Lorely' returns nothing - that briefly made this copy look like it had no leading lady at all.
For Dagmar use vivien-foster-1982, whose copyright page states it translates the Lemerre 1904.
OPEN DISCREPANCY, 2026-08-04. This scanned 1905 runs to printed p. 168 and contains no Dagmar chapters - an accent- and OCR-tolerant search of all 208 pages finds no 'dagmar', 'poetesse', 'saxe' or 'ressentais', while distinctive phrases elsewhere in the book are found normally, so it is not a search failure. But the French Wikisource text explicitly labelled 1905 (fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Une_femme_m'apparut/1905, in the Anna's Archive EPUB in this folder) has Lorély 207 times AND Dagmar 32 times, in chapters XXXV-XXXVIII. Both cannot be right. Either this printed copy is shorter than the text Wikisource transcribed, or Wikisource's 1905 is conflated. Until that is resolved, do not repeat the flat claim that Dagmar appears only in the 1904 - what IS established is that she is absent from this printed 1905 copy and present in the 1904.

about:
About

A working historical reference.

What this is

A map of the documented romantic and sexual relationships in Oscar Wilde's social circle. Every relationship carries quoted, cited sources; nothing rests on received anecdote. Click a person for a biography and a birth-to-death timeline of their engagements; click a connection for the evidence itself.

Reading the map

Node colour groups people by sphere (Wilde, aesthetes, the 1895 trials, society, spouse, the Order of Chaeronea, the later circle, outside the circle, beyond Europe). Node shape marks the subject's legally recognized gender in the genogram convention — squares for men, circles for women. Line style carries the certainty of each connection, below.

Outside the circle collects those who were never part of the propertied social world the rest of this map describes — a fisherman at Napoule, a waiter at the Café d'Égypte, a soldier in Reading Gaol, a servant who waited at table in a Paris boarding house. Most survive only under a first name, a nickname, or no name at all. They are here because the record of a life should not depend on its subject's status or class.

Narrowing the map

Every switch in the legend can be clicked to turn its category off. Right-click to solo that category — every other switch in the same row will turn off, and the one you picked will light up. Click it again, and the row goes back to how it was. Each row is independent, so soloing a sphere leaves Gender and Connections alone. The sphere chip above a person's name does the same thing for their sphere.

How a connection is evidenced (line styles)

The line style records how we know about a connection. This reference deliberately makes no claim about sexual acts in either direction. Criminal law was designed precisely to keep that evidence out of the record, so treating its absence as a finding would mistake the effect of prosecution for a fact about people's lives.

  • {{line:married}} Married — a legal marriage.
  • {{line:self-reported}} Self-Reported — a participant's own words survive: their letters, diaries, or sworn testimony. The speaker must be one of the two people connected.
  • {{line:second-hand}} Second-Hand — only non-participants attest it: observers, biographers, editors.
  • {{line:uncorroborated}} Uncorroborated — a claim with limited support: a lone source, or an allegation never tested — including those made only in Queensberry's 1895 plea of justification. Where someone genuinely contested the connection — testimony discredited at trial, a witness who recanted — that is stated in the note on the card.
  • {{line:attraction-expressed}} Attraction expressed — the record is one-sided: a declaration, an approach, or admiration noted in passing, the arrow pointing from the person who expressed it to its subject. Many of them — sailors, waiters, fishermen — left no papers of their own to confirm the nature of the connection.

Every classification is checked by hand against the sources before it is relied on.

Verification of quotes

Every quote carries a chip saying how far it has been checked. ⧖ means not yet confirmed on the printed page — either a passage found in a text search or index but not yet checked against the source page, or a source pointer: a claim recorded with nothing transcribed yet, naming only where to look.

These chips describe the research pass, not a final scholarly verdict. A separate audit runs by hand through a ledger kept beside the data, where each quotation is checked against the page it came from to characterize the connection. Not all connections are currently accurate. They may shift as more information is uncovered. And characterization will always remain somewhat inconclusive, as the classification of relationships is an inherently subjective endeavour. The goal of the project is to provide sources depicting warmth and affection in an easily searchable way, not to definitively prove things one way or another. The reader is welcome draw their own conclusions and contribute their own sources by opening a ticket in our open-source repository.

A note on the trial record

The 1895 trial record documents ages, sex work, and blackmail; the reference reproduces exactly what the court documents record, with citation.

Controls

To pan, click-and-drag.

To zoom, scroll or pinch-and-zoom.

To move a node, press-and-hold the node until it turns gold, then drag it.

To reset a node, press, hold, and release the node without moving.

To solo a filter, right-click the switch for the filter in the legend, and it will toggle on that filter and toggle off all the others in the same category.
